questions.explanation: Solve the point-mass equation for e: \(e = V^2/(15R) - f_s\). Forgetting to subtract the side friction factor is the classic error — it leads to the 12.0% trap.
questions.videoTitle: Critical SUPERELEVATION Calculations

questions.question: A crest vertical curve 400 ft long connects grades of +2% and −3%. If the elevation of the PVC is 98.00 ft, what is the elevation of a point on the curve 100 ft from the PVC?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the elevation \(y\) of the point 100 ft from the PVC. We can determine \(y\) from the parabolic vertical curve equation:

$$y = y_{PVC} + g_1 x + \frac{(g_2 - g_1)x^2}{2L}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(y\):

$$\begin{aligned} y_{PVC} &= 98.00\ \text{ft} \\ g_1 &= +2\% = 0.02 \\ g_2 &= -3\% = -0.03 \\ L &= 400\ \text{ft} \\ x &= 100\ \text{ft} \\ y &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$y = 98.00 + (0.02)(100) + \frac{(-0.03 - 0.02)(100)^2}{2(400)} = 100.00 - 0.625$$

$$y = 99.375\ \text{ft} \approx 99.38\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: On a vertical curve, elevation = tangent elevation plus the parabolic offset (g₂−g₁)x²/(2L); on a crest the offset is negative, so watch its sign.
questions.videoTitle: Vertical Curves: The Secret to Smooth Road Design

questions.question: A crest vertical curve connects grades of +4% and −4% on a highway with a required stopping sight distance of 196 ft. Assuming S > L, what is the minimum curve length?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the minimum crest curve length \(L\). Because \(S > L\), the governing equation is:

$$L = 2S - \frac{2158}{A}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(L\):

$$\begin{aligned} g_1 &= +4\% \\ g_2 &= -4\% \\ A &= |4 - (-4)| = 8\% \\ S &= 196\ \text{ft} \\ L &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$L = 2(196) - \frac{2158}{8} = 392 - 269.75$$

$$L = 122.25\ \text{ft} \approx 122\ \text{ft}$$

Since \(196 > 122\), the assumption \(S > L\) holds and the result is valid.
questions.explanation: Use L = 2S − 2158/A only when S > L, and always verify the assumption afterward — here 196 > 122 confirms it.
questions.videoTitle: Vertical Curves: The Secret to Smooth Road Design

questions.question: A directional freeway segment has 2 lanes, a peak-hour volume of 3,800 veh/hr, and a peak hour factor of 0.90. Using an ideal per-lane capacity of 2,400 pc/h/ln, what is the volume-to-capacity (v/c) ratio?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Flow Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The handbook (p. 311) prints the demand flow rate equation in this exact form:

$$v_p = \frac{V}{PHF \times N \times f_{HV}}$$

No heavy-vehicle data is given, so \(f_{HV} = 1\) and the handbook form reduces to \(v_p = V/(PHF \cdot N)\); the solution works this in two steps — \(v_p = V/PHF\), then the per-lane split inside \(v/c = (v_p/N)/c\):

$$v_p = \frac{V}{PHF}, \qquad v/c = \frac{v_p / N}{c}$$

Ultimately, we must solve for the volume-to-capacity ratio \(v/c\). First convert the hourly volume to the peak 15-minute flow rate, then compare the per-lane flow to per-lane capacity:

$$v_p = \frac{V}{PHF}, \qquad v/c = \frac{v_p / N}{c}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(v/c\):

$$\begin{aligned} V &= 3800\ \text{veh/hr} \\ PHF &= 0.90 \\ N &= 2\ \text{lanes} \\ c &= 2400\ \text{pc/h/ln} \\ v/c &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$v_p = \frac{3800}{0.90} = 4222.2\ \text{veh/hr}, \qquad v/c = \frac{4222.2/2}{2400} = \frac{2111.1}{2400}$$

$$v/c = 0.88$$
questions.explanation: Divide by the PHF (not multiply) to get the peak 15-minute rate, and compare per-lane flow against per-lane capacity — skipping the lane split gives the 1.76 trap.

questions.question: A signalized intersection has three phases whose critical lane groups have flow ratios (v/s) of 0.30, 0.25, and 0.20. What is the intersection's critical v/c ratio, Xc?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Signal Timing section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the critical v/c ratio \(X_c\), the sum of the flow ratios of the critical lane groups:

$$X_c = \sum \left(\frac{v}{s}\right)_{\text{critical}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(X_c\):

$$\begin{aligned} (v/s)_1 &= 0.30 \\ (v/s)_2 &= 0.25 \\ (v/s)_3 &= 0.20 \\ X_c &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$X_c = 0.30 + 0.25 + 0.20$$

$$X_c = 0.75$$
questions.explanation: The critical v/c ratio is the sum of the critical lane groups' flow ratios — the bottleneck is the total demand, not the single worst phase.

questions.question: According to the Highway Capacity Manual, the level of service of a two-lane highway is defined by which measure(s) of effectiveness?
choices: Percent time-spent-following and average travel speed
Density in passenger cars per mile per lane
questions.solution:
The Highway Capacity Manual assigns each facility type its own measure of effectiveness for level of service. For a basic freeway segment that measure is density — but a two-lane highway is different: its LOS is defined by percent time-spent-following together with average travel speed, because passing opportunities and platooning govern the driver's experience.

Control delay is the measure for signalized intersections, and v/c is a capacity check rather than a LOS measure.

Percent time-spent-following and average travel speed is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Two-lane highways are the odd ones out: LOS comes from percent time-spent-following and average travel speed, not density.

questions.question: A horizontal curve with a radius of 1,432.4 ft uses the arc definition of degree of curve. What is the degree of curve?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the degree of curve \(D\). Under the arc definition:

$$D = \frac{5729.58}{R}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(D\):

$$\begin{aligned} R &= 1432.4\ \text{ft} \\ D &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$D = \frac{5729.58}{1432.4} = 4.000$$

$$D = 4.00^{\circ}$$
questions.explanation: Arc definition: D = 5729.58/R. The 0.25° trap comes from inverting the relationship instead of dividing.

questions.question: In CPM scheduling, the free float of an activity is defined as:
choices: The scheduling slack that is always equal to the total float
The difference between the late start and the early finish of the activity
The amount an activity can be delayed without delaying project completion
The amount an activity can be delayed without delaying the early start of any successor activity
questions.solution:
Free float is the scheduling slack available to an activity without affecting any other activity: it is the amount an activity can be delayed without delaying the early start of any successor activity.

Total float, by contrast, is the amount an activity can be delayed without delaying project completion.

Free float can never exceed total float, and an activity with zero total float (on the critical path) has zero free float.

The correct definition is delaying without pushing back the early start of any successor.
questions.explanation: Free float protects successors; total float protects the project finish. Free float can never exceed total float.

questions.question: An activity has a normal duration of 10 days at a direct cost of $20,000. It can be crashed to a duration of 6 days at a direct cost of $28,000. What is the activity's cost slope?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the cost slope, the extra direct cost per day of shortening the activity:

$$\text{Cost slope} = \frac{\text{crash cost} - \text{normal cost}}{\text{normal time} - \text{crash time}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the cost slope:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Normal time} &= 10\ \text{days} \\ \text{Normal cost} &= \$20{,}000 \\ \text{Crash time} &= 6\ \text{days} \\ \text{Crash cost} &= \$28{,}000 \\ \text{Cost slope} &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$\text{Cost slope} = \frac{28000 - 20000}{10 - 6} = \frac{8000}{4}$$

$$\text{Cost slope} = \$2{,}000/\text{day}$$
questions.explanation: Cost slope = Δcost/Δtime using normal-minus-crash in both — dividing the cost difference by the crash duration alone is the $1,333/day trap.

questions.question: A project has a budget at completion (BAC) of $200,000. At the status date, BCWS = $100,000, BCWP = $90,000, and ACWP = $95,000. If cost performance continues at its current rate, what is the estimate at completion (EAC)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earned-Value Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The handbook (p. 317) prints the forecasting equations in this exact form:

$$ETC = \frac{BAC - BCWP}{CPI}, \qquad EAC = (ACWP + ETC)$$

Substituting the handbook's \(ETC\) into its \(EAC\) gives \(EAC = ACWP + (BAC - BCWP)/CPI\). Since the handbook prints \(CPI = BCWP/ACWP\), the term \(BCWP/CPI\) equals \(ACWP\), which cancels against the leading \(ACWP\), so the handbook form collapses to the working equation:

$$EAC = \frac{BAC}{CPI}$$

Ultimately, we must solve for the estimate at completion \(EAC\). Assuming the current cost efficiency continues, \(EAC = BAC/CPI\) where \(CPI = BCWP/ACWP\):

$$CPI = \frac{BCWP}{ACWP}, \qquad EAC = \frac{BAC}{CPI}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(EAC\):

$$\begin{aligned} BAC &= \$200{,}000 \\ BCWS &= \$100{,}000 \\ BCWP &= \$90{,}000 \\ ACWP &= \$95{,}000 \\ EAC &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$CPI = \frac{90000}{95000} = 0.9474, \qquad EAC = \frac{200000}{0.9474}$$

$$EAC = \$211{,}111$$
questions.explanation: EAC = BAC/CPI projects current cost efficiency forward; using the schedule index (SPI) instead gives the $222,222 trap.
questions.videoTitle: Your Project Is Already Over Budget (You Just Don't Know)

questions.question: A contractor submits a monthly progress payment request for $100,000 of completed work. The contract specifies 10% retainage. What is the amount of the payment due to the contractor?
questions.solution:
Retainage is the percentage of each progress payment that the owner withholds until the project reaches substantial completion. The payment due is the requested amount minus the retainage:

$$\text{Payment} = 100000 \times (1 - 0.10) = 90000$$

$$\text{Payment} = \$90{,}000$$

The correct payment is $90,000.
questions.explanation: Retainage is withheld from each payment — the contractor receives request × (1 − retainage), not the full request.
questions.videoTitle: Retainage for Contractors Explained

questions.question: A scraper with a 20-CY heaped bucket operates on a 6-minute cycle and works a 50-minute hour. The soil swells 25%. What is the hourly production rate in bank cubic yards?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the hourly production in bank cubic yards. Chain the adjustments — cycles per hour, the 50-minute-hour efficiency, and the swell correction from loose yards to bank yards:

$$\text{Production} = \frac{60}{\text{cycle time}} \times \text{bucket} \times \frac{50}{60} \times \frac{1}{1 + \text{swell}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the production:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cycle time} &= 6\ \text{min} \\ \text{Bucket} &= 20\ \text{CY (loose)} \\ \text{Efficiency} &= 50/60 \\ \text{Swell} &= 25\% = 0.25 \\ \text{Production} &= ?\ \text{BCY/hr} \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$\text{Production} = \frac{60}{6}(20)\left(\frac{50}{60}\right)\left(\frac{1}{1.25}\right) = \frac{166.67}{1.25}$$

$$\text{Production} = 133\ \text{BCY/hr}$$
questions.explanation: Bank yards come last: divide loose-yard production by (1 + swell). Skipping the swell correction leaves the 167 BCY/hr trap.
questions.videoTitle: FECivil 98 Production analysis of the Best Excavator

questions.question: Under OSHA excavation standards, a trench 4 ft or deeper must have a stairway, ladder, ramp, or other safe means of egress located so that no worker must travel more than what lateral distance to reach it?
questions.solution:
OSHA excavation standards are not printed in the FE Reference Handbook; under OSHA, trench excavations 4 ft or deeper require a stairway, ladder, ramp, or other safe means of egress, located so that no worker must travel more than 25 ft laterally to reach it.

The 25-ft limit is the correct choice — 50 ft and 100 ft are too lax, and 10 ft is stricter than the standard.
questions.explanation: Trench egress: 4 ft deep triggers the requirement, and no worker may be more than 25 ft of lateral travel from a ladder, stairway, or ramp.

questions.question: A contractor purchases a loader for $200,000 with an estimated salvage value of $20,000 after 5 years. The loader will operate 2,000 hours per year and the interest rate is 8%. What is the hourly ownership (fixed) cost of the loader?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the hourly ownership cost: the annual capital recovery on the depreciable amount, plus interest on the salvage value, divided by the annual operating hours:

$$\text{Hourly cost} = \frac{(P - S)(A/P, i, n) + S \cdot i}{\text{hours/year}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the hourly cost:

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \$200{,}000 \\ S &= \$20{,}000 \\ i &= 8\% = 0.08 \\ n &= 5\ \text{years} \\ \text{Hours} &= 2000\ \text{hr/yr} \\ (A/P, 8\%, 5) &= 0.2505 \\ \text{Hourly cost} &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$\text{Hourly cost} = \frac{(200000 - 20000)(0.25046) + (20000)(0.08)}{2000} = \frac{45082 + 1600}{2000}$$

$$\text{Hourly cost} = \$23.34/\text{hr}$$
questions.explanation: Ownership cost = capital recovery on (P − S) plus interest on S, all divided by annual hours. Forgetting the salvage value in the capital recovery is the $25.05/hr trap.

questions.question: What uniform end-of-year deposit is required for 5 years at 8% annual interest to accumulate $50,000?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the uniform annual deposit \(A\). We can determine \(A\) from the sinking fund factor:

$$A = F(A/F, i, n) = F\frac{i}{(1+i)^n - 1}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(A\):

$$\begin{aligned} F &= \$50{,}000 \\ i &= 8\% = 0.08 \\ n &= 5\ \text{years} \\ A &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$A = 50000\frac{0.08}{(1.08)^5 - 1} = 50000(0.17046)$$

$$A = \$8{,}523$$
questions.explanation: Sinking fund: A = F(A/F, i, n). The $10,000 trap ignores interest entirely; the $34,029 trap discounts instead of accumulating. Handbook table: also solvable with the compound-interest factor table (i = 8%) in the Engineering Economics chapter — look up (A/F, 8%, 5).

questions.tiTip: No — apply the geometric-gradient formula by hand; the calculator only does the arithmetic.
questions.question: Annual maintenance costs are $1,000 in year 1 and grow at 5% per year through year 5. At 10% annual interest, what is the present worth of these costs?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The handbook (p. 235) prints the single-payment present worth factor in this exact form:

$$(P/F, i\%, n) = (1+i)^{-n}$$

Each year's cash flow \(A_1(1+g)^{t-1}\) is discounted with this handbook factor, so \(P = \sum_{t=1}^{n} A_1(1+g)^{t-1}(1+i)^{-t}\). Summing this geometric series collapses to the working equation:

$$P = A_1\frac{1 - (1+g)^n(1+i)^{-n}}{i - g}$$

Ultimately, we must solve for the present worth \(P\) of a geometric gradient series, where each year's cost grows by the rate \(g\):

$$P = A_1\frac{1 - (1+g)^n(1+i)^{-n}}{i - g}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P\):

$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= \$1{,}000 \\ g &= 5\% = 0.05 \\ i &= 10\% = 0.10 \\ n &= 5\ \text{years} \\ P &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$P = 1000\frac{1 - (1.05)^5(1.10)^{-5}}{0.10 - 0.05} = 1000\frac{1 - 0.79247}{0.05}$$

$$P = \$4{,}151$$
questions.explanation: Geometric gradient: P = A₁[1 − (1+g)ⁿ(1+i)⁻ⁿ]/(i − g). Treating it as a level annuity gives the $3,791 trap.
questions.videoTitle: Engineering Economic Analysis - Gradient Series

questions.question: A project requires an investment of $8,000 today and returns $3,000, $4,000, and $5,000 at the ends of years 1, 2, and 3. At 10% annual interest, what is the present worth of the project?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the present worth \(P\) by discounting each cash flow at its own year:

$$P = \sum_{t=0}^{n}\frac{CF_t}{(1+i)^t}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P\):

$$\begin{aligned} CF_0 &= -\$8{,}000 \\ CF_1 &= \$3{,}000 \\ CF_2 &= \$4{,}000 \\ CF_3 &= \$5{,}000 \\ i &= 10\% = 0.10 \\ P &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$P = -8000 + \frac{3000}{1.10} + \frac{4000}{1.10^2} + \frac{5000}{1.10^3} = -8000 + 2727.27 + 3305.79 + 3756.57$$

$$P = \$1{,}790$$
questions.explanation: Discount each cash flow at its own year — averaging the inflows into an annuity gives the $1,947 trap. Handbook table: also solvable with the compound-interest factor table (i = 10%) in the Engineering Economics chapter — look up (P/F, 10%, 1), (P/F, 10%, 2), and (P/F, 10%, 3).
questions.videoTitle: Simple and Compound Interest Explained

questions.tiTip: No — discount each year's cash flow by hand until the investment is recovered; the calculator only does the arithmetic.
questions.question: A project requires an initial investment of $12,000 and generates $4,000 per year. At 10% annual interest, what is the discounted payback period?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The handbook (p. 236) states the payback definition in the Breakeven Analysis section, which prints no closed-form equation: "The payback period is the period of time required for the profit or other benefits of an investment to equal the cost of the investment."

Discounting each year's uniform benefit \(A\) with the handbook's single-payment present worth factor \((P/F, i\%, t) = (1+i)^{-t}\) (p. 235) gives the discounted-payback working equation:

$$\sum_{t=1}^{n}\frac{A}{(1+i)^t} \geq P$$

Ultimately, we must solve for the discounted payback period: the time until the cumulative discounted cash inflows recover the initial investment:

$$\sum_{t=1}^{n}\frac{A}{(1+i)^t} \geq P$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(n\):

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \$12{,}000 \\ A &= \$4{,}000/\text{yr} \\ i &= 10\% = 0.10 \\ n &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Accumulate the discounted inflows:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Year 1:} &\quad 4000/1.10 = 3636.36 \quad (\text{cum } 3636.36) \\ \text{Year 2:} &\quad 4000/1.10^2 = 3305.79 \quad (\text{cum } 6942.15) \\ \text{Year 3:} &\quad 4000/1.10^3 = 3005.26 \quad (\text{cum } 9947.41) \\ \text{Year 4:} &\quad 4000/1.10^4 = 2732.05 \quad (\text{cum } 12679.46) \end{aligned}$$

The investment is recovered during year 4:

$$n = 3 + \frac{12000 - 9947.41}{2732.05} = 3 + 0.75$$

$$n = 3.75\ \text{years}$$
questions.explanation: Discounted payback discounts first, then accumulates; the 3.00-year trap is the simple (undiscounted) payback. Handbook table: also solvable with the compound-interest factor table (i = 10%) in the Engineering Economics chapter — find the smallest n whose (P/A, 10%, n) covers the investment.

questions.question: A $100,000 piece of equipment is classified as 5-year property under MACRS. What is the depreciation deduction in year 2?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Depreciation section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the year-2 MACRS depreciation. For 5-year property, the MACRS recovery percentages are 20.00%, 32.00%, 19.20%, 11.52%, 11.52%, and 5.76%:

$$D_2 = (\text{cost}) \times (\text{year-2 rate})$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(D_2\):

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost} &= \$100{,}000 \\ \text{Year-2 rate} &= 32.00\% = 0.32 \\ D_2 &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$D_2 = 100000(0.32)$$

$$D_2 = \$32{,}000$$
questions.explanation: MACRS 5-year property: year-2 rate is 32.00% of the full cost. The 40% trap applies double-declining without the half-year convention.
questions.videoTitle: Depreciation

questions.tiTip: No — set up (benefits − disbenefits)/costs by hand; the calculator only does the arithmetic.
questions.question: A proposed project has benefits of $800,000, disbenefits of $100,000, and costs of $500,000 (all present worths). What is the conventional benefit-cost ratio?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Benefit-Cost Analysis section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the conventional benefit-cost ratio, in which disbenefits are subtracted from benefits:

$$B/C = \frac{\text{benefits} - \text{disbenefits}}{\text{costs}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(B/C\):

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Benefits} &= \$800{,}000 \\ \text{Disbenefits} &= \$100{,}000 \\ \text{Costs} &= \$500{,}000 \\ B/C &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$B/C = \frac{800000 - 100000}{500000} = \frac{700000}{500000}$$

$$B/C = 1.40$$
questions.explanation: Conventional B/C subtracts disbenefits from benefits: (800 − 100)/500 = 1.40. Adding them instead gives the 1.80 trap.
questions.videoTitle: Engineering Economics VI: Benefit–Cost Analysis

questions.question: An investment of $5,000 grows to $8,000 in 4 years with annual compounding. What is the annual effective interest rate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the annual effective interest rate \(i\). We can determine \(i\) from the single-payment compound amount relationship:

$$F = P(1+i)^n \quad\Rightarrow\quad i = \left(\frac{F}{P}\right)^{1/n} - 1$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(i\):

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \$5{,}000 \\ F &= \$8{,}000 \\ n &= 4\ \text{years} \\ i &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$i = \left(\frac{8000}{5000}\right)^{1/4} - 1 = (1.6)^{0.25} - 1 = 0.1247$$

$$i = 12.5\%$$
questions.explanation: Solve F = P(1+i)ⁿ for i: (F/P)^(1/n) − 1. Dividing the total 60% gain by 4 years gives the 15.0% trap. Handbook table: also solvable with the compound-interest factor table (i = 12%) in the Engineering Economics chapter — (F/P, 12%, 4) ≈ 1.5735 brackets the target 1.60, giving i ≈ 12.5%.

questions.question: Concrete compressive strengths are normally distributed with a mean of 500 psi and a standard deviation of 100 psi. Approximately what percentile is a strength of 600 psi?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Normal Distribution (Gaussian Distribution) section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the percentile of \(x = 600\). Standardize with the z-score, then read the cumulative area from the standard normal table:

$$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(z\):

$$\begin{aligned} \mu &= 500\ \text{psi} \\ \sigma &= 100\ \text{psi} \\ x &= 600\ \text{psi} \\ z &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$z = \frac{600 - 500}{100} = 1.00$$

From the standard normal table, \(\Phi(1.00) = 0.8413\), so a strength of 600 psi is at the 84.1st percentile.
questions.explanation: z = 1.00 → Φ(1) = 0.8413, the 84.1st percentile. The 68.3% trap confuses this with the within-one-σ empirical-rule band. Handbook table: also solvable with the unit normal distribution table in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter — convert 600 psi to z = 1.0 and read the cumulative area Φ(1) ≈ 84.1%, i.e., the 84.1st percentile.

questions.question: A manufactured part has a 5% defect rate, independently from part to part. If 4 parts are sampled, what is the probability that at least one is defective?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Laws of Probability section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (pp. 65-66).

The handbook (p. 65) prints the Law of Total Probability (Property 2) in this exact form:

$$P(A + B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A, B)$$

Taking \(B\) as the complement of \(A\): \(A + B\) is then certain (probability 1) and \(P(A, B) = 0\) (impossible) by Property 1, so \(P(A) + P(A') = 1\). Since the \(n\) sampled parts are independent, "none defective" is the joint event of \(n\) independent not-defective outcomes each with probability \(1 - p\), so the handbook form collapses to the working equation:

$$P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none defective}) = 1 - (1 - p)^n$$

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(\text{at least one defective})\). Use the complement rule:

$$P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none defective}) = 1 - (1 - p)^n$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P\):

$$\begin{aligned} p &= 5\% = 0.05 \\ n &= 4 \\ P &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$P = 1 - (0.95)^4 = 1 - 0.81451$$

$$P = 0.185$$
questions.explanation: “At least one” means use the complement: 1 − (1−p)ⁿ. The 0.815 trap is P(none defective).

questions.question: Steel yield strengths have a mean of 60 ksi and a standard deviation of 3 ksi. What is the coefficient of variation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Dispersion, Mean, Median, and Mode Values section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the coefficient of variation \(CV\), the relative (dimensionless) measure of spread:

$$CV = \frac{\sigma}{\mu}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(CV\):

$$\begin{aligned} \mu &= 60\ \text{ksi} \\ \sigma &= 3\ \text{ksi} \\ CV &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$CV = \frac{3}{60} = 0.05$$

$$CV = 5\%$$
questions.explanation: CV = σ/μ is unitless relative spread — the 20 trap inverts the ratio.

questions.question: In hypothesis testing, a Type I error is:
choices: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
Using a significance level that is too large
Accepting the alternative hypothesis when it is false
questions.solution:
Refer to the Hypothesis Testing section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

A Type I error is the error of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true — a false positive.

A Type II error is the opposite mistake: failing to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative).

The significance level \(\alpha\) of a test is exactly the probability of committing a Type I error.

Rejecting a true null hypothesis is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Type I = false positive (reject a true null); the significance level α is exactly P(Type I error).

questions.question: In a survey of 400 residents, 60% support a proposed transit project. What is the margin of error for a 95% confidence interval for the true proportion? (Use z = 1.96.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Confidence Intervals section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (pp. 75-76). Note: the handbook prints intervals for the mean, the difference of two means, and the variance -- it does not print a proportion interval, so memorize this one. It follows the same pattern as the handbook's mean interval: margin of error = z x (standard error), with the standard error of a sample proportion equal to \(\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}\):

Ultimately, we must solve for the margin of error \(E\) of a 95% confidence interval for a proportion:

$$E = z\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(E\):

$$\begin{aligned} \hat{p} &= 60\% = 0.60 \\ n &= 400 \\ z &= 1.96 \\ E &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$E = 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.60(0.40)}{400}} = 1.96(0.024495)$$

$$E = 0.048$$
questions.explanation: Margin of error = z√(p̂(1−p̂)/n). Forgetting the square root of n gives the 0.960 trap.

questions.question: X and Y are independent random variables with Var(X) = 4 and Var(Y) = 9. What is Var(3X − 2Y)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Combinations of Random Variables subsection under Expected Values in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (p. 66).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(Var(3X - 2Y)\). For independent random variables, variances add with squared coefficients — the minus sign does not survive squaring:

$$Var(aX + bY) = a^2Var(X) + b^2Var(Y)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(Var(3X - 2Y)\):

$$\begin{aligned} Var(X) &= 4 \\ Var(Y) &= 9 \\ a &= 3,\ b = -2 \\ Var(3X - 2Y) &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$Var(3X - 2Y) = (3)^2(4) + (-2)^2(9) = 36 + 36$$

$$Var(3X - 2Y) = 72$$
questions.explanation: Variance squares the coefficients and the minus sign vanishes: 9(4) + 4(9) = 72. The −18 trap keeps the sign.

questions.question: Vehicles arrive at a toll booth at an average rate of 3 per minute. What is the probability that at most 1 vehicle arrives in a given minute?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Probability and Density Functions: Means and Variances section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(X \le 1)\). Sum the probabilities for \(k = 0\) and \(k = 1\):

$$P(X = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{k}}{k!}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P(X \le 1)\):

$$\begin{aligned} \lambda &= 3 \\ k &= 0, 1 \\ P(X \le 1) &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$P(X \le 1) = \frac{e^{-3}3^0}{0!} + \frac{e^{-3}3^1}{1!} = e^{-3}(1 + 3) = 4(0.049787)$$

$$P(X \le 1) = 0.199$$
questions.explanation: P(X ≤ 1) = e^( −λ)(1 + λ). The 0.801 trap answers the complement instead.

questions.question: Under the NCEES Model Rules, an engineer who has knowledge of another engineer's violation of the licensure laws should:
choices: Confront the engineer privately and take no further action
Report it to the news media first
Report it to the appropriate licensing board
Ignore it unless it directly affects her own work
questions.solution:
The NCEES Model Rules provide that engineers having knowledge of any alleged violation of the licensure act or rules shall cooperate with the licensing board and furnish information or assistance as required.

An engineer who observes a violation therefore has an affirmative duty to report it to the appropriate licensing board — ignoring it, handling it only privately, or going to the media first does not satisfy that duty.

Reporting to the licensing board is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Knowledge of a licensure violation creates an affirmative duty to report it to the licensing board — private confrontation alone is not enough.

questions.question: An engineer uses her employer's licensed software and office equipment after hours to perform design work for a private client who competes with her employer. This conduct is:
choices: Unethical — misuse of employer resources and an undisclosed conflict of interest
Ethical, since the work was performed on her own time
Ethical, provided the design work meets professional standards
Ethical, as long as she charges the client a fair fee
questions.solution:
Under the NSPE Code of Ethics, engineers shall not use their employer's equipment, supplies, or staff for outside work without consent, and must disclose any conflict of interest to the affected parties.

Here the engineer commits both wrongs at once: using the employer's licensed software and equipment for private gain, and serving a competing client without disclosure.

Doing the work “on her own time” does not cure either violation.

The unethical — misuse of resources and undisclosed conflict — choice is correct.
questions.explanation: Employer resources are not for moonlighting, and competing side work without disclosure is a conflict of interest.

questions.question: An engineer retained as an expert witness in litigation must ensure that her testimony is:
choices: Withheld from the court until the retaining attorney approves it
Objective and based on technical facts, regardless of which side retained her
Limited to opinions that support the retaining client's position
As favorable as possible to the side that retained her
questions.solution:
The NSPE Code of Ethics requires that engineers testifying as experts be objective and truthful: testimony must be founded on adequate knowledge of the facts and honest conviction, and must not be slanted to favor the party paying the bill.

An expert who tailors opinions to the retaining client's position violates the duty of honesty to the tribunal and the public.

Objective and based on technical facts, regardless of which side retained her, is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: An expert witness serves the truth, not the retaining client — testimony must stay objective regardless of who pays.

questions.question: In most states, a licensed professional engineer must do which of the following to renew her license?
choices: Retake the FE exam every renewal cycle
Complete a required number of professional development (continuing education) hours
Publish one technical paper per renewal cycle
Maintain membership in a national engineering society
questions.solution:
Most state licensing boards require licensed professional engineers to complete a set number of professional development hours (continuing education) in each renewal cycle as a condition of license renewal.

Retaking the FE exam, publishing papers, and society membership are not renewal requirements.

Completing the required professional development hours is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: License renewal in most states hinges on completing the required professional development hours.

questions.question: A supervisor asks a junior engineer to backdate an inspection certification to a date before the inspection actually occurred. Under the NCEES Code of Ethics, the engineer should:
choices: Comply, but keep a private memo documenting the request
Backdate it only if the inspection results were satisfactory
Comply, since the supervisor assumes responsibility for the decision
Refuse — falsifying the date misrepresents facts and is dishonest
questions.solution:
The NCEES Code of Ethics requires engineers to be honest and to avoid deceptive acts: engineers shall not falsify or misrepresent facts.

Backdating an inspection certification misrepresents when the inspection occurred, regardless of whether the results were satisfactory — and a supervisor's order does not transfer the ethical responsibility.

Refusing because falsifying the date is dishonest is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Backdating any certification is falsification; a supervisor's instruction does not make it ethical.

questions.question: When an engineer issues a public statement on a technical matter (for example, testimony before a planning board), the NCEES Code of Ethics requires the statement to be:
choices: Limited to information the client has approved for release
Delivered only through the client's public relations office
Objective and truthful, disclosing any interest the engineer has in the matter
Supportive of the engineer's client position regardless of the facts
questions.solution:
Under the NSPE Code of Ethics, engineers shall be objective and truthful in professional reports, statements, and testimony, and shall include all relevant and pertinent information — and when issuing statements on behalf of an interested party, shall disclose that interest.

Slanting a public statement toward a client's position, or suppressing facts the client disfavors, violates that duty.

Objective and truthful, disclosing any interest, is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Public statements must be objective and truthful, with any interest disclosed — the facts come before the client's position.

questions.question: A materials supplier offers an engineer a 5% commission for specifying the supplier's products on a client's project, in addition to the engineer's normal design fee. Under the NSPE Code of Ethics, the engineer may accept the commission only if:
choices: The client is fully informed of the arrangement and consents to it
The supplier's products are technically equal to competitors
The engineer discloses the commission to the other engineers on the project
The commission is less than 10% of the design fee
questions.solution:
The NSPE Code of Ethics provides that engineers shall not accept compensation, financial or otherwise, from more than one party for services on the same project unless the circumstances are fully disclosed to and agreed to by all interested parties.

A secret supplier commission for specifying its products is a textbook violation; technical equivalence of the products and the size of the commission do not cure it.

Full disclosure to and consent of the client is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Compensation from two parties on one project is allowed only with full disclosure to and consent of all interested parties.

questions.question: Use one iteration of Newton's method for root extraction to estimate the root of \(f(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5\), starting from the initial estimate \(x_0 = 2\). What is \(x_1\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Newton's Method for Root Extraction section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(x_1\). The handbook gives the iteration formula:

$$x_{j+1} = x_j - \frac{f(x_j)}{f'(x_j)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(x_1\):

$$\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= x^3 - 2x - 5 \\
f'(x) &= 3x^2 - 2 \\
x_0 &= 2 \\
x_1 &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Evaluate \(f\) and \(f'\) at the initial estimate:

$$(f(2)) = (2)^3 - 2(2) - 5 \rightarrow 8 - 4 - 5 = -1$$

$$(f'(2)) = 3(2)^2 - 2 \rightarrow 12 - 2 = 10$$

Substitute into the iteration formula:

$$(x_1) = (2) - \frac{(-1)}{(10)} \rightarrow 2 + 0.10 = 2.10$$

$$x_1 = 2.10$$
questions.explanation: Newton's method improves each guess by subtracting f/f'. Watch the sign: a negative f value moves the guess upward.

questions.question: Evaluate the definite integral \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 x e^x\,dx\).
questions.solution:
Refer to the Indefinite Integrals section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\int_0^1 x e^x\,dx\). The handbook's integral equation #6 (integration by parts) gives:

$$\int u(x)\,dv(x) = u(x)v(x) - \int v(x)\,du(x)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to apply the formula:

$$\begin{aligned}
u &= x \\
dv &= e^x\,dx \\
du &= dx \\
v &= e^x
\end{aligned}$$

Substitute into the integration-by-parts formula and evaluate from 0 to 1:

$$\left(\int_0^1 x e^x\,dx\right) = \left[x e^x\right]_0^1 - \int_0^1 e^x\,dx$$

Evaluate the boundary term on its own line:

$$\left[x e^x\right]_0^1 = (1)(e) - (0)(1) = e$$

Evaluate the remaining integral on its own line:

$$\left(\int_0^1 e^x\,dx\right) = \left[e^x\right]_0^1 = e - 1$$

Combine the two results:

$$\left(\int_0^1 x e^x\,dx\right) = (e) - (e - 1) = 1$$

$$\int_0^1 x e^x\,dx = 1$$
questions.explanation: Integration by parts splits the integrand into u (the part that simplifies when differentiated) and dv (the part that is easy to integrate).

questions.tiTip: Setup by hand; use the numeric integral for the area and first-moment pieces.
questions.question: Consider the region bounded by the curve \(y = x^2\), the x-axis, and the vertical lines \(x = 0\) and \(x = 2\). What is the x-coordinate of the centroid of this region?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Centroids of Masses, Areas, Lengths, and Volumes section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(x_c\). The handbook gives, for an area bounded by the axes and the function \(y = f(x)\):

$$x_c = \frac{\int x\,dA}{A}, \qquad A = \int f(x)\,dx, \qquad dA = f(x)\,dx$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(x_c\):

$$\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= x^2 \\
dA &= x^2\,dx \\
A &= \int_0^2 x^2\,dx \\
\int x\,dA &= \int_0^2 x \cdot x^2\,dx = \int_0^2 x^3\,dx \\
x_c &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Compute the area on its own line:

$$(A) = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \frac{8}{3} - 0 = \frac{8}{3}$$

Compute the first moment with respect to the y-axis on its own line:

$$\left(\int x\,dA\right) = \left[\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^2 = \frac{16}{4} - 0 = 4$$

Divide the moment by the area:

$$(x_c) = \frac{(4)}{(8/3)} \rightarrow (4)\left(\frac{3}{8}\right) = \frac{12}{8} = 1.5$$

$$x_c = 1.5$$
questions.explanation: The x-centroid weights each vertical strip by its distance x from the y-axis; the taller strips on the right pull the centroid right of the midpoint.

questions.question: An engineering firm must select 3 engineers from a team of 8 to form a design review panel. How many distinct panels are possible?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Permutations and Combinations section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(C(8, 3)\). Because the order of the 3 engineers on the panel does not matter, the handbook's combination formula applies:

$$C(n, r) = \frac{n!}{r!(n - r)!}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(C(8, 3)\):

$$\begin{aligned}
n &= 8 \\
r &= 3 \\
C(8, 3) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Substitute into the combination formula:

$$(C(8, 3)) = \frac{8!}{3!(8 - 3)!} = \frac{8!}{3!\,5!}$$

Cancel the common factors on their own line:

$$\left(\frac{8!}{3!\,5!}\right) = \frac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6}{3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = \frac{336}{6}$$

Evaluate the result:

$$C(8, 3) = 56$$
questions.explanation: Order doesn't matter for a panel, so use combinations. If the 3 seats were distinct roles, you would use permutations instead.

questions.question: In a batch of castings, 30% have a surface flaw (event \(F\)) and 12% have both a surface flaw and a dimensional deviation (event \(D\)). Given that a randomly selected casting has a surface flaw, what is the probability it also has a dimensional deviation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Laws of Probability section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (pp. 65-66).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(D \mid F)\). Property 3 (Law of Compound or Joint Probability) gives:

$$P(A, B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A)$$

Rearranging for the conditional probability:

$$P(D \mid F) = \frac{P(D, F)}{P(F)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(P(D \mid F)\):

$$\begin{aligned}
P(F) &= 0.30 \\
P(D, F) &= 0.12 \\
P(D \mid F) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Substitute into the rearranged formula:

$$(P(D \mid F)) = \frac{(0.12)}{(0.30)}$$

Evaluate the result:

$$P(D \mid F) = 0.40$$
questions.explanation: Given the condition, divide the 'both' probability by the probability of the condition. The answer must be at least as large as the joint probability.

questions.question: A continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x) = 1/10\) for \(0 \le x \le 10\) (and zero otherwise). What is the expected value of \(X^2\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Expected Values section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(E[X^2]\). The handbook gives the expected value of a function \(Y = g(X)\) of a continuous random variable:

$$E[Y] = E[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)\,f(x)\,dx$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(E[X^2]\):

$$\begin{aligned}
g(x) &= x^2 \\
f(x) &= \frac{1}{10}, \quad 0 \le x \le 10 \\
E[X^2] &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Substitute into the expected-value formula, noting the density is zero outside \([0, 10]\):

$$(E[X^2]) = \int_0^{10} x^2 \left(\frac{1}{10}\right)\,dx = \frac{1}{10}\int_0^{10} x^2\,dx$$

Evaluate the integral on its own line:

$$\left(\int_0^{10} x^2\,dx\right) = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^{10} = \frac{1000}{3} - 0 = \frac{1000}{3}$$

Multiply by the constant factor:

$$(E[X^2]) = \left(\frac{1}{10}\right)\left(\frac{1000}{3}\right) = \frac{100}{3} \approx 33.33$$

$$E[X^2] = 33.33$$
questions.explanation: E[X²] is not the square of E[X]. Integrate x² against the density directly — the variance is the difference between the two.

questions.question: A proposal an engineer submits to a client states that she 'led the structural design of three high-rise projects,' when in fact she only assisted on one mid-rise project and played no role in the other two. Under the NCEES Model Rules, this conduct:
choices: Violates the rule against misrepresenting academic or professional qualifications and degree of responsibility in prior assignments
Is acceptable if no contract has been signed yet
Violates only the rule against political contributions
Is acceptable because proposal language is marketing, not engineering practice
questions.solution:
Refer to the Obligations of Licensees to Other Licensees section in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The Model Rules provide that licensees shall not falsify or permit misrepresentation of their, or their associates', academic or professional qualifications. They shall not misrepresent or exaggerate their degree of responsibility in prior assignments nor the complexity of said assignments.

Claiming to have led three high-rise designs when she only assisted on one mid-rise project exaggerates both her degree of responsibility and the complexity of her prior assignments, so it violates this rule. Proposal language is still a professional representation, and no signed contract is needed for the violation to occur.

Misrepresenting qualifications and degree of responsibility in prior assignments is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Marketing language doesn't excuse misrepresentation. The rule covers proposals and employment solicitations, not just sealed documents.

questions.question: An engineer is invited to form a joint venture with a firm she knows has been falsifying concrete test results on public projects. Under the NCEES Model Rules, she should:
choices: Decline only if her own current clients would find out about the partnership
Decline, because licensees must not partner or practice with any person or firm known to engage in fraudulent or dishonest business or professional practices
Accept the invitation, because the other firm's past conduct is not her responsibility
Accept the invitation, but report the firm only if a client asks about it
questions.solution:
Refer to the Obligations of Licensees to the Public section in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The Model Rules provide that licensees shall not partner, practice, or offer to practice with any person or firm that they know is engaged in fraudulent or dishonest business or professional practices.

Falsifying concrete test results on public projects is fraudulent and dishonest professional practice, and the engineer has knowledge of it. Accepting the joint venture would mean partnering with a known bad actor, which the rule prohibits regardless of whether her own clients ever learn of it. She also has a separate duty to report the violation to the board.

Declining the joint venture is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: You don't need to have participated in the fraud — knowingly associating your practice with it is itself the violation.

questions.question: To improve his firm's chances of winning a municipal design contract, an engineer makes a $5,000 personal contribution to the mayor's reelection campaign with the intent of influencing the contract award. Under the NCEES Model Rules, this is:
choices: Permitted, because the contribution went to a campaign rather than to an official directly
A violation, because licensees must not make a political contribution with the intent to influence the award of a contract by public authority
A violation only if the firm actually wins the contract
Permitted, because personal political contributions are a private matter
questions.solution:
Refer to the Obligations of Licensees to Other Licensees section in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The Model Rules provide that licensees shall not offer, give, solicit, or receive, either directly or indirectly, any commission, or gift, or other valuable consideration in order to secure work, and shall not make any political contribution with the intent to influence the award of a contract by public authority.

The engineer's contribution was made with the stated intent of influencing the award of a public contract, which is exactly what this rule prohibits. That the money went to a campaign rather than directly to an official does not change the intent, and the violation is complete when the contribution is made — whether or not the firm wins the contract is irrelevant.

A violation of the political-contribution rule is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: The intent to influence the award is what triggers the rule, whether or not the contract is actually won.

questions.question: A project cost is estimated in constant (year-0) dollars. If the market interest rate is 8% per year and general inflation is 3% per year, what inflation-adjusted interest rate should be used to compute the present worth of future costs stated in constant dollars?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Inflation section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(d\), the inflation-adjusted interest rate per interest period. The handbook gives:

$$d = i + f + (i \times f)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(d\):

$$\begin{aligned}
i &= 8\% = 0.08 \\
f &= 3\% = 0.03 \\
d &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Substitute into the inflation formula:

$$(d) = (0.08) + (0.03) + (0.08)(0.03)$$

Evaluate the cross term on its own line:

$$((0.08)(0.03)) = 0.0024$$

Add the terms:

$$(d) = 0.08 + 0.03 + 0.0024 = 0.1124 = 11.24\%$$

$$d = 11.24\%$$
questions.explanation: The cross term i×f is small but not zero — dropping it is the classic 11.00% trap.

questions.question: A 10-year bond with a $1,000 face value pays 6% annual coupons at each year end. If the market interest rate is 8% per year, what is the bond's value?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniform Series section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The Bonds section defines the bond value as the present worth of the payments the holder receives at interest rate \(i\). Ultimately, we must solve for the bond value \(V\):

$$V = C(P/A, i\%, n) + F(P/F, i\%, n)$$

The printed factor formulas are:

$$(P/A, i\%, n) = \frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i(1+i)^n}, \qquad (P/F, i\%, n) = (1+i)^{-n}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(V\):

$$\begin{aligned}
C &= (0.06)(1000) = \$60 \\
F &= \$1{,}000 \\
i &= 8\% = 0.08 \\
n &= 10 \\
V &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Compute the uniform-series present worth factor on its own line:

$$((P/A, 8\%, 10)) = \frac{(1.08)^{10} - 1}{(0.08)(1.08)^{10}} = \frac{1.158925}{0.172714} = 6.7101$$

Compute the single-payment present worth factor on its own line:

$$((P/F, 8\%, 10)) = (1.08)^{-10} = 0.4632$$

Substitute both factors into the bond-value equation:

$$(V) = (60)(6.7101) + (1000)(0.4632) \rightarrow 402.61 + 463.19 = 865.80$$

$$V = \$865.80$$
questions.explanation: A bond is worth the present worth of its coupon stream plus the discounted face value. When the market rate exceeds the coupon rate, the bond sells at a discount (below face value). Handbook table: also solvable with the compound-interest factor table (i = 8%) in the Engineering Economics chapter — look up (P/A, 8%, 10) and (P/F, 8%, 10).

questions.tiTip: No — price the annuity, then discount it through the deferral period by hand; the calculator only does the arithmetic.
questions.question: A machine upgrade will save $4,000 per year for 6 years, with the first savings occurring at the end of year 3 (the series is deferred 2 years). At 10% annual interest, what is the present worth of the savings?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniform Series section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the present worth \(P\). A deferred annuity is priced as an ordinary annuity at the start of its first payment year, then discounted back through the deferral period:

$$P = A(P/A, i\%, n)(P/F, i\%, k)$$

The printed factor formulas are:

$$(P/A, i\%, n) = \frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i(1+i)^n}, \qquad (P/F, i\%, k) = (1+i)^{-k}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(P\):

$$\begin{aligned}
A &= \$4{,}000 \\
i &= 10\% = 0.10 \\
n &= 6 \\
k &= 2 \\
P &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Compute the uniform-series present worth factor on its own line:

$$((P/A, 10\%, 6)) = \frac{(1.10)^6 - 1}{(0.10)(1.10)^6} = \frac{0.771561}{0.177156} = 4.3553$$

Compute the deferral (single-payment) factor on its own line:

$$((P/F, 10\%, 2)) = (1.10)^{-2} = 0.8264$$

Substitute both factors:

$$(P) = (4000)(4.3553)(0.8264) \rightarrow (4000)(3.5994) = 14{,}397.56$$

$$P = \$14{,}398$$
questions.explanation: Deferral is handled by discounting the whole annuity back through the gap years with a P/F factor — forgetting that step prices the annuity as if it started today. Handbook table: also solvable with the compound-interest factor table (i = 10%) in the Engineering Economics chapter — look up (P/A, 10%, 6) and (P/F, 10%, 2).

questions.explanation: On a frictionless incline the only thing pulling the crate downhill is the downhill component of its own weight, W·sinθ. The holding force must exactly balance that component: 400·sin25° ≈ 169 N up the plane.
questions.question: A 400 N crate rests on a frictionless plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal. What force P, applied parallel to the plane, is required to hold the crate in equilibrium?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
For equilibrium, the sum of force components along the plane must vanish: \(\sum F_{\parallel} = 0\).
The component of the crate's weight acting down the plane is \(W_{\parallel} = W \sin\theta\).
\(W_{\parallel} = (400\ \mathrm{N})(\sin 25^\circ)\).
\(W_{\parallel} = (400\ \mathrm{N})(0.4226) = 169\ \mathrm{N}\).
Therefore \(P = 169\ \mathrm{N}\) directed up the plane.

questions.explanation: Only the moment component along the hinge axis tends to rotate the bracket about its hinge. Using My = z·Fx − x·Fz gives (−15 + 24) = 9.0 N·m; the positive sign means it acts in the +y direction by the right-hand rule.
questions.question: A bracket is hinged along the y-axis (the hinge axis passes through the origin). A force \(\mathbf{F} = (-60\mathbf{i} + 25\mathbf{j} - 40\mathbf{k})\) N is applied at the point \((0.60, 0.10, 0.25)\) m measured from the origin. What is the scalar moment of the force about the y-axis?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Moments (Couples) section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
The moment about an axis is the corresponding component of \(\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\).
About the y-axis: \(M_y = zF_x - xF_z\).
\(M_y = (0.25\ \mathrm{m})(-60\ \mathrm{N}) - (0.60\ \mathrm{m})(-40\ \mathrm{N})\).
\(M_y = -15.0\ \mathrm{N{\cdot}m} + 24.0\ \mathrm{N{\cdot}m}\).
\(M_y = 9.0\ \mathrm{N{\cdot}m}\).

questions.explanation: Two things can happen: the crate can slide (when P beats maximum static friction, 200 N) or tip over its bottom corner (when P's overturning moment beats the weight's restoring moment, 161 N). The smaller one wins — the crate tips first at about 161 N.
questions.question: A 500 N rectangular crate is 0.9 m wide and 1.4 m tall. It rests on a horizontal surface with coefficient of static friction \(\mu_s = 0.40\). A horizontal force P is applied at the top edge of the crate and slowly increased. Does the crate tip or slip first, and at what value of P does motion impend?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Friction section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
Vertical equilibrium gives the normal force: \(N = 500\ \mathrm{N}\).
The limiting friction is \(F \le \mu_s N\).
\(F_{\max} = (0.40)(500\ \mathrm{N}) = 200\ \mathrm{N}\).
So slipping would impend at \(P = 200\ \mathrm{N}\).
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
For tipping, take moments about the bottom corner on the side toward which P pushes, at the instant the normal force acts at that corner:
\(\sum M = 0 \Rightarrow P(1.4\ \mathrm{m}) - (500\ \mathrm{N})(0.45\ \mathrm{m}) = 0\).
\(P = \dfrac{(500)(0.45)}{1.4} = 160.7\ \mathrm{N}\).
Since \(160.7\ \mathrm{N} < 200\ \mathrm{N}\), tipping impends first at \(P \approx 161\ \mathrm{N}\).
