questions.question: A sanitary sewer is being designed for a new subdivision. What minimum flowing-full velocity is typically required to prevent deposition of solids?
questions.explanation: The standard self-cleansing minimum is 2 ft/s (about 0.6 m/s) flowing full. Higher velocities risk scour of the pipe; lower velocities let solids settle.
questions.solution:
The 2 ft/s minimum flowing-full velocity is a design standard that is not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (the handbook's sewage flow ratio curves, Civil Engineering p.300, do not give it):

Sanitary sewers must maintain a self-cleansing velocity so suspended solids do not settle and clog the pipe. The long-standing design standard, used on the FE exam, is:

$$(V_{min}) = 2\\ \text{ft/s} \text{ (flowing full)}$$

Slopes are then selected so that the design flow produces at least this velocity, while staying below the maximum (typically 10 ft/s) that would scour the pipe.

questions.question: A 5-ft by 5-ft square spread footing carries a concentric column load of 180 kips (ignore the footing weight). What is the contact pressure at the base?
questions.explanation: q = P/A = 180/25 = 7.2 ksf. The 36.0 ksf answer divides by the side length instead of the area.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index); contact pressure under a concentric load is force divided by area:

Ultimately, we must solve for the contact pressure under a concentrically loaded footing:

$$q = \frac{P}{A}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 180\\ \text{kips} \\
A &= (5)(5) = 25\\ \text{ft}^2
\end{aligned}$$

$$(q) = \frac{180}{25}$$

$$(q) = 7.2\\ \text{ksf}$$

questions.question: A 6-ft by 6-ft square footing carries a 150-kip load with an eccentricity of 0.5 ft from the centroid. What is the maximum contact pressure?
questions.explanation: \(q_{max} = (P/A)(1 + 6e/B) = (150/36)(1 + 3/6) = 6.25\) ksf. The 4.17 ksf answer ignores the eccentricity.
questions.solution:
The toe pressure \(q_{toe} = \frac{\Sigma V}{B}\left(1 + \frac{6e}{B}\right)\) is printed under Retaining Walls (Civil Engineering, p.270), written for a wall base per unit length. Applying the same form to a square footing with eccentricity in one direction is an extension:

Ultimately, we must solve for the maximum contact pressure under eccentric loading. The handbook gives:

$$q_{max} = \frac{P}{A}\left(1 + \frac{6e}{B}\right)$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 150\\ \text{kips} \\
A &= (6)(6) = 36\\ \text{ft}^2 \\
e &= 0.5\\ \text{ft}, \quad B = 6\\ \text{ft}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(q_{max}) = \frac{150}{36}\left(1 + \frac{6(0.5)}{6}\right)$$

$$(q_{max}) = (4.167)(1.5)$$

$$(q_{max}) = 6.25\\ \text{ksf}$$

questions.question: A bearing wall imposes 8 kips per linear foot on a continuous wall footing. If the allowable soil bearing pressure is 4 ksf, what footing width is required (ignore footing weight)?
questions.explanation: For a 1-ft strip: \(B = P/q_{allow} = 8/4 = 2.0\) ft. The footing width is set so the contact pressure just reaches the allowable.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index); for a continuous wall footing, bearing pressure is load per unit length divided by width:

Ultimately, we must size the footing so the contact pressure equals the allowable bearing pressure. For a 1-ft-long strip of wall footing:

$$B = \frac{P}{q_{allow}}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 8\\ \text{kips/ft} \\
q_{allow} &= 4\\ \text{ksf}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(B) = \frac{8}{4}$$

$$(B) = 2.0\\ \text{ft}$$

questions.question: A mat (raft) foundation is most appropriate for a building when which condition holds?
choices: Column loads are light and widely spaced
Bedrock is within 3 ft of the surface
Individual footings would cover more than about half the building footprint
The soil is dense sand with high bearing capacity
questions.explanation: When footings grow so large they would cover over ~50% of the footprint, a single mat becomes more economical and settles more uniformly. Dense sand, light loads, or shallow bedrock all favor simple spread footings instead.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index); the one-half-of-footprint guideline is a common rule of thumb, not a handbook value:

Foundation type follows the soil and the loading:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Spread footings} &\rightarrow \text{competent soil, moderate loads} \\
\text{Mat foundation} &\rightarrow \text{footings would cover } > \sim 50\\% \text{ of footprint} \\
\text{Deep foundations} &\rightarrow \text{weak near-surface soil}
\end{aligned}$$

A mat spreads the building load over the entire footprint, cutting the contact pressure and bridging soft spots so the building settles as one unit.

questions.question: Quicklime is mixed into a highly plastic clay subgrade. What is the primary engineering purpose?
choices: Reduce plasticity and increase strength and workability
questions.explanation: Lime causes cation exchange and pozzolanic reactions that drop the plasticity index, raise strength, and make wet clay workable. It does the opposite of the other three choices.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index); this is standard geotechnical practice:

Chemical stabilization with lime treats the cause of poor subgrade behavior in plastic clays:

$$\text{lime} + \text{clay} \rightarrow \text{cation exchange} + \text{pozzolanic cementing}$$

The practical effects are:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Plasticity index} &\downarrow \\
\text{Strength / stiffness} &\uparrow \\
\text{Workability of wet clay} &\uparrow
\end{aligned}$$

This is why lime is the standard treatment for highly plastic (fat clay) subgrades.

questions.question: A geotextile is placed between a soft clay subgrade and a granular base course before paving. Which geosynthetic function is it primarily serving?
questions.explanation: Between dissimilar materials, the geotextile's job is separation — keeping the aggregate from punching into the clay and the clay from pumping up. Filtration passes water while retaining soil; reinforcement carries tension.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index); geosynthetic functions are standard geotechnical practice:

Geosynthetics are specified by function:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Separation} &\rightarrow \text{keep dissimilar layers from mixing} \\
\text{Filtration} &\rightarrow \text{pass water, retain soil} \\
\text{Reinforcement} &\rightarrow \text{carry tensile load} \\
\text{Drainage} &\rightarrow \text{transmit water in-plane}
\end{aligned}$$

A geotextile sandwiched between clay and aggregate blocks intermixing (which would destroy the base's strength), so its primary function here is separation.

questions.question: A geotextile wrapped around a subsurface drain must let groundwater in while keeping soil particles out. Which function is being specified?
questions.explanation: Passing water while retaining soil is the textbook definition of filtration. The key design property is the apparent opening size (AOS) relative to the soil gradation.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index); geosynthetic functions are standard geotechnical practice:

The geosynthetic functions are distinguished by what they move or hold:

$$\text{Filtration} = \text{transmit water across the plane } + \text{ retain soil particles}$$

Around a drain, the geotextile must do exactly this: admit groundwater into the drain while preventing soil migration that would clog it. Separation keeps layers apart (no flow requirement); reinforcement carries load.

questions.question: Portland cement is mixed into a granular base material. What is the primary engineering effect?
choices: Increased strength and stiffness of the stabilized layer
questions.explanation: Cement hydration cements the particles together, raising the layer's strength and stiffness (measured by unconfined compressive strength). It reduces — but does not eliminate — permeability and volume change.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index); this is standard geotechnical practice:

Soil-cement works through hydration of the cement:

$$\text{cement} + \text{water} \rightarrow \text{hydration products binding soil particles}$$

The design property is the unconfined compressive strength of the stabilized mixture:

$$(\text{strength}_{stabilized}) \gg (\text{strength}_{untreated})$$

The stabilized layer behaves as a semi-rigid slab, spreading wheel loads over a wider area of the subgrade.

questions.question: A site plan is drawn at a scale of 1 inch = 40 ft. A proposed driveway scales 3.25 inches on the drawing. How long is the driveway?
questions.explanation: Real length = 3.25 × 40 = 130 ft. Dividing by the scale factor instead of multiplying gives 0.08 ft — always check that the answer is bigger than the paper measurement.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index); scale conversion is multiplying the drawing length by the scale:

Ultimately, we must convert the paper measurement to a real length using the drawing scale:

$$L_{real} = L_{drawing} \times (\text{scale factor})$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
L_{drawing} &= 3.25\\ \text{in} \\
\text{scale} &= 40\\ \text{ft/in}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(L_{real}) = (3.25)(40)$$

$$(L_{real}) = 130\\ \text{ft}$$

questions.question: A water main runs from Sta 24+00 to Sta 27+50 along the alignment. What is its length?
questions.explanation: Station 27+50 = 2,750 ft and 24+00 = 2,400 ft from the origin, so the length is 350 ft. The '+' separates hundreds of feet from tens and ones.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index) (the mass-haul diagram on p.315 shows a STATION axis only); stationing is read in feet, 1 station = 100 ft:

Ultimately, we must convert station notation to feet. A station is written as hundreds of feet plus remaining feet:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Sta } 27{+}50 &= 2{,}750\\ \text{ft} \\
\text{Sta } 24{+}00 &= 2{,}400\\ \text{ft}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(L) = 2{,}750 - 2{,}400$$

$$(L) = 350\\ \text{ft}$$

questions.question: On a grading plan, two labeled contours read 98 ft and 108 ft, with four unlabeled contours between them. What is the contour interval?
questions.explanation: Six contours span 10 ft of elevation, creating 5 intervals: 10/5 = 2 ft. Counting contours instead of intervals gives 10/6, a classic trap.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index); contour interval is the elevation difference divided by the number of intervals:

Ultimately, we must solve for the contour interval — the elevation change between adjacent contours:

$$\text{interval} = \frac{\Delta Elev}{\text{number of intervals}}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\Delta Elev &= 108 - 98 = 10\\ \text{ft} \\
\text{intervals} &= 5\\ \ (6\\ \text{contours make } 5\\ \text{ gaps})
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\text{interval}) = \frac{10}{5}$$

$$(\text{interval}) = 2\\ \text{ft}$$

questions.question: On a highway plan set, which view shows the roadway elevations along the centerline alignment?
questions.explanation: Profile = elevations along the alignment (vertical alignment). Plan = bird's-eye layout. Cross-section = transverse slice at one station.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index); plan, profile and cross-section views are standard plan-reading conventions:

The three principal views each answer a different question:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Plan} &\rightarrow \text{horizontal layout (bird's eye)} \\
\text{Profile} &\rightarrow \text{elevations along the alignment} \\
\text{Cross-section} &\rightarrow \text{transverse slice at one station}
\end{aligned}$$

Grades, vertical curves, and earthwork depths are read from the profile, which plots centerline elevation against station.

questions.tiTip: Yes — the distance formula, straight in.
questions.question: What is the distance between the points (2, 3) and (7, 15)?
questions.explanation: d = √[(7−2)² + (15−3)²] = √(25+144) = 13. A 5-12-13 triangle hiding in plain sight.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the distance between two points:

$$d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
(x_1, y_1) &= (2, 3) \\
(x_2, y_2) &= (7, 15)
\end{aligned}$$

$$(d) = \sqrt{(7 - 2)^2 + (15 - 3)^2}$$

$$(d) = \sqrt{25 + 144}$$

$$(d) = \sqrt{169} = 13$$

questions.tiTip: Slope is quick arithmetic — punch in (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), then point-slope form.
questions.question: What is the equation of the line passing through (1, 2) and (5, 10)?
questions.explanation: Slope m = (10−2)/(5−1) = 2; using point (1,2): 2 = 2(1) + b gives b = 0, so y = 2x.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must find the line y = mx + b through both points. First the slope:

$$m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$$

$$(m) = \frac{10 - 2}{5 - 1} = \frac{8}{4} = 2$$

Insert one point to solve for the intercept:

$$(2) = (2)(1) + b \rightarrow (b) = 0$$

$$(y) = 2x$$

questions.tiTip: By hand — center-radius form (x−h)² + (y−k)² = r² straight from memory.
questions.question: What is the equation of the circle with center (3, −2) and radius 5?
questions.explanation: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² with (h,k) = (3,−2): the signs flip inside the parentheses and the radius is squared.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must write the standard circle equation:

$$(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
(h, k) &= (3, -2) \\
r &= 5
\end{aligned}$$

$$((x - 3)^2 + (y - (-2))^2) = (5)^2$$

$$((x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2) = 25$$

questions.tiTip: Yes — system solver: 2nd → sys-solv, enter FC + 500·VC = 10000 and FC + 1000·VC = 16000, then read FC.
questions.question: A contractor's total cost is $10,000 when producing 500 units and $16,000 when producing 1,000 units. Assuming cost is linear in quantity, what is the fixed cost?
questions.explanation: Variable cost = (16,000 − 10,000)/500 = $12/unit. Fixed = 10,000 − 12(500) = $4,000. The $6,000 answer is the variable-cost difference, not the fixed cost.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Cost section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must separate fixed from variable cost. Total cost is linear in quantity:

$$TC = FC + (VC_{unit})(Q)$$

First find the unit variable cost from the two data points:

$$(VC_{unit}) = \frac{16{,}000 - 10{,}000}{1{,}000 - 500} = \frac{6{,}000}{500} = 12\\ \text{dollars/unit}$$

Then back out the fixed cost:

$$(FC) = 10{,}000 - (12)(500)$$

$$(FC) = 10{,}000 - 6{,}000 = 4{,}000\\ \text{dollars}$$

questions.tiTip: No — divide total cost by quantity; the calculator only does the arithmetic.
questions.question: A precast plant spends $48,000 total to produce 3,000 identical concrete panels. What is the average cost per panel?
questions.explanation: Average cost = total cost / quantity = 48,000/3,000 = $16 per panel.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Cost section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the average (unit) cost:

$$AC = \frac{TC}{Q}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
TC &= 48{,}000\\ \text{dollars} \\
Q &= 3{,}000\\ \text{panels}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(AC) = \frac{48{,}000}{3{,}000}$$

$$(AC) = 16\\ \text{dollars/panel}$$

questions.tiTip: No — this is a conceptual question; the calculator can't help.
questions.question: A firm spent $200,000 developing a prototype that failed testing. It is now evaluating a redesigned product. How should the $200,000 be treated in the economic analysis?
choices: Depreciate it over the new product's life
Subtract it from the redesign's benefits
Add it to the redesign's cost
Ignore it — it is a sunk cost
questions.explanation: Sunk costs are unrecoverable regardless of the decision, so they are excluded from forward-looking analyses. Only incremental future costs and benefits matter.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Cost section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Costs are classified by their relevance to the decision:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Sunk cost} &\rightarrow \text{already incurred, unrecoverable} \\
\text{Decision rule} &\rightarrow \text{ignore sunk costs}
\end{aligned}$$

The $200,000 was spent whether or not the redesign proceeds, so it cannot change the ranking of alternatives. Only the incremental costs and benefits of the redesign itself enter the analysis.

questions.tiTip: No — weight each outcome by its probability by hand; the calculator only does the arithmetic.
questions.question: A project has a 60% chance of earning $100,000 and a 40% chance of losing $20,000. What is its expected monetary value?
questions.explanation: EMV = 0.6(100,000) + 0.4(−20,000) = 60,000 − 8,000 = $52,000. Forgetting the minus sign on the loss gives $68,000.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uncertainty section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must compute the expected monetary value:

$$EMV = \sum p_i x_i$$

List the outcomes:

$$\begin{aligned}
p_1 &= 0.60, \quad x_1 = 100{,}000\\ \text{dollars} \\
p_2 &= 0.40, \quad x_2 = -20{,}000\\ \text{dollars}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(EMV) = (0.60)(100{,}000) + (0.40)(-20{,}000)$$

$$(EMV) = 60{,}000 - 8{,}000$$

$$(EMV) = 52{,}000\\ \text{dollars}$$

questions.tiTip: No — compare the expected values by hand; the calculator only does the arithmetic.
questions.question: Alternative A has an expected value of $50,000. Alternative B has a 50% chance of $120,000 and a 50% chance of −$10,000. Using expected value, which should be selected?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uncertainty section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must compare expected values and select the larger:

$$(EMV_B) = (0.50)(120{,}000) + (0.50)(-10{,}000)$$

$$(EMV_B) = 60{,}000 - 5{,}000 = 55{,}000\\ \text{dollars}$$

$$(EMV_A) = 50{,}000\\ \text{dollars}$$

$$(55{,}000) > (50{,}000) \rightarrow \text{select Alternative B}$$

questions.tiTip: No — this is a definition question; the calculator can't help.
questions.question: In an engineering economic analysis under uncertainty, the term “risk” is best described as which of the following?
choices: The probability the project breaks even
Variability of outcomes around the expected value
The interest rate used for discounting
questions.explanation: Risk is the spread of possible outcomes — two projects can share an expected value while carrying very different risk. Expected value alone does not capture it.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uncertainty section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Under uncertainty, a decision is characterized by two things:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Expected value} &\rightarrow \text{probability-weighted mean outcome} \\
\text{Risk} &\rightarrow \text{variability of outcomes about that mean}
\end{aligned}$$

This is why analyses pair expected value with risk measures (range, variance, or probability of loss) rather than reporting the mean alone.

questions.question: A concrete mix contains 350 kg of cement with a specific gravity of 3.15. What volume does the cement occupy? (Density of water = 1000 kg/m³)
questions.explanation: V = mass/(SG × density of water) = 350/(3.15 × 1000) = 0.111 m³. Dividing by SG alone forgets the water-density conversion.
questions.solution:
Refer to the definition of specific gravity in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6, p. 181): \(SG = \rho/\rho_w\).

The handbook (p. 181) prints the specific gravity definition in this exact form:

$$SG = \gamma/\gamma_w = \rho/\rho_w$$

With density \(\rho = M/V\), this becomes \(SG = M/(V\rho_w)\); solving for the volume gives the working equation:

$$V = \frac{M}{(SG)(\rho_w)}$$

Ultimately, we must solve for the volume of cement:

$$V = \frac{M}{(SG)(\rho_w)}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
M &= 350\\ \text{kg} \\
SG &= 3.15 \\
\rho_w &= 1{,}000\\ \text{kg/m}^3
\end{aligned}$$

$$(V) = \frac{350}{(3.15)(1{,}000)}$$

$$(V) = \frac{350}{3{,}150}$$

$$(V) = 0.111\\ \text{m}^3$$

questions.question: A concrete batch contains 160 kg of water and 400 kg of cement. What is the water-cement ratio?
questions.explanation: w/c = 160/400 = 0.40. Lower ratios give higher strength; the 2.50 answer inverts the fraction.
questions.solution:
Refer to the water-cement ratio discussion in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6, p. 126).

Ultimately, we must solve for the water-cement ratio, the single most important predictor of concrete strength:

$$w/c = \frac{M_{water}}{M_{cement}}$$

$$(w/c) = \frac{160}{400}$$

$$(w/c) = 0.40$$

questions.question: In asphalt mix design, providing adequate voids in the mineral aggregate (VMA) is important primarily to ensure which of the following?
choices: Zero air voids in the compacted mix
Enough room for the binder film that gives durability
questions.explanation: VMA is the space available for binder plus air voids; too little VMA starves the mix of binder and the pavement ravels. Mixes are designed for 3–5% air voids, not zero.
questions.solution:
VMA is not tabulated in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6); use the definition stated here.

An asphalt mixture's volume is split three ways:

$$VMA = (\text{air voids}) + (\text{effective binder volume})$$

If VMA is too small, there is no room for an adequate binder film around each aggregate particle, and the pavement loses durability and ravels under traffic. This is why specifications set minimum VMA values by nominal aggregate size.

questions.question: A triangular inflow hydrograph peaks at 80 cfs with a 4-hour base. The basin outlet releases a constant 25 cfs. What detention storage volume is required?
questions.explanation: Storage = inflow volume − outflow volume = ½(80)(14,400) − 25(14,400) = 216,000 ft³ = 5.0 acre-ft.
questions.solution:
The storage balance comes from the Hydrologic Mass Balance (Budget) in the Civil Engineering chapter (printed p.296); the triangular hydrograph volume is computed directly:

The handbook (p. 296) prints the surface-water hydrologic budget in this exact form:

$$P + Q_{in} - Q_{out} + Q_g - E_s - T_s - I = \Delta S_s$$

For the detention basin during the storm, keeping only inflow, outflow, and the change in storage, the handbook form collapses to the working storage equation:

$$S = V_{in} - V_{out}$$

Ultimately, we must solve for the required storage as the difference between inflow and outflow volumes:

$$S = V_{in} - V_{out}$$

The inflow hydrograph is triangular; the outflow is constant over the same base time.

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{in} &= \tfrac{1}{2}(80)(4 \times 3{,}600) = 576{,}000\\ \text{ft}^3 \\
V_{out} &= (25)(4 \times 3{,}600) = 360{,}000\\ \text{ft}^3
\end{aligned}$$

$$(S) = 576{,}000 - 360{,}000 = 216{,}000\\ \text{ft}^3$$

$$(S) = \frac{216{,}000}{43{,}560} = 5.0\\ \text{acre-ft}$$

questions.question: A detention basin outlet is a 6-inch-diameter orifice with discharge coefficient 0.60. With 4 ft of head above the orifice centerline, what is the outflow?
questions.explanation: Q = Cd·A√(2gh) = 0.60 × 0.196 × √(257.6) = 1.9 cfs. Using the diameter instead of the area is the common error.
questions.solution:
The free-discharge orifice equation \(Q = C A_0\sqrt{2gh}\) is printed in Fluid Mechanics (p.190), with h measured to the orifice centroid:

Ultimately, we must solve for the orifice outflow:

$$Q = C_d A\sqrt{2gh}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
d &= 6\\ \text{in} = 0.5\\ \text{ft} \\
A &= \frac{\pi(0.5)^2}{4} = 0.1963\\ \text{ft}^2 \\
C_d &= 0.60, \quad h = 4\\ \text{ft}, \quad g = 32.2\\ \text{ft/s}^2
\end{aligned}$$

$$(Q) = (0.60)(0.1963)\sqrt{2(32.2)(4)}$$

$$(Q) = (0.1178)(16.05)$$

$$(Q) = 1.9\\ \text{cfs}$$

questions.question: A 2-acre parking lot (fully impervious) must capture the first 1 inch of runoff for water quality treatment. What storage volume is required?
questions.explanation: V = area × depth = 2(43,560)(1/12) = 7,260 ft³. The 87,120 answer forgets to convert inches to feet.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index); the capture volume is drainage area times design depth (unit conversion):

Ultimately, we must solve for the water-quality capture volume:

$$V = (\text{area})(\text{design depth})$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
A &= 2\\ \text{ac} = 87{,}120\\ \text{ft}^2 \\
d &= 1\\ \text{in} = \frac{1}{12}\\ \text{ft}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(V) = (87{,}120)\left(\frac{1}{12}\right)$$

$$(V) = 7{,}260\\ \text{ft}^3$$

questions.question: A stream flowing 10 cfs with BOD of 2 mg/L receives a 2-cfs wastewater discharge with BOD of 250 mg/L. Assuming complete mixing, what is the BOD just below the outfall?
questions.explanation: Flow-weighted average: (10×2 + 2×250)/12 = 43.3 mg/L. Averaging the concentrations without flow-weighting gives 126 mg/L — not among the choices for a reason.
questions.solution:
The mass balance \(\frac{dM}{dt} = \frac{dM_{in}}{dt} - \frac{dM_{out}}{dt}\) is printed in Environmental Engineering (p.327). The steady complete-mix result below is derived from it:

The handbook (p. 327) prints the mass-balance equation in this exact form:

$$\frac{dM}{dt} = \frac{dM_{in}}{dt} - \frac{dM_{out}}{dt} \pm rV, \quad \frac{dM_{in}}{dt} = C_{in}Q_{in}$$

At steady state (\(dM/dt = 0\)) with a conservative substance (\(r = 0\)) and two inflows mixing completely, the handbook form collapses to the working complete-mix equation:

$$C_{mix} = \frac{Q_s C_s + Q_w C_w}{Q_s + Q_w}$$

Ultimately, we must solve for the completely mixed concentration:

$$C_{mix} = \frac{Q_s C_s + Q_w C_w}{Q_s + Q_w}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
Q_s &= 10\\ \text{cfs}, \quad C_s = 2\\ \text{mg/L} \\
Q_w &= 2\\ \text{cfs}, \quad C_w = 250\\ \text{mg/L}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(C_{mix}) = \frac{(10)(2) + (2)(250)}{10 + 2}$$

$$(C_{mix}) = \frac{520}{12}$$

$$(C_{mix}) = 43.3\\ \text{mg/L}$$

questions.question: A wastewater sample has a 5-day BOD of 200 mg/L with a deoxygenation rate k = 0.23/day (base e). What is the ultimate BOD?
questions.explanation: BOD5 = L(1 − e^−kt), so L = 200/(1 − e^−1.15) = 293 mg/L. BOD5 is always less than ultimate BOD — the 200 answer confuses the two.
questions.solution:
The BOD exertion equation is printed in Environmental Engineering (p.327):

The handbook (p. 327) prints the BOD exertion equation in this exact form:

$$BOD_t = L_o\left(1 - e^{-kt}\right)$$

Solving the handbook form for the ultimate BOD \(L_o\) gives the working equation:

$$(L) = \frac{BOD_t}{1 - e^{-kt}}$$

Ultimately, we must solve for the ultimate (carbonaceous) BOD. The handbook gives the BOD exerted at time t:

$$BOD_t = L(1 - e^{-kt})$$

Solving for L:

$$(L) = \frac{BOD_t}{1 - e^{-kt}}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
BOD_5 &= 200\\ \text{mg/L} \\
k &= 0.23\\ \text{/day}, \quad t = 5\\ \text{days}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(L) = \frac{200}{1 - e^{-(0.23)(5)}}$$

$$(L) = \frac{200}{1 - 0.3166}$$

$$(L) = \frac{200}{0.6834} = 293\\ \text{mg/L}$$

questions.question: After a wastewater discharge, the dissolved oxygen sag curve reaches its minimum (critical deficit) at the point where which condition holds?
questions.explanation: The sag minimum is where the falling limb flattens: oxygen consumed by BOD exactly balances oxygen absorbed from the atmosphere. Downstream of that point, reaeration wins and DO recovers.
questions.solution:
The Streeter-Phelps oxygen-sag equations, including tc (time of minimum dissolved oxygen), are printed in Environmental Engineering (p.327-328). The rate-equality condition below is derived from them (set \(dD/dt = 0\)), not printed in words:

The Streeter-Phelps oxygen sag is governed by two competing rates:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Deoxygenation} &\rightarrow \text{oxygen consumed by BOD} \\
\text{Reaeration} &\rightarrow \text{oxygen absorbed from air}
\end{aligned}$$

The dissolved oxygen deficit grows while deoxygenation outpaces reaeration, peaks, then shrinks. At the minimum DO point the deficit stops growing:

$$(\text{deoxygenation rate}) = (\text{reaeration rate}) \text{ at the critical deficit}$$

questions.question: Two machines produce 85 dB and 79 dB individually at a property line. What is their combined noise level?
questions.explanation: Decibels add logarithmically: 10·log(10^8.5 + 10^7.9) = 86.0 dB. Adding them arithmetically (164 dB) ignores the log scale entirely.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Noise Pollution section in the Safety chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must combine two sound levels on the logarithmic decibel scale:

$$L_{total} = 10\log_{10}(10^{L_1/10} + 10^{L_2/10})$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
L_1 &= 85\\ \text{dB} \\
L_2 &= 79\\ \text{dB}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(L_{total}) = 10\log_{10}(10^{8.5} + 10^{7.9})$$

$$(L_{total}) = 10\log_{10}(3.162 \times 10^8 + 7.943 \times 10^7)$$

$$(L_{total}) = 10(8.597) = 86.0\\ \text{dB}$$

questions.question: The National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) set limits for criteria pollutants. Which of the following is a criteria pollutant with a NAAQS?
questions.explanation: The six criteria pollutants are PM, ozone, CO, NO2, SO2, and lead. Methane, radon, and asbestos are regulated under other programs.
questions.solution:
The criteria-pollutant list is not printed in the FE Reference Handbook; this is background knowledge for the exam.

The Clean Air Act directs EPA to set NAAQS for criteria pollutants — widespread pollutants judged harmful to health and welfare:

$$\text{Criteria pollutants} = \\{PM, O_3, CO, NO_2, SO_2, Pb\\}$$

Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is one of the six, with both annual and 24-hour standards. Methane is a greenhouse gas, radon is handled under indoor-air guidance, and asbestos under NESHAP — none carries a NAAQS.

questions.question: What is the EPA maximum contaminant level (MCL) for nitrate in drinking water, expressed as nitrogen?
questions.explanation: The nitrate MCL is 10 mg/L as N (about 44.3 mg/L as NO3, often rounded to 45). It protects infants against methemoglobinemia (blue-baby syndrome).
questions.solution:
The nitrate MCL is not printed in the FE Reference Handbook; this is background knowledge for the exam.

Under the Safe Drinking Water Act, EPA sets maximum contaminant levels for public water systems:

$$(MCL_{nitrate}) = 10\\ \text{mg/L as N}$$

Nitrate above this level risks methemoglobinemia in infants, so it is one of the primary standards every community system must meet. Expressed as nitrate ion rather than nitrogen, the same limit is 10 × (62.0 / 14.0) ≈ 44.3 mg/L as NO3, often rounded to 45.

questions.question: A rectangular sedimentation basin is 80 ft by 40 ft and treats 2 MGD. What is the surface overflow rate?
questions.explanation: SOR = Q/A = 2,000,000/3,200 = 625 gpd/ft². Typical design values run 500–1,000 gpd/ft², so this basin is reasonably sized.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Clarifier section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the surface overflow rate, the key sedimentation design parameter:

$$SOR = \frac{Q}{A}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
Q &= 2\\ \text{MGD} = 2{,}000{,}000\\ \text{gpd} \\
A &= (80)(40) = 3{,}200\\ \text{ft}^2
\end{aligned}$$

$$(SOR) = \frac{2{,}000{,}000}{3{,}200}$$

$$(SOR) = 625\\ \text{gpd/ft}^2$$

questions.question: In drinking water treatment, coagulants such as alum are added primarily to accomplish which of the following?
choices: Destabilize colloidal particles so they can be removed
Soften the water by removing hardness
questions.explanation: Colloids carry like charges that keep them suspended; coagulant neutralizes the charge so particles agglomerate into settleable floc. Disinfection and softening are separate unit processes.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Clarifier section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Conventional treatment follows a fixed sequence:

$$\text{Coagulation} \rightarrow \text{flocculation} \rightarrow \text{sedimentation} \rightarrow \text{filtration} \rightarrow \text{disinfection}$$

Colloidal turbidity particles repel each other electrostatically and will never settle on their own. Coagulant neutralizes that charge:

$$(\text{coagulant}) \rightarrow \text{charge neutralization} \rightarrow \text{floc formation} \rightarrow \text{settling}$$

questions.question: A clearwell provides 30 minutes of contact time at a free chlorine residual of 2 mg/L. What is the CT value?
questions.explanation: CT = concentration × time = 2 × 30 = 60 mg·min/L. Disinfection credit is awarded on this product, not on either factor alone.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Clarifier section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must compute the disinfection CT, the regulatory basis for pathogen inactivation credit:

$$CT = (C)(T)$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
C &= 2\\ \text{mg/L} \\
T &= 30\\ \text{min}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(CT) = (2)(30)$$

$$(CT) = 60\\ \text{mg}\cdot\text{min/L}$$

questions.question: A direct shear test on a sand gives c = 200 psf and φ = 25°. What is the shear strength at a normal stress of 1,000 psf?
questions.explanation: τ = c + σ·tanφ = 200 + 1,000(0.466) = 666 psf. Dropping the cohesion term gives 466 psf.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (Mohr-Coulomb failure, printed pages 268-269):

Ultimately, we must apply the Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion:

$$\tau = c + \sigma\tan\phi$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
c &= 200\\ \text{psf} \\
\phi &= 25^{\circ} \\
\sigma &= 1{,}000\\ \text{psf}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\tau) = 200 + (1{,}000)\tan(25^{\circ})$$

$$(\tau) = 200 + (1{,}000)(0.4663)$$

$$(\tau) = 666\\ \text{psf}$$

questions.question: An unconfined compression test on a saturated clay gives qu = 1,800 psf. What is the undrained shear strength (cohesion)?
questions.explanation: For φ = 0, the Mohr circle passes through the origin and qu, so su = c = qu/2 = 900 psf.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (Mohr-Coulomb failure, printed pages 268-269):

In an unconfined compression test the confining stress is zero and a saturated clay behaves with \(\phi = 0\). The Mohr circle then has diameter qu:

$$s_u = c = \frac{q_u}{2}$$

$$(s_u) = \frac{1{,}800}{2}$$

$$(s_u) = 900\\ \text{psf}$$

questions.question: A consolidated-drained triaxial test is run at confining stress 100 kPa on a soil with c = 20 kPa and φ = 30°. What is the major principal stress at failure?
questions.explanation: σ1 = σ3·tan²(45+φ/2) + 2c·tan(45+φ/2) = 100(3) + 40(1.732) = 370 kPa. The 300 kPa answer drops the cohesion term.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (Mohr-Coulomb failure, printed pages 268-269):

The handbook prints the Mohr-Coulomb criterion \(\tau_F = c + \sigma_N\tan\phi\) and the Rankine factor \(\tan^2(45^\circ + \phi/2)\), but not the principal-stress form below. This form is derived from them (derived relation, not printed). Ultimately, we must solve for the major principal stress at failure:

$$\sigma_1 = \sigma_3\tan^2\left(45 + \frac{\phi}{2}\right) + 2c\tan\left(45 + \frac{\phi}{2}\right)$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\sigma_3 &= 100\\ \text{kPa} \\
c &= 20\\ \text{kPa}, \quad \phi = 30^{\circ} \\
\tan(60^{\circ}) &= 1.732
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma_1) = (100)(1.732)^2 + (2)(20)(1.732)$$

$$(\sigma_1) = 300 + 69.3$$

$$(\sigma_1) = 370\\ \text{kPa}$$
questions.videoTitle: Use of Mohr's Circle in Geotechnical Engineering | Shear Strength of Soil

questions.question: A dry infinite slope of cohesionless soil has φ = 30° and a slope angle of 20°. What is the factor of safety against sliding?
questions.explanation: FS = tanφ/tanβ = 0.577/0.364 = 1.59. Inverting the ratio gives 0.63 — always check that FS > 1 for a standing slope.
questions.solution:
The planar slope-failure factor of safety \(FS = T_{FF}/T_{MOB}\), with \(T_{FF} = cL_S + W_M\cos\alpha_S\tan\phi\) and \(T_{MOB} = W_M\sin\alpha_S\), is printed (Civil Engineering, p.271). For \(c = 0\) the infinite-slope result below follows:

Ultimately, we must solve for the factor of safety of a dry infinite slope in cohesionless soil:

$$FS = \frac{\tan\phi}{\tan\beta}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\phi &= 30^{\circ} \\
\beta &= 20^{\circ}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(FS) = \frac{\tan(30^{\circ})}{\tan(20^{\circ})}$$

$$(FS) = \frac{0.5774}{0.3640}$$

$$(FS) = 1.59$$

questions.question: The same slope (φ = 30°, β = 20°) now has seepage parallel to the surface. If \(\gamma_{sat} = 125\ \text{pcf}\), what is the factor of safety?
questions.explanation: Seepage cuts FS by \(\gamma'/\gamma_{sat}\): (62.6/125)(1.59) = 0.79. The slope that was stable dry now fails — the classic seepage lesson.
questions.solution:
The dry planar-slope formula is printed (Civil Engineering, p.271), but the seepage-parallel-to-slope factor below is not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6; it is the standard infinite-slope result derived with effective stress:

Ultimately, we must correct the infinite-slope factor of safety for seepage parallel to the surface:

$$FS = \left(\frac{\gamma'}{\gamma_{sat}}\right)\frac{\tan\phi}{\tan\beta}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\gamma_{sat} &= 125\\ \text{pcf} \\
\gamma' &= 125 - 62.4 = 62.6\\ \text{pcf} \\
\frac{\tan(30^{\circ})}{\tan(20^{\circ})} &= 1.586
\end{aligned}$$

$$(FS) = \left(\frac{62.6}{125}\right)(1.586)$$

$$(FS) = (0.5008)(1.586)$$

$$(FS) = 0.79$$

questions.question: The ordinary method of slices (Fellenius) for slope stability analysis is based on which key assumption?
choices: Circular slip surface with interslice forces neglected
Planar slip surface with full interslice equilibrium
Log-spiral slip surface with seepage ignored
questions.explanation: Fellenius slices a circular slip mass and neglects interslice forces — simple and conservative. Bishop's simplified method keeps the circular surface but satisfies moment equilibrium including interslice normals.
questions.solution:
Not located in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (searched text and index); the method assumptions are standard geotechnical practice (only the planar failure surface is printed, Civil Engineering p.271):

Limit-equilibrium slope methods differ in their assumptions:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Ordinary (Fellenius)} &\rightarrow \text{circular surface, interslice forces neglected} \\
\text{Bishop simplified} &\rightarrow \text{circular surface, moment equilibrium with interslice normals}
\end{aligned}$$

Neglecting the interslice forces makes Fellenius statically determinate and quick to compute, at the cost of a somewhat conservative (lower) factor of safety.

questions.explanation: Magnitude is the 3D Pythagorean theorem. The traps: 11 adds the components, 49 forgets the square root, √13 drops a component.
questions.question: What is the magnitude of vector \(\mathbf{a} = (2, 3, 6)\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vectors section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(|\mathbf{a}|\). The handbook gives the length of a vector:

$$|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{a_x^2 + a_y^2 + a_z^2}$$

$$|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{2^2 + 3^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = \sqrt{49} = 7$$
questions.tiTip: Yes — vector menu: magnitude. Or punch in √(x² + y² + z²) directly.

questions.explanation: A unit vector keeps the direction and scales the length to 1: divide every component by the magnitude. (2,3,6) forgot the division; (1/2,1/3,1/6) took reciprocals; the /11 one divided by the component sum instead of the magnitude.
questions.question: What is the unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf{a} = (2, 3, 6)\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vectors section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The handbook (p. 60) prints the direction cosines of a vector in this exact form:

$$\cos\alpha = \frac{a_x}{|\mathbf{A}|}, \qquad \cos\beta = \frac{a_y}{|\mathbf{A}|}, \qquad \cos\gamma = \frac{a_z}{|\mathbf{A}|}$$

with \(\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1\). These are exactly the components of a unit vector in \(\mathbf{A}\)'s direction, so assembling them gives the working equation:

$$\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{a}|}$$

Ultimately, we must solve for the unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\). Divide each component by the vector's length:

$$\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{a}|}, \qquad |\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7$$

$$\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \left(\frac{2}{7}, \frac{3}{7}, \frac{6}{7}\right)$$
questions.tiTip: Yes — vector menu: get the magnitude, then divide each component by it.

questions.explanation: The dot product ties directly to the angle: a·b = |a||b|cos θ. 90° is the 'perpendicular guess' trap; 30°/60° are the other familiar angles.
questions.question: What is the angle between vectors \(\mathbf{a} = (1, 1, 0)\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (1, 0, 0)\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vectors section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The handbook (p. 61) prints the dot product in this exact form:

$$\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B} = a_xb_x + a_yb_y + a_zb_z = |\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}|\cos\theta = \mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{A}$$

Dividing both sides of the \(|\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}|\cos\theta\) equality by \(|\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}|\) isolates \(\cos\theta\), giving the working equation:

$$\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|}$$

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\theta\). The handbook gives the dot product as \(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = |\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\), so:

$$\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} \times 1}$$

$$\theta = \cos^{-1}(0.707) = 45^\circ$$
questions.tiTip: Yes — vector menu for the dot product and both magnitudes, then θ = cos⁻¹(a·b / (|a||b|)). Check degree mode.

questions.explanation: Projection = (scalar projection) × (unit vector along b) = ((a·b)/|b|²)b. (4,4,0) forgot to divide by |b|²; (1,1,0) is just the direction of b; (4,0,0) is a itself.
questions.question: What is the vector projection of \(\mathbf{a} = (4, 0, 0)\) onto \(\mathbf{b} = (1, 1, 0)\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vectors section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The handbook (p. 61) states that the dot product is a scalar product representing the projection of \(\mathbf{B}\) onto \(\mathbf{A}\) times \(|\mathbf{A}|\), and prints it in this exact form:

$$\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B} = a_xb_x + a_yb_y + a_zb_z = |\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}|\cos\theta$$

From this, the scalar projection of \(\mathbf{a}\) onto \(\mathbf{b}\) is \(|\mathbf{a}|\cos\theta = (\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})/|\mathbf{b}|\); multiplying by the unit vector \(\mathbf{b}/|\mathbf{b}|\) in \(\mathbf{b}\)'s direction gives the working equation:

$$\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{b}|^2}\,\mathbf{b}$$

Ultimately, we must solve for the projection of \(\mathbf{a}\) onto \(\mathbf{b}\). The handbook notes the dot product represents the projection of one vector onto another; scaling the vector \(\mathbf{b}\):

$$\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{b}|^2}\,\mathbf{b}$$

$$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 4, \qquad |\mathbf{b}|^2 = 2$$

$$\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{a} = \frac{4}{2}(1, 1, 0) = (2, 2, 0)$$
questions.tiTip: Mostly by hand — get the dot product and |b|² from the vector menu, then multiply. Formula: ((a·b)/|b|²)b.

questions.explanation: Area = |a × b| = |a||b|sin θ. Half of it (3) is the triangle area — the classic trap. 2√10 is |a||b| with sin θ forgotten.
questions.question: Vectors \(\mathbf{a} = (2, 0, 0)\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (1, 3, 0)\) form adjacent sides of a parallelogram. What is its area?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vectors section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The handbook (p. 61) prints the cross product magnitude relation in this exact form:

$$\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B} = |\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}|\mathbf{n}\sin\theta$$

where \(\mathbf{n}\) is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane of \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\). Since \(|\mathbf{n}| = 1\), taking magnitudes gives \(|\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B}| = |\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}|\sin\theta\) — the base-times-height area of the parallelogram — which is the working equation:

$$\text{Area} = |\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|$$

Ultimately, we must solve for the parallelogram area. The handbook gives the cross product a magnitude of \(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\), which is exactly the parallelogram area:

$$\text{Area} = |\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|$$

$$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = (0, 0, 6)$$

$$\text{Area} = \sqrt{0^2 + 0^2 + 6^2} = 6$$
questions.tiTip: Yes — vector menu: cross product, then magnitude. (Area = |a × b|.)

questions.explanation: Scale first, then add or subtract component by component. (8,2,5) added b instead of subtracting; (1,−5,1) is a−b without the 2; watch every sign.
questions.question: For vectors \(\mathbf{a} = (3, -1, 2)\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (2, 4, 1)\), what is \(2\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vectors section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(2\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}\). The handbook gives scalar multiplication and addition component-wise:

$$2\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b} = 2(3, -1, 2) - (2, 4, 1) = (6, -2, 4) - (2, 4, 1) = (4, -6, 3)$$
questions.tiTip: Yes — the vector menu handles scalar multiples and addition/subtraction directly.

questions.explanation: By symmetry the peak is at midspan: add the uniform-load term wL²/8 and the point-load term PL/4. The traps: 48 kN·m drops the point load, 136 kN·m uses wL²/4 for the uniform part, 128 kN·m uses PL/2 for the point load. Handbook table: also solvable with the Simply Supported Beam Slopes and Deflections table in the Mechanics of Materials chapter — superpose the two tabulated cases for full-span uniform load and center point load (wL²/8 + PL/4) to get the maximum moment.
questions.question: A simply supported floor beam spans 8 m. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 6 kN/m over its full length, plus a concentrated load of 20 kN at midspan from a partition wall. What is the maximum bending moment in the beam?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Simply Supported Beam tables in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(M_{max}\). By symmetry each reaction is:

$$R = \frac{wL}{2} + \frac{P}{2} = \frac{(6)(8)}{2} + \frac{20}{2} = 24 + 10 = 34\text{ kN}$$

The bending moment peaks at midspan, where the shear is zero:

$$M_{max} = R\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) - w\frac{(L/2)^2}{2} = (34)(4) - \frac{(6)(4)^2}{2}$$

$$M_{max} = 136 - 48 = 88\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}$$

Equivalently, superpose the two standard cases: \(M_{max} = wL^2/8 + PL/4 = 48 + 40 = 88\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}\).
questions.tiTip: No — set up wL²/8 + PL/4 by hand; the calculator only crunches the arithmetic.

questions.explanation: Shear is constant at P along the whole cantilever. The 36 kN trap is the maximum moment PL, not shear — watch the units.
questions.question: A cantilever balcony beam extends 3 m from its fixed support and carries a 12 kN planter load at its free tip. What is the maximum shear force in the beam?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Cantilever Beam tables in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(V_{max}\). With only a tip load \(P\), the shear is constant along the entire cantilever:

$$V(x) = P = 12\text{ kN} \quad \text{everywhere}$$

so \(V_{max} = 12\text{ kN}\). (The maximum bending moment is \(PL = (12)(3) = 36\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}\) at the fixed support — that is the 36 kN trap.)
questions.tiTip: No — the shear is just P here; use the calculator only to double-check PL for the moment.

questions.question: A simply supported warehouse beam spans 10 m and carries a uniformly distributed storage load of 5 kN/m over its full length. What is the maximum bending moment, and where does it occur?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Simply Supported Beam tables in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(M_{max}\) and its location. For a uniform load the shear diagram is linear, crossing zero at midspan — that is where the parabolic moment diagram peaks:

$$M_{max} = \frac{wL^2}{8} = \frac{(5)(10)^2}{8} = \frac{500}{8} = 62.5\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}$$

at \(x = L/2 = 5\text{ m}\), i.e., at midspan. (At the simple supports the moment is zero and the shear is maximum.)

questions.question: Three tugboat cables pull on a mooring bollard: 100 N due east, 80 N due north, and 60 N due west. What is the magnitude and direction of the single resultant force?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Resultant (Two Dimensions) section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(R\) and \(\theta\). Sum components (east and north positive):

$$R_x = \sum F_x = 100 - 60 = 40\text{ N} \qquad R_y = \sum F_y = 80\text{ N}$$

$$R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2} = \sqrt{40^2 + 80^2} = \sqrt{8{,}000} = 89.4\text{ N}$$

$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{R_y}{R_x}\right) = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{80}{40}\right) = 63.4^\circ$$

north of east.

choices: 600 N →, 3 m above the original line of action
200 N →, 0.33 m above the original line of action

questions.explanation: A couple shifts the line of action without changing the force: d = M/R. The side matters — below the line would give a counterclockwise moment, the wrong sense. 0.33 m inverts the division.
questions.question: A 200 N horizontal push acts on a shipping crate. Uneven loading adds a 600 N·m clockwise couple. What single force is equivalent to this force-couple system, and where must its line of action lie?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Moments (Couples) section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The handbook (p. 95) prints the moment equation in this exact form:

$$\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}$$

A single equivalent force \(R\) reproduces the force-couple system only if its moment about the original line of action equals the couple's moment, i.e. \(R\,d = M\); solving for the offset gives the working equation:

$$d = \frac{M}{R}$$

Ultimately, we must solve for the equivalent force and its offset \(d\). A couple does not change the force resultant, so:

$$R = 200\text{ N (horizontal) }$$

Shift its line of action a perpendicular distance \(d\) so its moment about the original line equals the couple:

$$d = \frac{M}{R} = \frac{600}{200} = 3\text{ m}$$

The offset must reproduce the clockwise sense: for a rightward force, the line of action lies 3 m above the original line (a force below would give a counterclockwise moment).

questions.question: A planar roof truss has 7 joints, 11 members, and 3 reaction components. Using the stability and determinacy check, how is this truss classified?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stability, Determinacy, and Classification of Structures section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must classify the truss. For a plane truss the handbook gives:

$$m + r < 2j \;\rightarrow\; \text{unstable} \qquad m + r = 2j \;\rightarrow\; \text{stable and statically determinate} \qquad m + r > 2j \;\rightarrow\; \text{stable and statically indeterminate}$$

Here \(m + r = 11 + 3 = 14\) and \(2j = 2(7) = 14\). Since \(m + r = 2j\), the truss is stable and statically determinate.

questions.explanation: Count reaction components, not supports: fixed = 3, roller = 1. 3m + r exceeds 3j + c by exactly one, so indeterminate to the first degree — not the second.
questions.question: A planar beam is fixed at support A and roller-supported at support B, with no internal hinges. Using the stability and determinacy check for a plane frame, how is this beam classified?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stability, Determinacy, and Classification of Structures section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must classify the beam. Treat it as a plane frame with \(m = 1\) member and \(j = 2\) joints. Reaction components: fixed support \(A = 3\), roller \(B = 1\), so \(r = 4\); no internal hinges, so \(c = 0\). The handbook gives:

$$3m + r = 3(1) + 4 = 7 \qquad 3j + c = 3(2) + 0 = 6$$

Since \(3m + r > 3j + c\) by exactly one, the beam (a propped cantilever) is stable and statically indeterminate to the first degree.

questions.explanation: Convert the manometer reading to head of the flowing fluid first: Δh = hm(SGm − 1). The traps: 138.9 L/s skips the (1 − β⁴) area correction, 149.0 L/s forgets the −1, 40.4 L/s uses the mercury head as if it were water head.
questions.question: A horizontal venturi meter is installed in a 30 cm water main. The throat diameter is 15 cm. A mercury manometer (specific gravity 13.6) connected between the inlet and the throat shows a 25 cm difference in the mercury columns. Assuming a discharge coefficient Cv = 1.0, what is most nearly the volumetric flow rate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Venturi Meters section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The handbook (p. 200) prints the venturi-meter equation in this exact form:

$$Q = \frac{C_v A_2}{\sqrt{1 - (A_2/A_1)^2}}\sqrt{2g\left(\frac{P_1}{\gamma} + z_1 - \frac{P_2}{\gamma} - z_2\right)}$$

For a horizontal meter \(z_1 = z_2\), so the bracket is the head difference \(\Delta h\) of the flowing fluid (converted from the manometer reading as \(\Delta h = h_m(SG_m - 1)\)), and \((A_2/A_1)^2 = (D_2/D_1)^4\), giving the working equation:

$$Q = C_v A_2\sqrt{\frac{2g\,\Delta h}{1 - (D_2/D_1)^4}}$$

Ultimately, we must solve for \(Q\). First convert the manometer reading to head of the flowing fluid (water):

$$\Delta h = h_m(SG_m - 1) = (0.25)(13.6 - 1) = 3.15\text{ m of water}$$

The venturi equation (horizontal, so \(z_1 = z_2\)):

$$Q = C_v A_2\sqrt{\frac{2g\,\Delta h}{1 - (D_2/D_1)^4}}$$

$$A_2 = \frac{\pi}{4}(0.15)^2 = 0.01767\text{ m}^2, \qquad \left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right)^4 = \left(\frac{15}{30}\right)^4 = 0.0625$$

$$Q = (1.0)(0.01767)\sqrt{\frac{2(9.81)(3.15)}{1 - 0.0625}} = (0.01767)\sqrt{65.92} = 0.1435\text{ m}^3\!/\!\text{s}$$

$$Q = 143.5\text{ L/s}$$

questions.question: A pitot tube in a water pipeline measures a stagnation pressure 12 kPa above the local static pressure. What is most nearly the flow velocity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Pitot Tubes section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6, p. 200).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(v\). From the stagnation pressure equation for an incompressible fluid:

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{2(P_0 - P_s)}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(12{,}000)}{1000}} = \sqrt{24} = 4.90\text{ m/s}$$

questions.question: A uniform slender rod has a mass of 8 kg and a length of 1.5 m. It is pinned at one end and swings as a pendulum. What is its mass moment of inertia about the pin?

Refer to the Mass Moment of Inertia table in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$I = \frac{1}{3}mL^2 = \frac{1}{3}(8)(1.5)^2 = \frac{1}{3}(8)(2.25) = 6.0\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$$

questions.question:
A geotechnical report includes this excerpt from a Terzaghi bearing capacity factor table:

φ = 30°: Nc = 37.2, Nq = 22.5, Nγ = 19.7
(The table also lists Nq = 2.7 for φ = 10°.)

For a footing bearing on soil with an internal friction angle of 30°, what is the bearing capacity factor Nq?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Ultimate Bearing Capacity section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6). where \(N_q\) is defined as the bearing capacity factor for depth (it multiplies the overburden term \(\gamma' D_f\) in \(q_{ULT} = cN_c + \gamma' D_f N_q + \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma' B N_\gamma\)).

Ultimately, we must read \(N_q\) for \(\phi = 30^\circ\). From the \(N_q\) column at the \(\phi = 30^\circ\) row:

$$N_q = 22.5$$

questions.explanation: Allowable = ultimate divided by FS. The 2,490 kPa trap multiplies by the factor of safety instead — FS always reduces the capacity. This is the pressure permitted by the bearing safety factor alone; settlement or other limits can govern the design.
questions.question: A strip footing analysis gives an ultimate bearing capacity of 830 kPa. The design requires a factor of safety of 3.0 against bearing failure. What is the allowable bearing capacity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Ultimate Bearing Capacity and Retaining Walls blocks in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (printed p.270). The handbook prints \(q_{ULT}\) and the bearing factor of safety \(FS = q_{ULT}/q_{toe}\); the allowable pressure below is that definition rearranged (the form \(q_{allow} = q_{ULT}/FS\) is not printed).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(q_{allow}\). The allowable capacity is the ultimate capacity divided by the factor of safety:

$$q_{allow} = \frac{q_{ULT}}{FS} = \frac{830}{3.0} = 276.7 = 277\text{ kPa}$$

questions.explanation: With continuous bracing only yielding governs, so \(M_n = F_y Z_x\), and LRFD applies \(\phi_b = 0.90\). Skipping \(\phi_b\) gives 541.7 kip-ft, and leaving the answer in kip-in gives 5,850.
questions.question: A compact doubly symmetric W-shape (\(F_y\) = 50 ksi, \(Z_x\) = 130 \(\text{in}^3\)) is braced continuously against lateral-torsional buckling and bent about its major axis. Using LRFD, what is the design flexural strength \(\phi_b M_n\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\phi_b M_n\). With continuous lateral bracing, lateral-torsional buckling does not apply, so the handbook gives yielding as the limit state:

$$M_n = M_p = F_y Z_x, \qquad \phi_b = 0.90$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
F_y &= 50\ \text{ksi} \\
Z_x &= 130\ \text{in}^3 \\
\phi_b &= 0.90 \\
\phi_b M_n &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(\phi_b M_n) &= 0.90(50)(130) \\
&= 5{,}850\ \text{kip-in} \\
&\rightarrow \frac{5{,}850}{12} \\
&= 487.5\ \text{kip-ft}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Because \(L_p < L_b \le L_r\), the strength is reduced below \(M_p\) by the linear LTB equation. Using \(\phi_b M_p\) alone (375.0 kip-ft) ignores the unbraced length, and stopping before \(\phi_b\) gives 360.6 kip-ft.
questions.question: A compact doubly symmetric W-shape (\(F_y\) = 50 ksi, \(Z_x\) = 100 \(\text{in}^3\), \(S_x\) = 90 \(\text{in}^3\)) has \(L_p\) = 6 ft and \(L_r\) = 17 ft. It is bent about its major axis with an unbraced length \(L_b\) = 10 ft and \(C_b\) = 1.0. Using LRFD, what is the design flexural strength \(\phi_b M_n\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\phi_b M_n\). Since \(L_p < L_b \le L_r\), the handbook gives the inelastic lateral-torsional buckling equation:

$$\begin{aligned}
M_n = C_b\Bigl[M_p &- (M_p - 0.7 F_y S_x) \\
&\times\left(\frac{L_b - L_p}{L_r - L_p}\right)\Bigr] \\
M_n &\le M_p
\end{aligned}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
M_p &= F_y Z_x = (50)(100) \\
&= 5{,}000\ \text{kip-in} \\
&= 416.7\ \text{kip-ft} \\
0.7 F_y S_x &= 0.7(50)(90) \\
&= 3{,}150\ \text{kip-in} \\
&= 262.5\ \text{kip-ft} \\
\frac{L_b - L_p}{L_r - L_p} &= \frac{10 - 6}{17 - 6} = 0.364 \\
M_n &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(M_n) &= (1.0)\left[416.7 - (154.2)(0.364)\right] \\
&= 416.7 - 56.1 \\
&= 360.6\ \text{kip-ft} \le M_p
\end{aligned}$$

$$\phi_b M_n = 0.90(360.6) = 324.5\ \text{kip-ft}$$

questions.explanation: Substituting the four moments into the handbook \(C_b\) equation gives 1.14, the same value the handbook table lists for a uniformly loaded, unbraced simple span. \(C_b = 1.00\) is the uniform-moment case and 1.32 is the midspan point-load value.
questions.question: In an unbraced segment of a simply supported steel beam, the absolute moments are \(M_{max}\) = 120 kip-ft, \(M_A\) = 90 kip-ft at the quarter point, \(M_B\) = 120 kip-ft at the centerline, and \(M_C\) = 90 kip-ft at the three-quarter point. What is the lateral-torsional buckling modification factor \(C_b\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(C_b\). The handbook prints:

$$C_b = \frac{12.5 M_{max}}{2.5 M_{max} + 3 M_A + 4 M_B + 3 M_C}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
M_{max} &= 120\ \text{kip-ft} \\
M_A &= 90\ \text{kip-ft} \\
M_B &= 120\ \text{kip-ft} \\
M_C &= 90\ \text{kip-ft} \\
C_b &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(C_b) &= \frac{12.5(120)}{300 + 270 + 480 + 270} \\
&= \frac{1{,}500}{1{,}320} \\
&= 1.14
\end{aligned}$$

questions.question: A rolled W-shape has an overall depth d = 21.0 in. and a web thickness \(t_w\) = 0.40 in. The steel has \(F_y\) = 50 ksi. Using LRFD, what is the design shear strength \(\phi_v V_n\)?

Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\phi_v V_n\). The handbook gives, for webs of rolled I-shaped members:

V_n = 0.6 F_y A_w C_{v1} \\
A_w = d\,t_w \\
C_{v1} = 1.0 \\
\phi_v = 1.00

A_w &= (21.0)(0.40) = 8.40\ \text{in}^2 \\

questions.question: A steel column (\(F_y\) = 50 ksi, \(A_g\) = 14.4 \(\text{in}^2\)) has KL/r = 80. Using LRFD, what is the design compressive strength \(\phi_c P_n\) for flexural buckling? (E = 29,000 ksi; no slender elements.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\phi_c P_n\). First compare the slenderness with the handbook limit:

$$\begin{aligned}
4.71\sqrt{\frac{E}{F_y}} &= 4.71\sqrt{\frac{29{,}000}{50}} \\
&= 113.4
\end{aligned}$$

Since \(KL/r = 80 \le 113.4\), the handbook gives:

$$\begin{gathered}
F_e = \frac{\pi^2 E}{(KL/r)^2} \\
F_{cr} = \left[0.658^{F_y/F_e}\right]F_y \\
P_n = F_{cr} A_g \\
\phi_c = 0.90
\end{gathered}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
F_e &= \frac{\pi^2 (29{,}000)}{(80)^2} = 44.72\ \text{ksi} \\
F_{cr} &= 0.658^{50/44.72}(50) = 31.3\ \text{ksi} \\
A_g &= 14.4\ \text{in}^2 \\
\phi_c P_n &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(\phi_c P_n) &= 0.90(31.3)(14.4) \\
&= 406\ \text{kip}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: \(KL/r = 140\) exceeds \(4.71\sqrt{E/F_y} = 113\), so elastic buckling governs with \(F_{cr} = 0.877 F_e\). Using the inelastic equation gives 123 kip, omitting \(\phi\) gives 147 kip, and using \(F_e\) without the 0.877 factor gives 151 kip.
questions.question: A steel column (\(F_y\) = 50 ksi, \(A_g\) = 11.5 \(\text{in}^2\)) has KL/r = 140. Using LRFD, what is the design compressive strength \(\phi_c P_n\) for flexural buckling? (E = 29,000 ksi; no slender elements.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\phi_c P_n\). The handbook slenderness limit is:

$$\begin{aligned}
4.71\sqrt{\frac{E}{F_y}} &= 4.71\sqrt{\frac{29{,}000}{50}} \\
&= 113.4
\end{aligned}$$

Since \(KL/r = 140 > 113.4\), the handbook gives:

$$\begin{gathered}
F_e = \frac{\pi^2 E}{(KL/r)^2} \\
F_{cr} = 0.877 F_e \\
P_n = F_{cr} A_g \\
\phi_c = 0.90
\end{gathered}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
F_e &= \frac{\pi^2 (29{,}000)}{(140)^2} = 14.60\ \text{ksi} \\
F_{cr} &= 0.877(14.60) = 12.81\ \text{ksi} \\
A_g &= 11.5\ \text{in}^2 \\
\phi_c P_n &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(\phi_c P_n) &= 0.90(12.81)(11.5) \\
&= 133\ \text{kip}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The tied-column maximum includes the 0.80 factor and \(\phi = 0.65\) (compression-controlled, tied). Dropping the 0.80 gives 798 kip, stopping before \(\phi\) gives 982 kip, and using \(\phi = 0.90\) gives 884 kip.
questions.question: A 16 in. x 16 in. tied short column is reinforced with eight #8 bars (\(A_{st}\) = 6.32 \(\text{in}^2\)). The concrete has \(f'_c\) = 4 ksi and the bars have \(f_y\) = 60 ksi. Under pure axial load, what is the design axial strength \(\phi P_n\) (maximum permitted by the handbook for a tied column)? Use ACI 318-14.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\phi P_n\). First check the longitudinal steel limits:

$$\begin{aligned}
\rho_g &= \frac{A_{st}}{A_g} \\
&= \frac{6.32}{256} \\
&= 2.47\%\ \text{(within 1\% to 8\%)}
\end{aligned}$$

The handbook prints for tied columns:

$$\begin{gathered}
P_n = 0.80\left[0.85 f'_c (A_g - A_{st}) + A_{st} f_y\right] \\
\phi = 0.65
\end{gathered}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
A_g &= 16 \times 16 = 256\ \text{in}^2 \\
A_{st} &= 6.32\ \text{in}^2 \\
f'_c &= 4\ \text{ksi}, \quad f_y = 60\ \text{ksi} \\
\phi P_n &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(P_n) &= 0.80\Bigl[0.85(4)(256 - 6.32) \\
&\qquad + (6.32)(60)\Bigr] \\
&= 0.80[849.0 + 379.2] \\
&= 982\ \text{kip}
\end{aligned}$$

$$\phi P_n = 0.65(982) = 639\ \text{kip}$$

questions.explanation: The net tensile strain (0.0094) is above 0.005, so the section is tension-controlled and \(\phi = 0.90\). Using \(\phi = 0.65\) (compression-controlled) gives 188.1 kip-ft, stopping at \(M_n\) gives 289.4 kip-ft, and using the full \(a\) instead of \(a/2\) in the lever arm gives 230.7 kip-ft.
questions.question: A singly reinforced rectangular beam has b = 12 in., d = \(d_t\) = 21.5 in., \(A_s\) = 3.00 \(\text{in}^2\) (three #9 bars), \(f'_c\) = 4,000 psi, and \(f_y\) = 60,000 psi. What is the design flexural strength \(\phi M_n\)? Use ACI 318-14.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\phi M_n\). Find the stress block depth, nominal moment, and then check the net tensile strain to pick phi:

$$\begin{gathered}
a = \frac{A_s f_y}{0.85 f'_c b} \\
M_n = A_s f_y\left(d - \frac{a}{2}\right) \\
\varepsilon_t = \frac{0.003(d_t - c)}{c} \\
c = \frac{a}{\beta_1}
\end{gathered}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
a &= \frac{(3.00)(60)}{0.85(4)(12)} \\
&= 4.412\ \text{in} \\
\beta_1 &= 0.85\ (f'_c = 4{,}000\ \text{psi}) \\
c &= \frac{4.412}{0.85} = 5.19\ \text{in} \\
\varepsilon_t &= \frac{0.003(21.5 - 5.19)}{5.19} \\
&= 0.0094 \ge 0.005 \\
&\Rightarrow \phi = 0.90 \\
\phi M_n &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(M_n) &= (3.00)(60)\left(21.5 - \frac{4.412}{2}\right) \\
&= 3473\ \text{kip-in}
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\phi M_n &= 0.90(3473) \\
&= 3126\ \text{kip-in} \\
&= 260.5\ \text{kip-ft}
\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: RC beam design flexural strength with strain check

questions.explanation: Strength alone requires \(s = 14.6\) in., but because \(V_s\) is below \(4 b_w d\sqrt{f'_c}\) the maximum permitted spacing is the smaller of \(d/2 = 11\) in. and 24 in., so 11 in. controls. Choosing 14.5 in. satisfies strength but violates the maximum spacing.
questions.question: A normal-weight concrete beam has \(b_w\) = 12 in., d = 22 in., \(f'_c\) = 4,000 psi, and #3 U-stirrups (\(A_v\) = 0.22 \(\text{in}^2\), two legs) with \(f_y\) = 60,000 psi. The factored shear at the critical section is \(V_u\) = 40.0 kip. What stirrup spacing should be used? Use ACI 318-14.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(s\). Compute the concrete shear strength and compare with the factored shear:

$$\begin{gathered}
\begin{aligned}
V_c &= 2\lambda\sqrt{f'_c}\,b_w d \\
&= 2(1.0)\sqrt{4000}(12)(22) \\
&= 33.4\ \text{kip}
\end{aligned} \\
\phi V_c = 0.75(33.4) = 25.0\ \text{kip}
\end{gathered}$$

Since \(V_u = 40.0 > \phi V_c\), use the right-hand column of the handbook table:

$$\begin{gathered}
V_s = \frac{V_u}{\phi} - V_c \\
s = \frac{A_v f_y d}{V_s}
\end{gathered}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
V_s &= \frac{40.0}{0.75} - 33.4 = 19.9\ \text{kip} \\
4 b_w d\sqrt{f'_c} &= 66.8\ \text{kip} \\
&> V_s \\
s_{required} &= \frac{(0.22)(60)(22)}{19.94} \\
&= 14.6\ \text{in} \\
s_{max} &= \min\left(\frac{d}{2}, 24\right) \\
&= \min(11, 24) = 11\ \text{in}
\end{aligned}$$

The smaller value controls:

$$s = \min(14.6,\ 11) = 11\ \text{in}$$
questions.subtopic: RC beam stirrup spacing (required vs maximum)

questions.explanation: An interior beam's tributary width equals its spacing (8 ft). Factored load is 204 psf \(\times\) 8 ft = 1.632 klf, so \(M_u = w_u L^2/8 = 183.6\) kip-ft. Using unfactored loads gives 135.0 kip-ft, a 4 ft tributary width gives 91.8 kip-ft, and a 16 ft width gives 367.2 kip-ft.
questions.question: An interior simply supported floor beam spans 30 ft and is spaced 8 ft on center from parallel beams. The floor carries a dead load of 90 psf and a live load of 60 psf (no live load reduction). Using the LRFD combination 1.2D + 1.6L, what is the maximum factored moment \(M_u\) in the beam?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Loads (ASCE 7-16) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(M_u\). An interior beam supports half the floor on each side, so its tributary width equals the beam spacing:

$$w_u = (1.2D + 1.6L)\,(\text{tributary width})$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
D &= 90\ \text{psf} \\
L &= 60\ \text{psf} \\
\text{tributary width} &= 8\ \text{ft} \\
w_u &= [1.2(90) + 1.6(60)](8) \\
&= (204)(8) \\
&= 1632\ \text{plf} = 1.632\ \text{klf} \\
M_u &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(M_u) &= \frac{w_u L^2}{8} \\
&= \frac{(1.632)(30)^2}{8} \\
&= 183.6\ \text{kip-ft}
\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Tributary width and LRFD factored moment

questions.explanation: Check both limit states: yielding on the gross area gives 113.4 kip and rupture on the effective net area (\(U = 1 - x/L = 0.80\)) gives 104.4 kip, so rupture governs. Forgetting the shear lag factor gives 130.5 kip, and omitting \(\phi\) from yielding gives 126.0 kip.
questions.question: A bolted angle tension member has \(A_g\) = 3.50 \(\text{in}^2\) and net area \(A_n\) = 3.00 \(\text{in}^2\). The connection eccentricity is x = 0.90 in. and the connection length is L = 4.50 in. The steel has \(F_y\) = 36 ksi and \(F_u\) = 58 ksi. Using LRFD and ignoring block shear, what is the design tensile strength?
questions.subtopic: Steel tension member strength (yielding vs rupture with shear lag)

questions.explanation: The handbook relation needs absolute temperature (298.15 K). Using 25 in place of 298.15 K gives 1,188 \(\mu\text{g/m}^3\), using the 0 °C molar volume (22.4 L/mol) gives 109 \(\mu\text{g/m}^3\), and skipping the \(P/RT\) factor gives 2,438.
questions.question: An air monitor reports 53 ppb of nitrogen dioxide (NO2, molecular weight 46 g/mol) at 25 deg C and 1 atm. What is the concentration in micrograms per cubic meter?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Air pollution section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the concentration in \(\mu g/m^3\). The handbook prints:

$$\frac{\mu g}{m^3} = \text{ppb} \times \frac{P(\text{MW})}{RT}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{ppb} &= 53 \\
P &= 1\ \text{atm} \\
\text{MW} &= 46\ \text{g/mol} \\
R &= 0.0821\ \text{L-atm/(mol-K)} \\
T &= 273.15 + 25 = 298.15\ \text{K} \\
\mu g/m^3 &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(\mu g/m^3) &= 53 \times \frac{(1)(46)}{(0.0821)(298.15)} \\
&= 100\ \mu g/m^3
\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Air pollutant ppb to ug/m3 conversion

questions.explanation: At \(z = 0\) and \(y = 0\) the two reflection terms in the handbook equation are equal, so the exponential term is doubled and the leading \(2\pi\) cancels to \(\pi\). Leaving out the \(\exp(-H^2/2\sigma_z^2)\) factor gives 3,979, and forgetting the reflection term (using \(2\pi\)) gives half the answer.
questions.question: A stack emits a pollutant at Q = 5.0 x \(10^7\) ug/s with an effective stack height H = 40 m. At a point on the ground directly downwind on the plume centerline, the wind speed is u = 5.0 m/s and the dispersion parameters are \(\sigma_y\) = 40 m and \(\sigma_z\) = 20 m. What is the ground-level concentration?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Atmospheric Dispersion Modeling (Gaussian) section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(C\). At ground level (\(z = 0\)) on the centerline (\(y = 0\)) the two exponentials inside the handbook bracket are equal, so the Gaussian equation reduces to:

$$C = \frac{Q}{\pi u \sigma_y \sigma_z}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{H^2}{\sigma_z^2}\right)$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
Q &= 5.0 \times 10^7\ \mu g/s \\
u &= 5.0\ \text{m/s} \\
\sigma_y &= 40\ \text{m}, \quad \sigma_z = 20\ \text{m} \\
H &= 40\ \text{m} \\
C &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(C) &= \frac{5.0 \times 10^7}{\pi (5.0)(40)(20)}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{(40)^2}{(20)^2}\right) \\
&= (3{,}979)(0.1353) \\
&= 538\ \mu g/m^3
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: For neutral conditions the handbook gives \(\sigma_z = H/\sqrt{2}\) at the maximum, so the exponential term is \(\exp(-1) = 0.368\). Dropping the exponential gives 2,001, using a \(2\pi\) denominator halves the result, and using \(\sigma_z = H\) gives 858.
questions.question: An elevated source (effective stack height H = 50 m) emits Q = 4.0 x \(10^7\) ug/s under neutral atmospheric conditions. The wind speed at stack height is u = 4.0 m/s and \(\sigma_y\) = 45 m at the point of maximum ground-level concentration. What is the maximum ground-level concentration?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Atmospheric Dispersion Modeling (Gaussian) section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(C_{max}\). For neutral conditions the handbook prints:

$$\begin{gathered}
C_{max} = \frac{Q}{\pi u \sigma_y \sigma_z}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{H^2}{\sigma_z^2}\right) \\
\sigma_z = \frac{H}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{gathered}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\sigma_z &= \frac{50}{\sqrt{2}} = 35.36\ \text{m} \\
\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{H^2}{\sigma_z^2}\right) &= \exp(-1) = 0.3679 \\
C_{max} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(C_{max}) &= \frac{4.0 \times 10^7}{\pi (4.0)(45)(35.36)}(0.3679) \\
&= (2001)(0.3679) \\
&= 736\ \mu g/m^3
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The handbook solids residence time counts solids leaving in both the waste sludge and the effluent. Ignoring effluent solids gives 7.5 days, using only the effluent term gives 33.3 days, and the ratio \(V/Q_w\) (20 days) ignores concentrations.
questions.question: An activated sludge aeration basin has V = 2,000 \(\text{m}^3\) and a mixed liquor concentration \(X_A\) = 3,000 mg/L. Waste sludge is withdrawn at \(Q_w\) = 100 \(\text{m}^3\)/d with \(X_w\) = 8,000 mg/L. The effluent flow is \(Q_e\) = 9,000 \(\text{m}^3\)/d with suspended solids \(X_e\) = 20 mg/L. What is the solids residence time (mean cell residence time)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Activated Sludge section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\theta_c\). The handbook gives:

$$\theta_c = \frac{V X_A}{Q_w X_w + Q_e X_e}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
V X_A &= (2{,}000)(3{,}000) \\
&= 6.0 \times 10^6\ \text{g} \\
Q_w X_w &= (100)(8{,}000) = 800{,}000 \\
Q_e X_e &= (9{,}000)(20) = 180{,}000 \\
\theta_c &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(\theta_c) &= \frac{6.0 \times 10^6}{800{,}000 + 180{,}000} \\
&= 6.1\ \text{days}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: \(F{:}M = Q_0 S_0 / (V X_A)\) with consistent units gives 0.20 per day. Dropping \(X_A\) from the denominator gives 600, using only the concentration ratio gives 0.07, and inverting the ratio gives 5.0.
questions.question: An aeration basin of volume 2,000 \(\text{m}^3\) receives \(Q_0\) = 6,000 \(\text{m}^3\)/d of wastewater with a BOD of \(S_0\) = 200 mg/L. The mixed liquor concentration is \(X_A\) = 3,000 mg/L. What is the food-to-mass (F:M) ratio?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Activated Sludge section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for F:M. The handbook gives the organic loading rate as:

$$F\!:\!M = \frac{Q_0 S_0}{\text{Vol}\,X_A}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
Q_0 &= 6{,}000\ \text{m}^3\text{/d} \\
S_0 &= 200\ \text{mg/L} = 200\ \text{g/m}^3 \\
\text{Vol} &= 2{,}000\ \text{m}^3 \\
X_A &= 3{,}000\ \text{mg/L} = 3{,}000\ \text{g/m}^3 \\
F\!:\!M &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(F\!:\!M) &= \frac{(6{,}000)(200)}{(2{,}000)(3{,}000)} \\
&= 0.20\ \text{d}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: SVI = (settled volume in mL/L \(\times\) 1,000) / MLSS in mg/L = 100 mL/g. Forgetting the 1,000 factor gives 0.1, and inverting the ratio gives 10.
questions.question: A 1-L sample of mixed liquor with MLSS = 3,000 mg/L is allowed to settle. After 30 minutes the settled sludge occupies 300 mL. What is the sludge volume index (SVI)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Activated Sludge section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for SVI. The handbook gives:

$$\text{SVI} = \frac{\text{settled volume (mL/L)} \times 1{,}000}{\text{MLSS (mg/L)}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{settled volume} &= 300\ \text{mL/L} \\
\text{MLSS} &= 3{,}000\ \text{mg/L} \\
\text{SVI} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(\text{SVI}) &= \frac{(300)(1{,}000)}{3{,}000} \\
&= 100\ \text{mL/g}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: P is the fraction of wastewater sample in the total volume (9/300 = 0.03), so BOD = \((D_1 - D_2)/P\) = 173 mg/L. Using the oxygen drop alone gives 5.2, using 9/291 as P gives 168, and multiplying by P gives 0.16.
questions.question: A BOD test uses 9 mL of wastewater diluted to a total volume of 300 mL with unseeded dilution water. The initial dissolved oxygen is 8.6 mg/L and after 5 days at 20 deg C it is 3.4 mg/L. What is the BOD5 of the wastewater?
questions.solution:
Refer to the BOD Test Solution and Seeding Procedures section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).
