Ultimately, we must solve for BOD5. The dilution water is not seeded, so the handbook gives:

$$\text{BOD},\ \text{mg/L} = \frac{D_1 - D_2}{P}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
D_1 &= 8.6\ \text{mg/L} \\
D_2 &= 3.4\ \text{mg/L} \\
P &= \frac{9}{300} = 0.030 \\
\text{BOD}_5 &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(\text{BOD}_5) &= \frac{8.6 - 3.4}{0.030} \\
&= 173\ \text{mg/L}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: \(X_A = \theta_c Y (S_0 - S_e) / [\theta (1 + k_d \theta_c)]\) gives 2.63 \(\text{kg/m}^3\). Ignoring endogenous decay gives 3.68, using \((1 - k_d \theta_c)\) gives 6.13, and omitting the hydraulic residence time gives 0.66.
questions.question: A completely mixed activated sludge system is designed with solids residence time 8 d, hydraulic residence time 0.25 d, yield Y = 0.5 kg biomass/kg BOD, and death coefficient \(k_d\) = 0.05 per day. The influent BOD is 0.25 kg/\(\text{m}^3\) and the effluent BOD is 0.02 kg/\(\text{m}^3\). What is the biomass concentration \(X_A\) in the aeration tank?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Activated Sludge section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(X_A\). The handbook gives:

$$X_A = \frac{\theta_c Y (S_0 - S_e)}{\theta(1 + k_d \theta_c)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\theta_c &= 8\ \text{d}, \quad \theta = 0.25\ \text{d} \\
Y &= 0.5, \quad k_d = 0.05\ \text{d}^{-1} \\
S_0 - S_e &= 0.25 - 0.02 = 0.23\ \text{kg/m}^3 \\
X_A &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(X_A) &= \frac{(8)(0.5)(0.23)}{(0.25)[1 + (0.05)(8)]} \\
&= \frac{0.92}{0.35} \\
&= 2.63\ \text{kg/m}^3
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The \(\text{CO}_2\) reaction and the calcium carbonate hardness reaction each use 1 mol of \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\) per mole removed. Counting only the hardness gives 89, counting only the \(\text{CO}_2\) gives 34, and doubling the hardness term (the magnesium ratio) gives 211. The linked video works a larger plant-design example (magnesium and soda ash included) with the same reaction stoichiometry.
questions.question: A groundwater contains 20 mg/L of dissolved \(\text{CO}_2\) and 120 mg/L (as \(\text{CaCO}_3\)) of calcium carbonate hardness. Using lime-soda softening, what lime dose, as \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\), is needed to remove both the \(\text{CO}_2\) and the calcium carbonate hardness? (Molecular weights: \(\text{CO}_2\) 44.01, \(\text{CaCO}_3\) 100.09, \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\) 74.09 g/mol.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Lime-Soda Softening Equations section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Step 1: pick the reactions. Rows 1 and 2 of the printed Lime-Soda Softening Equations table match the two things in this water:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{CO}_2 + \text{Ca(OH)}_2 &\\ \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \\
\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2 + \text{Ca(OH)}_2 &\\ \rightarrow 2\,\text{CaCO}_3 + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}
\end{aligned}$$

The arrow \(\rightarrow\) means "reacts to form": the left side is what reacts, the right side is what forms.

Step 2: read the lime ratio. No number stands before \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\), so each reaction uses 1 mole of lime per mole of substance removed. The 2 before \(\text{CaCO}_3\) in reaction 2 counts product, not lime: one calcium comes from the water, one from the added lime.

Step 3: turn moles into milligrams with the molecular weights in the question. Every 44 mg of \(\text{CO}_2\) needs 74 mg of lime, and every 100 mg of hardness reported as \(\text{CaCO}_3\) needs 74 mg of lime. The shorthand factors 74/44 and 74/100 are these ratios with the handbook rounded weights. "As \(\text{CaCO}_3\)" is only the reporting basis, so use 100 here, not the weight of \(\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2\).

Step 4: plug in the numbers and add the two demands, because both reactions consume lime.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Lime for CO}_2 &= \frac{20}{44.01}(74.09) \\
&= 33.7\ \text{mg/L} \\
\text{Lime for hardness} &= \frac{120}{100.09}(74.09) \\
&= 88.8\ \text{mg/L} \\
\text{Total} &= 33.7 + 88.8 \\
&= 122\ \text{mg/L}
\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Lime-soda softening (CO2 and calcium carbonate hardness)
questions.videoTitle: ENE 483: Lime Softening Example: Calculating Stoichiometric Amounts of Lime and Soda ash

questions.explanation: Calcium carbonate hardness uses 1 mol of lime per mole, but magnesium carbonate hardness uses 2 mol. Counting 1 mol for both gives 104, doubling the calcium instead gives 178, and treating only the magnesium gives 59.
questions.question: A water has no free \(\text{CO}_2\), 100 mg/L (as \(\text{CaCO}_3\)) of calcium carbonate hardness, and 40 mg/L (as \(\text{CaCO}_3\)) of magnesium carbonate hardness. What lime dose, as \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\), is needed to remove all of this carbonate hardness by lime-soda softening? (\(\text{CaCO}_3\) = 100.09 g/mol and \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\) = 74.09 g/mol.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Lime-Soda Softening Equations section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the lime dose. The handbook reactions are:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2 + \text{Ca(OH)}_2 &\\ \rightarrow 2\,\text{CaCO}_3 + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O} \\
\text{Mg(HCO}_3)_2 + 2\,\text{Ca(OH)}_2 &\\ \rightarrow 2\,\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{Mg(OH)}_2 \\ &\quad + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}
\end{aligned}$$

Calcium carbonate hardness needs 1 mol of \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\) per mole. Magnesium carbonate hardness needs 2 mol per mole.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Ca carbonate hardness} &= 100\ \text{mg/L} \\ &\quad \text{as CaCO}_3 \\
\text{Mg carbonate hardness} &= 40\ \text{mg/L} \\ &\quad \text{as CaCO}_3 \\
\text{Lime dose} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Lime} &= \frac{100 + 2(40)}{100.09}(74.09) \\
&= \frac{180}{100.09}(74.09) \\
&= 133\ \text{mg/L}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The filtration rate is the flow divided by the plan area of the filters in service, and the handbook defines it in m/s. Using all four filters gives \(0.0015\ \text{m/s}\), using one filter area instead of three gives \(0.0058\), and doubling the flow gives \(0.0039\).
questions.question: A treatment plant passes 0.35 m\(^3\)/s through four identical rapid sand filters, each with a plan area of 60 m\(^2\). With one filter out of service for backwashing, what is the filtration rate through each of the other three, in m/s?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Filtration Equations section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the filtration rate. The handbook defines it as the empty-bed approach velocity, in m/s:

$$v_s = \frac{Q}{A_{plan}}$$

With one of the four filters out of service, the flow passes through three filters.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
Q &= 0.35\ \text{m}^3/\text{s} \\
A_{plan} &= 3(60) = 180\ \text{m}^2 \\
v_s &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(v_s) &= \frac{0.35}{180} \\
&= 0.001944\ \text{m/s} \\
&\approx 0.0019\ \text{m/s}
\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Rapid filtration rate (one filter in backwash)

questions.explanation: The backwash velocity is the backwash flow divided by the plan area of the bed. Reading the answer in the wrong unit gives 1.5, an area factor of 4 gives 60, and inverting the ratio gives 67.
questions.question: A rapid sand filter with a plan area of 60 m\(^2\) is backwashed at 0.90 m\(^3\)/s. What is the backwash velocity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Filtration Equations section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the backwash velocity. The handbook gives:

$$v_B = \frac{Q_B}{A_{plan}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
Q_B &= 0.90\ \text{m}^3/\text{s} \\
A_{plan} &= 60\ \text{m}^2 \\
v_B &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(v_B) &= \frac{0.90}{60} \\
&= 0.015\ \text{m/s} \\
&= 15\ \text{mm/s}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Stokes' law uses the density difference (\(2{,}652 - 998\)) and the diameter squared. Using the radius in place of the diameter gives 0.56, using the particle density alone gives 3.60, and using \(9\) in place of \(18\) in the denominator gives 4.49.
questions.question: A spherical silt particle with a diameter of 0.050 mm and a density of 2,650 kg/m\(^3\) settles in still water at 20 °C (density 998 kg/m\(^3\), dynamic viscosity 1.002 × 10\(^{-3}\) Pa·s). Assuming laminar settling, what is the terminal settling velocity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Settling Equations section in the Environmental Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the terminal settling velocity. For laminar settling of a sphere the handbook gives Stokes' law:

$$v_t = \frac{g(\rho_p - \rho_f)d^2}{18\mu}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
g &= 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 \\
\rho_p &= 2{,}650\ \text{kg/m}^3 \\
\rho_f &= 998\ \text{kg/m}^3 \\
d &= 0.050\ \text{mm} = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m} \\
\mu &= 1.002 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{Pa}\cdot\text{s} \\
v_t &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(v_t) &= \frac{9.81(2{,}650 - 998)(5.0 \times 10^{-5})^2}{18(1.002 \times 10^{-3})} \\
&= 0.00225\ \text{m/s} \\
&= 2.25\ \text{mm/s}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The strut is a two-force member, so its force acts along BD. Moments about A give the vertical component (\(24\ \text{kN}\)), and the strut force is that divided by \(\sin 45^\circ\). Using only the vertical component gives 24.0, giving the pin force at A gives 26.8, and using the full \(4\ \text{m}\) beam length as the strut's moment arm gives 17.0.
questions.question: A horizontal beam AC is 4 m long. It is pinned to a vertical wall at A and pinned at its midpoint B to a strut BD. The other end D of the strut is pinned to the same wall 2 m directly below A, so the strut makes a 45° angle with the beam. A 12 kN downward load acts at end C. What is the force in strut BD?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the force in strut BD. The strut is pinned at both ends and carries no other load, so it is a two-force member and its force acts along line BD. Draw the free-body diagram of beam AC and write the moment equilibrium equation from the handbook about pin A:

$$\sum M_A = 0$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 12\ \text{kN at C}, \quad AC = 4\ \text{m} \\
AB &= 2\ \text{m}, \quad \theta = 45^\circ \\
F_{BD} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Only the vertical component of the strut force has a moment arm about A:

$$\begin{aligned}
F_{BD}\sin 45^\circ (2) - 12(4) &= 0 \\
F_{BD} &= \frac{48}{2\sin 45^\circ} \\
&= 33.9\ \text{kN}
\end{aligned}$$

The strut pushes up and to the right on the beam, so it is in compression.

choices: Stable and statically indeterminate to the second degree
Stable and statically indeterminate to the third degree
Stable and statically indeterminate to the first degree
questions.explanation: Count reaction components, not supports: each fixed base gives 3, so \(r = 6\). Then \(3m + r = 15\) exceeds \(3j + c = 12\) by three. Counting 2 components per fixed base would give first degree, and counting only 1 would give an unstable frame.
questions.question: A planar portal frame has two columns and one beam rigidly connected at the top corners, so it has 3 members and 4 joints (see the figure). Both column bases are fixed, and there are no internal hinges. How is the frame classified?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stability, Determinacy, and Classification of Structures section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must classify the frame. Use the handbook test for plane frames with \(m\) members, \(j\) joints, \(r\) reaction components, and \(c\) equations of condition:

$$\begin{aligned}
3m + r &< 3j + c \Rightarrow \text{unstable} \\
3m + r &= 3j + c \Rightarrow \text{determinate} \\
3m + r &> 3j + c \Rightarrow \text{indeterminate}
\end{aligned}$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
m &= 3, \quad j = 4 \\
r &= 3 + 3 = 6 \\
c &= 0
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
3m + r &= 3(3) + 6 = 15 \\
3j + c &= 3(4) + 0 = 12 \\
15 - 12 &= 3
\end{aligned}$$

Since \(3m + r\) exceeds \(3j + c\) by 3, the frame is statically indeterminate to the third degree. It is also stable: the rigid corners and fixed bases hold the frame in a fixed shape with no mechanism, so the count gives the degree of indeterminacy.

choices: Stable and statically indeterminate to the first degree
Stable and statically indeterminate to the second degree
questions.explanation: Pinned bases give \(r = 4\), and the hinge gives \(c = 1\). Then \(3m + r = 16\) equals \(3j + c = 16\), so the frame is determinate. Ignoring the hinge gives first degree, and counting the hinge as two conditions would give an unstable frame. The count is only a necessary check. Stability also needs the three hinges not to be collinear, which the problem states.
questions.question: A planar frame has two columns and a beam made of two segments joined by an internal hinge at midspan, so it has 4 members and 5 joints (see the figure). The column-to-beam corners are rigid, both column bases are pinned, and the two base pins and the midspan hinge do not lie on one straight line. How is the frame classified? Treat the hinge as one equation of condition.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stability, Determinacy, and Classification of Structures section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must classify the frame. Use the handbook test \(3m + r\) versus \(3j + c\) for plane frames.

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
m &= 4, \quad j = 5 \\
r &= 2 + 2 = 4 \\
c &= 1
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
3m + r &= 3(4) + 4 = 16 \\
3j + c &= 3(5) + 1 = 16
\end{aligned}$$

Since \(3m + r = 3j + c\), the count is consistent with a determinate frame. The count alone does not prove stability, so check the geometry. Each half of the frame is a rigid body pinned to the ground at its base, and the two halves are joined by the midspan hinge. With the two base pins and the midspan hinge not in a straight line, this is a stable three-hinged frame. The statement gives that non-collinear geometry, so the frame is stable and statically determinate.

questions.question: A lane closure on a street with a posted speed of 35 mph requires a merging taper across a lane offset of 12 ft. What merging taper length equals L? (Table 6B-3 gives a merging taper as at least L.) MUTCD Table 6B-4 gives the taper length L in feet as L = WS\(^2\)/60 for S of 40 mph or less and L = WS for S of 45 mph or more, where W is the offset width in feet and S is the posted speed limit (or off-peak 85th-percentile speed or anticipated operating speed) in mph.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA MUTCD, 11th Edition with Revision 1 (December 2025), the current edition on the FHWA site. The MUTCD is not part of the FE Reference Handbook, so the needed table values are given in the question. This is supplemental practice on MUTCD content, not a handbook-based item.

Ultimately, we must find the merging taper length. MUTCD Table 6B-4 gives \(L = \dfrac{WS^2}{60}\) for speeds of 40 mph or less and \(L = WS\) for 45 mph or more. Table 6B-3 says a merging taper is at least \(L\).

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
W &= 12\ \text{ft} \\
S &= 35\ \text{mph} \\
L &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Since \(S \le 40\) mph:

$$\begin{aligned}
L &= \frac{WS^2}{60} \\
&= \frac{(12)(35)^2}{60} \\
&= 245\ \text{ft}
\end{aligned}$$
questions.explanation: For speeds of 40 mph or less, L = WS\(^2\)/60 (MUTCD Table 6B-4), and a merging taper is at least L (Table 6B-3). Using L = WS gives 420, using a shifting taper (0.5 L) gives 122, and using a shoulder taper (0.33 L) gives 81.

questions.question: A freeway lane closure with a posted speed of 55 mph has a lane offset of 12 ft. What merging taper length equals L? (Table 6B-3 gives a merging taper as at least L.) MUTCD Table 6B-4 gives the taper length L in feet as L = WS\(^2\)/60 for S of 40 mph or less and L = WS for S of 45 mph or more, where W is the offset width in feet and S is the posted speed limit (or off-peak 85th-percentile speed or anticipated operating speed) in mph.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA MUTCD, 11th Edition with Revision 1 (December 2025), the current edition on the FHWA site. The MUTCD is not part of the FE Reference Handbook, so the needed table values are given in the question. This is supplemental practice on MUTCD content, not a handbook-based item.

Ultimately, we must find the merging taper length. MUTCD Table 6B-4 gives \(L = WS\) for speeds of 45 mph or more. A merging taper is at least \(L\) (Table 6B-3).

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
W &= 12\ \text{ft} \\
S &= 55\ \text{mph} \\
L &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
L &= WS \\
&= (12)(55) \\
&= 660\ \text{ft}
\end{aligned}$$
questions.explanation: For speeds of 45 mph or more, L = WS (MUTCD Table 6B-4), and a merging taper is at least L. Using WS\(^2\)/60 gives 605, a shifting taper gives 330, and a shoulder taper gives 218.

questions.question: A temporary lane shift on a road with a posted speed of 45 mph moves traffic laterally 10 ft. Table 6B-3 gives a shifting taper as at least 0.5 L. MUTCD Table 6B-4 gives the taper length L in feet as L = WS\(^2\)/60 for S of 40 mph or less and L = WS for S of 45 mph or more, where W is the offset width in feet and S is the posted speed limit (or off-peak 85th-percentile speed or anticipated operating speed) in mph. What is the shifting taper length equal to 0.5 L?
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA MUTCD, 11th Edition with Revision 1 (December 2025), the current edition on the FHWA site. The MUTCD is not part of the FE Reference Handbook, so the needed table values are given in the question. This is supplemental practice on MUTCD content, not a handbook-based item.

Ultimately, we must find the shifting taper length. At 45 mph or more, \(L = WS\) (Table 6B-4). A shifting taper is at least \(0.5L\) (Table 6B-3).

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
W &= 10\ \text{ft} \\
S &= 45\ \text{mph} \\
L_\text{shift} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
L &= WS = (10)(45) = 450\ \text{ft} \\
L_\text{shift} &= 0.5L \\
&= 0.5(450) \\
&= 225\ \text{ft}
\end{aligned}$$
questions.explanation: A shifting taper is at least 0.5 L (MUTCD Table 6B-3), and L = WS at 45 mph or more. Using the full merging length gives 450, applying the 40-mph-or-less formula gives 169, and using a shoulder taper gives 148.

questions.question: A closed shoulder 10 ft wide is tapered on a road with a posted speed of 40 mph. Table 6B-3 gives a shoulder taper as at least 0.33 L. MUTCD Table 6B-4 gives the taper length L in feet as L = WS\(^2\)/60 for S of 40 mph or less and L = WS for S of 45 mph or more, where W is the offset width in feet and S is the posted speed limit (or off-peak 85th-percentile speed or anticipated operating speed) in mph. What is the shoulder taper length equal to 0.33 L? (Round to the nearest foot.)
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA MUTCD, 11th Edition with Revision 1 (December 2025), the current edition on the FHWA site. The MUTCD is not part of the FE Reference Handbook, so the needed table values are given in the question. This is supplemental practice on MUTCD content, not a handbook-based item.

Ultimately, we must find the shoulder taper length. At 40 mph or less, \(L = WS^2/60\) (Table 6B-4). A shoulder taper is at least \(0.33L\) (Table 6B-3).

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
W &= 10\ \text{ft} \\
S &= 40\ \text{mph} \\
L_\text{shoulder} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
L &= \frac{(10)(40)^2}{60} = 266.7\ \text{ft} \\
L_\text{shoulder} &= 0.33L \\
&= 0.33(266.7) \\
&= 88\ \text{ft}
\end{aligned}$$
questions.explanation: A shoulder taper is at least 0.33 L (MUTCD Table 6B-3), and L = WS\(^2\)/60 at 40 mph or less, which gives L = 266.7 ft. Using 0.5 L gives 133, using the full L gives 267, and using L = WS gives 400.

questions.question: According to the MUTCD color code, which color has the general meaning of temporary traffic control?
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA MUTCD, 11th Edition with Revision 1 (December 2025), the current edition on the FHWA site. The MUTCD is not part of the FE Reference Handbook, so the needed table values are given in the question. This is supplemental practice on MUTCD content, not a handbook-based item.

Ultimately, we must match the color to its general meaning. MUTCD Section 1D.05 (Color Code) lists the general meaning of each color. Orange means temporary traffic control.

The other choices have different meanings. Yellow means warning. Fluorescent pink means incident management. Green means indicated movements or actions permitted and direction guidance.
questions.explanation: MUTCD Section 1D.05 assigns orange to temporary traffic control. Yellow is warning, fluorescent pink is incident management, and green is indicated movements or actions permitted and direction guidance.

questions.question: In a temporary traffic control zone, which area is the section of highway where road users are returned to their normal driving path?
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA MUTCD, 11th Edition with Revision 1 (December 2025), the current edition on the FHWA site. The MUTCD is not part of the FE Reference Handbook, so the needed table values are given in the question. This is supplemental practice on MUTCD content, not a handbook-based item.

Ultimately, we must identify which of the four areas of a TTC zone (MUTCD Section 6B.03) does this job.

The advance warning area informs road users of what is ahead. The transition area moves road users out of their normal path. The activity area contains the work space and traffic space. The termination area returns road users to their normal path.

The answer is the termination area (Section 6B.07).
questions.explanation: MUTCD Section 6B.07 defines the termination area as the section where road users return to their normal path, ending at the last TTC device such as END ROAD WORK signs. The advance warning area informs road users, the transition area moves them out of their normal path, and the activity area contains the work space and traffic space.

questions.question: In the termination area of a temporary traffic control zone, a downstream taper may be used. Which length criterion does MUTCD Table 6B-3 give for a downstream taper?
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA MUTCD, 11th Edition with Revision 1 (December 2025), the current edition on the FHWA site. The MUTCD is not part of the FE Reference Handbook, so the needed table values are given in the question. This is supplemental practice on MUTCD content, not a handbook-based item.

Ultimately, we must read the downstream taper criterion from MUTCD Table 6B-3 (Taper Length Criteria for Temporary Traffic Control Zones). A downstream taper may be useful in the termination area as a visual cue that the original lane is open again (Section 6B.08).

Table 6B-3 gives a merging taper at least L, a shifting taper at least 0.5 L and a shoulder taper at least 0.33 L. A downstream taper does not use L. It has a 50 feet minimum and a 100 feet maximum length.
questions.explanation: MUTCD Table 6B-3 gives a downstream taper a length of 50 feet minimum and 100 feet maximum, not a multiple of L. A merging taper is at least L, a shifting taper is at least 0.5 L, and a shoulder taper is at least 0.33 L.

questions.question: Horton's equation gives the infiltration capacity as \(f_p = f_\infty + (f_0 - f_\infty)e^{-k_d t}\), where \(f_0\) is the initial capacity, \(f_\infty\) is the final capacity and \(k_d\) is the decay coefficient. A soil has \(f_0 = 4.0\ \text{in/hr}\), \(f_\infty = 0.5\ \text{in/hr}\) and \(k_d = 3\ \text{hr}^{-1}\). What is the infiltration capacity 0.5 hr after the start of the storm?
questions.explanation: The exponent is \(k_d\)t = 1.5, so \(f_p\) = 0.5 + 3.5\(e^{-1.5}\). Using t = 1 hr gives 0.67, averaging \(f_0\) and \(f_\infty\) gives 2.25, and using t/\(k_d\) in the exponent gives 3.46.
questions.solution:
Source: EPA SWMM Reference Manual Volume I, Hydrology (EPA/600/R-15/162A), Chapter 4, Horton's method, Equations 4-1 to 4-3 (https://downloads.tuflow.com/SWMM/SWMM5_Reference_Manual_Volume1_Hydrology_P100NYRA.pdf). Horton's equation is not in the FE Reference Handbook, so it is given in the question. This is supplemental practice.

Ultimately, we must find the infiltration capacity at \(t = 0.5\) hr.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
f_0 &= 4.0\ \text{in/hr} \\
f_\infty &= 0.5\ \text{in/hr} \\
k_d &= 3\ \text{hr}^{-1} \\
t &= 0.5\ \text{hr} \\
f_p &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
f_p &= f_\infty + (f_0 - f_\infty)e^{-k_d t} \\
&= 0.5 + (4.0 - 0.5)e^{-(3)(0.5)} \\
&= 0.5 + 3.5(0.2231) \\
&= 1.28\ \text{in/hr}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.subtopic: Horton actual infiltration vs rainfall intensity
questions.question: Horton's equation gives the infiltration capacity as \(f_p = f_\infty + (f_0 - f_\infty)e^{-k_d t}\), where \(f_0\) is the initial capacity, \(f_\infty\) is the final capacity and \(k_d\) is the decay coefficient. The actual infiltration rate is the lesser of the infiltration capacity and the rainfall intensity. A soil has \(f_0 = 4.0\ \text{in/hr}\), \(f_\infty = 0.5\ \text{in/hr}\) and \(k_d = 3\ \text{hr}^{-1}\). At 0.5 hr into a storm the rainfall intensity is 1.0 in/hr. What is the actual infiltration rate?
questions.explanation: The capacity at 0.5 hr is 1.28 in/hr, which is more than the rainfall intensity of 1.0 in/hr, so all the rain infiltrates and the actual rate is 1.00 in/hr (no runoff). Choosing the capacity gives 1.28, taking the difference gives 0.28, and adding the two gives 2.28.

questions.question: Horton's equation gives the infiltration capacity as \(f_p = f_\infty + (f_0 - f_\infty)e^{-k_d t}\), where \(f_0\) is the initial capacity, \(f_\infty\) is the final capacity and \(k_d\) is the decay coefficient. Integrating gives the cumulative infiltration capacity \(F = f_\infty t + \dfrac{f_0 - f_\infty}{k_d}\left(1 - e^{-k_d t}\right)\). A soil has \(f_0 = 4.0\ \text{in/hr}\), \(f_\infty = 0.5\ \text{in/hr}\) and \(k_d = 3\ \text{hr}^{-1}\). What is the cumulative infiltration capacity over the first 1 hr, assuming infiltration equals capacity throughout?
questions.explanation: The integral of the capacity curve is the area under it. Leaving out the division by \(k_d\) gives 3.83, dropping the exponential term gives 1.67, and reporting the capacity at 1 hr (a rate, not a depth) gives 0.67.
questions.solution:
Source: EPA SWMM Reference Manual Volume I, Hydrology (EPA/600/R-15/162A), Chapter 4, Horton's method, Equations 4-1 to 4-3 (https://downloads.tuflow.com/SWMM/SWMM5_Reference_Manual_Volume1_Hydrology_P100NYRA.pdf). Horton's equation is not in the FE Reference Handbook, so it is given in the question. This is supplemental practice.

Ultimately, we must find the cumulative infiltration depth over \(1\) hr.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
f_0 &= 4.0\ \text{in/hr} \\
f_\infty &= 0.5\ \text{in/hr} \\
k_d &= 3\ \text{hr}^{-1} \\
t &= 1\ \text{hr} \\
F &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
F &= f_\infty t + \frac{f_0 - f_\infty}{k_d}\left(1 - e^{-k_d t}\right) \\
&= 0.5(1) + \frac{3.5}{3}\left(1 - e^{-3}\right) \\
&= 0.5 + 1.1667(0.9502) \\
&= 1.61\ \text{in}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.subtopic: Drilled shaft base resistance in clay
questions.question: FHWA GEC 10 gives the nominal unit base resistance of a drilled shaft in cohesive soil as \(q_{BN} = N_c^* s_u\), where \(s_u\) is the mean undrained shear strength over 2B below the base. For a shaft depth of at least 3 diameters and \(s_u\) of at least 2,000 psf, \(N_c^* = 9.0\). A drilled shaft is 4 ft in diameter and 40 ft deep, with \(s_u = 3{,}000\ \text{psf}\) below the base. What is the nominal base resistance?
questions.explanation: Since the depth (40 ft) is more than 3 diameters (12 ft) and \(s_u\) is above 2,000 psf, \(N_c^*\) = 9.0. The base area is \(\pi B^2/4\). Using \(\pi B^2\) for the area gives 1,357, using \(N_c^*\) = 6.5 gives 245, and using B\(^2\) for the area gives 432.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA GEC 10, Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and Design Methods (FHWA-NHI-18-024), Section 10 (Axial Loading), base resistance in cohesive soil, Equations 10-19 and 10-20 and Table 10-2 (https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/engineering/geotech/nhi18024.pdf). These equations are given in the question. This is supplemental practice, not a handbook-based item.

Ultimately, we must find the nominal base resistance \(R_{BN}\).

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
B &= 4\ \text{ft} \\
s_u &= 3{,}000\ \text{psf} \\
N_c^* &= 9.0 \\
R_{BN} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
q_{BN} &= N_c^* s_u \\
&= 9.0(3{,}000) \\
&= 27{,}000\ \text{psf}
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
R_{BN} &= q_{BN}\left(\frac{\pi B^2}{4}\right) \\
&= 27{,}000\left(\frac{\pi (4)^2}{4}\right) \\
&= 339{,}292\ \text{lb} \\
&= 339\ \text{kips}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.question: For a drilled shaft in cohesive soil with depth D less than 3 diameters B, FHWA GEC 10 gives \(q_{BN} = \frac{2}{3}\left[1 + \frac{1}{6}\frac{D}{B}\right]N_c^* s_u\). For \(s_u\) of at least 2,000 psf, \(N_c^* = 9.0\). A drilled shaft is 5 ft in diameter and 10 ft deep, with \(s_u = 2{,}000\ \text{psf}\) below the base. What is the nominal base resistance?
questions.explanation: Here D/B = 2, which is less than 3, so the reduced expression applies and the factor is 0.8889. Ignoring the reduction (using \(N_c^*\)\(s_u\) alone) gives 353, inverting D/B gives 255, and dropping the (1/6)(D/B) term gives 236.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA GEC 10, Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and Design Methods (FHWA-NHI-18-024), Section 10 (Axial Loading), base resistance in cohesive soil, Equations 10-19 and 10-20 and Table 10-2 (https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/engineering/geotech/nhi18024.pdf). These equations are given in the question. This is supplemental practice, not a handbook-based item.

Ultimately, we must find \(R_{BN}\). Since \(D/B = 10/5 = 2 < 3\), use the shallow-shaft expression.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
B &= 5\ \text{ft} \\
D &= 10\ \text{ft} \\
s_u &= 2{,}000\ \text{psf} \\
N_c^* &= 9.0 \\
R_{BN} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
q_{BN} &= \frac{2}{3}\left[1 + \frac{1}{6}\left(\frac{D}{B}\right)\right]N_c^* s_u \\
&= \frac{2}{3}\left[1 + \frac{1}{6}(2)\right](9.0)(2{,}000) \\
&= 16{,}000\ \text{psf}
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
R_{BN} &= q_{BN}\left(\frac{\pi B^2}{4}\right) \\
&= 16{,}000\left(\frac{\pi (5)^2}{4}\right) \\
&= 314{,}159\ \text{lb} \\
&= 314\ \text{kips}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.question: Which project delivery method combines design and construction services into a single contract with one entity?
questions.explanation: FHWA describes design-build as a delivery method that combines two usually separate services, design and construction, into a single contract. In design-bid-build the owner (or its consultant) designs the project and then awards a construction contract to the lowest responsive bidder. In CM/GC there are two phases, design and construction. Unit-price bidding is a payment method, not a delivery method.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA (Alternative Project Delivery, Design-Build and CM/GC pages, and the FHWA Design-Build Effectiveness Study glossary): https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/ipd/alternative_project_delivery/defined/new_build_facilities/design_build.aspx , https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/construction/contracts/acm/cmgc.cfm , https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/reports/designbuild/designbuilda1.htm . Supplemental practice; the FE Reference Handbook does not cover project delivery methods.

Ultimately, we must match the delivery method to its contract structure.

Design-build combines two usually separate services, architectural/engineering design and construction, in a single contract. The design-builder takes responsibility for most of the design and all of the construction.

Design-bid-build separates them: the owner designs (or hires a designer), solicits bids and awards construction to the lowest responsive bidder. CM/GC has a design phase and a construction phase, with the contractor advising during design.

questions.question: In the construction manager/general contractor (CM/GC) delivery method, what does the contractor do during the design phase?
choices: Acts as a consultant giving constructability and pricing feedback
Completes the design and the construction under one lump-sum contract
Has no role until a price is agreed by the owner
Waits for the design to be complete and then bids against other contractors
questions.explanation: FHWA describes CM/GC as having a design phase and a construction phase. During design the contractor acts as a consultant, offering constructability and pricing feedback and identifying risks. When the owner considers the design complete, the contractor has an opportunity to bid, and if the price is judged fair the contractor becomes the general contractor.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA (Alternative Project Delivery, Design-Build and CM/GC pages, and the FHWA Design-Build Effectiveness Study glossary): https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/ipd/alternative_project_delivery/defined/new_build_facilities/design_build.aspx , https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/construction/contracts/acm/cmgc.cfm , https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/reports/designbuild/designbuilda1.htm . Supplemental practice; the FE Reference Handbook does not cover project delivery methods.

Ultimately, we must recall the contractor's role during the design phase of CM/GC.

In the design phase the contractor is a consultant to the owner. The contractor gives constructability and pricing feedback on design options and identifies risks from its means and methods. This also lets the owner take an active part in design decisions.

After the design is complete, the contractor can bid based on the completed design. If the owner, designer and an independent cost estimator agree the price is fair, the owner issues a construction contract and the construction manager becomes the general contractor.

questions.question: A design-build procurement uses an adjusted bid. Technical proposals are scored from 0 to 1, and the adjusted bid is the price divided by the technical score. The lowest adjusted bid wins, but the winner is paid its stated price. Offeror A has a technical score of 0.9 and a price of USD 50 million. Offeror B has a technical score of 0.75 and a price of USD 44 million. Which statement is correct?
choices: B wins, with an adjusted bid of USD 33.0 million versus USD 45.0 million for A
B wins because its price is lower, and it is paid USD 44 million
A wins, with an adjusted bid of USD 55.6 million versus USD 58.7 million for B
A wins, with an adjusted bid of USD 45.0 million versus USD 33.0 million for B
questions.explanation: The adjusted bid is price divided by technical score: A is 50/0.9 = 55.6 and B is 44/0.75 = 58.7. A has the lower adjusted bid, so A wins even though B's price is lower, and A is paid its stated USD 50 million. Multiplying price by score gives 45.0 and 33.0, which reverses the ranking incorrectly.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA (Alternative Project Delivery, Design-Build and CM/GC pages, and the FHWA Design-Build Effectiveness Study glossary): https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/ipd/alternative_project_delivery/defined/new_build_facilities/design_build.aspx , https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/construction/contracts/acm/cmgc.cfm , https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/reports/designbuild/designbuilda1.htm . Supplemental practice; the FE Reference Handbook does not cover project delivery methods.

Ultimately, we must compare the adjusted bids. The adjusted bid is the price divided by the technical score (FHWA Design-Build Effectiveness Study glossary, Adjusted Bid).

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{A} &= \frac{50}{0.9} = 55.6\ \text{million} \\
\text{B} &= \frac{44}{0.75} = 58.7\ \text{million}
\end{aligned}$$

The lowest adjusted bid wins, so A is selected. The adjusted bid is used only for the award. A is paid its stated price of USD 50 million.

questions.question: The air voids of a compacted asphalt mixture are \(V_a = \left(1 - \dfrac{G_{mb}}{G_{mm}}\right)(100)\), where \(G_{mb}\) is the bulk specific gravity of the compacted mixture, \(G_{mm}\) is the maximum specific gravity of the mixture, \(P_s\) is the aggregate content as a percent by mass of the total mixture, and \(G_{sb}\) is the aggregate bulk specific gravity. A compacted sample has \(G_{mb} = 2.350\) and \(G_{mm} = 2.470\). What are the air voids?
questions.explanation: Va = (1 - 2.35/2.47)(100) = 4.9 percent. Inverting the ratio gives 5.1, subtracting the specific gravities and reading the result as a percent gives 0.1, and forgetting to subtract from 1 gives 95.1.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA, A Review of Aggregate and Asphalt Mixture Specific Gravity Measurements and Their Impacts on Asphalt Mix Design Properties and Mix Acceptance (FHWA-HIF-11-033), Equations 1 to 3 (https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/pavement/materials/pubs/hif11033/hif11033.pdf). The asphalt mixture volumetric equations are not in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (I searched for VMA, air voids and Gmb), so they are given in the question. Supplemental practice.

Ultimately, we must find the air voids \(V_a\).

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
G_{mb} &= 2.350 \\
G_{mm} &= 2.470 \\
V_a &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
V_a &= \left(1 - \frac{G_{mb}}{G_{mm}}\right)(100) \\
&= \left(1 - \frac{2.350}{2.470}\right)(100) \\
&= 4.9\%
\end{aligned}$$

questions.question: The voids in the mineral aggregate of a compacted asphalt mixture are \(VMA = 100 - \dfrac{G_{mb}P_s}{G_{sb}}\), where \(G_{mb}\) is the bulk specific gravity of the compacted mixture, \(G_{mm}\) is the maximum specific gravity of the mixture, \(P_s\) is the aggregate content as a percent by mass of the total mixture, and \(G_{sb}\) is the aggregate bulk specific gravity. A mixture has \(G_{mb} = 2.350\), \(P_s = 95.0\) percent and \(G_{sb} = 2.650\). What is the VMA?
questions.explanation: VMA = 100 - (2.35)(95.0)/2.65 = 15.8 percent. Forgetting to subtract from 100 gives 84.2, using the binder content (100 - P\(_s\)) in place of P\(_s\) gives 95.6, and dividing the product by 100 gives 99.2.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA, A Review of Aggregate and Asphalt Mixture Specific Gravity Measurements and Their Impacts on Asphalt Mix Design Properties and Mix Acceptance (FHWA-HIF-11-033), Equations 1 to 3 (https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/pavement/materials/pubs/hif11033/hif11033.pdf). The asphalt mixture volumetric equations are not in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (I searched for VMA, air voids and Gmb), so they are given in the question. Supplemental practice.

Ultimately, we must find \(VMA\).

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
G_{mb} &= 2.350 \\
P_s &= 95.0\% \\
G_{sb} &= 2.650 \\
VMA &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
VMA &= 100 - \frac{G_{mb}P_s}{G_{sb}} \\
&= 100 - \frac{(2.350)(95.0)}{2.650} \\
&= 15.8\%
\end{aligned}$$

questions.question: For a compacted asphalt mixture, \(V_a = \left(1 - \dfrac{G_{mb}}{G_{mm}}\right)(100)\), \(VMA = 100 - \dfrac{G_{mb}P_s}{G_{sb}}\) and \(VFA = \dfrac{VMA - V_a}{VMA}(100)\), where \(G_{mb}\) is the bulk specific gravity of the compacted mixture, \(G_{mm}\) is the maximum specific gravity of the mixture, \(P_s\) is the aggregate content as a percent by mass of the total mixture, and \(G_{sb}\) is the aggregate bulk specific gravity. A mixture has \(G_{mb} = 2.350\), \(G_{mm} = 2.470\), \(P_s = 95.0\) percent and \(G_{sb} = 2.650\). What is the VFA?
questions.explanation: First Va = 4.86% and VMA = 15.75%. Then VFA = (15.75 - 4.86)/15.75 x 100 = 69.2 percent. Reporting VMA - Va (the effective binder volume) gives 10.9, dividing Va by VMA gives 30.8, and dividing by Va instead of VMA gives 224.3.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA, A Review of Aggregate and Asphalt Mixture Specific Gravity Measurements and Their Impacts on Asphalt Mix Design Properties and Mix Acceptance (FHWA-HIF-11-033), Equations 1 to 3 (https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/pavement/materials/pubs/hif11033/hif11033.pdf). The asphalt mixture volumetric equations are not in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 (I searched for VMA, air voids and Gmb), so they are given in the question. Supplemental practice.

Ultimately, we must find \(VFA\), which needs \(V_a\) and \(VMA\) first.

$$\begin{aligned}
V_a &= \left(1 - \frac{2.350}{2.470}\right)(100) = 4.86\% \\
VMA &= 100 - \frac{(2.350)(95.0)}{2.650} = 15.75\%
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
VFA &= \frac{VMA - V_a}{VMA}(100) \\
&= \frac{15.75 - 4.86}{15.75}(100) \\
&= 69.2\%
\end{aligned}$$

questions.question: A proposed retail building has 120,000 square feet of floor area. For this problem, assume the average weekday PM peak hour rate is 3.5 vehicle trips per 1,000 square feet. How many PM peak hour vehicle trips does the building generate?
questions.explanation: Trips = rate x independent variable, with the floor area in thousands of square feet: 3.5 x 120 = 420. Using the area in square feet gives 420,000, dividing gives 34, and doubling the result gives 840.
questions.solution:
Source for the method: TxDOT Traffic Safety/Design manual, Chapter 16, Section 16.4 Analysis Methodology (https://www.txdot.gov/content/txdotoms/us/en/manuals/des/tsp/chapter-16-traffic-impact-analysis-/16-4-analysis-methodology.html): trips are generated from average rates or a fitted-curve equation for an independent variable, and a pass-by percentage is applied to the vehicle trips generated minus any internal capture. The rates and equation values in this question are assumed for practice and are not from the ITE Trip Generation Manual (paywalled). Supplemental practice, not handbook-based.

Ultimately, we must find the trips generated.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Rate} &= 3.5\ \text{trips per 1{,}000 sq ft} \\
X &= 120{,}000\ \text{sq ft} = 120\ (1{,}000\ \text{sq ft}) \\
T &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
T &= (\text{rate})(X) \\
&= (3.5)(120) \\
&= 420\ \text{trips}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.question: A residential development has 250 dwelling units. For this problem, assume the fitted-curve equation for daily vehicle trips is \(\ln(T) = 0.8\ln(X) + 1.2\), where \(T\) is the number of trips and \(X\) is the number of dwelling units. How many daily vehicle trips are generated?
questions.explanation: Evaluate the right side, ln(T) = 0.8(ln 250) + 1.2 = 5.617, then take the exponential: T = 275. Reporting ln(T) itself gives 5.6, treating the equation as linear gives 201, and multiplying instead of adding the constant gives 99.
questions.solution:
Source for the method: TxDOT Traffic Safety/Design manual, Chapter 16, Section 16.4 Analysis Methodology (https://www.txdot.gov/content/txdotoms/us/en/manuals/des/tsp/chapter-16-traffic-impact-analysis-/16-4-analysis-methodology.html): trips are generated from average rates or a fitted-curve equation for an independent variable, and a pass-by percentage is applied to the vehicle trips generated minus any internal capture. The rates and equation values in this question are assumed for practice and are not from the ITE Trip Generation Manual (paywalled). Supplemental practice, not handbook-based.

Ultimately, we must find \(T\) from the fitted curve.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
X &= 250\ \text{units} \\
a &= 0.8,\quad b = 1.2 \\
T &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\ln(T) &= 0.8\ln(250) + 1.2 \\
&= 5.617 \\
T &= e^{5.617} \\
&= 275\ \text{trips}
\end{aligned}$$

questions.question: A development generates 1,000 vehicle trips in the peak hour. For this problem, assume 10% of the trips are internal capture, and the pass-by percentage is 20% of the vehicle trips generated minus the internal capture. How many new (primary) trips does the development add to the surrounding street network?
questions.explanation: Internal capture removes 100 trips, leaving 900. The pass-by trips are 20% of 900, or 180, so the new trips are 720. Subtracting both percentages from the original total gives 700, ignoring internal capture gives 800, and reporting only the pass-by trips gives 180.
questions.solution:
Source for the method: TxDOT Traffic Safety/Design manual, Chapter 16, Section 16.4 Analysis Methodology (https://www.txdot.gov/content/txdotoms/us/en/manuals/des/tsp/chapter-16-traffic-impact-analysis-/16-4-analysis-methodology.html): trips are generated from average rates or a fitted-curve equation for an independent variable, and a pass-by percentage is applied to the vehicle trips generated minus any internal capture. The rates and equation values in this question are assumed for practice and are not from the ITE Trip Generation Manual (paywalled). Supplemental practice, not handbook-based.

Ultimately, we must find the new trips. The pass-by percentage applies to the trips generated minus the internal capture.

$$\begin{aligned}
G &= 1{,}000 \\
\text{Internal capture} &= 10\% \\
\text{Pass-by} &= 20\%
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Net} &= 1{,}000(1 - 0.1) = 900 \\
\text{Pass-by} &= 900(0.2) = 180 \\
\text{New} &= 900 - 180 \\
&= 720
\end{aligned}$$

questions.question: The moisture content of wood is the mass of water divided by the mass of the oven-dry wood, as a percentage, so \(MC = \dfrac{m_{wet} - m_{dry}}{m_{dry}}(100)\). A wood specimen has a mass of 580 g at its current moisture content and 450 g after oven drying. What is its moisture content?
questions.explanation: The water mass is 580 - 450 = 130 g, and the moisture content is 130/450 x 100 = 28.9 percent. Dividing by the wet mass gives 22.4, reporting the water mass as a percent gives 130.0, and forgetting to multiply by 100 gives 0.29.
questions.solution:
Source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material (FPL-GTR-282), Chapter 4, Moisture Relations and Physical Properties of Wood (https://www.fpl.fs.usda.gov/documnts/fplgtr/fplgtr282/chapter_04_fpl_gtr282.pdf). Wood moisture and shrinkage are not in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 text I searched. Supplemental practice.

Ultimately, we must find the moisture content.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
m_{wet} &= 580\ \text{g} \\
m_{dry} &= 450\ \text{g} \\
MC &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
MC &= \frac{m_{wet} - m_{dry}}{m_{dry}}(100) \\
&= \frac{580 - 450}{450}(100) \\
&= 28.9\%
\end{aligned}$$

questions.question: As wood dries below the fiber saturation point, in which direction does it shrink the most?
questions.explanation: Wood is anisotropic. The Wood Handbook says it shrinks most in the direction of the annual growth rings (tangentially), about half as much across the rings (radially), and only slightly along the grain. Longitudinal shrinkage from green to oven-dry is generally 0.1 to 0.2 percent.
questions.solution:
Source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material (FPL-GTR-282), Chapter 4, Moisture Relations and Physical Properties of Wood (https://www.fpl.fs.usda.gov/documnts/fplgtr/fplgtr282/chapter_04_fpl_gtr282.pdf). Wood moisture and shrinkage are not in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 text I searched. Supplemental practice.

Ultimately, we must rank the shrinkage directions of wood.

Below the fiber saturation point, wood shrinks most tangentially (along the growth rings). Radial shrinkage across the rings is about half as large as tangential. Longitudinal shrinkage along the grain is very small, generally 0.1 to 0.2 percent from green to oven-dry.

So the greatest shrinkage is tangential.

questions.question: The fiber saturation point of wood is the moisture content below which most wood properties start to change. About what moisture content is it, on average?
questions.explanation: The Wood Handbook says the point below which most wood properties start to change averages about 30 percent moisture content, though it varies by several percentage points among species and pieces. Wood properties do not change with moisture content above this point.
questions.solution:
Source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material (FPL-GTR-282), Chapter 4, Moisture Relations and Physical Properties of Wood (https://www.fpl.fs.usda.gov/documnts/fplgtr/fplgtr282/chapter_04_fpl_gtr282.pdf). Wood moisture and shrinkage are not in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 text I searched. Supplemental practice.

Ultimately, we must recall the average fiber saturation point.

Above the fiber saturation point, physical and mechanical properties of wood do not change with moisture content. Below it, wood begins to shrink and its properties change. The average value is about 30 percent moisture content.

questions.question: What does the concrete slump test (AASHTO T 119 / ASTM C143) determine?
choices: The consistency of the fresh concrete
The compressive strength of the hardened concrete
The unit weight of the hardened concrete
The air content of the fresh concrete
questions.explanation: The FHWA lab manual says the slump test is used to determine the consistency of concrete, in other words how wet or dry it is. Strength comes from cylinder tests, and air content has its own pressure or volumetric test.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA Highway Materials Engineering Course, Module G, Testing Fresh Concrete Laboratory Manual, AASHTO T 119 / ASTM C143 slump test (https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/pavement/materials/hmec/pubs/module_g/lab_manual_fresh.pdf). The slump test procedure is not in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 text I searched (it only mentions a slump value in a mix example). Supplemental practice.

Ultimately, we must state what the slump test measures.

The test determines and monitors the consistency of plastic hydraulic cement concrete, meaning how wet or dry it is. The slump value is generally specified in the project documents.

questions.question: In the standard slump test (AASHTO T 119 / ASTM C143), how is the cone filled and consolidated?
choices: Two equal layers, each rodded 15 times
Three equal layers by volume, each rodded 10 times
Three equal layers by volume, each rodded 25 times
questions.explanation: The FHWA lab manual describes filling the cone in three equal layers by volume, rodding each layer 25 times, keeping the final layer heaped, striking off the top, and lifting the cone straight up in 5 plus or minus 2 seconds.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA Highway Materials Engineering Course, Module G, Testing Fresh Concrete Laboratory Manual, AASHTO T 119 / ASTM C143 slump test (https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/pavement/materials/hmec/pubs/module_g/lab_manual_fresh.pdf). The slump test procedure is not in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 text I searched (it only mentions a slump value in a mix example). Supplemental practice.

Ultimately, we must recall the filling procedure for the slump cone.

The cone is filled in three equal layers by volume. Each layer is rodded 25 times. The second and third layers are rodded to penetrate about an inch into the layer below. After the final layer the top is struck off and the cone is lifted straight up in 5 plus or minus 2 seconds.

questions.question: A slump test gives a measured slump of 98 mm. The standard reports slump to the nearest 5 mm. What value is recorded?
questions.explanation: The FHWA lab manual says the slump is measured and recorded to the nearest 5 mm (1/4 in.). 98 mm is 2 mm from 100 mm and 3 mm from 95 mm, so 100 mm is recorded.
questions.solution:
Source: FHWA Highway Materials Engineering Course, Module G, Testing Fresh Concrete Laboratory Manual, AASHTO T 119 / ASTM C143 slump test (https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/pavement/materials/hmec/pubs/module_g/lab_manual_fresh.pdf). The slump test procedure is not in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6 text I searched (it only mentions a slump value in a mix example). Supplemental practice.

Ultimately, we must round the measured slump to the nearest 5 mm.

The slump is recorded to the nearest 5 mm [1/4 in.]. The two nearest multiples of 5 are 95 mm and 100 mm.

$$\begin{aligned}
98 - 95 &= 3\ \text{mm} \\
100 - 98 &= 2\ \text{mm}
\end{aligned}$$

98 mm is closer to 100 mm, so 100 mm is recorded.

questions.explanation: SP would need \(C_u < 6\) or \(C_c\) outside 1 to 3. SM needs more than 12% fines. GW is the gravel symbol, so the 4 and 3 limits do not apply here.
questions.question: A clean sand has less than 5% fines. Its grain-size curve gives \(D_{10} = 0.12\) mm, \(D_{30} = 0.50\) mm and \(D_{60} = 1.20\) mm. Using the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) criteria, what is the group symbol?
questions.solution:
Refer to the USCS criteria table (ASTM D2487) and the \(C_u\), \(C_c\) definitions in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 273 (PDF page 279).

The handbook defines \(C_u = D_{60}/D_{10}\) and \(C_c = (D_{30})^2/(D_{10} \times D_{60})\).

$$\begin{aligned}C_u &= \frac{1.20}{0.12} \\ &= 10.0, \quad C_c \\ &= \frac{(0.50)^2}{(0.12)(1.20)} \\ &= 1.74\end{aligned}$$

For clean sands (less than 5% fines) the table gives SW when \(C_u \ge 6\) and \(1 \le C_c \le 3\). Both are met, so the sand is well graded: SW.

questions.explanation: 10.00 is \(C_u = D_{60}/D_{10}\), the coefficient of uniformity. The other two skip the squaring or the \(D_{60}\) term.
questions.question: A soil has \(D_{10} = 0.15\) mm, \(D_{30} = 0.60\) mm and \(D_{60} = 1.50\) mm. What is the coefficient of concavity (curvature) \(C_c\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Coefficient of concavity (or curvature) in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 272 (PDF page 278).

The handbook gives \(C_c = (D_{30})^2/(D_{10} \times D_{60})\), where \(D_{\#\#}\) is the grain diameter in mm at ##% passing by weight.

$$\begin{aligned}C_c &= \frac{(0.60)^2}{(0.15)(1.50)} \\ &= \frac{0.36}{0.225} \\ &= 1.60\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The gravel limit for \(C_u\) is 4, not the 6 used for sands. Because \(C_u\) fails, GW is out even though \(C_c\) is inside 1 to 3.
questions.question: A clean gravel with less than 5% fines has \(D_{10} = 0.40\) mm, \(D_{30} = 1.1\) mm and \(D_{60} = 1.3\) mm. Which USCS group symbol applies?
questions.solution:
Refer to the USCS criteria table in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 273 (PDF page 279).

$$\begin{aligned}C_u &= \frac{D_{60}}{D_{10}} \\ &= \frac{1.3}{0.40} \\ &= 3.25, \quad C_c \\ &= \frac{(1.1)^2}{(0.40)(1.3)} \\ &= 2.33\end{aligned}$$

For clean gravels the table requires \(C_u \ge 4\) and \(1 \le C_c \le 3\) for GW. Here \(C_u = 3.25 < 4\), so the gravel is poorly graded: GP.

questions.explanation: A-7-6 needs \(PI > LL - 30 = 15\). A-6 and A-5 have \(LL \le 40\) in the table, so they do not fit \(LL = 45\).
questions.question: A soil has more than 36% passing the No. 200 sieve, a liquid limit of 45 and a plasticity index of 14. Using the AASHTO classification table, what is the group?
questions.solution:
Refer to the AASHTO soil classification table in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 272 (PDF page 278).

With 36% or more passing the No. 200 sieve and \(LL \ge 41\), the soil is A-7 when \(PI \ge 11\). The footnote splits the group: A-7-5 when \(PI \le LL - 30\), A-7-6 when \(PI > LL - 30\).

$$LL - 30 = 45 - 30 = 15$$

\(PI = 14 \le 15\), so the soil is A-7-5.

questions.explanation: The void ratio 0.65 is voids over solids, while porosity is voids over total volume. \(1/(1+e)\) is the solids fraction.
questions.question: A soil has a void ratio of 0.65. What is its porosity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Phase Relationships in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 265 (PDF page 271).

The handbook gives porosity \(n = V_V/V = e/(1 + e)\).

$$n = \frac{0.65}{1 + 0.65} = 0.394$$

questions.explanation: Porosity is voids over total volume. Void ratio is voids over solids, so it is larger than \(n\). 0.58 is the solids fraction.
questions.question: A soil has a porosity of 0.42. What is its void ratio?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Phase Relationships in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 265 (PDF page 271).

The handbook gives \(n = e/(1 + e)\). Solving that for \(e\) (algebra, not printed in the handbook) gives \(e = n/(1 - n)\).

$$e = \frac{0.42}{1 - 0.42} = 0.724$$

questions.explanation: 97.2 is the dry unit weight formula (no \(e\) in the numerator). 60.9 is the submerged unit weight.
questions.question: A saturated soil has \(G_s = 2.68\) and a void ratio of 0.72. Using \(\gamma_w = 62.4\) lb/ft³, what is the saturated unit weight?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Saturated unit weight in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 265 (PDF page 271).

The handbook gives \(\gamma_{sat} = \dfrac{(G_s + e)\gamma_w}{1 + e}\).

$$\begin{aligned}\gamma_{sat} &= \frac{(2.68 + 0.72)(62.4)}{1 + 0.72} \\ &= 123.3\ \text{lb/ft}^3\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 19.07 is the saturated unit weight. The effective unit weight subtracts the unit weight of water.
questions.question: A saturated soil has \(G_s = 2.70\) and a void ratio of 0.80. Using \(\gamma_w = 9.81\) kN/m³, what is the effective (submerged) unit weight?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Saturated unit weight and Effective (submerged) unit weight in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 265 (PDF page 271).

$$\begin{aligned}\gamma_{sat} &= \frac{(G_s + e)\gamma_w}{1 + e} \\ &= \frac{(2.70 + 0.80)(9.81)}{1 + 0.80} \\ &= 19.07\ \text{kN/m}^3\end{aligned}$$

The handbook gives \(\gamma' = \gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w\).

$$\gamma' = 19.07 - 9.81 = 9.26\ \text{kN/m}^3$$

questions.explanation: Using \(e/(\omega G_s)\) flips the ratio. A degree of saturation cannot exceed 100%, which also rules out that choice here.
questions.question: A soil sample has a water content of 22%, \(G_s = 2.70\) and a void ratio of 0.70. What is the degree of saturation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Degree of saturation in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 266 (PDF page 272).

The handbook gives \(S = \omega G_S / e\) (with \(\omega\) as a decimal).

$$\begin{aligned}S &= \frac{(0.22)(2.70)}{0.70} \\ &= 0.8486 \rightarrow 84.9\%\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 13.6% divides by the total weight. Water content divides by the dry weight.
questions.question: A soil sample weighs 3.30 lb at its natural moisture content and 2.85 lb after oven drying. What is its water content?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Water content (%) in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 265 (PDF page 271).

The handbook gives \(\omega = (W_W/W_S) \times 100\), where \(W_S\) is the weight of solids.

$$\begin{aligned}W_W &= 3.30 - 2.85 \\ &= 0.45\ \text{lb}, \quad \omega \\ &= \frac{0.45}{2.85}(100) \\ &= 15.8\%\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Multiplying by \(1 - \omega\) gives 109.2, which is close but wrong. Water content is based on dry weight, so divide by \(1 + \omega\).
questions.question: A soil has a total unit weight of 127 lb/ft³ and a water content of 14%. What is its dry unit weight?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Total unit weight, Dry unit weight and Water content in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 265 (PDF page 271).

The handbook defines \(\gamma = W/V\), \(\gamma_D = W_S/V\) and \(\omega = W_W/W_S\). Since \(W = W_S(1 + \omega)\), the dry unit weight is \(\gamma_D = \gamma/(1 + \omega)\). That last step is derived from the definitions and is not printed in the handbook.

$$\begin{aligned}\gamma_D &= \frac{127}{1 + 0.14} \\ &= 111.4\ \text{lb/ft}^3\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Dry unit weight from total unit weight and water content

questions.explanation: 0.496 is the porosity (voids over total volume). Void ratio uses the solids volume in the denominator.
questions.question: A soil specimen of total volume 1.2 ft³ contains 100 lb of solids. The specific gravity of solids is 2.65. Using \(\gamma_w = 62.4\) lb/ft³, what is the void ratio?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Specific gravity of soil solids and Void ratio in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 265 (PDF page 271).

The handbook gives \(G_S = (W_S/V_S)/\gamma_W\), so \(V_S = W_S/(G_S\gamma_W)\).

$$\begin{aligned}V_S &= \frac{100}{(2.65)(62.4)} \\ &= 0.6047\ \text{ft}^3, \quad V_V \\ &= 1.2 - 0.6047 \\ &= 0.5953\ \text{ft}^3\end{aligned}$$

\(e = V_V/V_S\):

$$e = \frac{0.5953}{0.6047} = 0.984$$
questions.subtopic: Void ratio from weight of solids

questions.explanation: 127.4 divides by 0.95 and exceeds the lab maximum, which a field fill cannot normally reach.
questions.question: The specification requires 95% relative compaction. The laboratory maximum dry unit weight is 121 lb/ft³. What minimum field dry unit weight must the contractor achieve?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Relative compaction (%) in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 266 (PDF page 272).

From \(RC = (\gamma_{D\ field}/\gamma_{D\ max}) \times 100\):

$$\begin{aligned}\gamma_{D\ field} &= 0.95(\gamma_{D\ max}) \\ &= 0.95(121) \\ &= 115.0\ \text{lb/ft}^3\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 36.2% measures from \(e_{min}\) instead of \(e_{max}\). That gives how loose the sand is, not how dense.
questions.question: A sand has \(e_{max} = 0.92\) and \(e_{min} = 0.45\). In the field its void ratio is 0.62. What is the relative density?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Relative density in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 266 (PDF page 272).

The handbook gives \(D_r = [(e_{max} - e)/(e_{max} - e_{min})] \times 100\).

$$\begin{aligned}D_r &= \frac{0.92 - 0.62}{0.92 - 0.45}(100) \\ &= 63.8\%\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 61.1% leaves out the \(\gamma_{D\ max}/\gamma_{D\ field}\) factor. The unit-weight form is not a straight interpolation.
questions.question: A sand has \(\gamma_{D\ min} = 94\), \(\gamma_{D\ max} = 112\) and a field \(\gamma_{D\ field} = 105\), all in lb/ft³. What is the relative density?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Relative density in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 266 (PDF page 272).

The handbook gives the unit-weight form \(D_r = [(\gamma_{D\ field} - \gamma_{D\ min})/(\gamma_{D\ max} - \gamma_{D\ min})][\gamma_{D\ max}/\gamma_{D\ field}] \times 100\).

$$\begin{aligned}D_r &= \left(\frac{105 - 94}{112 - 94}\right)\left(\frac{112}{105}\right)(100) \\ &= (0.6111)(1.0667)(100) \\ &= 65.2\%\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Relative density from dry unit weights

questions.explanation: 1,825 psf is the total stress. Pore pressure acts over the 10 ft below the water table only, not over the full depth.
questions.question: A soil profile has 5 ft of moist soil (\(\gamma = 115\) lb/ft³) above the water table and 10 ft of saturated soil (\(\gamma_{sat} = 125\) lb/ft³) below it, as shown. Using \(\gamma_w = 62.4\) lb/ft³, what is the effective vertical stress at point A, at the bottom of the saturated layer?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Stress Profiles in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 270 (PDF page 276).

The handbook profile gives \(\sigma = \gamma_1 H_1 + \gamma_2 H_2\), \(u = \gamma_w H_2\) and \(\sigma' = \sigma - u\).

$$\begin{aligned}\sigma &= (115)(5) + (125)(10) \\ &= 1{,}825\ \text{psf}\end{aligned}$$

$$u = (62.4)(10) = 624\ \text{psf}$$

$$\sigma' = 1{,}825 - 624 = 1{,}201\ \text{psf}$$
questions.subtopic: Effective vertical stress with a water table

questions.explanation: 691.2 psf leaves out the surcharge. A surcharge raises both total stress and effective stress; it does not change the pore pressure here.
questions.question: A 12-ft sand layer (\(\gamma_{sat} = 120\) lb/ft³) lies below a water table at the ground surface. A uniform surcharge of 400 psf is applied at the surface, as shown. Using \(\gamma_w = 62.4\) lb/ft³, what is the effective vertical stress at point B at the bottom of the layer?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Stress Profiles with Surcharge in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 270 (PDF page 276).

The handbook gives \(\sigma' = S + [(\gamma_2)(H_2)] - (\gamma_w H_2)\) for a saturated layer, with surcharge \(S\) acting in both total and effective stress.

$$\begin{aligned}\sigma' &= 400 + (120)(12) - (62.4)(12) \\ &= 400 + 1440 - 748.8 \\ &= 1{,}091.2\ \text{psf}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Pore pressure carries part of the total stress, so effective stress is smaller than total stress. Adding the pore pressure reverses the relationship.
questions.question: At a point in a clay layer the total vertical stress is 2,400 psf. A piezometer at that point shows water standing 25 ft above it. Using \(\gamma_w = 62.4\) lb/ft³, what is the effective vertical stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Effective stress in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 269 (PDF page 275).

The handbook gives \(\sigma' = \sigma - u\) with \(u = h_u\gamma_w\).

$$\begin{aligned}u &= (25)(62.4) \\ &= 1{,}560\ \text{psf}, \quad \sigma' \\ &= 2{,}400 - 1{,}560 \\ &= 840\ \text{psf}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 3.255 is the passive coefficient. 0.470 is the at-rest coefficient \(K_0\). 0.554 forgot to square the tangent.
questions.question: A smooth wall retains level, cohesionless backfill with an angle of internal friction of 32°. What is the Rankine active earth pressure coefficient?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Active forces on retaining wall in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 269 (PDF page 275).

The handbook gives \(K_A = \tan^2(45° - \phi/2)\).

$$\begin{aligned}K_A &= \tan^2(45° - 32°/2) \\ &= \tan^2(29°) \\ &= (0.5543)^2 \\ &= 0.307\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 0.36 is \(K_A\), the active coefficient. 1.66 is the unsquared tangent.
questions.question: What is the Rankine passive earth pressure coefficient for a smooth wall and level, cohesionless backfill with \(\phi = 28°\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Passive forces on retaining wall in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 269 (PDF page 275).

The handbook gives \(K_P = \tan^2(45° + \phi/2)\).

$$K_P = \tan^2(59°) = (1.6643)^2 = 2.77$$

questions.explanation: 7,709 drops the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) from the triangular pressure diagram. 275 is the pressure at the base, not the force. Dividing by \(K_A\) gives a passive-type value.
questions.question: A smooth 14-ft-high wall retains level backfill with \(\gamma = 118\) lb/ft³ and \(\phi = 30°\), as shown. Ignoring groundwater, what is the Rankine active force per foot of wall length?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Stress Profiles and Forces in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 269 (PDF page 275).

The handbook gives \(K_A = \tan^2(45° - \phi/2)\) and, for one soil layer with no water, \(P_A = \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma H^2 K_A\) per unit wall length.

$$K_A = \tan^2(45° - 15°) = 0.3333$$

$$\begin{aligned}P_A &= \tfrac{1}{2}(118)(14)^2(0.3333) \\ &= 3{,}855\ \text{lb/ft}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Active force on a retaining wall

questions.explanation: 0.50 is the normally consolidated value, \(1 - \sin\phi\). 2.00 multiplies by OCR instead of raising it to the power \(\sin\phi\). 0.33 is the Rankine active coefficient.
questions.question: A clay has \(\phi = 30°\) and an overconsolidation ratio of 4. Using the handbook relation, what is the at-rest earth pressure coefficient \(K_0\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the At-rest forces on wall per unit length of wall in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 269 (PDF page 275).

For an overconsolidated soil the handbook gives \(K_0 = (1 - \sin\phi)\,OCR^{\sin\phi}\).

$$\begin{aligned}K_0 &= (1 - \sin 30°)(4)^{\sin 30°} \\ &= (0.50)(4)^{0.5} \\ &= (0.50)(2.0) \\ &= 1.00\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 0.33 inverts the ratio. A safe wall has resisting moment larger than overturning moment, so FS is above 1.
questions.question: A retaining wall has a resisting moment of 18,400 ft-lb per foot of wall about the toe and an overturning moment of 6,100 ft-lb per foot about the toe. What is the factor of safety against overturning?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Retaining Walls in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 270 (PDF page 276).

The handbook gives \(FS_{overturning} = \Sigma M_R / \Sigma M_O\).

$$\begin{aligned}FS_{overturning} &= \frac{18{,}400}{6{,}100} \\ &= 3.02\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 1.40 leaves out the passive resistance. 4.15 skips the friction factor \(\tan\delta\), which converts vertical load to a sliding resistance.
questions.question: A retaining wall carries a total vertical force \(\Sigma V = 15{,}000\) lb/ft. The base friction angle is \(\delta = 20°\), adhesion is neglected (\(C_a = 0\)), the horizontal active force is \(P_A = 3{,}900\) lb/ft acting horizontally (\(\alpha = 0\)), and the passive resistance is \(P_P = 1{,}200\) lb/ft, as shown. What is the factor of safety against sliding?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Retaining Walls in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 270 (PDF page 276).

The handbook gives \(FS_{sliding} = \dfrac{(\Sigma V)\tan\delta + C_a B + P_p}{P_a \cos\alpha}\).

$$\begin{aligned}FS_{sliding} &= \frac{(15{,}000)\tan 20° + 0 + 1{,}200}{(3{,}900)\cos 0°} \\ &= \frac{5{,}459.6 + 1{,}200}{3{,}900} \\ &= 1.71\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 1,063 psf leaves out the cohesion. Using \(\sin\phi\) in place of \(\tan\phi\) is a common slip.
questions.question: A soil has cohesion \(c = 300\) psf and an angle of internal friction \(\phi = 28°\). What shear stress at failure develops on a plane with a normal stress of 2,000 psf?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Shear stress at failure in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 269 (PDF page 275).

The handbook gives \(\tau_F = c + \sigma_N \tan\phi\).

$$\begin{aligned}\tau_F &= 300 + (2{,}000)\tan 28° \\ &= 300 + 1{,}063.4 \\ &= 1{,}363\ \text{psf}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 125.0 kPa is the normal stress, not the shear stress. Multiplying the force by \(\tan\phi\) before dividing by the area mixes units: the cohesion is a stress, so convert the force to stress first.
questions.question: In a direct shear test, a normal force of 450 N acts on a square specimen 60 mm by 60 mm. The soil has \(c = 10\) kPa and \(\phi = 30°\). What shear stress is needed to fail the specimen?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Total normal stress and Shear stress at failure in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 269 (PDF page 275).

The handbook gives \(\sigma_N = P/A\) and \(\tau_F = c + \sigma_N\tan\phi\).

$$\begin{aligned}A &= (0.060)(0.060) \\ &= 0.0036\ \text{m}^2, \quad \sigma_N \\ &= \frac{450}{0.0036} \\ &= 125{,}000\ \text{Pa} \\ &= 125\ \text{kPa}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\tau_F &= 10 + (125)\tan 30° \\ &= 10 + 72.2 \\ &= 82.2\ \text{kPa}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Using \(\tan 30°\) assumes a friction angle the data do not give. Using 48 kPa takes the first shear stress as cohesion. A line through the origin and the second point ignores the intercept.
questions.question: Two direct shear tests on the same soil give these failure points: \(\sigma_N = 50\) kPa with \(\tau_F = 48\) kPa, and \(\sigma_N = 120\) kPa with \(\tau_F = 82\) kPa. Assuming a straight Mohr-Coulomb envelope, what is the cohesion?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Shear stress at failure in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 269 (PDF page 275).

The handbook line is \(\tau_F = c + \sigma_N\tan\phi\). Two points fix the slope and the intercept.

$$\begin{aligned}\tan\phi &= \frac{82 - 48}{120 - 50} \\ &= 0.4857 \quad (\phi \\ &= 25.9°)\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}c &= \tau_F - \sigma_N\tan\phi \\ &= 48 - (50)(0.4857) \\ &= 23.7\ \text{kPa}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Cohesion from two direct shear tests

questions.explanation: 6,624 is only the depth term. 17,376 drops the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) in the unit-weight term.
questions.question: A strip footing has a base width of \(B = 4\) ft, and the base bearing surface is \(D_f = 3\) ft below the ground surface in cohesionless soil (\(c = 0\)) with \(\gamma = 120\) lb/ft³. The groundwater table is far below the footing. For this soil \(N_q = 18.4\) and \(N_\gamma = 22.4\). Using the handbook equation, what is the ultimate bearing capacity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Ultimate Bearing Capacity in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 270 (PDF page 276).

The handbook gives \(q_{ULT} = cN_c + \gamma' D_f N_q + \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma' B N_\gamma\). With \(c = 0\) and no groundwater near the footing, \(\gamma' = \gamma = 120\) lb/ft³.

$$\begin{aligned}q_{ULT} &= 0 + (120)(3)(18.4) \\ &\quad + \tfrac{1}{2}(120)(4)(22.4) \\ &= 6{,}624 + 5{,}376 \\ &= 12{,}000\ \text{psf}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 0.36 inverts the ratio. 0.69 compares a pressure with a line load, which have different units.
questions.question: A strip footing 4 ft wide has an ultimate bearing capacity of 9,600 psf. It carries a line load of 14 kips per foot of footing length. Treating the pressure as uniform, what is the factor of safety against bearing capacity failure?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Retaining Walls, factor of safety against bearing capacity in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 270 (PDF page 276).

The handbook gives \(FS = q_{ULT}/q\) for bearing capacity (the retaining-wall equation uses \(q_{toe}\); a uniform pressure takes its place here). Bearing pressure is load per area, with a 1-ft strip.

$$\begin{aligned}q &= \frac{14{,}000\ \text{lb/ft}}{4\ \text{ft}} \\ &= 3,500\ \text{psf}\end{aligned}$$

$$FS = \frac{9{,}600}{3{,}500} = 2.74$$
questions.subtopic: Factor of safety against bearing failure

questions.explanation: 10,200 uses the saturated unit weight in both terms and ignores buoyancy. The other two choices use the effective weight in only one term.
questions.question: A strip footing has a base width of \(B = 5\) ft, and the base bearing surface is \(D_f = 3\) ft below the ground surface in cohesionless soil (\(c = 0\)). The water table is at the ground surface and \(\gamma_{sat} = 125\) lb/ft³. For this soil \(N_q = 14.7\) and \(N_\gamma = 15.0\). Using \(\gamma_w = 62.4\) lb/ft³, what is the ultimate bearing capacity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Ultimate Bearing Capacity in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 270 (PDF page 276).

The handbook equation is \(q_{ULT} = cN_c + \gamma' D_f N_q + \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma' B N_\gamma\), and \(\gamma'\) is the effective unit weight. Both soil terms are below the water table, so both use \(\gamma' = \gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w\) (page 265).

$$\begin{aligned}\gamma' &= 125 - 62.4 \\ &= 62.6\ \text{lb/ft}^3\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}q_{ULT} &= (62.6)(3)(14.7) \\ &\quad + \tfrac{1}{2}(62.6)(5)(15.0) \\ &= 2{,}761 + 2{,}348 \\ &= 5{,}108\ \text{psf}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Bearing capacity with a high water table

questions.explanation: 6,840 leaves out the overburden term. 9,462 uses \(N_c\) where \(N_q\) belongs.
questions.question: A strip footing in saturated clay (\(\phi = 0\)) has \(c = 1{,}200\) psf and \(\gamma = 115\) lb/ft³. The base is 4 ft below the ground surface and groundwater is deep. For \(\phi = 0\), \(N_c = 5.7\), \(N_q = 1.0\) and \(N_\gamma = 0\). What is the ultimate bearing capacity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Ultimate Bearing Capacity in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 270 (PDF page 276).

The handbook gives \(q_{ULT} = cN_c + \gamma' D_f N_q + \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma' B N_\gamma\). With \(N_\gamma = 0\) the width term drops out.

$$\begin{aligned}q_{ULT} &= (1{,}200)(5.7) + (115)(4)(1.0) + 0 \\ &= 6{,}840 + 460 \\ &= 7{,}300\ \text{psf}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 0.468 forgets to subtract 10. 0.063 divides by 6, which is the recompression relation.
questions.question: A clay has a liquid limit of 52. Using the handbook correlation, what is the approximate compression index \(C_C\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Compression index in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 267 (PDF page 273).

The handbook gives \(C_C = 0.009(LL - 10)\).

$$C_C = 0.009(52 - 10) = 0.378$$

questions.explanation: Recompression happens along the flatter part of the curve, so \(C_R\) is smaller than \(C_C\). Multiplying by 6 reverses that.
questions.question: A clay has a compression index \(C_C = 0.42\). Using the handbook correlation, what is the approximate recompression index \(C_R\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Recompression index in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 267 (PDF page 273).

The handbook gives \(C_R = C_C/6\).

$$C_R = \frac{0.42}{6} = 0.07$$

questions.explanation: 0.37 is the answer in feet, not inches. The natural log gives 10.2 in. The handbook equation uses base-10 log. Dropping the \(1 + e_o\) denominator gives 8.6 in.
questions.question: A 10-ft layer of normally consolidated clay has \(e_0 = 0.95\) and \(C_C = 0.3\). At mid-depth the initial effective stress is 1,500 psf and the load raises it to 2,600 psf, as shown. Using the mid-depth stress for the whole layer, what is the primary consolidation settlement?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Settlement equations in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 267 (PDF page 273).

For a normally consolidated layer (\(\sigma'_0 \ge \sigma'_c\) and \(\sigma'_f \ge \sigma'_c\)) the handbook gives \(\Delta H = \dfrac{H_o}{1 + e_o}\,C_C \log\dfrac{\sigma'_f}{\sigma'_0}\).

$$\begin{aligned}\Delta H &= \frac{10}{1 + 0.95}(0.3)\log\frac{2{,}600}{1{,}500} \\ &= (1.5385)(0.3)(0.2389) \\ &= 0.3675\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

$$\Delta H = (0.3675)(12) = 4.4\ \text{in}$$
questions.subtopic: Primary consolidation settlement, normally consolidated clay

questions.explanation: 3.38 in uses \(C_C\) although the stress never passes \(\sigma'_c\). 0.78 in stops at \(\sigma'_c\) instead of the final stress.
questions.question: An overconsolidated clay layer 8 ft thick has \(e_0 = 0.80\), \(C_C = 0.36\), \(\sigma'_0 = 2{,}000\) psf and a preconsolidation stress \(\sigma'_c = 3{,}500\) psf. A new load raises the stress to \(\sigma'_f = 3{,}000\) psf. Using \(C_R = C_C/6\), what is the primary consolidation settlement?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Settlement equations and Recompression index in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 267 (PDF page 273).
