Here \(\sigma'_0 < \sigma'_c\) and \(\sigma'_f < \sigma'_c\), so the whole change is in the recompression range. The handbook gives \(\Delta H = \dfrac{H_o}{1 + e_o}\,C_R \log\dfrac{\sigma'_f}{\sigma'_0}\) with \(C_R = C_C/6 = 0.06\).

$$\begin{aligned}\Delta H &= \frac{8}{1 + 0.80}(0.06)\log\frac{3{,}000}{2{,}000} \\ &= (4.4444)(0.06)(0.1761) \\ &= 0.0470\ \text{ft} \\ &= 0.56\ \text{in}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Using \(C_C\) for the whole range overstates settlement. Using \(C_R\) for the whole range understates it. Using only the virgin-compression part leaves out the recompression from \(\sigma'_0\) to \(\sigma'_c\).
questions.question: A clay layer 5 m thick has \(e_0 = 0.90\), \(C_C = 0.45\) and \(C_R = 0.075\). The initial effective stress is 80 kPa and the preconsolidation stress is 120 kPa. A new load raises the effective stress to 200 kPa. What is the primary consolidation settlement?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Settlement equations in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 267 (PDF page 273).

Because \(\sigma'_0 < \sigma'_c < \sigma'_f\), the handbook gives \(\Delta H = \dfrac{H_o}{1 + e_o}\left[C_R \log\dfrac{\sigma'_c}{\sigma'_0} + C_C \log\dfrac{\sigma'_f}{\sigma'_c}\right]\).

$$\begin{aligned}\Delta H &= \frac{5}{1 + 0.90}\Big[0.075\log\frac{120}{80} \\ &\quad + 0.45\log\frac{200}{120}\Big] \\ &= (2.6316)[0.01321 + 0.09983]\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\Delta H &= 0.2975\ \text{m} = 297\ \text{mm}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 3.68 uses the full 6 m as the drainage path, which is right only for one-way drainage. 8.29 multiplies by \(c_v\) instead of dividing.
questions.question: A 6-m clay layer drains at both its top and bottom. Its coefficient of consolidation is \(c_v = 3.0\) m²/year. How long does it take to reach 62% average consolidation? Use the handbook time-factor table.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Variation of time factor with degree of consolidation in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 268 (PDF page 274).

The table gives \(T_v = 0.307\) at \(U = 62\%\). With drainage at both faces the drainage path is half the layer thickness, \(H_{dr} = 6/2 = 3\) m. The handbook defines \(T_v = c_v t / H_{dr}^2\), so \(t = T_v H_{dr}^2/c_v\).

$$\begin{aligned}t &= \frac{(0.307)(3)^2}{3.0} \\ &= 0.921\ \text{years}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 91.2 mm is the settlement still to come. Dividing by the fraction gives a value larger than the ultimate settlement, which cannot be right.
questions.question: The ultimate consolidation settlement of a clay layer is 240 mm. What is the approximate settlement when the average degree of consolidation is 62%?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Approximate settlement (at time t = tC) in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 267 (PDF page 273).

The handbook gives \(S_T = U_{AV} S_{ULT}\).

$$S_T = (0.62)(240) = 148.8\ \text{mm}$$
questions.subtopic: Settlement at a given degree of consolidation

questions.explanation: 480 mm leaves out the \(1 + e_0\) divisor. Strain is change in void ratio over the initial total (solids plus voids) volume, so the denominator is \(1 + e_0\).
questions.question: A 4.0-m clay layer has an initial void ratio of 0.85. Loading changes the void ratio by a total of 0.12 (recompression plus virgin compression). What is the ultimate consolidation settlement?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Ultimate consolidation settlement in soil layer in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 267 (PDF page 273).

The handbook gives \(S_{ULT} = \varepsilon_v H_S\) with \(\varepsilon_v = \Delta e_{TOT}/(1 + e_0)\).

$$\begin{aligned}\varepsilon_v &= \frac{0.12}{1 + 0.85} \\ &= 0.06486, \quad S_{ULT} \\ &= (0.06486)(4.0) \\ &= 0.2595\ \text{m} \\ &= 259\ \text{mm}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Ultimate settlement from void ratio change

questions.explanation: 1.48 counts cohesion only. 0.41 inverts the ratio. Swapping \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) on the weight components gives 0.90.
questions.question: A soil wedge above an assumed planar slip surface weighs \(W_M = 12{,}000\) lb per foot measured perpendicular to the page (out-of-plane width), not along the slope. The slip surface is inclined at \(\alpha_S = 25°\) to the horizontal and is \(L_S = 30\) ft long, as shown. The soil has \(c = 250\) psf and \(\phi = 24°\). What is the factor of safety against slope instability?
questions.solution:
Refer to the slope failure along a planar surface in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 271 (PDF page 277).

The handbook gives \(FS = T_{FF}/T_{MOB}\), with \(T_{FF} = cL_S + W_M\cos\alpha_S\tan\phi\) and \(T_{MOB} = W_M\sin\alpha_S\).

$$\begin{aligned}T_{FF} &= (250)(30) \\ &\quad + (12{,}000)\cos 25°\tan 24° \\ &= 7{,}500 + 4{,}842 \\ &= 12{,}342\ \text{lb/ft}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}T_{MOB} &= (12{,}000)\sin 25° \\ &= 5{,}071\ \text{lb/ft}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}FS &= \frac{12{,}342}{5{,}071} = 2.43\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Planar slope failure, factor of safety

questions.explanation: 0.63 leaves out cohesion. 2.21 drops \(\tan\phi\) from the friction term.
questions.question: For a planar slip surface, \(W_M = 900\) kN/m, \(\alpha_S = 30°\), \(L_S = 18\) m, \(c = 12\) kPa and \(\phi = 20°\). What is the factor of safety?
questions.solution:
Refer to the slope failure along a planar surface in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 271 (PDF page 277).

The handbook gives \(FS = T_{FF}/T_{MOB}\).

$$\begin{aligned}T_{FF} &= cL_S + W_M\cos\alpha_S\tan\phi \\ &= (12)(18) + (900)\cos 30°\tan 20° \\ &= 216 + 283.7 \\ &= 499.7\ \text{kN/m}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}T_{MOB} &= W_M\sin\alpha_S \\ &= (900)\sin 30° \\ &= 450\ \text{kN/m}\end{aligned}$$

$$FS = \frac{499.7}{450} = 1.11$$
questions.subtopic: Planar slope failure in SI units

questions.explanation: 0.72 inverts the ratio. 1.31 divides the angles directly, which is not how the safety factor works.
questions.question: A dry, cohesionless sand slope (\(c = 0\)) is analyzed for sliding along a planar surface at \(\alpha_S = 26°\). The friction angle is \(\phi = 34°\). What is the factor of safety?
questions.solution:
Refer to the slope failure along a planar surface in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 271 (PDF page 277).

Set \(c = 0\) in the handbook equations. Then \(T_{FF} = W_M\cos\alpha_S\tan\phi\) and \(T_{MOB} = W_M\sin\alpha_S\), so the weight cancels (algebra, not printed in the handbook):

$$\begin{aligned}FS &= \frac{\cos\alpha_S\tan\phi}{\sin\alpha_S} \\ &= \frac{\tan\phi}{\tan\alpha_S} \\ &= \frac{\tan 34°}{\tan 26°} \\ &= \frac{0.6745}{0.4877} \\ &= 1.38\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Infinite-type planar slide in clean sand

questions.explanation: 14,095 is the component normal to the slip surface, \(W_M\cos\alpha_S\), which drives friction. Only the component along the surface is mobilized.
questions.question: A soil mass weighing 15,000 lb per foot of slope sits on a planar slip surface inclined at 20° to the horizontal. What is the mobilized shear force along the slip surface?
questions.solution:
Refer to the slope failure along a planar surface in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), Civil Engineering: Geotechnical, printed page 271 (PDF page 277).

The handbook gives \(T_{MOB} = W_M\sin\alpha_S\).

$$\begin{aligned}T_{MOB} &= (15{,}000)\sin 20° \\ &= 5{,}130\ \text{lb/ft}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Mobilized shear force on a slip plane

questions.explanation: Using P/F gives the present worth factor, which shrinks the amount. F/A is for a series of equal payments. Simple interest would give $11,200.
questions.question: A deposit of $8,000 earns 4% interest per year, compounded annually. Using the handbook interest-rate table, what is the balance after 10 years?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics interest-rate table for i = 4% in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 240 (PDF page 246), and the factor formulas, printed page 235 (PDF page 241). 

The factor \((F/P, 4\%, 10)\) converts a present amount to a future amount.

$$\begin{aligned}F &= P(F/P, 4\%, 10) \\ &= (8{,}000)(1.4802) \\ &= \$11{,}842\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Single payment compound amount from the table

questions.explanation: Compounding the future value forward answers a different question and gives a number larger than the target. A/F is the annual deposit factor.
questions.question: A city needs $50,000 in 15 years for a bridge replacement fund. At 8% interest compounded annually, how much must be set aside today?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics interest-rate table for i = 8% in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 241 (PDF page 247), and the factor formulas, printed page 235 (PDF page 241). 

$$\begin{aligned}P &= F(P/F, 8\%, 15) \\ &= (50{,}000)(0.3152) \\ &= \$15{,}760\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Present worth of a future sum

questions.explanation: The sinking fund factor gives $2,628, which leaves out the interest on the borrowed balance. Dividing by n ignores interest completely.
questions.question: A contractor finances $120,000 of equipment with a 20-year loan at 8% per year, paid in equal annual payments at the end of each year. What is the annual payment?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics interest-rate table for i = 8% in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 241 (PDF page 247), and the factor formulas, printed page 235 (PDF page 241). 

The capital recovery factor converts a present amount P to a uniform series A.

$$\begin{aligned}A &= P(A/P, 8\%, 20) \\ &= (120{,}000)(0.1019) \\ &= \$12{,}228\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Loan payment using the capital recovery factor

questions.explanation: A/P would be the payment that repays a present amount of $90,000. Equal deposits of $7,500 ignore the interest the account earns.
questions.question: A utility will deposit equal amounts at the end of each year for 12 years at 4% annual interest so that the account holds $90,000 immediately after the last deposit. What is each deposit?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics interest-rate table for i = 4% in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 240 (PDF page 246), and the factor formulas, printed page 235 (PDF page 241). 

$$\begin{aligned}A &= F(A/F, 4\%, 12) \\ &= (90{,}000)(0.0666) \\ &= \$5{,}994\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: P/A gives the present worth of the same series. Adding the deposits without interest gives $25,000.
questions.question: An engineer deposits $2,500 at the end of each year for 10 years into an account that pays 12% per year. What is the balance right after the last deposit?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics interest-rate table for i = 12% in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 242 (PDF page 248), and the factor formulas, printed page 235 (PDF page 241). 

$$\begin{aligned}F &= A(F/A, 12\%, 10) \\ &= (2{,}500)(17.5487) \\ &= \$43{,}872\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Future worth of an annual series

questions.explanation: The F/A factor gives the future worth at the end of the lease. The simple total of $7,200 ignores the time value of money.
questions.question: A lease requires $300 at the end of each month for 24 months. The interest rate is 1.5% per month. What is the present worth of the lease payments?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics interest-rate table for i = 1.5% in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 239 (PDF page 245), and the factor formulas, printed page 235 (PDF page 241). The rate is per month, so n counts months.

$$\begin{aligned}P &= A(P/A, 1.5\%, 24) \\ &= (300)(20.0304) \\ &= \$6{,}009\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: A/G converts the gradient to an equivalent uniform annual amount ($3,871); it is not a present worth. P/A treats $1,000 as a level annual cost.
questions.question: Maintenance cost on a pump is $0 in year 1 and increases by $1,000 each year after that (year 2 = $1,000, year 3 = $2,000, and so on) through year 10. At 8% interest, what is the present worth of these costs?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics interest-rate table for i = 8% in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 241 (PDF page 247), and the factor formulas, printed page 235 (PDF page 241). The gradient factor assumes the first gradient amount arrives at the end of year 2.

$$\begin{aligned}P &= G(P/G, 8\%, 10) \\ &= (1{,}000)(25.9768) \\ &= \$25{,}977\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Present worth of a gradient series

questions.explanation: Averaging the costs without interest gives $2,250. P/G gives a present worth, not an annual amount.
questions.question: Annual repair costs for a vehicle start at $0 in year 1 and rise by $500 each year through year 10. At 4% interest, what is the equivalent uniform annual cost?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics interest-rate table for i = 4% in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 240 (PDF page 246), and the factor formulas, printed page 235 (PDF page 241). 

$$\begin{aligned}A &= G(A/G, 4\%, 10) \\ &= (500)(4.1773) = \$2{,}089\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Equivalent annual amount of a gradient

questions.explanation: The quoted 10% would only be effective with annual compounding. 5% is the rate per half year. 10.38% assumes quarterly compounding.
questions.question: A bond fund quotes 10% per year compounded semiannually. What is its effective annual yield?
questions.solution:
Use \(i_e = (1 + r/m)^m - 1\) from the Non-Annual Compounding section, Engineering Economics, printed page 236 (PDF page 242).

$$\begin{aligned}i_e &= (1 + 0.10/2)^2 - 1 \\ &= 0.1025 = 10.25\%\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Adding the rates without the cross term gives 13%. Subtracting gives 5%. The ratio form 4.81% is the real rate, which is the other direction.
questions.question: A project is evaluated in then-current dollars. The market interest rate is 9% per year and general inflation is 4% per year. What inflation-adjusted rate d should be used to find present worth?
questions.solution:
The handbook gives \(d = i + f + (i \times f)\) in the Inflation section, Engineering Economics, printed page 236 (PDF page 242).

$$\begin{aligned}d &= 0.09 + 0.04 + (0.09)(0.04) \\ &= 0.1336 = 13.36\%\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The bond sells below face value because its coupon rate is lower than the required yield. Dropping the face-value payment or using F/P on it gives wrong results.
questions.question: A bond with a face value of $1,000 pays 6% interest each year ($60 per year) and matures in 10 years. Investors require an 8% yield. What is the bond value?
questions.solution:
Bond value is the present worth of the payments the holder receives (Bonds, Engineering Economics, printed page 236 (PDF page 242)). Use the 8% table, printed page 241 (PDF page 247).

$$\begin{aligned}V &= 60(P/A, 8\%, 10) \\ &\quad + 1{,}000(P/F, 8\%, 10) \\ &= 60(6.7101) + 1{,}000(0.4632) \\ &= \$866\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Bond value at a market yield

questions.explanation: Adding the salvage term instead of subtracting it overstates the cost. Ignoring salvage gives $7,450. Straight division by n ignores interest.
questions.question: A machine costs $50,000, lasts 10 years, and has a salvage value of $8,000. Ignoring operating costs, what is its equivalent uniform annual cost at 8% interest?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics interest-rate table for i = 8% in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 241 (PDF page 247), and the factor formulas, printed page 235 (PDF page 241). 

$$\begin{aligned}A &= P(A/P, 8\%, 10) - S(A/F, 8\%, 10) \\ &= (50{,}000)(0.1490) - (8{,}000)(0.0690) \\ &= \$6{,}898\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: A/F (the sinking fund factor) is smaller than A/P because it leaves out the interest on the unpaid balance.
questions.question: A truck costs $24,000 and is financed with equal monthly payments for 40 months. The interest rate is 0.5% per month. What is the monthly payment?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics interest-rate table for i = 0.5% in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 238 (PDF page 244), and the factor formulas, printed page 235 (PDF page 241). The rate and the period are both monthly.

$$\begin{aligned}A &= P(A/P, 0.5\%, 40) \\ &= (24{,}000)(0.0276) \\ &= \$662\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Monthly payment from a monthly rate

questions.explanation: At 4% the same investment would need only $2,246 per year, so $2,505 is a higher return. At 12% it would need $2,774.
questions.question: An investment of $10,000 returns $2,505 at the end of each year for 5 years. Which interest rate in the handbook tables is the rate of return?
questions.solution:
The rate of return is the interest rate that makes benefits equal costs (Rate-of-Return, printed page 236 (PDF page 242)). Compute \((A/P, i, 5) = 2505/10{,}000 = 0.2505\).

The 8% table, printed page 241 (PDF page 247), gives \((A/P, 8\%, 5) = 0.2505\). At 4% the factor is 0.2246 and at 12% it is 0.2774, so the rate is 8%.
questions.subtopic: Rate of return from a capital recovery factor

questions.explanation: Dividing by the price alone gives 4,000. Dividing by the variable cost alone gives 6,667. Each unit contributes price minus variable cost toward fixed cost.
questions.question: A plant has fixed costs of $120,000 per year. Variable cost is $18 per unit and each unit sells for $30. How many units must be sold per year to break even?
questions.solution:
Refer to Breakeven Analysis, Engineering Economics, printed page 236 (PDF page 242): the breakeven point is where income just covers expenses. Setting revenue equal to total cost: \(pc\,x = F + vc\,x\) (algebra, not printed in the handbook).

$$\begin{aligned}x &= \frac{F}{p - v} \\ &= \frac{120{,}000}{30 - 18} \\ &= 10{,}000\ \text{units}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 20.0% divides fixed cost by revenue only. 53.3% is the contribution margin, not the break-even point.
questions.question: At full capacity a plant earns revenue of $1,500,000 per year with variable costs of $700,000 and fixed costs of $300,000. At what percent of capacity does income just cover expenses?
questions.solution:
Breakeven analysis is described as the percentage of capacity at which income just covers expenses (Engineering Economics, printed page 236 (PDF page 242)). With revenue and variable cost both scaling with output, \(x\,(R - V) = F\) (algebra, not printed).

$$\begin{aligned}x &= \frac{300{,}000}{1{,}500{,}000 - 700{,}000} \\ &= 0.375 \\ &= 37.5\%\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Break-even as a percent of capacity

questions.explanation: Buying saves nothing on fixed cost but costs more per part, so the quantity depends on the per-part difference.
questions.question: A company can make a part with $50,000 of fixed cost per year plus $8 per part, or buy it for $14 per part with no fixed cost. At what annual quantity are the two options equally costly?
questions.solution:
This is a breakeven problem (Breakeven Analysis, Engineering Economics, printed page 236 (PDF page 242)): vary one quantity until the alternatives cost the same. Set \(F + v_m x = v_b x\) (algebra, not printed).

$$\begin{aligned}x &= \frac{F}{v_b - v_m} \\ &= \frac{50{,}000}{14 - 8} \\ &= 8{,}333\ \text{parts}\end{aligned}$$

Above this quantity making is cheaper.

questions.explanation: A simple payback period does not discount cash flows. 7.2 years comes from multiplying instead of dividing.
questions.question: A $60,000 energy retrofit saves $12,000 each year. What is the simple payback period?
questions.solution:
The handbook defines payback as the time for the benefits to equal the cost of the investment (Breakeven Analysis, printed page 236 (PDF page 242)).

$$\begin{aligned}\text{payback} &= \frac{60{,}000}{12{,}000} \\ &= 5.0\ \text{years}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Leaving out O&M gives 1.64. Dividing capital by life ignores interest and gives 2.22. The inverse 0.76 is the cost-benefit ratio.
questions.question: A flood-control project costs $2,400,000 to build, has annual O&M of $60,000, and produces annual benefits of $400,000. Use a 20-year life and 8% interest. What is the benefit-cost ratio?
questions.solution:
The handbook requires B/C \(\ge 1\) (Benefit-Cost Analysis, printed page 237 (PDF page 243)). Annualize the capital cost with the 8% table, printed page 241 (PDF page 247).

$$\begin{aligned}C &= 2{,}400{,}000(A/P, 8\%, 20) + 60{,}000 \\ &= 2{,}400{,}000(0.1019) + 60{,}000 \\ &= \$304{,}560\end{aligned}$$

$$B/C = \frac{400{,}000}{304{,}560} = 1.31$$

questions.explanation: 32% is the year 2 rate and 11.52% is the year 4 rate. Straight-line would give $16,000.
questions.question: Equipment costing $80,000 is 5-year MACRS property. What is the depreciation in year 3?
questions.solution:
Use the MACRS factors in the handbook, Engineering Economics, printed page 237 (PDF page 243): for 5-year property the rates are 20.00, 32.00, 19.20, 11.52, 11.52, 5.76 percent. \(D_j = (\text{factor})C\).

$$D_3 = (0.1920)(80{,}000) = \$15{,}360$$

questions.explanation: Leaving out depreciation gives $72,000. Adding depreciation back gives $99,000. $150,000 is the taxable income, not the tax.
questions.question: A project has annual income of $500,000, ordinary expenses of $260,000 and depreciation of $90,000. The tax rate is 30%. How much income tax is paid?
questions.solution:
The handbook defines taxable income as total income less depreciation and ordinary expenses (Taxation, Engineering Economics, printed page 236 (PDF page 242)).

$$\begin{aligned}\text{taxable income} &= 500{,}000 - 260{,}000 \\ &\quad - 90{,}000 \\ &= \$150{,}000\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\text{tax} &= (0.30)(150{,}000) \\ &= \$45{,}000\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Leaving out the construction cost gives $300,000. A 20-year series would give a smaller upkeep value than a perpetual one. Multiplying by i instead of dividing is a common slip.
questions.question: A park needs $100,000 for construction now and $12,000 per year for upkeep forever. At 4% interest, what is the capitalized cost?
questions.solution:
Capitalized costs are present worth values for a perpetual period, \(P = A/i\) (Engineering Economics, printed page 236 (PDF page 242)).

$$\begin{aligned}P &= 100{,}000 + \frac{12{,}000}{0.04} \\ &= 100{,}000 + 300{,}000 \\ &= \$400{,}000\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Capitalized cost with an initial cost

questions.explanation: After year 2 the project has returned $33,000 of the $45,000, so payback is not yet reached.
questions.question: A $45,000 investment returns $15,000 in year 1, $18,000 in year 2, $20,000 in year 3 and $22,000 in year 4. Using cumulative undiscounted cash flow, in which year does payback occur?
questions.solution: Payback is the time required for benefits to equal the cost (Engineering Economics, printed page 236 (PDF page 242)). Cumulative benefits: $15{,}000, $33{,}000, $53{,}000. The total passes $45,000 during year 3, at about \(2 + 12/20 = 2.6\) years.

questions.explanation: The plain average of the three outcomes ignores probability. Leaving out the loss gives $115,000.
questions.question: A contractor estimates three outcomes for a bid: 50% chance of a $200,000 profit, 30% chance of a $50,000 profit and 20% chance of an $80,000 loss. What is the expected value?
questions.solution:
Use \(EV = (C_1)(p_1) + (C_2)(p_2) + \ldots\) (Economic Decision Trees, Engineering Economics, printed page 237 (PDF page 243)).

$$\begin{aligned}EV &= (0.5)(200{,}000) \\ &\quad + (0.3)(50{,}000) \\ &\quad + (0.2)(-80{,}000) \\ &= \$99{,}000\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Choosing B because it is less risky is a different criterion. The EV rule picks the larger expected value. The other values leave out the loss branch.
questions.question: Project A has a 60% chance of earning $90,000 and a 40% chance of losing $30,000. Project B has an 80% chance of earning $40,000 and a 20% chance of losing $5,000. Based on expected value, which should be chosen and what is its expected value?
questions.solution:
Compute EV for each branch set (Engineering Economics, printed page 237 (PDF page 243)).

$$\begin{aligned}EV_A &= (0.6)(90{,}000) + (0.4)(-30{,}000) \\ &= \$42{,}000\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}EV_B &= (0.8)(40{,}000) + (0.2)(-5{,}000) \\ &= \$31{,}000\end{aligned}$$

Project A has the higher expected value.

choices: Repair now, saving $10,000 in expected cost
Repair now, saving $160,000 in expected cost
questions.explanation: Waiting looks cheaper only if the failure branch is ignored. Weighted by its probability that branch adds $50,000 of expected cost, which exceeds the certain repair cost.
questions.question: An agency can repair a culvert now for $40,000, or wait. If it waits there is a 25% chance of a failure costing $200,000 and a 75% chance of no cost. Using expected cost, what is the better choice and by how much?
questions.solution: On the waiting branch, \(EV = (0.25)(200{,}000) + (0.75)(0) = \$50{,}000\) (Economic Decision Trees, Engineering Economics, printed page 237 (PDF page 243)). Repairing costs a certain $40,000, which is $10,000 lower than the expected cost of waiting.
questions.subtopic: Decision tree with a cost outcome

choices: Seal the plan if a senior colleague in the firm also agrees to approve it
Seal only plans that conform to accepted standards and safeguard the public
Seal the plan if the client signs a written release of liability for the engineer
Seal the plan and add a note on the drawings that the standards were not met
questions.explanation: A release, a disclaimer note, or a colleague's agreement does not change what the rule requires. The seal is tied to conformance with accepted standards and public safety.
questions.question: A client pressures a licensed engineer to seal a drainage plan that meets the client's budget but falls short of accepted standards for stormwater capacity. What does the Model Rules direct?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 4 (PDF page 10).

Rule A.2: Licensees shall sign and seal only those plans, surveys, and other documents that conform to accepted engineering and surveying standards and that safeguard the health, safety, and welfare of the public.

choices: Comply quietly, because the project manager has the authority to decide
Wait until a failure actually occurs, and then report it to the authorities
Resign from the project and say nothing about the safety concern to anyone
Notify the employer or client and any other appropriate authority
questions.explanation: Silence, a quiet resignation, or waiting for failure all leave the endangered public uninformed. The rule requires notification.
questions.question: A project manager overrules an engineer's recommendation to add scour protection at a bridge pier. The engineer believes public safety is endangered. What should the engineer do under the Model Rules?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 4 (PDF page 10).

Rule A.3: Licensees shall notify their employer or client and such other authority as may be appropriate when their professional judgment is overruled when the health, safety, or welfare of the public is endangered.

choices: Include all relevant and pertinent information, including the weaker results
Include the weaker results only in an internal memo that the client never sees
Leave out the results because the client is paying for the report
Round the results in the report so that they look less adverse to the client
questions.explanation: Omitting, hiding, or rounding results makes the report less than objective and truthful.
questions.question: While preparing a report, an engineer finds test results that weaken the case the client hopes to make. Which action fits the Model Rules?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 4 (PDF page 10).

Rule A.4: Licensees shall, to the best of their knowledge, include all relevant and pertinent information in an objective and truthful manner within all professional documents, statements, and testimony.

choices: Any opinion at all, because the engineer is a licensed professional
A public opinion only if it rests on adequate knowledge and competent evaluation
An opinion based only on the photographs and quotes published in the news story
A confident opinion, as long as it is labeled as a personal view
questions.explanation: A license or a personal label does not supply the facts. Press photographs are not an adequate basis for a competent evaluation.
questions.question: A local newspaper asks an engineer to comment on the cause of a dam spillway failure. The engineer has not seen the site, plans or inspection records. What do the Model Rules allow?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule A.5: Licensees shall express a professional opinion publicly only when it is founded upon an adequate knowledge of the facts and a competent evaluation of the subject matter.

choices: Publish it, provided the opinion expressed in the letter is technically correct
Publish the letter under a neighbor's name instead of the engineer's
Explicitly identify the company and disclose any interest in the matter
Publish under the engineer's name without mentioning the payment
questions.explanation: A correct opinion is not enough. The rule is about disclosing who is behind the statement.
questions.question: A pipeline company pays an engineer to write a letter to the editor supporting a route. Under the Model Rules, what must the engineer do?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule A.6: Licensees shall issue no statements, criticisms, or arguments on engineering and surveying matters that are inspired or paid for by interested parties, unless they explicitly identify the interested parties on whose behalf they are speaking and reveal any interest they have in the matters.
questions.subtopic: Statements paid for by interested parties

choices: Do nothing unless the firm begins competing for the engineer's own clients in the region
Report it to the board and cooperate with it and other authorities
Warn the firm privately about the problem and take no further action about it afterward
Report it only to the local newspaper and leave the board out of it
questions.explanation: The rule says shall report to the board. A private warning or a press release does not meet it.
questions.question: An engineer learns that a firm in the same city has been stamping designs prepared by unlicensed staff. What does the Model Rules require?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule A.8: Licensees who have knowledge or reason to believe that any person or firm has violated any rules or laws applying to the practice of engineering or surveying shall report it to the board, may report it to appropriate legal authorities, and shall cooperate with the board and those authorities as requested.

choices: Undertake only assignments that fit the engineer's education or experience
Accept it if the client agrees in writing to accept the risk of the unfamiliar work
Accept it if the fee is large enough to cover hiring a second engineer later in the job
Accept it and learn on the job, because the client is local and the firm knows them well
questions.explanation: Client consent or a fee arrangement does not substitute for qualification.
questions.question: A civil engineer with no electrical background is offered a substation protection design. What do the Model Rules say?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule B.1: Licensees shall undertake assignments only when qualified by education or experience in the specific technical fields of engineering or surveying involved.

choices: Seal them after a quick page-turn review of the sheets for obvious mistakes
Seal them if the firm that prepared them gives the engineer written permission
Decline, because they were not prepared under the engineer's responsible charge
Seal them if the client agrees in writing to accept liability for any errors in them
questions.explanation: Permission from another firm or a liability transfer from the client does not create responsible charge.
questions.question: An engineer is asked to seal a set of structural drawings that were prepared by another firm and that the engineer has not reviewed or directed. What is the correct response?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule B.2: Licensees shall not affix their signatures or seals to any plans or documents dealing with subject matter in which they lack competence, nor to any such plan or document not prepared under their responsible charge.

choices: Share it if the competitor signs a nondisclosure agreement covering the rates shared
Share it if the client has not paid the engineer's fee on time, since the duty ends then
Share it, because production rates are not usually considered to be secret
Refuse, since facts learned in a professional capacity need the client's prior consent
questions.explanation: Only the client's prior consent, or a legal requirement, allows disclosure. An NDA with a third party or an unpaid fee does not.
questions.question: An engineer, while designing a client's new process line, learns the client's production rate. A competitor of the client offers money for it. What should the engineer do?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule B.4: Licensees shall not reveal facts, data, or information obtained in a professional capacity without the prior consent of the client, employer, or public body on which they serve except as authorized or required by law or rules.

choices: Disclose it, but only after the contract with the lab has been signed
Select the brother's lab without comment, because its price is the lowest bid
Say nothing about it, as long as the brother's lab is technically qualified
Disclose the relationship to the client before the selection
questions.explanation: The rule covers circumstances that could influence or even appear to influence judgment. Disclosure has to come before the decision.
questions.question: An engineer is selecting a geotechnical lab for a client. The engineer's brother owns one of the bidding labs. What must the engineer do?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule B.6: Licensees shall disclose to their employers or clients all known or potential conflicts of interest or other circumstances that could influence or appear to influence their judgment or the quality of their professional service or engagement.

choices: Only if fully disclosed and agreed to in writing by all interested parties
If the contractor agrees verbally and the owner is not told about it
If the extra fee from the contractor is modest compared with the owner's fee and no one asks
If the engineer reviews all of the requests honestly and with care
questions.explanation: The condition is full disclosure and written agreement by all interested parties. Amount, verbal agreement, or personal honesty do not substitute.
questions.question: An engineer is paid by an owner to review a contractor's pay requests. The contractor offers an extra fee for faster approvals. Under which condition could the engineer accept payment from both?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule B.7: Licensees shall not accept compensation, financial or otherwise, from more than one party for services pertaining to the same project, unless the circumstances are fully disclosed and agreed to in writing by all interested parties.
questions.subtopic: Compensation from more than one party

choices: Marketing material and proposals are exempt from the Model Rules when they are not sealed
Only written degrees and license numbers need to be stated accurately
Licensees shall not exaggerate their responsibility or the complexity of past work
Exaggeration is fine as long as the client does not object to it later or ask for proof
questions.explanation: The rule covers responsibility and complexity of past work, and it applies to solicitations for business.
questions.question: In a proposal, a firm describes a junior engineer's work on a small culvert as leading the design of a regional interchange. Which rule applies?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule C.1: Licensees shall not falsify or permit misrepresentation of their, or their associates', academic or professional qualifications. They shall not misrepresent or exaggerate their degree of responsibility in prior assignments nor the complexity of said assignments.

choices: Licensees may not attend public meetings at which other designers' work is discussed in any way
Licensees shall not maliciously or falsely injure other licensees' reputations or criticize their work indiscriminately
Licensees must keep the results of all bids private at every stage of the selection process
Licensees must always publicly agree with the designs of other licensees, even when they see errors
questions.explanation: The rule does not require agreement or silence. It prohibits malicious, false or indiscriminate attacks.
questions.question: A competing engineer's design was selected over yours. At a public meeting, you say the winning engineer has always been careless, without evidence. Which rule does this conflict with?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule C.3: Licensees shall not injure or attempt to injure, maliciously or falsely, directly or indirectly, the professional reputation, prospects, practice, or employment of other licensees, nor indiscriminately criticize other licensees' work.

choices: Negligence, incompetence, or misconduct in practice
Presenting the seal of another licensee
Failure to comply with a continuing education audit
questions.explanation: The other grounds are not supported by the facts given. Harm to someone is not required for this ground to apply.
questions.question: A board finds that a licensed engineer's calculations contained a serious error caused by carelessness, and no one was harmed. Which ground in the Model Law applies?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Law, Section 150.10 (Grounds for Disciplinary Action, Licensees and Interns) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 10 (PDF page 16).

Section 150.10.A.2 lists any negligence, incompetence, or misconduct in the practice of engineering or surveying as grounds. The board may suspend, revoke, place on probation, fine, recover costs, or reprimand. The handbook text does not itself define professional liability or the standard of care.

choices: Failing to provide information that the board requested during an inquiry into a complaint
Providing services outside the licensee's areas of competence
Aiding an unlicensed person in the practice of engineering
Conviction of a felony that relates to the practice of engineering
questions.explanation: No facts point to the other grounds. The key fact is the field the licensee has no background in.
questions.question: A licensee agrees to design a tall building's wind bracing, a field in which the licensee has no education or experience. Which Model Law ground is most directly implicated?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Law, Section 150.10 (Grounds for Disciplinary Action, Licensees and Interns) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 10 (PDF page 16).

Section 150.10.A.14 lists providing engineering or surveying services outside any of the licensee's areas of competence as a ground for disciplinary action.

choices: Violating an order that the board issued to the licensee in writing after a hearing
Providing false or misleading testimony to the board during an official inquiry
Failure to renew a license on time, before the expiration date stated on the license
Sealing documents not prepared under the licensee's responsible charge
questions.explanation: The seal was used on documents outside the licensee's responsible charge. That is what ground 10 covers.
questions.question: A licensee lets a vendor's drawings carry his seal without having prepared them or supervised the work. Which Model Law ground applies?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Law, Section 150.10 (Grounds for Disciplinary Action, Licensees and Interns) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 10 (PDF page 16).

Section 150.10.A.10 names signing, affixing, or permitting the licensee's seal or signature to be affixed to specifications, reports, drawings, plans, or calculations that have not been prepared by the licensee or under the licensee's responsible charge.
questions.subtopic: Signing work not prepared by the licensee

choices: Order the licensee to give up all personal income earned during the year
Assign the licensee's active projects to the board's own staff to complete
Suspend, revoke, place on probation, fine, recover costs, or reprimand
Cancel the license of the licensee's employer without any further hearing
questions.explanation: The listed powers are about the license of the licensee, including fines and costs. The other options go beyond that list.
questions.question: Which of the following is among the actions the Model Law lets a board take against a licensee found guilty of a listed ground?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Law, Section 150.10 (Grounds for Disciplinary Action, Licensees and Interns) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 10 (PDF page 16).

Section 150.10.A: the board shall have the power to suspend, revoke, place on probation, fine, recover costs, and/or reprimand, or to refuse to issue, restore, or renew a license or intern certification.

choices: Section 110.20, which only defines terms used elsewhere in the law and sets no duties
Section 240.15, which applies to the firm's required insurance coverage and bonding
Section 160.70, which covers discipline of firms holding a certificate of authorization
Section 150.30, which covers only unlicensed individuals who use the title in advertising
questions.explanation: Section 150.30 is for unlicensed individuals and section 110.20 is the definitions section. Section 240.15 is the rules of conduct and does not cover insurance.
questions.question: A firm holding a certificate of authorization is found to have knowingly signed false statements in connection with an engineering project. Which section lets the board act against the firm?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Law, Section 160.70 in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 12 (PDF page 18).

Section 160.70.A.7 lists knowingly making false statements, or signing false statements, certifications, or affidavits in connection with the practice of engineering or surveying as grounds for discipline of a firm holding a certificate of authorization.

choices: Only the NCEES FE exam and nothing else
The NCEES FE exam and an exam set by the employing company
Only the NCEES PE exam and a state ethics test given by the board
The NCEES FE exam, the NCEES PE exam, and any jurisdiction-specific exam
questions.explanation: The FE exam alone covers only the first step. The Model Law lists the FE, the PE and any jurisdiction-specific exam.
questions.question: Under the Model Law, which examinations must an individual pass to be licensed as a professional engineer?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Law, Section 130.10 (Examination Requirements) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 9 (PDF page 15).

An individual seeking licensure as a professional engineer shall take and pass the NCEES FE examination and the NCEES PE examination, and any jurisdiction-specific examination.

questions.explanation: Four years is the base requirement without the master's substitution. Five years applies to the master's route after a degree in a(1)(c), a different qualifying path.
questions.question: Using the Model Law's substitution for experience, how many years of progressive experience after a qualifying bachelor's degree (a(1)(a)) does an applicant with an acceptable engineering master's degree need?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Law, Section 130.10 (Experience Requirements) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 9 (PDF page 15).

The base requirement is four years of progressive engineering experience after the qualifying degree in a(1)(a), a(1)(b) or a(1)(d). A master's degree acceptable to the board allows three years of experience after the qualifying bachelor's degree in a(1)(a) or a(1)(d).
questions.subtopic: Experience requirement with a master's degree

questions.explanation: Four years is the figure for a doctorate holder who chose not to take the FE exam. Three years is the master's substitution.
questions.question: An applicant has an earned doctoral degree in engineering acceptable to the board and has passed the FE exam. How many years of experience does the Model Law list for that applicant?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Law, Section 130.10 (Experience Requirements) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 9 (PDF page 15).

The substitution for an individual with an earned doctoral degree in engineering acceptable to the board and who has passed the FE exam is two years of experience. If the individual elected not to take the FE exam, four years of experience is listed.

choices: Yes, as long as the board has not formally objected to the credit being used twice
No, one graduate degree cannot count toward both education and experience
Yes, if the applicant is also working full time during the whole degree program
Yes, any graduate degree counts twice, once for each requirement
questions.explanation: Full-time work does not change the rule. The handbook says concurrent credit is not allowed.
questions.question: An applicant used a master's degree to satisfy the education requirement for licensure. May the same graduate degree also be applied as experience credit?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Law, Section 130.10 (Experience Requirements) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 9 (PDF page 15).

A graduate degree that is used to satisfy education requirements cannot be applied for experience credit toward licensure. Experience credit for a graduate degree also cannot be earned concurrently with work experience credit.

choices: Section 150.30, on unlicensed use of the title
Section 150.10, which applies only to people who already hold a current license
Section 160.10, which applies only to firms and needs no action by the board
Section 110.20, which only defines the term 'Board' and nothing else
questions.explanation: Section 150.10 covers licensees and interns, so it is not the section for an unlicensed person.
questions.question: An unlicensed designer prints business cards reading "Professional Engineer." Which Model Law section covers this conduct?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Law, Section 150.30 in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 11 (PDF page 17).

Section 150.30.A lists engaging in the practice of engineering without a license and using or advertising any title tending to convey the impression of being a professional engineer unless duly licensed. The board may fine and recover costs.

choices: When it is done by a graduate of an accredited engineering program with several years of practice
When the employee has passed the FE exam and is only waiting for a PE license to be issued
When it excludes final designs and is verified by a licensed individual in responsible charge
When the work is not sealed by anyone and never leaves the firm's own offices
questions.explanation: Neither a degree nor an FE pass substitutes for responsible charge. The exemption is about supervision and verification, not about who seals.
questions.question: A staff engineer who is not yet licensed prepares calculations for a licensed principal. Under the Model Law, when does the work of an employee or subordinate fall within the exemption?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Law, exemptions for employees and subordinates in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 13 (PDF page 19).

The work of an employee or a subordinate of a licensee is covered, provided the work does not include final engineering or surveying designs or decisions and is done under the responsible charge of and verified by an individual holding a certificate of licensure.

choices: No firm needs one as long as every one of its employees is licensed individually
Only firms with more than 10 employees are required to hold one, and then only for large projects
Only firms that do government work are required to hold one in any state
A firm offering engineering services needs one, except for work only for itself or a parent or subsidiary
questions.explanation: The exception is for work for the firm itself or its parent or subsidiary. Size, licensed employees or government work do not decide it.
questions.question: A firm that wants to offer engineering services in a jurisdiction asks whether it needs a certificate of authorization. Which statement matches the Model Law?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Law, Section 160.10 in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 11 (PDF page 17).

Section 160.10.A requires a firm that practices or offers to practice engineering or surveying to obtain a certificate of authorization. 160.10.B says a certificate is not required for a firm performing engineering or surveying for the firm itself or for a parent or subsidiary.

choices: It is allowed if the principal abstains from the council vote on the contract in question
It is allowed if the total value of the contract is under $50,000 and the work is routine
The licensee shall not solicit or accept a contract from a governmental body on which a principal or officer serves
It is allowed if the fee charged is below the city's usual rate for such work and is bid openly
questions.explanation: The rule has no abstention, price or size exception. The relationship itself bars soliciting or accepting the contract.
questions.question: A principal of an engineering firm is also a member of a city council. The firm wants to bid on a city design contract. What do the Model Rules say?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule B.8: Licensees shall not solicit or accept a professional contract from a governmental body on which a principal or officer of their organization serves as a member.

choices: Gifts are acceptable if the officer receiving them is not on the selection panel for the project
Licensees shall not offer, give, solicit, or receive gifts or other valuable consideration to secure work
Gifts are acceptable if they are reported to the client after the contract award is made
Gifts are acceptable if they cost much less than the design fee itself and are given openly
questions.explanation: The rule is about intent to secure work. Reporting it, its cost, or the officer's role does not remove the prohibition.
questions.question: To win a design contract, an engineer offers a procurement officer a gift. Which rule applies?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule C.2: Licensees shall not offer, give, solicit, or receive, either directly or indirectly, any commission, or gift, or other valuable consideration in order to secure work, and shall not make any political contribution with the intent to influence the award of a contract by public authority.

choices: Do not solicit or accept gratuities from contractors in connection with the work
Accept it, provided that the engineer discloses it to a coworker or friend in the firm
Accept it, provided that the contractor is not bidding on any more work with the firm
Accept it, provided that it is shared with everyone else in the whole office
questions.explanation: Sharing the gift or mentioning it to a coworker does not change that it is a gratuity from a contractor tied to the work.
questions.question: A contractor on a project the engineer administers sends the engineer a holiday gift basket worth several hundred dollars. What do the Model Rules direct?
questions.solution:
Refer to the NCEES Model Rules, Section 240.15 (Rules of Professional Conduct) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 5 (PDF page 11).

Rule B.5: Licensees shall not solicit or accept gratuities, directly or indirectly, from contractors, their agents, or other parties in connection with work for employers or clients.

choices: Life of the inventor plus 70 years
questions.explanation: 17 years from issue was the older rule. Life plus 70 years is a copyright-style term and is not in the handbook patent text.
questions.question: A company files a U.S. utility patent application on a new bridge bearing. Generally, how long is the term of a new patent from the filing date?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Intellectual Property section in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 13 (PDF page 19).

Generally, the term of a new patent is 20 years from the date on which the application for the patent was filed in the United States, subject to payment of maintenance fees. U.S. patent grants are effective only within the United States, its territories, and its possessions.

choices: Patents, trademarks, copyrights, and trade secrets
Copyrights, liens, warranties, and trade secrets of the owner
Patents, licenses, warranties, and performance bonds
questions.explanation: Licenses, warranties, bonds, easements and liens are business or property terms, not the four protection categories listed.
questions.question: Which list gives the four protection categories for intellectual property in the handbook?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Intellectual Property section in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 13 (PDF page 19).

There are four protection categories used to offer varying degrees of protection to intellectual property owners: Patents, Trademarks, Copyrights, and Trade Secrets.

choices: Making the same kind of geotextile product under any name at all, even a different one
Using any single word that appears anywhere in the registered mark, even as a common term
Using a confusingly similar mark; a clearly different mark is not covered
Selling any kind of geotextile at all within the same country, whatever its brand
questions.explanation: A trademark protects the source-identifying mark, not the goods themselves.
questions.question: A company holds a trademark on the name of its geotextile product. What can the trademark owner prevent others from doing?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Intellectual Property section (Trademarks) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 13 (PDF page 19).

Trademark rights may be used to prevent others from using a confusingly similar mark, but not to prevent others from making the same goods or from selling the same goods or services under a clearly different mark.

questions.explanation: A utility patent covers function. A plant patent covers plants. There is no patent called a trade secret patent.
questions.question: A firm invents a new, original, and ornamental shape for a manhole cover. Which type of patent fits best?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Intellectual Property section (Patents) in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 13 (PDF page 19).

Design patents may be granted to anyone who invents a new, original, and ornamental design for an article of manufacture. Utility patents cover new and useful processes, machines, articles of manufacture, or compositions of matter. Plant patents cover new varieties of plants.

choices: Tax rate, interest rate, land value, the inflation outlook, and local labor wages
Safety, public health, quality of life, resource allocation, and non-renewable resource use
Shop drawing review time, change-order markups, bid-day attendance, and punch-list length
Schedule float, bid price, warranty length, insurance premium, and contract type
questions.explanation: The other lists are project management or finance terms. They are not the sustainability principles in the handbook.
questions.question: Which of the following is listed among the sustainable principles engineers should consider in planning, design and construction?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Societal Considerations section in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 14 (PDF page 20).

Sustainable principles include consideration of safety, public health, quality of life, resource allocation, and non-renewable resources. Life-cycle analysis (cradle to grave) assesses potential environmental consequences from design through utilization and disposal.

questions.explanation: Dropping the factor 2 on the deceleration gives 7.6 s. Leaving out the reaction time gives 3.3 s. The last choice adds a red clearance term that is not part of y.
questions.question: A signalized intersection has an approach speed of 45 mph (66.15 ft/s) on a level grade. Use a driver reaction time of 1.0 s and a deceleration of 10 ft/s². Using the handbook equation, what is the yellow interval to the nearest 0.1 s?
questions.solution:
Refer to Traffic Signal Timing in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 306 (PDF page 312).

The handbook gives \(y = t + \dfrac{v}{2a \pm 64.4G}\) (the red clearance \(r = (W + l)/v\) is a separate interval).

$$\begin{aligned}y &= 1.0 + \frac{66.15}{2(10) + 64.4(0)} \\ &= 1.0 + 3.31 \\ &= 4.31 \approx 4.3\ \text{s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The vehicle has to clear the full intersection width plus its own length. Using width alone leaves the vehicle length out.
questions.question: An intersection is 64 ft wide curb to curb and the design vehicle is 20 ft long. The approach speed is 66.15 ft/s. Using the handbook, what red clearance interval to the nearest 0.1 s is needed?
questions.solution:
Refer to Traffic Signal Timing in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 306 (PDF page 312).

The handbook gives \(r = \dfrac{W + l}{v}\).

$$\begin{aligned}r &= \frac{64 + 20}{66.15} \\ &= 1.27 \approx 1.3\ \text{s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The walking time alone leaves out the start-up allowance and the extra time for the group of pedestrians.
questions.question: A crosswalk is 48 ft long. The handbook default pedestrian speed is used and 12 pedestrians are in the crossing interval. What is the minimum pedestrian green time?
questions.solution:
Refer to Traffic Signal Timing in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 306 (PDF page 312).

The handbook gives \(G_p = 3.2 + \dfrac{L}{S_p} + 0.27N_{ped}\) with \(S_p = 3.5\) ft/s.

$$\begin{aligned}G_p &= 3.2 + \frac{48}{3.5} + 0.27(12) \\ &= 3.2 + 13.71 + 3.24 \\ &= 20.2\ \text{s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The reaction distance alone is 220 ft and the braking distance alone is 345 ft. Using a directly instead of a/32.2 gives 231 ft.
questions.question: A highway has a design speed of 60 mph. Use a driver reaction time of 2.5 s and a deceleration of 11.2 ft/s² on a level road. What is the stopping sight distance?
questions.solution:
Refer to Stopping Sight Distance in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 306 (PDF page 312).

The handbook gives \(SSD = 1.47Vt + \dfrac{V^2}{30\left[\dfrac{a}{32.2} \pm G\right]}\).

$$\begin{aligned}SSD &= 1.47(60)(2.5) + \frac{60^2}{30(11.2/32.2)} \\ &= 220.5 + 345.0 \\ &= 566\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Stopping sight distance on level grade

questions.explanation: The level-grade value 566 ft ignores the grade. Using +0.03 gives the uphill answer, 538 ft, which is shorter.
questions.question: For a design speed of 60 mph, reaction time 2.5 s and deceleration 11.2 ft/s², what is the stopping sight distance on a 3% downgrade?
questions.solution:
Refer to Stopping Sight Distance in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 306 (PDF page 312).

The handbook uses \(\pm G\) with uphill grades positive, so a 3% downgrade is \(G = -0.03\).

$$\begin{aligned}SSD &= 220.5 + \frac{60^2}{30(11.2/32.2 - 0.03)} \\ &= 220.5 + 377.6 \\ &= 598\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Stopping sight distance on a downgrade

questions.explanation: Without the 1.47 factor the speed is still in mph and the result is not in feet. 1.47 converts mph to ft/s.
questions.question: The major road has a design speed of 45 mph. A driver on the minor road needs a time gap of 7.5 s to enter. What intersection sight distance is required?
questions.solution:
Refer to Stopping Sight Distance (ISD) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 306 (PDF page 312).

The handbook gives \(ISD = 1.47V_{major}t_g\).

$$ISD = 1.47(45)(7.5) = 496\ \text{ft}$$

questions.explanation: The factor 4 converts the peak 15-minute volume to an hourly flow rate. A PHF above 1.0 is not physically possible.
questions.question: A roadway carries 2,400 veh in the peak hour. The highest 15-minute volume within that hour is 680 veh. What is the peak hour factor?
questions.solution:
Refer to Peak Hour Factor in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 306 (PDF page 312).

The handbook gives \(PHF = \dfrac{V}{4 \times V_{15}}\).

$$PHF = \frac{2{,}400}{4(680)} = 0.882$$

questions.explanation: The S greater than L equation gives 220 ft, which is shorter than S and does not apply here. The 400 + 3.5S form is for sag curves.
questions.question: A crest vertical curve joins grades of +4% and -8%. Use the standard criteria (eye height 3.50 ft, object height 2.0 ft). What curve length gives a sight distance of 200 ft, assuming S is less than L?
questions.solution:
Refer to Vertical Curves: Sight Distance Related to Curve Length in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 308 (PDF page 314).

Here \(A = |-8 - 4| = 12\). For a crest curve with the standard criteria and \(S \le L\), \(L = AS^2/2{,}158\).

$$L = \frac{(12)(200)^2}{2{,}158} = 222\ \text{ft}$$

Since \(L = 222 > S = 200\), the assumption holds.
questions.subtopic: Crest vertical curve length, S less than L

questions.explanation: The S less than L equation gives 500 ft, which exceeds S and is inconsistent with its own assumption. Adding the term instead of subtracting it overstates the length.
questions.question: A crest vertical curve has an algebraic grade difference of 3%. Using the standard criteria, what is the minimum curve length for a sight distance of 600 ft, given that S is greater than L?
questions.solution:
Refer to Vertical Curves: Sight Distance Related to Curve Length in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 308 (PDF page 314).

For \(S > L\) with the standard criteria, \(L = 2S - 2{,}158/A\).

$$\begin{aligned}L &= 2(600) - \frac{2{,}158}{3} \\ &= 1200 - 719.3 \\ &= 481\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

This is less than S, which confirms that S is greater than L.
questions.subtopic: Crest vertical curve length, S greater than L

questions.explanation: The 2,158 denominator belongs to crest curves. In the sag equation the 3.5 is multiplied by S, not added alone.
questions.question: A sag vertical curve has an algebraic grade difference of 8%. Based on the standard headlight criteria, what length is needed for a sight distance of 250 ft (S less than L)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Sag Vertical Curve (based on standard headlight criteria) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 308 (PDF page 314).

$$\begin{aligned}L &= \frac{AS^2}{400 + 3.5S} \\ &= \frac{(8)(250)^2}{400 + 3.5(250)} \\ &= \frac{500{,}000}{1275} \\ &= 392\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Speed is squared in the comfort criterion because the centripetal acceleration scales with V squared.
questions.question: A sag vertical curve on a 60 mph road has an algebraic grade difference of 6%. Using the riding comfort criterion, what is the minimum length?
questions.solution:
Refer to Sag Vertical Curve (based on riding comfort) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 308 (PDF page 314).

$$\begin{aligned}L &= \frac{AV^2}{46.5} \\ &= \frac{(6)(60)^2}{46.5} \\ &= 465\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Sag curve length for riding comfort

questions.explanation: 510.8 ft is the elevation on the back tangent at the high point's station and skips the parabolic drop. Adding the parabola term instead of subtracting it gives 516.2 ft.
questions.question: A crest vertical curve has \(g_1 = +3\%\), \(g_2 = -2\%\) and \(L = 600\) ft, as shown. The PVC is at elevation 500 ft. What is the elevation of the high point on the curve?
questions.solution:
Refer to Vertical Curves in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 307 (PDF page 313).

The handbook gives \(x_m = \dfrac{g_1 L}{g_1 - g_2}\) and curve elevation \(Y = Y_{PVC} + g_1x + \dfrac{g_2 - g_1}{2L}x^2\).

$$\begin{aligned}x_m &= \frac{(0.03)(600)}{0.03 - (-0.02)} \\ &= 360\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}Y &= 500 + (0.03)(360) \\ &\quad + \frac{-0.02 - 0.03}{2(600)}(360)^2 \\ &= 500 + 10.80 - 5.40 \\ &= 505.4\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: High point of a crest curve

questions.explanation: The offset at the PVI is one quarter of what you would get from a straight A times L over 200 slope, because the parabola changes grade over half the curve on each side.
questions.question: A vertical curve has an algebraic grade difference of 5% and a length of 600 ft. What is the tangent offset E at the PVI?
questions.solution:
Refer to Vertical Curves in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 307 (PDF page 313).

The handbook gives \(E = a\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)^2\) with \(a = \dfrac{g_2 - g_1}{2L}\). With \(A\) in percent this reduces to \(E = AL/800\) (algebra, not printed).

$$\begin{aligned}|a| &= \frac{0.05}{2(600)} \\ &= 0.000042, \quad E \\ &= 0.000042(300)^2 \\ &= 3.75\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: A sharper curve (larger D) has a smaller radius, so multiplying by D reverses the relationship.
questions.question: A horizontal curve has a degree of curve (arc definition) of 4°. What is its radius?
questions.solution:
Refer to Horizontal Curves in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 308 (PDF page 314).

The handbook gives \(R = \dfrac{5729.58}{D}\).

$$R = \frac{5729.58}{4} = 1{,}432\ \text{ft}$$

questions.explanation: Using the full angle I instead of I/2 overstates T. The tangent distance is measured from the PI back to the PC along the tangent.
questions.question: A simple horizontal curve has a radius of 1,000 ft and an intersection angle I of 36°, as shown. What is the tangent distance T?
questions.solution:
Refer to Horizontal Curves in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 308 (PDF page 314).

The handbook gives \(T = R\tan(I/2)\).

$$T = 1{,}000\tan(18°) = 324.9\ \text{ft}$$
questions.subtopic: Tangent distance of a horizontal curve

questions.explanation: 51.5 ft is the external distance E, measured from the PI to the midpoint of the curve. M is measured from the midpoint of the long chord to the midpoint of the curve.
questions.question: For a horizontal curve with R = 1,000 ft and I = 36°, what is the middle ordinate M?
questions.solution:
Refer to Horizontal Curves in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 309 (PDF page 315).

The handbook gives \(M = R[1 - \cos(I/2)]\) and \(E = R[1/\cos(I/2) - 1]\).

$$M = 1{,}000[1 - \cos 18°] = 48.9\ \text{ft}$$

questions.explanation: The chord is shorter than the arc length. The value R sin(I/2) is half the chord.
questions.question: A horizontal curve has R = 1,000 ft and I = 36°. What is the long chord?
questions.solution:
Refer to Horizontal Curves in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 308 (PDF page 314).

The handbook gives \(LC = 2R\sin(I/2)\).

$$LC = 2(1{,}000)\sin 18° = 618.0\ \text{ft}$$
questions.subtopic: Long chord of a horizontal curve

questions.explanation: Using e = 6 instead of 0.06 mixes percent with decimal. Using friction alone ignores the superelevation. Multiplying instead of dividing reverses the relationship.
questions.question: A curve is designed for 45 mph with a superelevation of 6% and a side friction factor of 0.12. What is the minimum radius?
questions.solution:
Refer to Horizontal Curves (side friction factor) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 309 (PDF page 315).

The handbook gives \(0.01e + f = \dfrac{V^2}{15R}\) with e in percent.

$$\begin{aligned}R &= \frac{V^2}{15(0.01e + f)} \\ &= \frac{45^2}{15(0.06 + 0.12)} \\ &= 750\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Minimum radius from superelevation and friction

questions.explanation: Speed is cubed in this equation. Dropping the 3.15 constant also changes the units of the answer.
questions.question: A spiral transition is to be provided for a 50 mph design speed and a 1,000 ft radius curve. Use the handbook rate of increase of lateral acceleration. What is the spiral length?
questions.solution:
Refer to Spiral Transition Length in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 309 (PDF page 315).

The handbook gives \(L_s = \dfrac{3.15V^3}{RC}\) with \(C = 1\) ft/s³ unless stated otherwise.

$$\begin{aligned}L_s &= \frac{3.15(50)^3}{(1000)(1)} \\ &= 394\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The small-angle approximation S squared over 8R gives a nearby but different value. The sine and secant forms are other curve quantities, not the offset.
questions.question: A horizontal curve has a radius of 1,200 ft. A driver needs 480 ft of sight distance. How far must the line of sight clear the inside edge of the lane (the horizontal sight line offset)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Sight Distance (to see around obstruction) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 309 (PDF page 315).

The handbook gives \(HSO = R\left[1 - \cos\left(\dfrac{28.65S}{R}\right)\right]\), with the angle in degrees.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{28.65S}{R} &= \frac{28.65(480)}{1{,}200} \\ &= 11.46°\end{aligned}$$

$$HSO = 1{,}200[1 - \cos(11.46°)] = 23.9\ \text{ft}$$

questions.explanation: The breakpoint, 1,200, is where speed begins to fall below free-flow speed and is not the capacity. The third choice forgets to subtract 50 from FFS (and would exceed the 2,400 cap).
questions.question: A basic freeway segment has a free-flow speed of 70 mph under base conditions. Using the handbook relation, what is the base capacity in pc/h/ln?
questions.solution:
Refer to Basic Freeway Segment Highway Capacity in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 310 (PDF page 316).

The handbook gives \(c = 2{,}200 + 10(FFS - 50)\) for \(55 \le FFS \le 75\), with \(c \le 2{,}400\).

$$\begin{aligned}c &= 2{,}200 + 10(70 - 50) \\ &= 2{,}400\ \text{pc/h/ln}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: A lower free-flow speed raises the breakpoint, so subtracting the term instead of adding it reverses the trend.
questions.question: A basic freeway segment has an adjusted free-flow speed of 70 mph and a capacity adjustment factor of 1.00. What is the breakpoint in pc/h/ln?
questions.solution:
Refer to Basic Freeway Segment Highway Capacity in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 310 (PDF page 316).

The handbook gives \(BP_{adj} = [1{,}000 + 40(75 - FFS_{adj})]\,CAF^2\).

$$\begin{aligned}BP &= [1{,}000 + 40(75 - 70)](1.00)^2 \\ &= 1{,}200\ \text{pc/h/ln}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Dropping the ramp-density term gives 72.7 mph. Using TRD without the 0.84 exponent gives 67.9 mph. The last choice uses the wrong clearance value (1.2 is for 2 lanes at 4 ft).
questions.question: A freeway has 11.5-ft average lane widths (adjustment 1.9 mph from the handbook table), 3 lanes in one direction with a 4-ft right-side lateral clearance (adjustment 0.8 mph), and a total ramp density of 1.5 ramps/mi. Use the default base free-flow speed. What is the FFS?
questions.solution:
Refer to Basic Freeway Segment Highway Capacity in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 310 (PDF page 316).

The handbook gives \(FFS = BFFS - f_{LW} - f_{RLC} - 3.22\,TRD^{0.84}\) with BFFS = 75.4 mph. The lane width table (printed page 310) gives 1.9 mph for widths from 11 up to 12 ft. The lateral clearance table (printed page 311, PDF page 317) gives 0.8 mph for 4 ft clearance with 3 lanes.

$$\begin{aligned}FFS &= 75.4 - 1.9 - 0.8 - 3.22(1.5)^{0.84} \\ &= 75.4 - 1.9 - 0.8 - 4.53 \\ &= 68.2\ \text{mph}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Free-flow speed of a basic freeway segment

questions.explanation: Ignoring trucks gives 1,304. Multiplying by \(f_{HV}\) instead of dividing lowers the flow rate. Using \(E_T\) instead of \(E_T - 1\) in \(f_{HV}\) overcounts trucks.
questions.question: A three-lane freeway direction (level terrain) carries 3,600 veh/h with PHF = 0.92. Trucks are 10% of traffic. Use the handbook passenger car equivalent for level terrain. What is the demand flow rate vp in pc/h/ln?
questions.solution:
Refer to Basic Freeway Segment Highway Capacity in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 311 (PDF page 317).

The handbook gives \(v_p = \dfrac{V}{PHF \times N \times f_{HV}}\) and \(f_{HV} = \dfrac{1}{1 + P_T(E_T - 1)}\), with \(E_T = 2.0\) for level terrain.

$$f_{HV} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.10(2.0 - 1)} = 0.9091$$

$$\begin{aligned}v_p &= \frac{3{,}600}{(0.92)(3)(0.9091)} \\ &= 1,435\ \text{pc/h/ln}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Demand flow rate with heavy vehicles

questions.explanation: A density of 15 is above 11, so it is not LOS A, and below 18, so it is not LOS C.
questions.question: A basic freeway segment with a free-flow speed of 70 mph carries a demand flow rate of 1,050 pc/h/ln, which is below the breakpoint. What are the density and level of service?
questions.solution:
Refer to Basic Freeway Segment Highway Capacity in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 311 (PDF page 317).

Below the breakpoint the mean speed is the free-flow speed (printed page 310), and \(D = v_p/S\).

$$D = \frac{1,050}{70} = 15.0\ \text{pc/mi/ln}$$

The LOS table gives A for densities up to 11 and B for more than 11 up to 18, so this is LOS B.
questions.subtopic: Freeway density and level of service

questions.explanation: Speed falls linearly from the free-flow speed as density rises. The value 30 mph is the speed at optimum density, which is half the jam density, not 60.
questions.question: Under the Greenshields model, free-flow speed is 60 mph and jam density is 180 veh/mi/ln. What is the speed when the density is 60 veh/mi/ln?
questions.solution:
Refer to Traffic Flow Relationships (Greenshields Model) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 312 (PDF page 318).

The handbook gives \(S = S_f - \dfrac{S_f}{D_j}D\).

$$\begin{aligned}S &= 60 - \frac{60}{180}(60) \\ &= 60 - 20 \\ &= 40\ \text{mph}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Greenshields model, speed at a given density

questions.explanation: Flow is a product of speed and density. At \(D_j/2\) both are half their extreme values, so the maximum is one quarter of \(D_j S_f\).
questions.question: Using the Greenshields model with free-flow speed 60 mph and jam density 180 veh/mi/ln, what is the maximum flow?
questions.solution:
