Refer to Traffic Flow Relationships (Greenshields Model) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 312 (PDF page 318).

The handbook gives \(V_m = \dfrac{D_jS_f}{4}\), reached at the optimum density \(D_o = D_j/2\).

$$\begin{aligned}V_m &= \frac{(180)(60)}{4} \\ &= 2{,}700\ \text{veh/h/ln}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The speed (40 mph) is not the flow. The value 3,600 ignores the density-dependent speed drop. The maximum flow occurs at 90 veh/mi/ln, not at 60.
questions.question: With free-flow speed 60 mph and jam density 180 veh/mi/ln, what is the flow when the density is 60 veh/mi/ln?
questions.solution:
Refer to Traffic Flow Relationships (Greenshields Model) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 312 (PDF page 318).

The handbook gives \(V = S_fD - \dfrac{S_f}{D_j}D^2\).

$$\begin{aligned}V &= (60)(60) - \frac{60}{180}(60)^2 \\ &= 3{,}600 - 1{,}200 \\ &= 2{,}400\ \text{veh/h/ln}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Greenshields model, flow at a density

questions.explanation: Using ADT directly gives a rate per million vehicle-days, not per million entering vehicles in a year.
questions.question: An intersection had 18 crashes in one year. The average daily traffic entering the intersection is 24,000 veh/day. What is the crash rate per million entering vehicles?
questions.solution:
Refer to Traffic Safety Equations (Crash Rates at Intersections) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 313 (PDF page 319).

The handbook gives \(R_{MEV} = \dfrac{A \times 1{,}000{,}000}{V}\) with \(V = ADT \times 365\).

$$V = 24{,}000(365) = 8{,}760{,}000$$

$$\begin{aligned}R_{MEV} &= \frac{18(1{,}000{,}000)}{8{,}760{,}000} \\ &= 2.05\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Using one year of days with three years of crashes triples the rate. Leaving out the segment length gives a rate per million vehicles instead of per million vehicle miles.
questions.question: A 4.5 mi roadway segment had 42 crashes during a 3-year study period (1,095 days). ADT is 12,000 veh/day. What is the crash rate per million vehicle miles?
questions.solution:
Refer to Traffic Safety Equations (Crash Rates for Roadway Segments) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 313 (PDF page 319).

The handbook gives \(R_{MVM} = \dfrac{A \times 1{,}000{,}000}{VMT}\) with \(VMT = ADT \times (\text{days}) \times (\text{length})\).

$$\begin{aligned}VMT &= 12{,}000(1{,}095)(4.5) \\ &= 59{,}130{,}000\ \text{veh-mi}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}R_{MVM} &= \frac{42(1{,}000{,}000)}{59{,}130{,}000} \\ &= 0.71\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Adding the factors gives 0.50, which double-counts crashes already removed by the first measure. Leaving out the traffic ratio gives 8.80. Dividing by it applies the ratio in the wrong direction.
questions.question: A site is expected to have 20 crashes per year without improvement. Two mutually exclusive countermeasures have crash reduction factors of 0.3 and 0.2. Traffic after the improvements is expected to be 1.10 times the traffic before. How many crashes are prevented?
questions.solution:
Refer to Crash Reduction in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 313 (PDF page 319).

The handbook gives \(CR = CR_1 + (1 - CR_1)CR_2\) for two countermeasures and \(\text{crashes prevented} = N \times CR \times \dfrac{ADT_{after}}{ADT_{before}}\).

$$CR = 0.30 + (0.70)(0.20) = 0.44$$

$$\text{prevented} = (20)(0.44)(1.10) = 9.68$$

questions.explanation: Using attractions alone ignores travel time and gives 230.8. Using friction factors alone ignores zone size.
questions.question: Zone i produces 1,000 trips. Zones 1, 2 and 3 attract 400, 300 and 600 trips with friction factors 1.0, 0.8 and 0.5 for travel from zone i. Take all K factors as 1. How many trips go from zone i to zone 2?
questions.solution:
Refer to Gravity Model in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 312 (PDF page 318).

The handbook gives \(T_{ij} = P_i\left[\dfrac{A_jF_{ij}K_{ij}}{\sum_j A_jF_{ij}K_{ij}}\right]\).

$$\begin{aligned}\sum A_jF_{ij} &= (400)(1.0) + (300)(0.8) \\ &\quad + (600)(0.5) \\ &= 940\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}T_{i2} &= 1{,}000\frac{(300)(0.8)}{940} = 255.3\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 0.574 is the probability of choosing transit. Taking the ratio of utilities is not a probability.
questions.question: A logit mode choice model uses utility \(U = a_1(\text{time, min}) + a_2(\text{cost, \$})\) with \(a_1 = -0.05\) and \(a_2 = -0.30\). Auto takes 20 min and costs $6.00. Transit takes 35 min and costs $2.50. What is the probability of choosing auto?
questions.solution:
Refer to Logit Models in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 313 (PDF page 319).

The handbook gives \(U_x = \sum a_iX_i\) and \(P(A) = \dfrac{e^{U_A}}{e^{U_A} + e^{U_T}}\).

$$\begin{aligned}U_A &= (-0.05)(20) + (-0.30)(6.00) \\ &= -2.80, \quad U_T \\ &= (-0.05)(35) + (-0.30)(2.50) \\ &= -2.50\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}P(A) &= \frac{e^{-2.80}}{e^{-2.80} + e^{-2.50}} \\ &= 0.426\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Leaving out the drainage coefficient on the subbase gives a thinner base than needed. Using the whole SN over the base coefficient ignores the other layers.
questions.question: A pavement needs SN = 4.5. It has 4 in. of asphalt concrete (a = 0.44) and 10 in. of subbase (a = 0.11, m = 0.9). The base course has a = 0.14 and m = 1.0. What base thickness is required?
questions.solution:
Refer to Highway Pavement Design (AASHTO Structural Number Equation) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 314 (PDF page 320).

Rearrange \(SN = a_1D_1 + a_2D_2m_2 + a_3D_3m_3\) for \(D_2\) (algebra, not printed).

$$\begin{aligned}D_2 &= \frac{SN - a_1D_1 - a_3D_3m_3}{a_2m_2} \\ &= \frac{4.5 - 1.76 - 0.99}{0.14(1.0)} \\ &= 12.5\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Required base thickness for a target SN

questions.explanation: 11.18 is the single-axle factor for 34,000 lb and 0.0144 is the tandem factor for 12,000 lb. Each axle has to use the column that matches its type.
questions.question: Each truck in a traffic stream has one 12,000-lb single axle and one 34,000-lb tandem axle. Using the handbook load equivalency factors, how many ESALs result from 5,000 truck passes?
questions.solution:
Refer to Highway Pavement Design (Load Equivalency Factors) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 314 (PDF page 320).

The table gives 0.189 for a 12,000-lb single axle and 1.095 for a 34,000-lb tandem axle.

$$\text{ESAL per truck} = 0.189 + 1.095 = 1.284$$

$$\text{ESAL} = (1.284)(5{,}000) = 6{,}420$$
questions.subtopic: ESALs from axle load equivalency factors

questions.explanation: The ratio of loads, 1.67, understates the damage because pavement damage rises much faster than load. 0.658 is the tandem-axle factor for 30,000 lb.
questions.question: Using the handbook load equivalency factors, how many 18,000-lb single-axle passes does one pass of a 30,000-lb single axle damage the pavement as much as?
questions.solution:
Refer to Highway Pavement Design (Load Equivalency Factors) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 314 (PDF page 320).

The handbook table gives a load equivalency factor of 1.000 for an 18,000-lb single axle and 6.97 for a 30,000-lb single axle. One pass of the heavier axle is equivalent to 6.97 passes of the standard axle.
questions.subtopic: Relative damage from heavier single axles

questions.explanation: A drainage coefficient below 1.0 reduces the layer's contribution. Dividing by it would increase the contribution instead.
questions.question: A granular base has a = 0.14 and D = 10 in. What is the base's structural number contribution when the drainage coefficient is 0.8?
questions.solution:
Refer to Highway Pavement Design (AASHTO Structural Number Equation) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 314 (PDF page 320).

Each layer contributes \(a_iD_im_i\).

$$a_2D_2m_2 = (0.14)(10)(0.8) = 1.12$$

questions.explanation: Values below 1.0 represent poor drainage and are used only when given. A value of 0 would remove the layer.
questions.question: A problem gives layer coefficients and thicknesses but does not give drainage coefficients. What value should be used for m in the structural number equation?
questions.solution:
Refer to Highway Pavement Design (AASHTO Structural Number Equation) in the Civil Engineering: Transportation section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 314 (PDF page 320).

The handbook states that m is the drainage coefficient and to assume m equals 1.0 unless otherwise given.

questions.explanation: Leaving out the division by 2 gives 31,100 ft². The last choice converts to acres by mistake, 0.357, but keeps the ft² unit.
questions.question: A lot has corners A (0, 0), B (120, 0), C (150, 80), D (60, 130) and E (-20, 70), listed in order around the boundary (coordinates in ft), as shown. What is its area?
questions.solution:
Refer to Area formulas (Area by Coordinates) in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 316 (PDF page 322).

The handbook gives \(A = [X_A(Y_B - Y_N) + X_B(Y_C - Y_A) + \ldots + X_N(Y_A - Y_{N-1})]/2\).

$$\begin{aligned}2A &= 0(0-70) + 120(80-0) \\ &\quad + 150(130-0) \\ &\quad + 60(70-80) + (-20)(0-130) \\ &= 0 + 9{,}600 + 19{,}500 \\ &\quad - 600 + 2{,}600 \\ &= 31{,}100\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}A &= 15{,}550\ \text{ft}^2\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The rectangle alone ignores the triangle at the top. Skipping the factor of 1/2 doubles the area. The last choice forgets to convert ft² to acres.
questions.question: A parcel has corners at (0, 0), (200, 0), (200, 150), (100, 220) and (0, 150) in ft, listed counterclockwise. What is its area in acres? (1 acre = 43,560 ft²)
questions.solution:
Refer to Area formulas (Area by Coordinates) in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 316 (PDF page 322).

Using the handbook formula (the last term wraps to the first point):

$$\begin{aligned}2A &= 0(0-150) + 200(150-0) \\ &\quad + 200(220-0) \\ &\quad + 100(150-150) + 0(0-220) \\ &= 0 + 30{,}000 + 44{,}000 + 0 + 0 \\ &= 74{,}000\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}A &= 37{,}000\ \text{ft}^2 \\ &= \frac{37{,}000}{43{,}560} \\ &= 0.849\ \text{acres}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Area by coordinates, house lot with pitched corner

questions.explanation: Halving the offset sum gives 123, which averages all offsets instead of weighting interior ones fully. Simpson's rule gives 257, a different method.
questions.question: Seven offsets are measured at a common interval of 10 ft from a straight baseline to an irregular boundary: 0, 4.2, 5.1, 6.0, 5.5, 3.8 and 0 ft, as shown. What is the area using the trapezoidal rule?
questions.solution:
Refer to Area formulas (Trapezoidal Rule) in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 316 (PDF page 322).

The handbook gives \(A = w\left[\dfrac{h_1 + h_n}{2} + h_2 + h_3 + \ldots + h_{n-1}\right]\).

$$\begin{aligned}A &= 10\Big[\frac{0 + 0}{2} + 4.2 + 5.1 \\ &\quad + 6.0 + 5.5 + 3.8\Big] \\ &= 10(24.6) \\ &= 246\ \text{ft}^2\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Swapping the 2 and 4 multipliers gives a different, wrong result. Dropping the 1/3 factor triples the area.
questions.question: Seven equally spaced offsets (0, 4.2, 5.1, 6.0, 5.5, 3.8, 0 ft) at w = 10 ft, what is the area by Simpson's 1/3 rule?
questions.solution:
Refer to Area formulas (Simpson's 1/3 Rule) in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 316 (PDF page 322).

The handbook gives, for an odd number of measurements (n = 7 here):

$$\begin{aligned}A &= \frac{w}{3}\Big[h_1 + 2\sum_{k=3,5,\ldots}^{n-2}h_k \\ &\quad + 4\sum_{k=2,4,\ldots}^{n-1}h_k + h_n\Big]\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}A &= \frac{10}{3}\big[0 + 2(5.1 + 5.5) \\ &\quad + 4(4.2 + 6.0 + 3.8) + 0\big] \\ &= \frac{10}{3}[21.2 + 56.0] \\ &= 257.3\ \text{ft}^2\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The rule fits parabolas to pairs of intervals, so it needs an even number of intervals, which means an odd number of offsets.
questions.question: For which number of equally spaced offset measurements does the handbook allow Simpson's 1/3 rule?
questions.solution:
Refer to Area formulas (Simpson's 1/3 Rule) in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 316 (PDF page 322).

The handbook states that n must be an odd number of measurements for Simpson's 1/3 rule. That gives an even number of intervals.

questions.explanation: The ft³ value must be divided by 27 to get cubic yards. Leaving out the division by 2 doubles the volume.
questions.question: Two cross sections 100 ft apart have end areas of 450 ft² and 380 ft². What is the volume between them in cubic yards by the average end area method?
questions.solution:
Refer to Earthwork formulas (Average End Area Formula) in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 315 (PDF page 321).

The handbook gives \(V = L(A_1 + A_2)/2\).

$$\begin{aligned}V &= \frac{100(450 + 380)}{2} \\ &= 41{,}500\ \text{ft}^3 \\ &= \frac{41{,}500}{27} \\ &= 1{,}537\ \text{yd}^3\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The average end area result is 1,537 yd³. The prismoidal result is slightly larger here because the mid-section area is above the average of the end areas (415 ft²). Leaving out the factor 4 on the mid-section understates its weight.
questions.question: Two cross sections 100 ft apart have areas of 450 ft² and 380 ft². The section midway between them has an area of 420 ft². What volume in cubic yards does the prismoidal formula give?
questions.solution:
Refer to Earthwork formulas (Prismoidal Formula) in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 315 (PDF page 321).

The handbook gives \(V = L(A_1 + 4A_m + A_2)/6\).

$$\begin{aligned}V &= \frac{100(450 + 4(420) + 380)}{6} \\ &= 41{,}833\ \text{ft}^3 \\ &= 1{,}549\ \text{yd}^3\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The prism volume would be height times base area. A pyramid holds one third of that. The last choice converts to yd³ without being asked.
questions.question: A pyramid-shaped stockpile has a rectangular base of 40 ft by 30 ft and a height of 12 ft. What is its volume?
questions.solution:
Refer to Earthwork formulas (Pyramid or Cone) in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 315 (PDF page 321).

The handbook gives \(V = h(\text{area of base})/3\).

$$V = \frac{(12)(40)(30)}{3} = 4{,}800\ \text{ft}^3$$

questions.explanation: Leaving out the 1/3 gives the volume of a cylinder. The value in ft³ is not in the requested unit.
questions.question: A conical stockpile of sand has a base radius of 15 ft and a height of 20 ft. What volume of sand is in the pile, in cubic yards?
questions.solution:
Refer to Earthwork formulas (Pyramid or Cone) in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 315 (PDF page 321).

Use \(V = h(\text{area of base})/3\) with a circular base.

$$A_b = \pi(15)^2 = 706.9\ \text{ft}^2$$

$$\begin{aligned}V &= \frac{(20)(706.9)}{3} \\ &= 4,712\ \text{ft}^3 \\ &= 174.5\ \text{yd}^3\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Dividing by the factor reduces the volume instead of increasing it. The increment alone, 2,400, is only the extra amount.
questions.question: The design requires 12,000 yd³ of compacted fill. The handbook adjusts earthwork for shrinkage by increasing fill by the shrinkage factor. Using a shrinkage factor of 1.20, what volume of fill must be provided?
questions.solution:
Refer to Mass haul diagram (shrinkage note) in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 315 (PDF page 321).

The handbook says earthwork may be adjusted to account for shrinkage by increasing fill at each station by the shrinkage factor.

$$V = (12{,}000)(1.20) = 14{,}400\ \text{yd}^3$$

questions.explanation: Adding the absolute values gives the gross quantity moved. The sign-reversed choice treats fill as positive. The cumulative value after two segments, 2,000, is where the ordinate peaks before fill begins.
questions.question: A roadway has the following net quantities between successive stations: +1,200 yd³ (cut), +800 yd³ (cut), -600 yd³ (fill), -1,500 yd³ (fill), +500 yd³ (cut). The mass haul ordinate is zero at the start. Counting cut as positive and fill as negative, what is the ordinate at the end of the last segment?
questions.solution:
Refer to Earthwork formulas (Mass Haul Diagram) in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 315 (PDF page 321).

The handbook defines the mass haul ordinate as the cumulative total of excavation and embankment at a given station. Counting cut as positive and fill as negative (the usual sign convention, consistent with the handbook diagram, where the ordinate rises through a cut and falls through a fill):

$$\begin{aligned}\text{net} &= 1{,}200 + 800 - 600 \\ &\quad - 1{,}500 + 500 \\ &= 400\ \text{yd}^3\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Sine and cosine are swapped in the first wrong choice. The other choices flip a sign: a northeast bearing has both a north latitude and an east departure.
questions.question: A traverse course is 250 ft long with a bearing of N 40° E. What are its latitude and departure?
questions.solution:
Refer to Latitudes and Departures in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 315 (PDF page 321).

The handbook diagram shows north latitude positive and east departure positive. For a bearing, latitude is \(L\cos\) and departure is \(L\sin\) of the bearing angle measured from the north-south line (the cosine/sine split is standard trigonometry; the handbook shows the sign convention).

$$\begin{aligned}\text{lat} &= 250\cos 40° \\ &= 191.5\ \text{ft (north)}, \quad \text{dep} \\ &= 250\sin 40° \\ &= 160.7\ \text{ft (east)}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Latitude and departure of a course

questions.explanation: A southwest bearing has negative latitude and negative departure. Swapping sine and cosine would apply the angle to the wrong axis.
questions.question: A course is 180 ft long with a bearing of S 25° W. What are its latitude and departure, using the handbook sign convention (north and east positive)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Latitudes and Departures in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 315 (PDF page 321).

South latitudes and west departures are negative in the handbook diagram.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{lat} &= -180\cos 25° \\ &= -163.1\ \text{ft}, \quad \text{dep} \\ &= -180\sin 25° \\ &= -76.1\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Height of collimation = known RL + backsight; every reading from the same setup subtracts from that one HoC. 51.460 m is the HoC itself, 50.630 m is station B, and 48.540 m subtracts the backsight.
questions.question: A leveling run is booked in the table below. The reduced level (RL) of BM-A is 50.000 m and the instrument stays at one setup for all three readings. What is the RL of station C?
questions.solution:
Leveling booking tables (BS/IS/FS/HoC/RL) are standard surveying practice; this method is not printed in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Height of collimation (HoC) = RL + backsight. Every reading taken from the same setup subtracts from that one HoC.

1. HoC \(= 50.000 + 1.46 = 51.460\ \text{m}\)
2. RL of B \(= 51.460 - 0.83 = 50.630\ \text{m}\)
3. RL of C \(= 51.460 - 1.22 = 50.240\ \text{m}\)

Completed table (rows in station order BM-A, B, C):

$${\small \begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \textbf{BS} & \textbf{IS} & \textbf{FS} & \textbf{HoC} & \textbf{RL} \\ \hline 1.46 & - & - & 51.460 & 50.000 \\ - & 0.83 & - & & 50.630 \\ - & - & 1.22 & & 50.240 \\ \hline 1.46 & & 1.22 & & \end{array}}$$

Arithmetic check: \(\Sigma BS - \Sigma FS = 1.46 - 1.22 = +0.24\ \text{m} = 50.240 - 50.000\).
questions.subtopic: Height of collimation booking table, single setup

questions.explanation: The CP1 foresight (1.68) comes off the first HoC (88.320); the CP1 backsight (1.44) starts the second HoC (88.080). 87.630 m flips the sign of the -0.63 m difference, 88.080 m is the second HoC, and 87.110 m is IS2.
questions.question: A leveling run from BM-1 to BM-2 is booked in the table below with one change point (CP1), where the instrument is moved to a new setup. The RL of BM-1 is 87.000 m. What is the RL of BM-2?
questions.solution:
Leveling booking tables (BS/IS/FS/HoC/RL) are standard surveying practice; this method is not printed in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

At a change point (CP) the foresight closes the old setup and the backsight opens the new one.

1. HoC at setup 1 \(= 87.000 + 1.32 = 88.320\ \text{m}\)
2. RL of CP1 \(= 88.320 - 1.68 = 86.640\ \text{m}\)
3. HoC at setup 2 \(= 86.640 + 1.44 = 88.080\ \text{m}\)
4. RL of BM-2 \(= 88.080 - 1.71 = 86.370\ \text{m}\)

Completed table (rows in station order BM-1, IS1, CP1, IS2, BM-2):

$${\small \begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \textbf{BS} & \textbf{IS} & \textbf{FS} & \textbf{HoC} & \textbf{RL} \\ \hline 1.32 & - & - & 88.320 & 87.000 \\ - & 1.05 & - & & 87.270 \\ 1.44 & - & 1.68 & 88.080 & 86.640 \\ - & 0.97 & - & & 87.110 \\ - & - & 1.71 & & 86.370 \\ \hline 2.76 & & 3.39 & & \end{array}}$$

Arithmetic check: \(\Sigma BS - \Sigma FS = 2.76 - 3.39 = -0.63\ \text{m} = 86.370 - 87.000\). The check verifies the booking arithmetic, not field blunders.
questions.subtopic: Height of collimation booking table with change point

choices: Yes: because \(\Sigma BS + \Sigma FS = 8.77\ \text{m}\) equals twice the rise
No: the check only works if the run closes back on the starting BM
No: the backsight and foresight totals must be equal
questions.explanation: The check is sum(BS) - sum(FS) = last RL - first RL. The totals need not be equal, and closing back on the starting BM is a separate closure check, not part of this arithmetic check.
questions.question: A leveling run from BM-A (RL 50.000 m) to BM-B is booked with total backsight \(\Sigma BS = 4.55\ \text{m}\) and total foresight \(\Sigma FS = 4.22\ \text{m}\). The booked RL of BM-B is 50.330 m. Does the arithmetic check pass?
questions.solution:
The arithmetic check is standard leveling-booking practice; it is not printed in the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

1. \(\Sigma BS - \Sigma FS = 4.55 - 4.22 = +0.33\ \text{m}\)
2. Last RL - first RL \(= 50.330 - 50.000 = +0.33\ \text{m}\)
3. The two differences match, so the booking arithmetic checks out.

Intermediate sights do not enter the check, and equal totals are not required: a net rise is normal when the closing BM is higher. The check verifies the arithmetic only; it does not catch field blunders.
questions.subtopic: Leveling arithmetic check, sum BS minus sum FS

questions.explanation: The path A-C-E-F is only 15 days. Adding every duration, 24 days, ignores that B-D and C-E run in parallel.
questions.question: Activity A (3 days) precedes B (4) and C (6). B precedes D (5). C precedes E (2). D and E both precede F (4). All relationships are finish-to-start, as shown. What is the project duration?
questions.solution:
Refer to CPM Precedence Relationships and Nomenclature in the Civil Engineering (Construction) chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 316 (PDF page 322).

Forward pass with ES = latest EF of predecessors and EF = ES + D:

A: 0 to 3. B: 3 to 7. C: 3 to 9. D: 7 to 12. E: 9 to 11. F: ES = max(12, 11) = 12, EF = 16.

The project duration is 16 days along A-B-D-F.

questions.explanation: Activities A, B, D and F have zero float and form the critical path. E is on the shorter path, so it has one day of float.
questions.question: In a project network (A 3 d, B 4 d, C 6 d, D 5 d, E 2 d, F 4 d; A precedes B and C, B precedes D, C precedes E, D and E precede F), what is the total float of activity E?
questions.solution:
Refer to CPM Precedence Relationships and Nomenclature in the Civil Engineering (Construction) chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 316 (PDF page 322).

Forward pass: E has ES = 9, EF = 11. Backward pass with LF = earliest LS of successors: F has LF = 16, LS = 12. E has LF = 12, LS = 10.

$$\text{Float} = LS - ES = 10 - 9 = 1\ \text{day}$$

(equivalently \(LF - EF = 12 - 11\)).

questions.explanation: A-C-E-F is one day shorter. The other sequences use links that do not exist in the network.
questions.question: In a project network (A 3 d, B 4 d, C 6 d, D 5 d, E 2 d, F 4 d; A precedes B and C, B precedes D, C precedes E, D and E precede F), which sequence is the critical path?
questions.solution:
Refer to CPM Precedence Relationships and Nomenclature in the Civil Engineering (Construction) chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 316 (PDF page 322).

The critical path has zero float. A-B-D-F totals 3 + 4 + 5 + 4 = 16 days, and A-C-E-F totals 3 + 6 + 2 + 4 = 15 days, so the longer one is critical.

questions.explanation: Swapping the two variances compares the wrong pairs. Positive values would mean under budget and ahead of schedule.
questions.question: At a status date a project has BCWS (planned) of $200,000, BCWP (earned) of $180,000 and ACWP (actual) of $210,000. What are the cost variance and the schedule variance?
questions.solution:
Refer to Earned-Value Analysis in the Civil Engineering (Construction) chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 316 (PDF page 322).

The handbook gives \(CV = BCWP - ACWP\) and \(SV = BCWP - BCWS\).

$$\begin{aligned}CV &= 180{,}000 - 210{,}000 \\ &= -30{,}000, \quad SV \\ &= 180{,}000 - 200{,}000 \\ &= -20{,}000\end{aligned}$$

Both are negative: over budget and behind schedule.

questions.explanation: The inverted ratios, 1.167 and 1.111, would suggest the project is doing better than planned. Both indices below 1.0 mean over budget and behind schedule.
questions.question: For BCWS = $200,000, BCWP = $180,000 and ACWP = $210,000, what are CPI and SPI?
questions.solution:
Refer to Earned-Value Analysis (Indices) in the Civil Engineering (Construction) chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 317 (PDF page 323).

The handbook gives \(CPI = BCWP/ACWP\) and \(SPI = BCWP/BCWS\).

$$\begin{aligned}CPI &= \frac{180{,}000}{210{,}000} \\ &= 0.857, \quad SPI \\ &= \frac{180{,}000}{200{,}000} \\ &= 0.900\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Adding the remaining budget at face value gives $530,000, which assumes the rest is done exactly on budget. $373,333 is the estimate to complete, not the estimate at completion.
questions.question: A project has BAC = $500,000, BCWP = $180,000, ACWP = $210,000, so CPI = BCWP/ACWP = 0.857 (carry the unrounded ratio). Assuming the current cost performance continues, what is the estimate at completion?
questions.solution:
Refer to Earned-Value Analysis (Forecasting) in the Civil Engineering (Construction) chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 317 (PDF page 323).

The handbook gives \(ETC = (BAC - BCWP)/CPI\) and \(EAC = ACWP + ETC\).

$$\begin{aligned}ETC &= \frac{500{,}000 - 180{,}000}{0.857143} \\ &= 373{,}333\end{aligned}$$

$$EAC = 210{,}000 + 373{,}333 = 583{,}333$$

questions.explanation: Finish-to-start would stop B from starting until A finishes. Start-to-start ties the two starts together. Start-to-finish is not one of the three shown.
questions.question: In an activity-on-node schedule, activity B cannot finish until activity A finishes. Which precedence relationship is this?
questions.solution:
Refer to CPM Precedence Relationships in the Civil Engineering (Construction) chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 316 (PDF page 322).

The handbook diagram labels the three relationships: start-to-start (the start of B depends on the start of A), finish-to-finish (the finish of B depends on the finish of A) and finish-to-start (the start of B depends on the finish of A). B finishing only after A finishes is finish-to-finish.

questions.explanation: Using only 1.4D gives 56 kip and the roof-live-load-dominant combination gives 140 kip. Both are smaller than the governing floor-live-load combination. The unfactored sum 100 kip is not a handbook strength combination.
questions.question: A floor beam carries nominal loads of D = 40 kip, L = 60 kip and Lr = 20 kip. Using the handbook LRFD basic combinations that involve only D, L and Lr, what is the governing factored load?
questions.solution:
Refer to Loads (ASCE 7-16) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 278 (PDF page 284).

The combinations with D, L and Lr are 1.4D, \(1.2D + 1.6L + 0.5L_r\) and \(1.2D + 1.6L_r + L\).

$$\begin{aligned}1.4D &= 56,\quad 1.2D+1.6L+0.5L_r \\ &= 154,\quad 1.2D+1.6L_r+L \\ &= 140\end{aligned}$$

The largest is 154 kip.

questions.explanation: Using 1.2D gives 20 kip and ignoring the load factor on D gives 10 kip. Wind uplift opposes dead load, so the smaller dead-load factor 0.9 is the one that checks uplift. Adding W as downward gives 85 kip.
questions.question: A roof connection has a nominal dead load of 50 kip downward and a nominal wind uplift of 40 kip. Using the handbook LRFD combination 0.9D + 1.0W, taking uplift as negative, what is the factored net force (positive downward)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Load Combinations using Strength Design (LRFD) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 278 (PDF page 284).

$$\begin{aligned}0.9D + 1.0W &= 0.9(50) + 1.0(-40) \\ &= 5\ \text{kip}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The reduced three-load combination is 66.50 kip and D + Lr is 32 kip, both smaller. Adding all three at full value (82 kip) is not one of the handbook combinations.
questions.question: Nominal loads on a column are D = 20 kip, L = 50 kip and Lr = 12 kip. Using the handbook ASD combinations D + L, D + (Lr or S or R) and D + 0.75L + 0.75(Lr or S or R), what is the governing allowable-stress-design load?
questions.solution:
Refer to Load Combinations using Allowable Stress Design (ASD) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 278 (PDF page 284).

$$\begin{aligned}D+L &= 70,\quad D+L_r \\ &= 32,\quad D+0.75L+0.75L_r \\ &= 66.50\end{aligned}$$

The largest is 70 kip.

questions.explanation: Using \(K_{LL} = 4\) (the column value) gives 27.8 psf, and leaving \(K_{LL}\) out gives 43.1 psf. Dropping the 0.25 term gives 21.7 psf.
questions.question: A typical floor beam supports a tributary area of 600 ft² and the unreduced floor live load is 50 psf. Using the handbook live load reduction model for a member supporting one floor, what is the reduced live load?
questions.solution:
Refer to Live Load Reduction (page 278 for the model, page 279 for the \(K_{LL}\) values) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 279 (PDF page 285).

For a typical beam \(K_{LL} = 2\).

$$\begin{aligned}L &= L_o\left(0.25 + \frac{15}{\sqrt{K_{LL}A_T}}\right) \\ &= 50\left(0.25 + \frac{15}{\sqrt{2(600)}}\right) \\ &= 34.2\ \text{psf}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Using Ce = Ct = 1.0 gives 21.0 psf. Using Ct = 1.0 with Ce = 0.9 gives 18.9 psf, and using Ce = 1.0 with Ct = 1.2 gives 25.2 psf.
questions.question: A fully exposed, unheated open-air shelter in open terrain (Terrain C) has a ground snow load of 30 psf and importance factor Is = 1.0. Using the handbook, what is the flat roof snow load?
questions.solution:
Refer to Flat Roof Snow Loads in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 279 (PDF page 285).

From the tables: Ce = 0.9 (Terrain C, fully exposed) and Ct = 1.2 (unheated and open air).

$$\begin{aligned}P_f &= 0.7C_eC_tI_sP_g \\ &= 0.7(0.9)(1.2)(1.0)(30) \\ &= 22.7\ \text{psf}\end{aligned}$$

choices: cannot be classified without knowing the member lengths
questions.explanation: Compare m + r with 2j. Here m + r = 12 and 2j = 12. The handbook notes that a proper arrangement of members is also needed for stability.
questions.question: A plane truss has 9 members, 3 reaction components and 6 joints. Using the handbook classification and assuming the members are arranged properly, the truss is:
questions.solution:
Refer to Stability, Determinacy, and Classification of Structures in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 277 (PDF page 283).

$$m + r = 9 + 3 = 12,\qquad 2j = 12$$

Since \(m + r = 2j\), the truss is stable and statically determinate.

choices: unstable because it has a hinge
questions.explanation: Compare 3m + r = 13 with 3j + c = 13. Forgetting the condition equations from the hinges changes the right side to 12.
questions.question: A plane frame has m = 3 members, r = 4 reaction components, j = 4 joints and c = 1 condition equation (internal hinges). Assuming a proper arrangement, the frame is:
questions.solution:
Refer to Stability, Determinacy, and Classification of Structures in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 277 (PDF page 283).

$$\begin{aligned}3m + r &= 3(3) + 4 \\ &= 13,\qquad 3j + c \\ &= 3(4) + 1 \\ &= 13\end{aligned}$$

So the frame is stable and statically determinate.

questions.explanation: Equating the downward load deflection to the upward redundant deflection gives 3wL/8. The fixed end then carries 5wL/8, which is the value in the first wrong choice.
questions.question: A cantilever of length L carries a uniform load w and is propped at its free end. Using the force method in the handbook with deflections \(\Delta = wL^4/(8EI)\) from the load and \(\delta = B_yL^3/(3EI)\) from the redundant, what is the prop reaction in terms of wL?
questions.solution:
Refer to Elementary Statically Indeterminate Structures by Force Method of Analysis in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 276 (PDF page 282).

Compatibility requires the net deflection at the prop to be zero:

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{wL^4}{8EI} &= \frac{B_yL^3}{3EI}\quad\Rightarrow\quad B_y \\ &= \frac{3wL}{8}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The span in the handbook formulas is the full length, 2L. The middle support carries more than half of the total load wL \(\cdot\) 2 \(/ 2\) = wL. The end reactions are each 3wL/8.
questions.question: A two-span continuous beam has equal spans L (total length 2L) and a uniform load w. Using the force method in the handbook with the middle support removed, where \(\Delta_{BB} = 5w(2L)^4/(384EI)\) and \(\delta_{BB} = B_y(2L)^3/(48EI)\), what is the middle reaction?
questions.solution:
Refer to Elementary Statically Indeterminate Structures by Force Method of Analysis in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 276 (PDF page 282).

Set the net deflection to zero with the total span \(2L\):

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{5w(2L)^4}{384EI} &= \frac{B_y(2L)^3}{48EI}\quad\Rightarrow\quad B_y \\ &= \frac{5w(2L)}{8} \\ &= \frac{5wL}{4}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: wL²/8 is the simply supported midspan moment (216 kip-ft). wL²/12 is the fixed-end value.
questions.question: A fixed-fixed beam spans 24 ft and carries a uniform load of 3 kip/ft. Using the handbook fixed-end moment formula, what is the magnitude of the end moment?
questions.solution:
Refer to Member Fixed-End Moments (Magnitudes) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 277 (PDF page 283).

$$\begin{aligned}FEM &= \frac{wL^2}{12} \\ &= \frac{3(24)^2}{12} \\ &= 144\ \text{kip-ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The end nearer the load carries the larger fixed-end moment. Swapping the two formulas reverses the answer, and PL/8 applies only to a load at midspan.
questions.question: A fixed-fixed beam has a 30 kip point load at 8 ft from end A and 12 ft from end B. Using the handbook formulas, what are the fixed-end moment magnitudes at A and B?
questions.solution:
Refer to Member Fixed-End Moments (Magnitudes) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 277 (PDF page 283).

$$\begin{aligned}FEM_{AB} &= \frac{Pab^2}{L^2} \\ &= \frac{30(8)(12)^2}{20^2} \\ &= 86.4,\qquad FEM_{BA} \\ &= \frac{Pa^2b}{L^2} \\ &= 57.6\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 833 kip-ft is the nominal Mp without φb. Dividing by Ω = 1.67 gives the ASD allowable (499 kip-ft). The last choice is in kip-in, not kip-ft.
questions.question: A compact W-shape has Fy = 50 ksi and Zx = 200 in³ and is fully braced (Lb ≤ Lp). Using the handbook with φb = 0.90, what is the design flexural strength φbMn?
questions.solution:
Refer to Design of Steel Components (Beams) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 287 (PDF page 293).

When \(L_b \le L_p\), lateral-torsional buckling does not apply and \(M_n = M_p = F_yZ_x\).

$$\begin{aligned}\phi_bM_n &= 0.90\left(\frac{50(200)}{12}\right) \\ &= 750\ \text{kip-ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Ω = 1.67 for flexure. The factor 1.50 is the shear Ω, and φb = 0.90 belongs to LRFD.
questions.question: For a W-shape (Fy = 50 ksi, Zx = 200 in³, fully braced), what is the ASD allowable flexural strength Mn/Ωb using the handbook value of Ω?
questions.solution:
Refer to Design of Steel Components (Beams) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 287 (PDF page 293).

\(M_n = F_yZ_x/12 = 833\) kip-ft and \(\Omega = 1.67\) for flexure.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{M_n}{\Omega} &= \frac{833}{1.67} \\ &= 499\ \text{kip-ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: φv = 1.00 for rolled I-shaped webs, so no 0.90 reduction applies. 180 kip is the ASD value with Ω = 1.50.
questions.question: A rolled I-shape has overall depth 18.0 in., web thickness 0.5 in. and Fy = 50 ksi. Using the handbook shear provisions for rolled I-shaped webs, what is the LRFD design shear strength?
questions.solution:
Refer to Design of Steel Components (Shear) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 287 (PDF page 293).

\(A_w = d\,t_w = 18.0(0.5) = 9.0\) in², with \(C_{v1} = 1.0\) and \(\phi_v = 1.00\).

$$\phi_vV_n = 1.00(0.6)(50)(9.0) = 270\ \text{kip}$$

questions.explanation: Every term in the denominator is needed. Dropping MC gives a larger Cb, the reciprocal gives a value below 1, and using MA for all three points ignores the centerline moment.
questions.question: In an unbraced segment, the absolute moments are Mmax = 100 kip-ft, MA = 75 kip-ft at the quarter point, MB = 100 kip-ft at the center and MC = 75 kip-ft at the three-quarter point. Using the handbook equation, what is Cb?
questions.solution:
Refer to Design of Steel Components (Lateral-Torsional Buckling) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 287 (PDF page 293).

$$\begin{aligned}C_b &= \frac{12.5M_{max}}{2.5M_{max} + 3M_A + 4M_B + 3M_C} \\ &= \frac{12.5(100)}{2.5(100) + 3(75) + 4(100) + 3(75)} \\ &= 1.14\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 0.877Fe = 39.2 ksi applies only above the slenderness limit 113.4. Fe itself is the elastic Euler stress, and Fy is the upper bound that Fcr does not reach.
questions.question: A steel column without slender elements has KL/r = 80 and Fy = 50 ksi (E = 29,000 ksi). Using the handbook, what is the critical stress Fcr?
questions.solution:
Refer to Design of Steel Components (Columns; Fe defined on printed page 288) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 287 (PDF page 293).

The limit is \(4.71\sqrt{E/F_y} = 113.4\). Since KL/r = 80 is below it, use \(F_{cr} = 0.658^{F_y/F_e}F_y\) with \(F_e = \pi^2E/(KL/r)^2 = 44.7\) ksi.

$$F_{cr} = 0.658^{50/44.7}(50) = 31.3\ \text{ksi}$$

questions.explanation: 4.71 is the coefficient in the handbook. The 0.877 appears as a multiplier on Fe in the elastic equation, not in the limit.
questions.question: For flexural buckling of members without slender elements, which expression gives the KL/r value that separates the inelastic equation from the elastic one, per the handbook?
questions.solution:
Refer to Design of Steel Components (Columns) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 287 (PDF page 293).

The handbook uses (a) \(F_{cr} = 0.658^{F_y/F_e}F_y\) when \(KL/r \le 4.71\sqrt{E/F_y}\) and (b) \(F_{cr} = 0.877F_e\) when \(KL/r > 4.71\sqrt{E/F_y}\).

questions.explanation: The design strength φMn is 240 kip-ft (φ = 0.9, if tension-controlled). Using d instead of d − a/2 overstates the arm, and using d − a understates it.
questions.question: A singly reinforced rectangular beam has b = 12 in., d = 20 in., As = 3.0 in², f'c = 4,000 psi and fy = 60,000 psi. Using the handbook equations, what is the nominal flexural strength Mn?
questions.solution:
Refer to Beams-Flexure, Singly-Reinforced Beams in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 281 (PDF page 287).

$$\begin{aligned}a &= \frac{A_sf_y}{0.85f'_cb} \\ &= \frac{3.0(60{,}000)}{0.85(4{,}000)(12)} \\ &= 4.41\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}M_n &= A_sf_y\left(d - \frac{a}{2}\right) \\ &= 3.0(60{,}000)\left(20 - 2.21\right) \\ &= 3{,}202{,}941\ \text{in.-lb}\end{aligned}$$

This equals 267 kip-ft.

questions.explanation: εt above 0.005 means tension-controlled with φ = 0.90. Using a in place of c in the strain formula gives a different strain, and φ = 0.65 is for compression-controlled tied sections.
questions.question: For the beam with a = 4.41 in., d = dt = 20 in. and β1 = 0.85, the neutral axis depth is c = a/β1. Using the handbook strain relationship, what is the net tensile strain εt, and what φ applies?
questions.solution:
Refer to Beams-Flexure and Resistance Factors in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 281 (PDF page 287).

$$\begin{aligned}c &= \frac{a}{\beta_1} \\ &= 5.19\ \text{in.},\qquad \varepsilon_t \\ &= 0.003\,\frac{d_t - c}{c} \\ &= 0.0086\end{aligned}$$

Since \(\varepsilon_t \ge 0.005\), the section is tension-controlled and \(\phi = 0.90\).

questions.explanation: 30.4 kip is the nominal Vc without φ. Half of φVc is the threshold below which no stirrups are required.
questions.question: A beam web has bw = 12 in., d = 20 in. and f'c = 4,000 psi (normal weight concrete). Using the handbook, what is the design shear strength provided by the concrete, φVc, with φ = 0.75?
questions.solution:
Refer to Beams-Shear in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 282 (PDF page 288).

$$\begin{aligned}V_c &= 2\sqrt{f'_c}\,b_wd \\ &= 2\sqrt{4{,}000}(12)(20) \\ &= 30{,}358\ \text{lb}\end{aligned}$$

$$\phi V_c = 0.75(30{,}358) = 22.8\ \text{kip}$$

questions.explanation: In the handbook table this is one of the two expressions whose smaller value governs; the other uses 0.75 bw sqrt(f'c). The 24 in. cap and d/2 are separate maximum-spacing limits.
questions.question: Two-leg #3 stirrups give Av = 0.22 in² with fy = 60,000 psi on a web with bw = 12 in. Using the handbook minimum-area expression Av fy/(50 bw), what is the spacing s from this expression alone?
questions.solution:
Refer to Beams-Shear (required and maximum-permitted stirrup spacing) in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 282 (PDF page 288).

$$\begin{aligned}s &= \frac{A_vf_y}{50b_w} \\ &= \frac{0.22(60{,}000)}{50(12)} \\ &= 22.0\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 1153 kip is Pn without φ. Omitting the 0.80 factor for accidental eccentricity or using the gross area for the concrete term overstates the strength.
questions.question: A short tied column has Ag = 324 in², Ast = 6.0 in², f'c = 4,000 psi and fy = 60,000 psi. Using the handbook, what is the design axial strength φPn with φ = 0.65?
questions.solution:
Refer to Short Columns, Design Column Strength, Tied Columns in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 284 (PDF page 290).

$$\begin{aligned}P_n &= 0.80\left[0.85f'_c(A_g - A_{st}) + A_{st}f_y\right] \\ &= 0.80\big[0.85(4000)(324-6.0) \\ &\quad + 6.0(60000)\big] \\ &= 1{,}152{,}960\ \text{lb}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\phi P_n &= 0.65(1153) \\ &= 749\ \text{kip}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: ρg is the steel area over the gross area, here 0.0185, which lies between 0.01 and 0.08.
questions.question: A square column is 18 in. by 18 in. (Ag = 324 in²) with 6.0 in² of longitudinal steel. Using the handbook limits 0.01 ≤ ρg ≤ 0.08, what is ρg and is it acceptable?
questions.solution:
Refer to Short Columns, Limits for Longitudinal Reinforcements in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 284 (PDF page 290).

$$\begin{aligned}\rho_g &= \frac{A_{st}}{A_g} \\ &= \frac{6.0}{324} \\ &= 0.0185\end{aligned}$$

This lies between 0.01 and 0.08.

questions.explanation: The load scales with 1/K². The wrong choices use the K values of other end conditions.
questions.question: A steel column (E = 29,000 ksi) has I = 100 in⁴ about the buckling axis and an actual length of 15 ft. With the effective length factor K for pinned-pinned ends, what is the Euler buckling load?
questions.solution:
Refer to Table C-A-7.1 AISC Approximate Values of Effective Length Factor, K in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 293 (PDF page 299).

For pinned-pinned ends the theoretical K is 1.0. \(P_{cr} = \dfrac{\pi^2EI}{(KL)^2}\).

$$\begin{aligned}P_{cr} &= \frac{\pi^2(29{,}000)(100)}{(1.0\times180)^2} \\ &= 883\ \text{kip}\end{aligned}$$

choices: It increases by a factor of 2
It increases by a factor of 4
It increases by a factor of 16
It decreases by a factor of 4
questions.explanation: Because K is squared, halving K quadruples the buckling load.
questions.question: A column is changed from pinned-pinned ends to fixed-fixed ends with the same length, E and I. Using the theoretical effective length factors, how does the Euler buckling load change?
questions.solution:
Refer to Table C-A-7.1 AISC Approximate Values of Effective Length Factor, K in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 293 (PDF page 299).

The theoretical K is 1.0 for pinned-pinned and 0.5 for fixed-fixed. Since \(P_{cr} \propto 1/K^2\), the ratio is \((1.0/0.5)^2 = 4\).
questions.subtopic: Euler load ratio, fixed-fixed vs pinned-pinned

questions.explanation: Length must be in inches to match E in ksi, and the length term is squared.
questions.question: A pinned-pinned steel column (E = 29,000 ksi) is 15 ft long. What moment of inertia about the buckling axis is needed for an Euler buckling load of 500 kip?
questions.solution:
Refer to Table C-A-7.1 AISC Approximate Values of Effective Length Factor, K in the Civil Engineering: Structural Engineering section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 293 (PDF page 299).

With K = 1.0, solve \(P_{cr} = \pi^2EI/(KL)^2\) for I:

$$\begin{aligned}I &= \frac{P_{cr}(KL)^2}{\pi^2E} \\ &= \frac{500(180)^2}{\pi^2(29{,}000)} \\ &= 56.6\ \text{in}^4\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Required moment of inertia for a given Euler load

questions.explanation: The initial abstraction 0.2S is subtracted from P and squared, and the denominator adds 0.8S. Subtracting 0.2S only gives too large a runoff, and a CN that is too high overstates the runoff.
questions.question: A watershed has a curve number of 80. Using the handbook NRCS/SCS method, what is the runoff depth for a 4.0 in. storm?
questions.solution:
Refer to NRCS/SCS Rainfall-Runoff in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 296 (PDF page 302).

$$\begin{aligned}S &= \frac{1000}{CN} - 10 \\ &= \frac{1000}{80} - 10 \\ &= 2.50\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}Q &= \frac{(P - 0.2S)^2}{P + 0.8S} \\ &= \frac{(4.0 - 0.50)^2}{4.0 + 2.00} \\ &= 2.04\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Forgetting the 10 or adding it instead of subtracting changes the result by 10 in. or 20 in.
questions.question: A basin has a curve number of 65. Using the handbook relationship, what is the maximum basin retention S?
questions.solution:
Refer to NRCS/SCS Rainfall-Runoff in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 296 (PDF page 302).

$$\begin{aligned}S &= \frac{1000}{CN} - 10 \\ &= \frac{1000}{65} - 10 \\ &= 5.38\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: CN = 1000/(S + 10). Dividing by S alone gives 400, which is above the CN range of 100.
questions.question: A watershed has a maximum retention S of 2.5 in. Using the handbook, what is the curve number?
questions.solution:
Refer to NRCS/SCS Rainfall-Runoff in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 296 (PDF page 302).

$$\begin{aligned}CN &= \frac{1000}{S + 10} \\ &= \frac{1000}{2.5 + 10} \\ &= 80\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Q = CIA with A in acres and I in in./hr gives cfs directly. Leaving C out gives the unreduced flow and leaving A out gives only CI.
questions.question: A 45 acre watershed has a runoff coefficient of 0.35 and a design rainfall intensity of 2.8 in./hr. Using the handbook rational formula, what is the peak discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to Rational Formula in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 296 (PDF page 302).

$$Q = CIA = 0.35(2.8)(45) = 44.1\ \text{cfs}$$

questions.explanation: Inflows (P, Qin, Qg) are added and outflows and losses (Qout, Es, Ts, I) are subtracted. Sign errors flip the result.
questions.question: For a surface water system in one month (all values in inches over the basin): P = 9.0, Qin = 1.5, Qout = 2.0, Qg = 0.4, evaporation Es = 1.1, transpiration Ts = 0.6, infiltration I = 3.0. Using the handbook budget, what is the change in surface water storage?
questions.solution:
Refer to Hydrologic Mass Balance (Budget) in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 296 (PDF page 302).

$$\begin{aligned}\Delta S_s &= P + Q_{in} - Q_{out} \\ &\quad + Q_g - E_s - T_s - I \\ &= 9.0+1.5-2.0+0.4 \\ &\quad -1.1-0.6-3.0 \\ &= 4.2\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The handbook gives Pc between 0.3 and 0.85 with 0.7 as the common value. Dividing by Pc is a reversal, and the end values 0.3 and 0.85 are the range limits.
questions.question: The measured pan evaporation is 0.28 in./day. Using the handbook's common pan coefficient, what is the lake evaporation?
questions.solution:
Refer to Pan Evaporation in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 296 (PDF page 302).

$$E_L = P_cE_p = 0.7(0.28) = 0.196\ \text{in./day}$$

questions.explanation: The gradient is dh/dx = 0.02, not its inverse. Dropping A gives the Darcy velocity, not the discharge.
questions.question: An aquifer has hydraulic conductivity K = 0.0004 ft/s and a cross-sectional flow area of 25.0 ft². The head drops 2.0 ft over a flow path of 100 ft. Using the handbook form of Darcy's law, what is the magnitude of the discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to Darcy's Law in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 298 (PDF page 304).

$$\begin{aligned}Q &= KA\left|\frac{dh}{dx}\right| \\ &= 0.0004(25.0)\left(\frac{2.0}{100}\right) \\ &= 2.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{ft}^3/\text{s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Water moves only through the pores, so the seepage velocity is larger than the Darcy velocity by 1/n. Multiplying by n gives a smaller value.
questions.question: Groundwater flows through sand with K = 0.0004 ft/s, a hydraulic gradient of 0.02 and effective porosity n = 0.25. Using the handbook, what is the average seepage velocity?
questions.solution:
Refer to Darcy's Law (specific discharge and seepage velocity) in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 298 (PDF page 304).

The specific discharge is \(q = K\,|dh/dx| = 0.0004(0.02) = 8.0\times10^{-6}\) ft/s.

$$\begin{aligned}v &= \frac{q}{n} \\ &= \frac{8.0\times10^{-6}}{0.25} \\ &= 3.2\times10^{-5}\ \text{ft/s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: T has units of length squared per time (L²T⁻¹). Dividing K by b gives 0.00005, which has the wrong units.
questions.question: A confined aquifer has hydraulic conductivity K = 0.002 ft/s and thickness b = 40 ft. What is its transmissivity, using the handbook definition?
questions.solution:
Refer to Transmissivity, T in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 298 (PDF page 304).

The handbook defines transmissivity as the product of hydraulic conductivity and aquifer thickness.

$$T = Kb = 0.002(40) = 0.08\ \text{ft}^2/\text{s}$$

questions.explanation: The head terms are squared, and the logarithm is natural (ln), as the handbook says. A common-log value, no squares, or an extra factor of 2 gives the wrong choices.
questions.question: A well in an unconfined aquifer (K = 0.001 ft/s) has a water surface 40 ft above the aquifer bottom at the well wall (r1 = 0.5 ft) and 48 ft at r2 = 300 ft. Using Dupuit's formula, what is the well discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to Dupuit's Formula in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 299 (PDF page 305).

$$\begin{aligned}Q &= \frac{\pi K(h_2^2 - h_1^2)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)} \\ &= \frac{\pi(0.001)(48^2 - 40^2)}{\ln(300/0.5)} \\ &= 0.346\ \text{cfs}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The confined-aquifer form uses the head difference, not the squared heads, and a factor 2π. Using log base 10 or dropping the 2 changes the answer.
questions.question: A confined aquifer has transmissivity T = 0.05 ft²/s. Piezometric heights above the aquifer bottom are 20 ft at r1 = 0.5 ft and 26 ft at r2 = 200 ft. Using the Thiem equation, what is the pumping rate?
questions.solution:
Refer to Thiem Equation in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 299 (PDF page 305).

$$\begin{aligned}Q &= \frac{2\pi T(h_2 - h_1)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)} \\ &= \frac{2\pi(0.05)(26-20)}{\ln(200/0.5)} \\ &= 0.315\ \text{cfs}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Specific capacity is discharge per unit drawdown. The inverse (40) is drawdown per cfs.
questions.question: A well is pumped at 0.30 cfs and the drawdown in the well is 12 ft. Using the handbook definition, what is the specific capacity?
questions.solution:
Refer to Dupuit's Formula (specific capacity Q/Dw) in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 299 (PDF page 305).

The handbook lists specific capacity as Q/Dw.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{Q}{D_w} &= \frac{0.30}{12} \\ &= 0.025\ \text{cfs/ft}\end{aligned}$$

choices: The volume of water taken into or released from storage per unit surface area per unit change in head
The volume of water per unit time passing a unit width under a unit gradient
The product of hydraulic conductivity and aquifer thickness
The ratio of the flow velocity to the effective porosity
questions.explanation: The other choices describe transmissivity and seepage velocity or a flow rate. Storativity is dimensionless.
questions.question: Which statement matches the handbook definition of storativity (storage coefficient) of an aquifer?
questions.solution:
Refer to Storativity or storage coefficient of an aquifer, S in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 298 (PDF page 304).

The handbook defines storativity as the volume of water taken into or released from storage per unit surface area of aquifer per unit change in potentiometric head.

choices: The hydrograph of total streamflow at a gauge for one year
The direct runoff hydrograph resulting from one unit of rainfall occurring uniformly in space and time over a specified period
The base flow hydrograph resulting from one unit of groundwater recharge
The peak flow resulting from one unit of rainfall intensity over any duration
questions.explanation: It applies to direct runoff only, and the rainfall occurs uniformly over a specified duration.
questions.question: The handbook defines a unit hydrograph as:
questions.solution:
Refer to Unit hydrograph in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 298 (PDF page 304).

The handbook states that a unit hydrograph is the direct runoff hydrograph that would result from one unit of rainfall occurring uniformly in space and time over a specified period of time.

questions.explanation: The unit discharge q is squared, then divided by g, then the cube root is taken. Using Q instead of q or q without squaring gives different depths.
questions.question: A rectangular channel is 20 ft wide and carries 300 cfs. Using the handbook equation, what is the critical depth?
questions.solution:
Refer to Critical depth for rectangular channels in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 302 (PDF page 308).

$$\begin{aligned}q &= \frac{Q}{B} \\ &= \frac{300}{20} \\ &= 15.0\ \text{cfs/ft}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}y_c &= \left(\frac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3} \\ &= \left(\frac{15.0^2}{32.2}\right)^{1/3} \\ &= 1.91\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Using the area in place of the hydraulic depth, or not taking the square root, gives different values. Fr < 1 means subcritical.
questions.question: A channel flows with a velocity of 3.0 ft/s, a flow area of 60 ft² and a top width of 20 ft. Using the handbook hydraulic depth, what is the Froude number and flow regime?
questions.solution:
Refer to Froude number and flow regimes in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 302 (PDF page 308).

The hydraulic depth is \(y_h = A/T = 60/20 = 3.0\) ft.

$$\begin{aligned}Fr &= \frac{V}{\sqrt{g\,y_h}} \\ &= \frac{3.0}{\sqrt{32.2(3.0)}} \\ &= 0.31\end{aligned}$$

Since Fr < 1 the flow is subcritical.

choices: Supercritical flow, inertial forces exceed gravity forces
Critical flow, depth equals the alternate depth
Subcritical flow, gravity forces exceed inertial forces
Subcritical flow because the velocity is less than the wave speed
questions.explanation: Fr = 1.6 is greater than 1.
questions.question: Which description is correct for a channel flow with Froude number 1.6?
questions.solution:
Refer to Froude number in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 302 (PDF page 308).

The handbook gives supercritical flow for Fr > 1, subcritical for Fr < 1 and critical for Fr = 1. The Froude number is the ratio of inertial forces to gravity forces.

questions.explanation: The velocity head is V²/2g. Omitting the 2 or using V instead of V² gives the wrong choices.
questions.question: Water flows at a depth of 4.0 ft with velocity 6.0 ft/s. Taking α = 1, what is the specific energy using the handbook expression?
questions.solution:
Refer to Specific Energy Diagram in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 302 (PDF page 308).

$$\begin{aligned}E &= \frac{\alpha V^2}{2g} + y \\ &= \frac{(1)(6.0)^2}{2(32.2)} + 4.0 \\ &= 4.56\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

choices: The normal and critical depths for the same flow
Two flow depths with the same specific energy
The depths on either side of a hydraulic jump
Two flow depths with the same momentum
questions.explanation: Sequent depths share momentum and are used for hydraulic jumps.
questions.question: In the handbook specific energy diagram, alternate depths are:
questions.solution:
Refer to Specific Energy Diagram in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 302 (PDF page 308).

The handbook defines alternate depths as depths with the same specific energy. Sequent (conjugate) depths are depths with the same momentum.

questions.explanation: The hydraulic radius uses the wetted perimeter with both sides and the bottom. Using S instead of the square root, K = 1.0 in USCS units, or width for the perimeter gives other values.
questions.question: A rectangular concrete channel (n = 0.013) is 6 ft wide and flows 3 ft deep on a slope of 0.0009. Using Manning's equation with K = 1.486, what is the discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to Manning's Equation in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 303 (PDF page 309).

\(A = 6(3) = 18\) ft², \(P = 6 + 2(3) = 12\) ft, \(R_H = A/P = 1.50\) ft.

$$\begin{aligned}Q &= \frac{1.486}{n}AR_H^{2/3}S^{1/2} \\ &= \frac{1.486}{0.013}(18)(1.50)^{2/3}(0.0009)^{1/2} \\ &= 81\ \text{cfs}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Free discharge suppressed uses CLH¹.5. The contracted form subtracts 0.2H from L and the V-notch uses H².5.
questions.question: A suppressed rectangular weir is 8 ft long with a head of 1.2 ft over the crest. Using the handbook with C = 3.33, what is the discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to Weir Formulas in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 303 (PDF page 309).

$$\begin{aligned}Q &= CLH^{3/2} \\ &= 3.33(8)(1.2)^{1.5} \\ &= 35.0\ \text{cfs}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The contraction reduces the effective length by 0.2H. Using 0.1H or the V-notch exponent gives wrong values.
questions.question: A contracted rectangular weir with free discharge is 8 ft long with a head of 1.2 ft. Using the handbook with C = 3.33, what is the discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to Weir Formulas in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 303 (PDF page 309).

$$\begin{aligned}Q &= C(L - 0.2H)H^{3/2} \\ &= 3.33(8 - 0.2(1.2))(1.2)^{1.5} \\ &= 34.0\ \text{cfs}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The V-notch discharge varies as H².5 and C = 2.54 in USCS units. The 3.33 is the rectangular weir value and 1.40 is the SI value.
questions.question: A 90° V-notch weir has a head of 0.9 ft. Using the handbook with C = 2.54, what is the discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to Weir Formulas (V-notch) in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 303 (PDF page 309).

$$Q = CH^{5/2} = 2.54(0.9)^{2.5} = 1.95\ \text{cfs}$$

questions.explanation: Diameter must be in feet and flow in cfs for this form, and the flow exponent is 1.852. Using Q² or D in inches gives the other values.
questions.question: A 12 in. pipe (1.0 ft) is 2000 ft long with C = 120 and carries 3.0 cfs. Using the handbook head loss equation, what is hf?
questions.solution:
Refer to Circular Pipe Head Loss Equation (Head Loss Expressed in Feet) in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 304 (PDF page 310).

$$\begin{aligned}h_f &= \frac{4.73L}{C^{1.852}D^{4.87}}Q^{1.852} \\ &= \frac{4.73(2000)}{120^{1.852}(1.0)^{4.87}}(3.0)^{1.852} \\ &= 10.2\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: This form uses Q in gpm and D in inches. Converting the diameter to feet or applying a head conversion gives wrong values.
questions.question: A 6 in. pipe with C = 120 carries 300 gpm. Using the handbook pressure-loss equation for U.S. customary units, what is the pressure loss per foot of pipe?
questions.solution:
Refer to Circular Pipe Head Loss Equation (Head Loss Expressed as Pressure) in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 304 (PDF page 310).

$$\begin{aligned}P &= \frac{4.52Q^{1.85}}{C^{1.85}D^{4.87}} \\ &= \frac{4.52(300)^{1.85}}{120^{1.85}(6)^{4.87}} \\ &= 0.0040\ \text{psi/ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: A lower C means more friction loss, and older cast iron has the lowest value of these.
questions.question: Using the handbook table of Hazen-Williams coefficients, which pipe has the lowest C among these?
questions.solution:
Refer to Values of Hazen-Williams Coefficient C in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 304 (PDF page 310).

From the table: ductile iron 140, concrete 130, new cast iron 130, 5-year-old cast iron 120 and 20-year-old cast iron 100.
questions.subtopic: Hazen-Williams C for old cast iron

questions.explanation: The ratio is HR/HF with exponent 0.54. Inverting the ratio or exponent gives the other choices.
questions.question: A hydrant flow test gives a total test flow of 1000 gpm with static pressure 60 psi and residual pressure 40 psi. Using the handbook formula, what is the rated capacity at 20 psi?
questions.solution:
Refer to Formula for Calculating Rated Capacity at 20 psi from Fire Hydrant in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 305 (PDF page 311).

\(H_R = P_S - 20 = 40\) psi and \(H_F = P_S - P_R = 20\) psi.

$$\begin{aligned}Q_R &= Q_F\left(\frac{H_R}{H_F}\right)^{0.54} \\ &= 1000\left(\frac{40}{20}\right)^{0.54} \\ &= 1454\ \text{gpm}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The coefficient depends on outlet geometry: 0.90, 0.80 or 0.70. Pressure enters as a square root.
questions.question: A hydrant outlet is 2.5 in. in diameter, smooth and well-rounded, with a pitot pressure of 10 psi. Using the handbook, what is the discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to Fire Hydrant Discharging to Atmosphere in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 305 (PDF page 311).

A smooth, well-rounded outlet has \(C_d = 0.90\).

$$\begin{aligned}Q &= 29.8D^2C_dP^{1/2} \\ &= 29.8(2.5)^2(0.90)(10)^{1/2} \\ &= 530\ \text{gpm}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Pan evaporation overstates lake evaporation, so Pc is below 1.
questions.question: What range does the handbook give for the pan coefficient Pc used to convert pan evaporation to lake evaporation?
questions.solution:
Refer to Pan Evaporation in the Civil Engineering: Hydrology/Water Resources section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 296 (PDF page 302).

The handbook states that Pc ranges from 0.3 to 0.85, with a common value of 0.7.

questions.explanation: bh³/36 is the centroidal value. The base axis is a parallel axis one-third of the height away.
questions.question: A right triangle has base b = 6 in. and height h = 12 in. What is its area moment of inertia about the base axis (x axis along the base)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the table of area properties (triangle) in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 99 (PDF page 105).

The handbook gives \(I_{x_c} = bh^3/36\) and \(I_x = bh^3/12\) about the base.

$$\begin{aligned}I_x &= \frac{bh^3}{12} \\ &= \frac{6(12)^3}{12} \\ &= 864\ \text{in}^4\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Triangle moment of inertia about base

questions.explanation: The offset distance is squared. Using d instead of d², or dropping Ic, gives the other choices.
questions.question: A rectangle 6 in. wide and 12 in. tall has a centroidal moment of inertia about its horizontal centroidal axis. What is its moment of inertia about an axis parallel to it and 10 in. away?
questions.solution:
Refer to the parallel axis theorem in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 97 (PDF page 103).

\(I_c = bh^3/12 = 864\) in⁴ and \(A = 72\) in².

$$\begin{aligned}I &= I_c + Ad^2 \\ &= 864 + 72(10)^2 \\ &= 8064\ \text{in}^4\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: With the radius a, \(I = \pi a^4/4\). \(\pi a^4/2\) is the polar J, and \(5\pi a^4/4\) is the value about a tangent axis.
questions.question: A solid circular section has radius a = 5 in. What is its centroidal area moment of inertia?
questions.solution:
Refer to the table of area properties (circle) in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 100 (PDF page 106).

$$\begin{aligned}I_{x_c} &= \frac{\pi a^4}{4} \\ &= \frac{\pi(5)^4}{4} \\ &= 491\ \text{in}^4\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: J equals Ix + Iy, so for a circle it is twice the centroidal Ix.
questions.question: For a solid circle of radius a = 5 in., what is the polar moment of inertia J?
questions.solution:
Refer to the table of area properties (circle) in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 100 (PDF page 106).

$$J = \frac{\pi a^4}{2} = 982\ \text{in}^4$$

questions.explanation: Each centroid distance is weighted by its area. Averaging the two distances or swapping the weights gives wrong values.
questions.question: A T-shaped area is split into two rectangles: area 48 in² with centroid 3 in. above the base, and area 36 in² with centroid 12 in. above the base. How far above the base is the centroid of the whole area?
questions.solution:
Refer to the centroid of area definitions (discrete sum) in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 96 (PDF page 102).

$$\begin{aligned}\bar y &= \frac{\sum y_na_n}{\sum a_n} \\ &= \frac{48(3) + 36(12)}{48+36} \\ &= 6.86\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The centroid of a right triangle is b/3 and h/3 from the legs, while 2b/3 and 2h/3 would be measured from the opposite vertex.
questions.question: A right triangle has its right angle at the origin, base b = 9 ft along the x axis and height h = 6 ft along the y axis. What are the centroid coordinates?
questions.solution:
Refer to the table of area properties (right triangle) in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 99 (PDF page 105).

The handbook table gives \(x_c = b/3\) and \(y_c = h/3\) measured from the right-angle corner, so \(x_c = 9/3 = 3\) ft and \(y_c = 6/3 = 2\) ft.

questions.explanation: θ is the total contact angle in radians, 1.5 turns = 3π rad. Using 1.5 turns as the angle, a linear product, or dividing gives wrong values.
questions.question: A rope wraps 1.5 turns (3π rad) around a fixed post. The coefficient of static friction is 0.25 and the holding force is 80 lb. What is the largest force F1 that can be resisted using the handbook belt friction equation?
questions.solution:
Refer to Belt Friction in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 98 (PDF page 104).

$$\begin{aligned}F_1 &= F_2e^{\mu\theta} \\ &= 80\,e^{0.25(3\pi)} \\ &= 844\ \text{lb}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Both terms are needed. v0t alone is 96 ft; the acceleration term alone is 128 ft; using the final velocity for the whole time overstates the distance.
questions.question: A particle with initial velocity 12 ft/s accelerates uniformly at 4 ft/s² for 8 s. How far does it travel?
questions.solution:
Refer to Particle Rectilinear Motion (constant acceleration) in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 103 (PDF page 109).

$$\begin{aligned}s - s_0 &= v_0t + \tfrac{1}{2}a_0t^2 \\ &= 12(8) + \tfrac{1}{2}(4)(8)^2 \\ &= 224\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The equation uses squared speeds and the factor 2. Using unsquared speeds or dropping the 2 gives wrong values.
questions.question: A car speeds up from 10 ft/s to 30 ft/s over 200 ft with constant acceleration. What is the acceleration?
questions.solution:
Refer to Particle Rectilinear Motion (constant acceleration) in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 103 (PDF page 109).

$$\begin{aligned}v^2 &= v_0^2 + 2a_0(s - s_0)\ \Rightarrow\ a_0 \\ &= \frac{30^2 - 10^2}{2(200)} \\ &= 2.0\ \text{ft/s}^2\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The range equals v₀² sin 2θ/g. Using only sin θ, halving, or cos² gives other values.
questions.question: A projectile launches at 80 ft/s at 35° above horizontal from level ground (g = 32.2 ft/s²). Using constant-acceleration kinematics in x and y, what is the horizontal range?
questions.solution:
Refer to Particle Curvilinear Motion (x, y coordinates) and constant acceleration in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 103 (PDF page 109).

The flight time follows from \(y = v_0\sin\theta\,t - \tfrac12gt^2 = 0\): \(t = 2.85\) s (derived).

$$\begin{aligned}x &= v_0\cos\theta\,t \\ &= 80\cos35°(2.85) \\ &= 187\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: a = F/m. Inverting the ratio or forgetting the time step gives wrong speeds.
questions.question: A 50 slug block starts at rest and is pushed by a constant 120 lb force for 6 s on a frictionless surface. What is its speed?
questions.solution:
Refer to constant force equations (ax = Fx/m) in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 107 (PDF page 113).

$$\begin{aligned}a_x &= \frac{F_x}{m} \\ &= \frac{120}{50} \\ &= 2.4\ \text{ft/s}^2,\qquad v_x \\ &= a_xt \\ &= 14.4\ \text{ft/s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The mass drops out. Leaving out the 2 or the square root gives wrong values.
questions.question: A 3.0 slug object falls from rest through 15.0 ft with no energy loss (g = 32.2 ft/s²). Using the handbook energy equation, what is its speed at the bottom?
questions.solution:
Refer to Principle of Work and Energy in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 107 (PDF page 113).

\(T_2 + V_2 = T_1 + V_1\) with \(T_1 = 0\), so \(\tfrac12mv^2 = mgh\) (mass cancels).

$$\begin{aligned}v &= \sqrt{2gh} \\ &= \sqrt{2(32.2)(15.0)} \\ &= 31.1\ \text{ft/s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The handbook notes that forces such as friction that dissipate energy have negative work. The weight times distance would ignore μ.
questions.question: A 80 lb crate slides 50 ft on a level floor with a kinetic friction coefficient of 0.25. Using the handbook work-energy equation with nonconservative forces, what is the work U₁→₂ done by friction?
questions.solution:
Refer to Principle of Work and Energy (nonconservative forces) in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 107 (PDF page 113).

Friction dissipates energy, so its work is negative: \(U_{1\to2} = -\mu_kN\,d = -0.25(80)(50) = -1{,}000\) ft-lb.

questions.explanation: The length must be in inches (120 in.). Using feet gives a result 12 times too small, and dropping A gives the wrong units.
questions.question: A steel rod (E = 29,000,000 psi) with area 0.5 in² and length 10 ft carries a 20,000 lb tensile load. What is the elongation?
questions.solution:
Refer to Uniaxial Loading and Deformation in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 131 (PDF page 137).

$$\begin{aligned}\delta &= \frac{PL}{AE} \\ &= \frac{20{,}000(120)}{0.5(29{,}000{,}000)} \\ &= 0.1655\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: With L in inches the result is in inches. Using feet gives a value 12 times too small.
questions.question: A 100 ft steel member (α = 6.5×10⁻⁶ /°F) heats up by 60°F and is free to expand. What is the change in length?
questions.solution:
Refer to Thermal Deformations in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 131 (PDF page 137).

$$\begin{aligned}\delta_t &= \alpha L(T - T_0) \\ &= (6.5\times10^{-6})(1200)(60) \\ &= 0.468\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The factor is (1 − 2ν). Using 1 + 2ν, or E/[2(1 + ν)] (the shear modulus), gives other values.
questions.question: A material has E = 29,000 ksi and Poisson's ratio 0.30. What is its bulk modulus using the handbook relation?
questions.solution:
Refer to Bulk (Volume) Modulus of Elasticity in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 131 (PDF page 137).

$$\begin{aligned}K &= \frac{E}{3(1 - 2\nu)} \\ &= \frac{29{,}000}{3(1 - 0.60)} \\ &= 24{,}167\ \text{ksi}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The transverse stress reduces the strain through ν. Adding it, ignoring it, or using the y equation gives the wrong choices.
questions.question: In plane stress (σz = 0), σx = 20 ksi and σy = 8 ksi, with E = 29,000 ksi and ν = 0.30. What is the strain εx?
questions.solution:
Refer to Hooke's Law, plane stress case in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 134 (PDF page 140).

$$\begin{aligned}\varepsilon_x &= \frac{1}{E}(\sigma_x - \nu\sigma_y) \\ &= \frac{20 - 0.30(8)}{29{,}000} \\ &= 607\times10^{-6}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: M must be in kip-in. Leaving it in kip-ft gives a stress 12 times too small.
questions.question: A beam section has I = 300 in⁴ and c = 6 in. to the extreme fiber. What is the maximum bending stress at a section with M = 120 kip-ft?
questions.solution:
Refer to Maximum normal stresses in a beam due to bending in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 136 (PDF page 142).

Convert M to kip-in: \(120(12) = 1440\).

$$\begin{aligned}\sigma &= \frac{Mc}{I} \\ &= \frac{1440(6)}{300} \\ &= 28.8\ \text{ksi}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The width b is in the denominator. Leaving it out or multiplying by it gives wrong values.
questions.question: At a point in a beam, V = 30 kip, Q = 48 in³, I = 300 in⁴ and the width is b = 4 in. What is the shear stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to Transverse shear stress in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 136 (PDF page 142).

$$\begin{aligned}\tau &= \frac{VQ}{Ib} \\ &= \frac{30(48)}{300(4)} \\ &= 1.20\ \text{ksi}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The handbook defines n as E1/E2 with E1 > E2, so n > 1. The inverse is below 1.
questions.question: A composite beam uses steel (E = 29,000 ksi) and wood (E = 1,800 ksi). Using the handbook transformed-section method with steel as material 1, what is the modular ratio n?
questions.solution:
Refer to Composite Sections in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 137 (PDF page 143).

$$\begin{aligned}n &= \frac{E_1}{E_2} \\ &= \frac{29{,}000}{1{,}800} \\ &= 16.1\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The center alone is the average normal stress. The principal stress is the center plus the radius.
