questions.question: At a point in plane stress, σx = 60 ksi, σy = 20 ksi and τxy = 15 ksi. What is the larger principal stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to Mohr's circle (center and radius) in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 133 (PDF page 139).

Center \(C = (\sigma_x+\sigma_y)/2 = 40\) ksi and radius \(R = \sqrt{((\sigma_x-\sigma_y)/2)^2 + \tau_{xy}^2} = 25.00\) ksi.

$$\sigma_1 = C + R = 65.0\ \text{ksi}$$

questions.explanation: The in-plane maximum shear stress equals the radius of Mohr's circle. Twice the radius is the diameter.
questions.question: For the stress state (σx = 60 ksi, σy = 20 ksi, τxy = 15 ksi), what is the maximum in-plane shear stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to Mohr's circle (maximum in-plane shear stress) in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 134 (PDF page 140).

The handbook gives \(\tau_{in} = R = 25.00\) ksi.

questions.explanation: Pressure in pascals must be divided by 1,000 for kPa. Using ρ instead of γ gives the mass density times depth.
questions.question: What is the gauge pressure at a depth of 12 m in fresh water (γ = 9,810 N/m³)?
questions.solution:
Refer to hydrostatic pressure (P = γh) in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 182 (PDF page 188).

$$\begin{aligned}P &= \gamma h \\ &= 9{,}810(12) \\ &= 117{,}720\ \text{Pa} \\ &= 117.7\ \text{kPa}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: A smaller area means a higher velocity. The inverted ratio gives a lower value.
questions.question: Water flows at 3 m/s through a pipe with area 0.05 m². The pipe contracts to 0.02 m². What is the velocity in the smaller pipe?
questions.solution:
Refer to the continuity equation (A1v1 = A2v2) in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 185 (PDF page 191).

For incompressible flow the discharge is the same: \(A_1v_1 = A_2v_2\).

$$\begin{aligned}v_2 &= \frac{A_1v_1}{A_2} \\ &= \frac{0.05(3)}{0.02} \\ &= 7.5\ \text{m/s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The velocity is squared and divided by 2g. The Fanning form has a factor of 4 on f only when f is the Fanning factor.
questions.question: Water flows at 2.5 m/s in a 0.2 m diameter pipe, 100 m long, with friction factor f = 0.02. Using the Darcy-Weisbach equation, what is the head loss?
questions.solution:
Refer to Head Loss Due to Flow (Darcy-Weisbach) in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 187 (PDF page 193).

$$\begin{aligned}h_f &= f\frac{L}{D}\frac{v^2}{2g} \\ &= 0.02\left(\frac{100}{0.2}\right)\frac{(2.5)^2}{2(9.81)} \\ &= 3.19\ \text{m}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The 1.18 ratio is for fully turbulent flow and 1.5 applies to parallel planes (1.2 m/s).
questions.question: The average velocity in a circular pipe with fully developed laminar flow is 0.8 m/s. What is the centerline velocity?
questions.solution:
Refer to velocity distribution for laminar flow in circular tubes in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 187 (PDF page 193).

For laminar flow in a circular tube the handbook gives \(v_{max} = 2\bar v\).

$$v_{max} = 2(0.8) = 1.6\ \text{m/s}$$
questions.subtopic: Maximum velocity in laminar pipe flow

questions.explanation: The stress increases linearly from zero at the centerline to the wall value. The inverse ratio gives 150 Pa.
questions.question: In a circular pipe of radius 0.10 m the shear stress at the wall is 60 Pa. What is the shear stress at r = 0.04 m?
questions.solution:
Refer to the shear stress distribution (τ/τw = r/R) in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 187 (PDF page 193).

The shear stress varies linearly with radius: \(\tau/\tau_w = r/R\).

$$\begin{aligned}\tau &= 60\left(\frac{0.04}{0.10}\right) \\ &= 24\ \text{Pa}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: A sample uses n − 1. Dividing by n gives the population value, and without the square root you get the variance.
questions.question: A sample has the values 12, 15, 11, 18, 14, 20, 16. What is the sample standard deviation?
questions.solution:
Refer to sample statistics (mean, variance, standard deviation) in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 64 (PDF page 70).

Mean \(\bar x = 15.14\). \(\sum(x-\bar x)^2 = 60.86\).

$$\begin{aligned}s &= \sqrt{\frac{\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2}{n-1}} \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{60.86}{6}} \\ &= 3.18\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The binomial coefficient counts the arrangements and the (1−p)^(n−x) term covers the successes. The last choice is P(X ≤ 3).
questions.question: A process fails with probability 0.3 on each independent trial. What is the probability of exactly 3 failures in 10 trials?
questions.solution:
Refer to Binomial distribution b(x; n, p) in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 85 (PDF page 91).

$$\begin{aligned}b(3;10,0.3) &= \binom{10}{3}(0.3)^3(0.7)^7 \\ &= 0.2668\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The variance includes the factor (1 − p).
questions.question: For a binomial variable with n = 40 and p = 0.25, what are the mean and variance?
questions.solution:
Refer to Probability and Density Functions: Means and Variances (Binomial) in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 85 (PDF page 91).

The handbook gives mean \(np = 10\) and variance \(np(1-p) = 40(0.25)(0.75) = 7.5\).

questions.explanation: The x! term divides by 2. The last choice is the cumulative P(X ≤ 2).
questions.question: Defects occur at an average rate of 4 per day (Poisson). What is the probability of exactly 2 defects in a day?
questions.solution:
Refer to Poisson distribution in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 85 (PDF page 91).

$$\begin{aligned}f(2;4) &= \frac{\lambda^xe^{-\lambda}}{x!} \\ &= \frac{4^2e^{-4}}{2!} \\ &= 0.1465\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Mean and variance are equal. 2.45 is the standard deviation.
questions.question: For a Poisson distribution with λ = 6, what are the mean and variance?
questions.solution:
Refer to Probability and Density Functions: Means and Variances (Poisson) in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 85 (PDF page 91).

The handbook lists mean λ and variance λ for the Poisson distribution.

questions.explanation: The slope is rise over run. The inverse is the run over rise, and the negative inverse is the perpendicular slope.
questions.question: What is the slope of the line through (2, 3) and (8, 12)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Straight Line in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 37 (PDF page 43).

$$\begin{aligned}m &= \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \\ &= \frac{12-(3)}{8-(2)} \\ &= 1.5\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Slope of a line through two points

questions.explanation: The slope is rise over run. The inverse is the run over rise, and the negative inverse is the perpendicular slope.
questions.question: What is the slope of the line through (-1, 4) and (5, -8)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Straight Line in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 37 (PDF page 43).

$$\begin{aligned}m &= \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \\ &= \frac{-8-(4)}{5-(-1)} \\ &= -2\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Slope of a line through two points

questions.explanation: The perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal.
questions.question: A line has slope 2. What is the slope of a line perpendicular to it?
questions.solution:
Refer to Straight Line (perpendicular lines) in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 37 (PDF page 43).

Two lines are perpendicular if \(m_1 = -1/m_2\). With \(m_1 = 2\), \(m_2 = -1/2 = -0.5\).

questions.explanation: The denominator is 1 + m2m1. Using only the slope difference or adding the slopes in the numerator gives other angles.
questions.question: Two lines have slopes 1 and 3. Using the handbook formula, what is the angle between them?
questions.solution:
Refer to Straight Line (angle between lines) in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 37 (PDF page 43).

$$\begin{aligned}\alpha &= \arctan\frac{m_2 - m_1}{1 + m_2m_1} \\ &= \arctan\frac{3-1}{1+3(1)} \\ &= \arctan(0.5) \\ &= 26.6°\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The roots sum to 6 and multiply to 5.
questions.question: What are the roots of x² − 6x + 5 = 0?
questions.solution:
Refer to Quadratic Equation in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 37 (PDF page 43).

$$\begin{aligned}x &= \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \\ &= \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 20}}{2} \\ &= \frac{6 \pm 4}{2}\end{aligned}$$

So x = 5 and x = 1.

questions.explanation: The signs of the center coordinates are opposite the signs in the equation. The right side is r squared.
questions.question: Which is the center and radius of the surface (x − 2)² + (y + 1)² + (z − 4)² = 25?
questions.solution:
Refer to Quadric Surface (Sphere) in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 37 (PDF page 43).

The standard form is \((x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 + (z-m)^2 = r^2\), so \(h = 2\), \(k = -1\), \(m = 4\) and \(r^2 = 25\), giving \(r = 5\).

questions.explanation: The magnitude is the root of the sum of squares. The angle is tan⁻¹(b/a), not its complement.
questions.question: Express z = 3 + j4 in polar form.
questions.solution:
Refer to Algebra of Complex Numbers in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 38 (PDF page 44).

$$\begin{aligned}c &= \sqrt{a^2+b^2} \\ &= \sqrt{3^2+4^2} \\ &= 5,\qquad \theta \\ &= \tan^{-1}(b/a) \\ &= \tan^{-1}(4/3) \\ &= 53.1°\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Since j² = −1, the −j²·3 term becomes +3. The sum 6 + j2 is z₁ + z₂.
questions.question: If z₁ = 2 + j3 and z₂ = 4 − j1, what is z₁z₂ in rectangular form?
questions.solution:
Refer to Algebra of Complex Numbers in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 38 (PDF page 44).

$$\begin{aligned}z_1z_2 &= (2+j3)(4-j1) \\ &= 8 - j2 + j12 - j^23 \\ &= (8+3) + j(12-2) \\ &= 11 + j10\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The dot product is a scalar sum of component products.
questions.question: A = 2i -1j +3k and B = 4i +2j -1k. What is A·B?
questions.solution:
Refer to Dot product in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 61 (PDF page 67).

$$\begin{aligned}A\cdot B &= a_xb_x + a_yb_y + a_zb_z \\ &= 2(4) + (-1)(2) + 3(-1) \\ &= 3\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The i component is the determinant of the y and z entries: \(a_y b_z - a_z b_y\). The opposite sign is the B × A value.
questions.question: A = 2i − 1j + 3k and B = 4i + 2j − 1k. What is the i-component of A × B?
questions.solution:
Refer to Cross product (determinant form) in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 61 (PDF page 67).

$$\begin{aligned}(A\times B)_x &= a_yb_z - a_zb_y \\ &= (-1)(-1) - (3)(2) \\ &= -5\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Setting the dot product to zero gives k = −6. The values 1.5 and 6 come from sign or ratio slips.
questions.question: For what value of k are A = 3i + 2j and B = 4i + kj perpendicular?
questions.solution:
Refer to Dot product (A·B = 0 for perpendicular vectors) in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 61 (PDF page 67).

Perpendicular vectors have zero dot product: \(3(4) + 2k = 0\), so \(k = -6\).

questions.explanation: Divide the dot product by both magnitudes. The wrong choices are the individual angles of B and A from the x axis, and the complement.
questions.question: A = 3i + 4j and B = 5i + 12j. What is the angle between them?
questions.solution:
Refer to Dot product (A·B = |A||B| cos θ) in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 61 (PDF page 67).

$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta &= \frac{A\cdot B}{|A||B|} \\ &= \frac{3(5)+4(12)}{5(13)} \\ &= 0.9692\ \Rightarrow\ \theta \\ &= 14.3°\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The correction is f divided by f′, subtracted. Adding it, using f/x or inverting the ratio gives other values.
questions.question: Using Newton's method for f(x) = x² − 10 with initial estimate 3, what is the next estimate?
questions.solution:
Refer to Newton's Method for Root Extraction in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 62 (PDF page 68).

$$\begin{aligned}a_{j+1} &= a_j - \frac{f(a_j)}{f'(a_j)} \\ &= 3 - \frac{3^2 - 10}{2(3)} \\ &= 3 - \frac{-1}{6} \\ &= 3.1667\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The change depends on the difference of squares, not the square of the difference. Dropping the 1/2 doubles the answer.
questions.question: A spring with k = 40 lb/in. is stretched from s₁ = 0.4 in. to s₂ = 1.5 in. What is the change in stored potential energy?
questions.solution:
Refer to Elastic Potential Energy in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 108 (PDF page 114).

$$\begin{aligned}V_2 - V_1 &= \frac{k(s_2^2 - s_1^2)}{2} \\ &= \frac{40(1.5^2 - 0.4^2)}{2} \\ &= 42\ \text{in.-lb}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The halves cancel. Keeping a factor of 2 on one side gives a speed √2 too large.
questions.question: A 0.5 kg block is pressed against a spring (k = 800 N/m) compressed 0.10 m and released on a frictionless surface. What is its speed leaving the spring?
questions.solution:
Refer to Elastic Potential Energy and conservation of energy (page 107) in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 108 (PDF page 114).

Conservation of energy: \(\tfrac12ks^2 = \tfrac12mv^2\).

$$\begin{aligned}v &= s\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \\ &= 0.10\sqrt{\frac{800}{0.5}} \\ &= 4.00\ \text{m/s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Input power is larger than output. Multiplying by the efficiency or converting to horsepower without changing the unit label gives wrong choices.
questions.question: A motor lifts a 500 lb load 20 ft in 10 s. The motor is 80% efficient. What power must the motor draw (input)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Power and Efficiency in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 108 (PDF page 114).

Output power: \(P_{out} = U/t = 500(20)/10 = 1000\) ft-lb/s. With efficiency \(\varepsilon = P_{out}/P_{in}\):

$$P_{in} = \frac{1000}{0.80} = 1250\ \text{ft-lb/s}$$

questions.explanation: The common velocity after a perfectly plastic impact is (0.80); here e = 0.6, so the bodies separate. The first choice is the velocity of the other body.
questions.question: A 4 kg body moving at 5 m/s hits a 6 kg body moving at -2 m/s in the same line (positive = right). The coefficient of restitution is 0.6. What is the velocity of the 6 kg body after impact?
questions.solution:
Refer to Impact in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 109 (PDF page 115).

Momentum: \(m_1v_1 + m_2v_2 = m_1v_1' + m_2v_2'\) gives 8 = 4v₁′ + 6v₂′. The relative velocity relation gives \(v_2' - v_1' = e(v_1 - v_2) = 4.2\).

Solving: \(v_2' = 2.48\) m/s and \(v_1' = -1.72\) m/s.

choices: 6 cfs, and the head loss is the same in both pipes
6 cfs, and the head loss in B is 1.5 times that in A
4 cfs, because each pipe carries half
6 cfs, and the head loss adds across the two pipes
questions.explanation: Head loss adds only for pipes in series. Parallel pipes share the same head loss and split the flow.
questions.question: Two parallel pipes carry a total flow of 10 cfs. Pipe A carries 4 cfs. What is the flow in pipe B, and what does the handbook say about head loss?
questions.solution:
Refer to Multipath Pipeline Problems (pipes in parallel) in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 191 (PDF page 197).

The total flow is the sum of the flows in the parallel pipes, so \(Q_B = 10 - 4 = 6\) cfs. For pipes in parallel the head loss is the same in each pipe.

questions.explanation: The ideal flow is multiplied by the discharge coefficient Cd = Cc·Cv. Leaving out Cd or the factor 2 in 2gh gives the wrong choices.
questions.question: A sharp-edged orifice has area A0 = 0.01 m², a head of 4 m to its centroid and a discharge coefficient of 0.61. Using Q = Cd A0 √(2gh) (the handbook free-discharge form), what is Q?
questions.solution:
Refer to Orifice Discharging Freely into Atmosphere in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 190 (PDF page 196).

$$\begin{aligned}Q &= C_dA_0\sqrt{2gh} \\ &= 0.61(0.01)\sqrt{2(9.81)(4)} \\ &= 0.0540\ \text{m}^3/\text{s} \\ &= 54.0\ \text{L/s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The support nearer the load carries more. The other support carries 30 · 8/20 = 12 kip.
questions.question: The simply supported beam shown carries a 30 kip point load 8 ft from support A on a 20 ft span. What is the reaction at A?
questions.solution:
Refer to Beams (shear force and bending moment relations) in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 135 (PDF page 141).

Moments about B: \(R_A(20) = 30(12)\), so \(R_A = 18\) kip (derived from statics; \(R_A + R_B = 30\)).

questions.explanation: PL/4 applies only to a midspan load. The moment must use the reaction, not the load, times the distance from the near support.
questions.question: For the beam shown (P = 30 kip at 8 ft from A, span 20 ft), what is the maximum bending moment?
questions.solution:
Refer to Beams (V and M relationship, dM/dx = V) in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 135 (PDF page 141).

\(R_A = 18\) kip. The shear is positive between A and the load and changes sign at the load, so the maximum moment is under the load. From the handbook relation \(dM/dx = V\), the moment grows linearly with slope \(R_A\):

$$M_{max} = R_A a = 18(8) = 144\ \text{kip-ft}$$

questions.explanation: The shear jumps by the load P at the load. A positive 12 kip would have the wrong sign for the right segment.
questions.question: For the simply supported beam shown (P = 30 kip at 8 ft from A, span 20 ft), what is the shear just to the right of the point load? Use the handbook sign convention (positive when the right portion tends to shear downward).
questions.solution:
Refer to Shearing Force and Bending Moment Sign Conventions in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 135 (PDF page 141).

Just left of the load V = \(R_A\) = 18 kip. The load drops it by P: \(V = 18 - 30 = -12\) kip.
questions.subtopic: Shear just right of the load

questions.explanation: wL²/8 is the midspan moment of a uniformly loaded simple span. wL/2 is the reaction (in kip, not kip-ft).
questions.question: The simply supported beam shown carries 2.5 kip/ft over a 16 ft span. What is the maximum bending moment?
questions.solution:
Refer to Beams (V and M relationship, dM/dx = V) in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 135 (PDF page 141).

Each reaction is \(wL/2 = 20\) kip and the shear is zero at midspan, where M is maximum.

$$\begin{aligned}M_{max} &= \frac{wL^2}{8} \\ &= \frac{2.5(16)^2}{8} \\ &= 80\ \text{kip-ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The shear decreases linearly at rate w. Zero shear is where the moment peaks.
questions.question: For the uniformly loaded beam shown (w = 2.5 kip/ft, L = 16 ft, reactions 20 kip), how far from A is the shear zero?
questions.solution:
Refer to Beams (V and M relationship, w = -dV/dx) in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 135 (PDF page 141).

With \(V(x) = R_A - wx\) (derived): zero shear at \(x = R_A/w = 20/2.5 = 8\) ft, which is midspan.

choices: The area under the shear diagram to that point
The shear force at that point
The load intensity at that point
questions.explanation: The slope of the moment diagram is the shear. The area under the shear diagram between two points is the change in moment, not the slope.
questions.question: According to the handbook relationships between load, shear and moment, the slope of the moment diagram at a point equals:
questions.solution:
Refer to relationship between w, V and M in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 135 (PDF page 141).

The handbook gives \(w(x) = -dV/dx\) (load intensity, with the handbook sign convention) and \(dM/dx = V\).

questions.explanation: Y divides the toughness when solving for stress. Multiplying by Y, omitting Y or π gives other values.
questions.question: A plate of a material with \(K_{Ic}\) = 40 ksi√in. has an exterior edge crack of length a = 0.2 in. using Y = 1.1. What stress causes fracture?
questions.solution:
Refer to Fracture toughness (\(K_{Ic} = Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}\)) in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 123 (PDF page 129).

$$\begin{aligned}K_{Ic} &= Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}\ \Rightarrow\ \sigma \\ &= \frac{K_{Ic}}{Y\sqrt{\pi a}} \\ &= \frac{40}{1.1\sqrt{\pi(0.2)}} \\ &= 45.9\ \text{ksi}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The ratio is squared and divided by π. Skipping π or the square gives other answers. The handbook's interior crack figure uses a crack length of 2a, and Y = 1.
questions.question: An interior crack (Y = 1) in a part with \(K_{Ic}\) = 40 ksi√in. is loaded to 30 ksi. What is the critical crack length a?
questions.solution:
Refer to Fracture toughness (\(K_{Ic} = Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}\)) in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 123 (PDF page 129).

$$\begin{aligned}a &= \frac{1}{\pi}\left(\frac{K_{Ic}}{Y\sigma}\right)^2 \\ &= \frac{1}{\pi}\left(\frac{40}{30}\right)^2 \\ &= 0.57\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: D depends exponentially on 1/T. The temperature ratio 1.11 greatly underestimates the change, and the inverse is the ratio D1/D2.
questions.question: A diffusion process has activation energy Q = 120,000 J/mol (R = 8.314 J/mol·K). By what factor does the diffusion coefficient D increase when the temperature rises from 900 K to 1,000 K?
questions.solution:
Refer to Diffusion Coefficient (D = D0 e^(−Q/RT)) in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 117 (PDF page 123).

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{D_2}{D_1} &= \exp\left[\frac{Q}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)\right] \\ &= \exp\left[\frac{120{,}000}{8.314}\left(\frac{1}{900} - \frac{1}{1000}\right)\right] \\ &= 5.0\end{aligned}$$

choices: Leaves both strength and ductility unchanged
questions.explanation: Strengthening by plastic deformation comes at the cost of ductility. Heating (recovery, recrystallization) reverses it.
questions.question: According to the handbook, cold working a metal:
questions.solution:
Refer to Thermal and Mechanical Processing in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 117 (PDF page 123).

The handbook states that cold working (plastically deforming) a metal increases strength and lowers ductility.

choices: To measure the hardness of the surface
To measure the elastic modulus of the material
To measure the creep rate at constant load
To find the energy required to fracture a sample and identify the ductile-to-brittle transition
questions.explanation: Impact tests give fracture energy and the transition temperature, not modulus, hardness or creep.
questions.question: What is the Charpy impact test used for, according to the handbook?
questions.solution:
Refer to Impact Test in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 126 (PDF page 132).

The handbook says the Charpy impact test is used to find the energy required to fracture and to identify the ductile-to-brittle transition, with tests repeated across a range of temperatures.

choices: The metal with the larger area
questions.explanation: The anode corrodes. The more noble (less electropositive) metal is the cathode.
questions.question: When two dissimilar metals are in electrical contact in an electrolyte, which metal becomes the anode according to the handbook?
questions.solution:
Refer to Corrosion in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 117 (PDF page 123).

The handbook states that, when dissimilar metals are in contact, the more electropositive one becomes the anode in a corrosion cell, where oxidation occurs.

questions.explanation: Oxygen-rich regions and the bulk grain interior are the cathodic ones in these pairs.
questions.question: In a piece of carbon steel, which region is anodic to the others, according to the handbook?
questions.solution:
Refer to Corrosion in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 117 (PDF page 123).

The handbook lists cold-worked regions as anodic to non-cold-worked regions, grain boundary regions as anodic to the bulk grain, and oxygen-deficient regions as cathodic to oxygen-rich regions.

questions.explanation: Flow varies with N, head with N² and power with N³. Inverting the ratio increases the flow.
questions.question: A pump delivers 500 gpm at 1,750 rpm. Using the affinity laws with the same impeller, what is the flow at 1,450 rpm?
questions.solution:
Refer to Fans, Pumps, and Compressors: Scaling Laws; Affinity Laws in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 199 (PDF page 205).

Flow is proportional to speed at constant diameter (derived from the handbook's \(Q/(ND^3)\) group).

$$\begin{aligned}Q_2 &= Q_1\frac{N_2}{N_1} \\ &= 500\left(\frac{1450}{1750}\right) \\ &= 414\ \text{gpm}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The head scales with N². Using N or N³ gives the wrong choices, and the inverse ratio raises the head.
questions.question: A pump develops 100 ft of head at 1,750 rpm. What head does it develop at 1,450 rpm with the same impeller (affinity laws)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Fans, Pumps, and Compressors: Scaling Laws; Affinity Laws in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 199 (PDF page 205).

Head is proportional to the square of the speed at constant diameter (the handbook group \(H/(N^2D^2)\)).

$$\begin{aligned}H_2 &= H_1\left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^2 \\ &= 100\left(\frac{1450}{1750}\right)^2 \\ &= 68.7\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Power scales with N³. The exponent 5 applies to the diameter, not the speed.
questions.question: A pump uses 30 hp at 1,750 rpm. Using the affinity laws with the same impeller and fluid, what power at 1,450 rpm?
questions.solution:
Refer to Fans, Pumps, and Compressors: Scaling Laws; Affinity Laws in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 199 (PDF page 205).

Power is proportional to the cube of the speed at constant diameter (the handbook power group \(\dot W/(\rho N^3D^5)\)).

$$\begin{aligned}P_2 &= 30\left(\frac{1450}{1750}\right)^3 \\ &= 17.1\ \text{hp}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Dividing by n gives the population form (10.00). 3.46 is the standard deviation, and 60.00 is the unscaled sum of squares.
questions.question: A sample of 6 concrete cylinder strengths (ksi x 0.1) reads 12, 15, 11, 18, 14, 20. What is the sample variance?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 64 (PDF page 70).

The mean is 15.00. The handbook sample variance divides by n - 1:

$$\begin{aligned}s^2 &= \frac{1}{n-1}\sum (X_i-\bar X)^2 \\ &= \frac{60.00}{5} \\ &= 12.00\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The simple average (84.3) ignores the weights. 830 is the numerator before dividing by the sum of weights.
questions.question: A course grade uses homework (weight 2) with a score of 85, a midterm (weight 3) with 90 and a final (weight 5) with 78. What is the weighted mean?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 64 (PDF page 70).

$$\begin{aligned}\bar X_w &= \frac{\sum w_iX_i}{\sum w_i} \\ &= \frac{2(85)+3(90)+5(78)}{10} \\ &= 83.0\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The mean is 7.2. Using only the 3rd or the 4th item ignores that n is even.
questions.question: What is the median of the data set 7, 3, 9, 4, 8, 12?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 64 (PDF page 70).

Sorted: 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 12. With n = 6 (even) the median is the average of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th items: (7 + 8)/2 = 7.5.

questions.explanation: \(\sigma\sqrt n\) is the series (sum) form. Dividing by n instead of \(\sqrt n\) over-reduces the spread.
questions.question: Individual measurements have a standard deviation of 6.0 psi. What is the standard deviation of the mean of 25 independent measurements?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 64 (PDF page 70).

The handbook gives \(\sigma_{mean} = \sigma/\sqrt{n}\):

$$\begin{aligned}\sigma_{mean} &= \frac{6.0}{\sqrt{25}} \\ &= 1.20\ \text{psi}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Adding the standard deviations directly assumes perfect correlation. The sum of variances is a variance, not a standard deviation.
questions.question: Three independent loads have standard deviations of 3, 4 and 12 kips. What is the standard deviation of their sum?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 64 (PDF page 70).

Independent standard deviations add in quadrature (\(\sigma_{sum} = \sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2+\dots}\)):

$$\begin{aligned}\sigma_{sum} &= \sqrt{3^2+4^2+12^2} \\ &= \sqrt{169} \\ &= 13.0\ \text{kips}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 7.50 is the arithmetic mean and 9.22 is the root-mean-square value.
questions.question: What is the geometric mean of 2, 8, 4, 16?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 64 (PDF page 70).

$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt[n]{X_1X_2\cdots X_n} &= \sqrt[4]{1024} \\ &= 5.66\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 85.00 is the mean square before taking the root.
questions.question: What is the sample root-mean-square value of 2, 8, 4, 16?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 64 (PDF page 70).

$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2} &= \sqrt{\frac{340}{4}} \\ &= 9.22\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 1.80 is the mean. 1.24 is the standard deviation.
questions.question: A binomial experiment has n = 12 trials and p = 0.15. What is its variance?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 85 (PDF page 91).

From the table, the binomial variance is \(np(1-p)\) = 12(0.15)(0.85) = 1.53.

questions.explanation: The standard deviation is 1.79. The variance equals the mean for Poisson.
questions.question: A Poisson count has a mean of 3.2 events per interval. What is its variance?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 85 (PDF page 91).

For the Poisson distribution the table gives mean = \(\lambda\) and variance = \(\lambda\), so the variance is 3.2.

questions.explanation: The variance is the square of the mean for the exponential distribution.
questions.question: An exponential distribution has a mean of 4.0 hours (the handbook parameter beta). What is its variance?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 85 (PDF page 91).

In the handbook table the exponential mean is \(\beta\) and the variance is \(\beta^2\) = 16.0.

questions.explanation: 16.0 is the mean, not the variance. Dividing by 4 instead of 12 is the wrong constant.
questions.question: A random variable is uniformly distributed between 10 and 22. What is its variance?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 85 (PDF page 91).

The table gives \((b-a)^2/12\) = 144/12 = 12.0. The mean is (a + b)/2 = 16.0.

questions.explanation: 20.0 is the variance, \((1-p)/p^2\).
questions.question: A test passes with probability 0.2 on each independent trial. Using the geometric distribution, what is the expected number of trials until the first pass?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 85 (PDF page 91).

The handbook geometric mean is 1/p = 1/0.2 = 5.0 trials.

questions.explanation: 3.50 is the expected number of good bolts.
questions.question: A lot of 20 bolts contains 6 defective bolts. 5 are drawn without replacement. What is the expected number of defectives in the sample?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 85 (PDF page 91).

The hypergeometric mean is \(nr/N\) = 5(6)/20 = 1.50.

questions.explanation: The PERT weighting (a + 4m + b)/6 is not the triangular mean in the handbook table. The midrange ignores the mode.
questions.question: A task duration follows a triangular distribution with minimum 2, mode 5 and maximum 14 days. What is the mean?
questions.solution:
Refer to Engineering Probability and Statistics in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 85 (PDF page 91).

The table gives mean = (a + b + m)/3 = (2 + 14 + 5)/3 = 7.00 days.

questions.explanation: The plain average (7.5 in.) ignores the areas. 576 is the first moment of area, not yet divided by A.
questions.question: A composite section is made of a 48 in.² flange whose centroid is 3 in. above the base and a 36 in.² web whose centroid is 12 in. above the base. How far above the base is the centroid of the whole section?
questions.solution:
Refer to Centroid of Area in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 96 (PDF page 102).

The handbook gives \(y_{ac} = \sum y_na_n/A\):

$$\begin{aligned}y_{ac} &= \frac{48(3) + 36(12)}{48+36} \\ &= \frac{576}{84} \\ &= 6.86\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 333 is the centroidal value only. 2560 omits the centroidal term. Using d instead of d squared underestimates the shift.
questions.question: A rectangle 4 in. wide and 10 in. deep has its centroidal moment of inertia about the horizontal axis. What is its moment of inertia about a parallel axis 8 in. from the centroid?
questions.solution:
Refer to Moment of Inertia Parallel Axis Theorem in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 96 (PDF page 102).

\(I_{xc} = bh^3/12 = 4(10)^3/12 = 333.3\) in.⁴. The handbook gives \(I_x = I_{xc} + d_y^2A\):

$$I_x = 333.3 + (8)^2(40) = 2893.3\ \text{in.}^4$$

questions.explanation: Forgetting the square root gives I/A (in.²). Multiplying instead of dividing is dimensionally wrong.
questions.question: A section has \(I_x = 2400\) in.⁴ and an area of 30 in.². What is the radius of gyration \(r_x\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Radius of Gyration in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 97 (PDF page 103).

The handbook gives \(r_x = \sqrt{I_x/A} = \sqrt{2400/30} = 8.94\) in.

questions.explanation: The polar moment of inertia is the sum of the two axis values, not either one alone or their difference.
questions.question: An area of 20 in.² has \(I_x = 500\) in.⁴ and \(I_y = 300\) in.⁴. What is its polar radius of gyration \(r_p\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Polar moment of inertia and Radius of Gyration in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 97 (PDF page 103).

\(J = I_x + I_y = 800\) in.⁴ (printed page 96), then \(r_p = \sqrt{J/A} = \sqrt{800/20} = 6.32\) in. (printed page 97).
questions.subtopic: Polar moment of inertia of an area

questions.explanation: 1143 lb divides by the coefficient. The full weight is the normal force, not the friction force.
questions.question: A 400 lb crate rests on a level floor with a coefficient of static friction of 0.35. What is the largest friction force the floor can supply before the crate slips?
questions.solution:
Refer to Friction in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 97 (PDF page 103).

The handbook gives the limiting friction \(F \le \mu_sN\). On a level floor N = W = 400 lb, so \(F_{max} = 0.35(400) = 140\) lb.

choices: It does not slip; friction is 60 lb
It does not slip; friction is 150 lb
questions.explanation: Limiting friction (150 lb) is the maximum available, not the force that actually acts. Friction only reaches the limit when the pull does.
questions.question: A 500 lb block rests on a level surface with \(\mu_s = 0.3\). A horizontal pull of 60 lb is applied. Does the block slip, and what friction force acts?
questions.solution:
Refer to Friction in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 97 (PDF page 103).

The limit is \(\mu_sN = 0.3(500) = 150\) lb. The pull of 60 lb is below this, so the block is in equilibrium and the actual friction force equals the applied pull, 60 lb.
questions.subtopic: Friction on a horizontal surface with applied pull

questions.explanation: 0.98 cfs omits the discharge coefficient. Leaving out the square root or the factor 2 gives the other values.
questions.question: A sharp-edged orifice with C = 0.61 and an area of 0.05 ft² discharges freely into the atmosphere under a head of 6.0 ft measured to the orifice centroid. What is the flow?
questions.solution:
Refer to Orifice Discharging Freely into Atmosphere in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 190 (PDF page 196).

The handbook gives \(Q = CA_0\sqrt{2gh}\):

$$\begin{aligned}Q &= 0.61(0.05)\sqrt{2(32.2)(6.0)} \\ &= 0.60\ \text{cfs}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The driving head for a submerged orifice is the difference of the two water levels, not the upstream depth alone and not their sum.
questions.question: A submerged orifice (C = 0.6, A = 0.02 ft²) connects two tanks. The upstream water surface is 9.0 ft above the orifice centerline and the downstream surface is 4.0 ft above it. What is the flow?
questions.solution:
Refer to Submerged Orifice Operating under Steady-Flow Conditions in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 190 (PDF page 196).

The handbook gives \(Q = CA\sqrt{2g(h_1-h_2)}\), with the head difference between the two surfaces:

$$\begin{aligned}Q &= 0.6(0.02)\sqrt{2(32.2)(9.0-4.0)} \\ &= 0.215\ \text{cfs}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Dropping the 2 halves the time. Using h instead of its square root, or omitting the 1/sqrt(2g) factor, gives values that are off by large factors.
questions.question: A tank with a cross-sectional area of 4.0 ft² drains through a bottom orifice of area 0.01 ft² (take C = 1.0). How long does the water level take to fall from 5.0 ft to 1.0 ft above the orifice?
questions.solution:
Refer to Time required to drain a tank in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 190 (PDF page 196).

The handbook gives \(\Delta t = \dfrac{2(A_t/A_0)}{\sqrt{2g}}\left(h_1^{1/2} - h_2^{1/2}\right)\):

$$\begin{aligned}\Delta t &= \frac{2(400)}{\sqrt{2(32.2)}}(\sqrt{5.0}-\sqrt{1.0}) \\ &= 123\ \text{s}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Tank drain time through an orifice

questions.explanation: The factor 4 comes from using the tube diameter, not the radius. Using the radius would give half the rise.
questions.question: Water (surface tension 0.005 lb/ft, specific weight 62.4 lb/ft³, contact angle 0 degrees) rises in a clean glass tube of 0.125 in. diameter. What is the capillary rise?
questions.solution:
Refer to Surface Tension and Capillarity in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 182 (PDF page 188).

The handbook gives \(h = \dfrac{4\sigma\cos\beta}{\gamma d}\):

$$\begin{aligned}h &= \frac{4(0.005)(1)}{62.4(0.01042)} \\ &= 0.0308\ \text{ft} \\ &= 0.37\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Dilatant fluids have n > 1. A Newtonian fluid would be the n = 1 case, which is not what the handbook calls out here.
questions.question: A fluid follows \(\tau = K(dv/dy)^n\) with n = 0.6. How does the handbook classify it?
questions.solution:
Refer to For a power law (non-Newtonian) fluid in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 182 (PDF page 188).

The handbook lists n < 1 as pseudoplastic and n > 1 as dilatant. n = 0.6 is below 1.

questions.explanation: 300 s^-1 is the velocity gradient, not a stress. Multiplying by the film thickness reverses the dependence on gap.
questions.question: A plate moves at 3.0 ft/s over a stationary surface separated by a 0.01 ft oil film with a viscosity of 0.02 lb-s/ft². Assuming a linear velocity profile, what is the shear stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to For a thin Newtonian fluid film and a linear velocity profile in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 182 (PDF page 188).

For a linear profile \(dv/dy = v/\delta\) (printed page 182) and \(\tau = \mu\,dv/dy\):

$$\begin{aligned}\tau &= 0.02\left(\frac{3.0}{0.01}\right) \\ &= 6.0\ \text{psf}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Shear stress in a thin fluid film

questions.explanation: 10.83 is the value in psi, not psf. Dividing instead of multiplying by h is dimensionally wrong.
questions.question: Two points in static water are 25.0 ft apart vertically. What is the pressure difference between them?
questions.solution:
Refer to The Pressure Field in a Static Liquid in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 182 (PDF page 188).

The handbook gives \(P_2 - P_1 = -\gamma(z_2 - z_1) = -\gamma h\), so the magnitude is \(\gamma h = 62.4(25) = 1560\) psf.
questions.subtopic: Pressure difference in a static liquid

questions.explanation: 18.7 psi would add the vacuum reading, which applies to positive gauge readings only.
questions.question: A vacuum gauge reads 4 psi (below atmospheric) where atmospheric pressure is 14.7 psi. What is the absolute pressure?
questions.solution:
Refer to The Pressure Field in a Static Liquid in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 182 (PDF page 188).

The handbook states absolute pressure = atmospheric pressure - vacuum gauge pressure reading: 14.7 - 4 = 10.7 psi.
questions.subtopic: Absolute pressure from a vacuum gauge

questions.explanation: 1.5 applies to laminar flow between parallel planes and 1.18 to fully turbulent flow.
questions.question: Water flows in a circular pipe in the laminar regime with an average velocity of 10.0 ft/s. What is the centerline velocity?
questions.solution:
Refer to Velocity distribution for laminar flow in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 187 (PDF page 193).

The handbook gives \(v_{max} = 2\bar v\) for circular tubes in laminar flow: 2(10.0) = 20.0 ft/s.

questions.explanation: The Fanning factor is one fourth of the Darcy factor; mixing them changes the answer by 4. The velocity must be squared.
questions.question: A 500 ft pipe of 6 in. diameter carries water at 6.0 ft/s with a Darcy friction factor of 0.025. What is the friction head loss?
questions.solution:
Refer to Head Loss Due to Flow in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 187 (PDF page 193).

The handbook gives \(h_f = f\dfrac{L}{D}\dfrac{v^2}{2g}\):

$$\begin{aligned}h_f &= 0.025\left(\frac{500}{0.5}\right)\frac{6.0^2}{2(32.2)} \\ &= 14.0\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 0.99 ft is one velocity head, before multiplying by the coefficient.
questions.question: A valve has a loss coefficient C = 2.5 and the water velocity through it is 8.0 ft/s. What is the head loss?
questions.solution:
Refer to Minor Losses in Pipe Fittings in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 187 (PDF page 193).

The handbook gives \(h_{f,fitting} = C\dfrac{v^2}{2g}\):

$$h_f = 2.5\frac{8.0^2}{2(32.2)} = 2.48\ \text{ft}$$

questions.explanation: Keep the units consistent: kips, in. and ksi. Converting L to feet again would scale the answer by 12.
questions.question: A steel rod (E = 29,000 ksi) with an area of 0.5 in.² and a length of 120 in. carries an axial load of 30 kips. What is the elongation?
questions.solution:
Refer to Uniaxial Loading and Deformation in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 131 (PDF page 137).

The handbook gives \(\delta = PL/(AE)\):

$$\begin{aligned}\delta &= \frac{30(120)}{0.5(29{,}000)} \\ &= 0.248\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The length and the temperature change are both multipliers; omitting L gives a strain-like quantity.
questions.question: A steel member 240 in. long (α = 6.5 × 10⁻⁶ per °F) is heated by 80 degrees F and is free to expand. What is the change in length?
questions.solution:
Refer to Thermal Deformations in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 131 (PDF page 137).

The handbook gives \(\delta_t = \alpha L(T - T_o)\):

$$\begin{aligned}\delta_t &= (6.5\times10^{-6})(240)(80) \\ &= 0.1248\ \text{in.}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Section modulus is I/c; stress is M divided by it. Multiplying by I instead of dividing is incorrect.
questions.question: A beam section has I = 300 in.⁴ and c = 5 in. to the extreme fiber. What is the maximum bending stress for a moment of 120 kip-in.?
questions.solution:
Refer to Stresses in Beams in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 136 (PDF page 142).

The handbook gives \(\sigma_x = \pm Mc/I\):

$$\sigma = \frac{120(5)}{300} = 2.00\ \text{ksi}$$

questions.explanation: 2.400 is the shear flow q = VQ/I (kip/in.), which has not been divided by the width.
questions.question: At a point in a beam, V = 18 kips, Q = 40 in.³, I = 300 in.⁴ and the width is 4 in. What is the transverse shear stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to Stresses in Beams (transverse shear stress) in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 136 (PDF page 142).

The handbook gives \(\tau_{xy} = VQ/(Ib)\):

$$\tau = \frac{18(40)}{300(4)} = 0.600\ \text{ksi}$$

questions.explanation: Shear flow is per unit length and does not include the width b. Dividing by b gives a stress.
questions.question: A built-up beam carries V = 18 kips with Q = 40 in.³ for the connected part and I = 300 in.⁴. What shear flow must the connectors carry per inch of length?
questions.solution:
Refer to Stresses in Beams (transverse shear flow) in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 136 (PDF page 142).

The handbook gives \(q = VQ/I\):

$$q = \frac{18(40)}{300} = 2.40\ \text{kip/in.}$$
questions.subtopic: Shear flow in a built-up section

questions.explanation: n is the ratio of the larger modulus to the smaller, so it exceeds 1.
questions.question: A composite beam has steel (E = 29,000 ksi) and concrete (E = 3,000 ksi). What modular ratio n transforms the concrete into an equivalent steel section when the handbook defines n = E1/E2 with E1 > E2?
questions.solution:
Refer to Composite Sections in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 137 (PDF page 143).

The handbook defines \(n = E_1/E_2\) with \(E_1 > E_2\): n = 29000/3000 = 9.67.
questions.subtopic: Modular ratio in a composite beam

questions.explanation: The radial stress at the inside wall is \(-P_i = -500\) psi. The thin-wall formula Pr/t gives 1000 psi, which is only an approximation.
questions.question: A cylinder has an inside radius of 4.0 in., outside radius of 6.0 in. and internal pressure 500 psi only. What is the hoop stress at the inside wall?
questions.solution:
Refer to Cylindrical Pressure Vessel in the Mechanics of Materials section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 131 (PDF page 137).

The handbook gives \(\sigma_t = P_i\dfrac{r_o^2 + r_i^2}{r_o^2 - r_i^2}\):

$$\begin{aligned}\sigma_t &= 500\frac{6^2+4^2}{6^2-4^2} \\ &= 1300\ \text{psi}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 875 is the MPa value, not psi. The factor is 500, not 5,000.
questions.question: A plain carbon steel has a Brinell hardness of 250 BHN. Using the handbook relation, what is the approximate tensile strength?
questions.solution:
Refer to Relationship Between Hardness and Tensile Strength in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 123 (PDF page 129).

The handbook gives TS(psi) ~ 500 BHN: 500(250) = 125,000 psi (equivalently 3.5 BHN = 875 MPa).
questions.subtopic: Hardness and tensile strength of steel

questions.explanation: Omitting Y gives 23.8. For an interior crack the length is 2a and Y = 1.
questions.question: An edge crack of length a = 2 mm in a plate under an applied stress of 300 MPa has Y = 1.1. What is the stress intensity K (MPa m¹/2)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Fracture toughness in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 123 (PDF page 129).

The handbook gives \(K_{IC} = Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}\) with Y = 1.1 for an exterior crack:

$$\begin{aligned}K &= 1.1(300)\sqrt{\pi(0.002)} \\ &= 26.2\ \text{MPa}\sqrt{\text{m}}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 2^n = 64 forgets the n - 1 exponent.
questions.question: Using the handbook relation N = 2^(n-1) for the number of grains per 0.0645 mm², how many grains are in that area for ASTM grain size n = 6?
questions.solution:
Refer to ASTM Grain Size in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 123 (PDF page 129).

\(N = 2^{n-1} = 2^{5} = 32\) grains in 0.0645 mm².

questions.explanation: Slump and aggregate size affect workability and mix proportions but are not named as the primary strength factor.
questions.question: According to the handbook, what is the primary factor affecting the strength of concrete?
questions.solution:
Refer to Concrete in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 126 (PDF page 132).

The handbook states that the water-cement (W/C) ratio is the primary factor affecting the strength of concrete, with strength decreasing as W/C increases.

questions.explanation: Air entrainment, not extra water, is used to improve durability.
questions.question: A crew adds water to a concrete mix to improve workability but adds no cement. According to the handbook, what is the consequence?
questions.solution:
Refer to Concrete in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 126 (PDF page 132).

The handbook says that an increase in water without a corresponding increase in cement reduces concrete strength. Superplasticizers are the typical way to raise workability.
questions.subtopic: Effect of adding water without cement

questions.explanation: Adding water without cement reduces strength; air entrainment targets durability.
questions.question: Which approach does the handbook name as the most typical way to increase concrete workability without sacrificing strength?
questions.solution:
Refer to Concrete in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 126 (PDF page 132).

The handbook says superplasticizers are the most typical way to increase workability, and air entrainment is used to improve durability.

questions.explanation: 18.2 hp is the water power with no efficiency loss. Multiplying by the efficiency instead of dividing understates the input power.
questions.question: A pump lifts 2.0 cfs of water through a total head of 80 ft. The total (pump times motor) efficiency is 0.7. What input power is required?
questions.solution:
Refer to Pump Power Equation in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 197 (PDF page 203).

The handbook gives \(\dot W = Q\gamma h/\eta_t\):

$$\begin{aligned}\dot W &= \frac{2.0(62.4)(80)}{0.7} \\ &= 14{,}263\ \text{ft-lbf/s}\end{aligned}$$

Dividing by 550 ft-lbf/s per hp gives 25.9 hp (the conversion is a standard unit factor).

questions.explanation: 19.6 kW is the fluid power (no efficiency). Multiplying by the efficiency, or dividing twice, uses the efficiency incorrectly.
questions.question: A pump delivers 0.05 m³/s of water with a head increase of 40 m at a pump efficiency of 0.78. What is the pump (brake) power?
questions.solution:
Refer to Pump (brake) power in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 196 (PDF page 202).

The handbook gives pump (brake) power \(\dot W = \rho gHQ/\eta_{pump}\):

$$\begin{aligned}\dot W &= \frac{1000(9.81)(40)(0.05)}{0.78} \\ &= 25.2\ \text{kW}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The brake power already includes the pump efficiency. Dividing by the pump efficiency again double counts it.
questions.question: A pump has a brake (shaft) power of 25.2 kW and is driven by a motor with efficiency 0.92. What is the purchased electrical power?
questions.solution:
Refer to Purchased power in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 196 (PDF page 202).

The handbook gives \(\dot W_{purchased} = \dot W/\eta_{motor}\):

$$\begin{aligned}\dot W_{purchased} &= \frac{25.2}{0.92} \\ &= 27.4\ \text{kW}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The efficiencies multiply; they are not averaged or added.
questions.question: A pump has an efficiency of 0.80 and its motor has an efficiency of 0.90. What total efficiency applies in the pump power equation?
questions.solution:
Refer to Pump Power Equation in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 197 (PDF page 203).

The handbook defines the total efficiency as \(\eta_t = \eta_{pump}\times\eta_{motor}\) = 0.80(0.90) = 0.72.
questions.subtopic: Total efficiency of a pump and motor

questions.explanation: A flooded suction adds static head. Friction loss and vapor pressure head both reduce the available head.
questions.question: A pump draws water from an open sump at sea level (atmospheric head 33.9 ft). The liquid surface is 8.0 ft above the impeller centerline, the suction line friction loss is 2.5 ft and the vapor pressure head is 0.8 ft. What is NPSH available?
questions.solution:
Refer to Net Positive Suction Head Available in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 196 (PDF page 202).

The handbook gives \(NPSH_A = H_{pa} + H_s - \sum h_L - H_{vp}\):

$$\begin{aligned}NPSH_A &= 33.9 + 8.0 - 2.5 - 0.8 \\ &= 38.6\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: A lift reduces the available head. Using +12 treats the pump as flooded.
questions.question: A pump sits 12 ft above the water surface in a sump (a suction lift, so the handbook static suction head is negative). With atmospheric head 33.9 ft, friction loss 2.5 ft and vapor pressure head 0.8 ft, what is NPSH available?
questions.solution:
Refer to Net Positive Suction Head Available in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 196 (PDF page 202).

The handbook defines \(H_s\) as the height of the liquid surface above the pump centerline, so a lift makes it negative:

$$\begin{aligned}NPSH_A &= 33.9 + (-12) - 2.5 - 0.8 \\ &= 18.6\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: NPSH available with a suction lift

questions.explanation: Pressures must be in psf for the specific weight in lb/ft³. The velocity head adds; vapor pressure subtracts.
questions.question: At a pump inlet the absolute pressure is 22 psi, the velocity is 6.0 ft/s and the vapor pressure is 0.26 psi (water, \(\gamma\) = 62.4 lb/ft³). What is NPSH available?
questions.solution:
Refer to Net Positive Suction Head Available in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 196 (PDF page 202).

The handbook also gives \(NPSH_A = \dfrac{P_{inlet}}{\rho g} + \dfrac{v_{inlet}^2}{2g} - \dfrac{P_{vapor}}{\rho g}\). Convert pressures to psf (x144):

$$\begin{aligned}NPSH_A &= \frac{3168}{62.4} + \frac{6.0^2}{2(32.2)} - \frac{37.4}{62.4} \\ &= 50.7\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

choices: It first decreases then equals zero
questions.explanation: \(\mathrm{NPSH}_R\) is shown rising with \(Q\), in contrast to head H, which falls.
questions.question: On the handbook's centrifugal pump performance curves (constant \(N\), \(D\), \(\rho\)), how does the required net positive suction head, \(\mathrm{NPSH}_R\), change as flow rate increases?
questions.solution:
Refer to Centrifugal Pump Characteristics in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 195 (PDF page 201).

The \(NPSH_R\) curve on the handbook's pump performance chart rises with flow rate, so a pump needs more suction head at higher flow.
questions.subtopic: NPSH required trend on a pump curve

choices: It is independent of impeller speed
questions.explanation: Head decreases with flow while the \(\mathrm{NPSH}_R\) curve rises.
questions.question: On the handbook's centrifugal pump performance curves (constant \(N\), \(D\), \(\rho\)), how does the pump head H change as flow rate increases?
questions.solution:
Refer to Centrifugal Pump Characteristics in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 195 (PDF page 201).

The H curve on the handbook's pump chart falls as flow rate increases.
questions.subtopic: Head trend on a pump curve

questions.explanation: 94 ft-lbf/s is the air power with no efficiency loss. Efficiency divides the output power to give the input power.
questions.question: A backward curved fan raises the pressure by 31.2 psf while moving 3.0 cfs at a fan efficiency of 0.65. What is the fan power?
questions.solution:
Refer to Fan Characteristics in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 197 (PDF page 203).

The handbook gives \(\dot W = \Delta PQ/\eta_f\):

$$\begin{aligned}\dot W &= \frac{31.2(3.0)}{0.65} \\ &= 144\ \text{ft-lbf/s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 76.8 Btu/lbm is the work per unit mass. Using the absolute exit temperature alone overstates the work.
questions.question: An adiabatic air compressor (\(c_p = 0.24\) Btu/lbm-R, constant) takes in 2.0 lbm/s at 540 R and delivers it at 860 R. What is the magnitude of the compressor power?
questions.solution:
Refer to Compressors in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 197 (PDF page 203).

The handbook gives \(\dot W_{comp} = -\dot mc_p(T_e - T_i)\); the magnitude is:

$$\begin{aligned}|\dot W| &= 2.0(0.24)(860-540) \\ &= 153.6\ \text{Btu/s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: For a compressor the ideal (isentropic) temperature rise is in the numerator. Inverting it gives a value above 1, which is not an efficiency.
questions.question: A compressor takes in air at 540 R. The isentropic exit temperature would be 800 R, but the actual exit temperature is 860 R. What is the compressor isentropic efficiency?
questions.solution:
Refer to Compressor Isentropic Efficiency in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 197 (PDF page 203).

The handbook gives \(\eta_C = \dfrac{T_{es} - T_i}{T_e - T_i}\):

$$\eta_C = \frac{800-540}{860-540} = 0.81$$

questions.explanation: 130 Btu/lbm is the work per unit mass.
questions.question: An adiabatic gas turbine (\(c_p = 0.26\) Btu/lbm-R) passes 3.0 lbm/s, entering at 1600 R and leaving at 1100 R. What is the turbine power output?
questions.solution:
Refer to Turbines in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 199 (PDF page 205).

The handbook gives \(\dot W_{turb} = \dot mc_p(T_i - T_e)\):

$$\begin{aligned}\dot W &= 3.0(0.26)(1600-1100) \\ &= 390\ \text{Btu/s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: For a turbine the actual temperature drop is the numerator and the ideal drop is in the denominator, the reverse of a compressor.
questions.question: A turbine enters gas at 1600 R and exits at 1100 R. The isentropic exit temperature would be 1000 R. What is the isentropic efficiency?
questions.solution:
Refer to Turbine Isentropic Efficiency in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 199 (PDF page 205).

The handbook gives \(\eta_T = \dfrac{T_i - T_e}{T_i - T_{es}}\):

$$\eta_T = \frac{1600-1100}{1600-1000} = 0.83$$

questions.explanation: The flow downstream of a normal shock is always subsonic, so \(Ma_2 < 1\).
questions.question: A normal shock forms in air (k = 1.4) at an upstream Mach number of 2.0. What is the downstream Mach number?
questions.solution:
Refer to Normal Shock Relationships in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 195 (PDF page 201).

The handbook gives \(Ma_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{(k-1)Ma_1^2 + 2}{2kMa_1^2 - (k-1)}}\):

$$\begin{aligned}Ma_2 &= \sqrt{\frac{(1.4-1)(2.0)^2+2}{2(1.4)(2.0)^2-(1.4-1)}} \\ &= 0.577\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Mach number downstream of a normal shock

questions.explanation: Dropping the -(k - 1) term gives 4.67. The pressure rises across a shock, so the ratio exceeds 1.
questions.question: For a normal shock in air (k = 1.4) with \(Ma_1 = 2.0\), what is the static pressure ratio \(P_2/P_1\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Normal Shock Relationships in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 195 (PDF page 201).

The handbook gives \(P_2/P_1 = \dfrac{1}{k+1}\left[2kMa_1^2 - (k-1)\right]\):

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{P_2}{P_1} &= \frac{2(1.4)(2.0)^2-(1.4-1)}{1.4+1} \\ &= 4.50\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Pressure ratio across a normal shock

questions.explanation: The gas is compressed through the shock, so density increases. The velocity ratio V1/V2 equals the same ratio.
questions.question: For a normal shock in air (k = 1.4) with \(Ma_1 = 2.0\), what is the density ratio \(\rho_2/\rho_1\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Normal Shock Relationships in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 195 (PDF page 201).

The handbook gives \(\rho_2/\rho_1 = V_1/V_2 = \dfrac{(k+1)Ma_1^2}{(k-1)Ma_1^2+2}\):

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} &= \frac{(1.4+1)(2.0)^2}{(1.4-1)(2.0)^2+2} \\ &= 2.667\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Density ratio across a normal shock

choices: It drops to the upstream static temperature
questions.explanation: The static temperature increases across the shock; stagnation temperature does not.
questions.question: Across a normal shock, how does the stagnation temperature change, according to the handbook relations?
questions.solution:
Refer to Normal Shock Relationships in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 195 (PDF page 201).

The handbook lists \(T_{01} = T_{02}\): stagnation temperature is conserved across a normal shock, although static temperature rises.
questions.subtopic: Stagnation temperature across a normal shock

questions.explanation: The pressure difference must be in psf for consistent units, and g must appear in the numerator when using specific weight.
questions.question: A pitot tube in a water pipe (\(\gamma\) = 62.4 lb/ft³) reads a stagnation pressure 0.5 psi above the static pressure. What is the fluid velocity?
questions.solution:
Refer to Pitot Tubes in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 200 (PDF page 206).

The handbook gives \(v = \sqrt{2g(P_0-P_s)/\gamma}\). Convert to psf (x144):

$$\begin{aligned}v &= \sqrt{\frac{2(32.2)(72)}{62.4}} \\ &= 8.6\ \text{ft/s}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The factor of 2 sits in the numerator, and kPa must be converted to Pa.
questions.question: A pitot tube measures a pressure difference P0 - Ps of 0.8 kPa in a stream of air with density 1.2 kg/m³ (Mach number below 0.3). What is the velocity?
questions.solution:
Refer to Pitot Tubes in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 200 (PDF page 206).

The handbook gives \(v = \sqrt{(2/\rho)(P_0-P_s)}\), valid for a compressible fluid when Ma \(\le\) 0.3:

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{2(800)}{1.2}} = 36.5\ \text{m/s}$$

questions.explanation: Above Ma = 0.3 compressibility effects are no longer negligible.
questions.question: Up to what Mach number does the handbook allow the incompressible pitot tube equation to be used for a compressible fluid?
questions.solution:
Refer to Pitot Tubes in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 200 (PDF page 206).

The handbook states to use the incompressible equation if the Mach number is 0.3 or less.

questions.explanation: Leaving out the area-ratio correction, squaring it incorrectly, or using the inlet area in the numerator all give wrong flows.
questions.question: A horizontal venturi meter has an inlet diameter of 12 in and a throat diameter of 6 in. The piezometric head difference between inlet and throat is 5.0 ft of water and \(C_v = 0.98\). What is the flow rate?
questions.solution:
Refer to Venturi Meters in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 200 (PDF page 206).

The handbook gives the venturi flow as \(Q = \dfrac{C_vA_2}{\sqrt{1-(A_2/A_1)^2}}\sqrt{2g\,\Delta h}\), where \(\Delta h = (P_1/\gamma+z_1)-(P_2/\gamma+z_2)\) is the piezometric head difference. With \(A_1 = 0.7854\ \text{ft}^2\) and \(A_2 = 0.1963\ \text{ft}^2\) and a head difference of 5.0 ft:

$$\begin{aligned}Q &= \frac{0.98(0.1963)}{\sqrt{1-(0.250)^2}}\sqrt{2(32.2)(5.0)} \\ &= 3.57\ \text{cfs}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The equation uses a single constant density.
questions.question: For which kind of fluid is the handbook's venturi meter equation written?
questions.solution:
Refer to Venturi Meters in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 200 (PDF page 206).

The handbook notes that the venturi equation is for incompressible fluids.

choices: The valve flow coefficient at full open
questions.explanation: \(C_v\) corrects the ideal flow for real velocity losses.
questions.question: In the handbook's venturi meter equation, what does \(C_v\) represent?
questions.solution:
Refer to Venturi Meters in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 200 (PDF page 206).

The handbook defines \(C_v\) as the coefficient of velocity.

questions.explanation: Components must be summed with signs before squaring; adding magnitudes overstates the resultant.
questions.question: Three forces act on a particle. Their x-components are 30, 40 and -10 lb and their y-components are 20, -50 and 60 lb. What is the magnitude of the resultant?
questions.solution:
Refer to Resultant (Two Dimensions) in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 95 (PDF page 101).

The handbook gives \(F = [(\sum F_x)^2 + (\sum F_y)^2]^{1/2}\). \(\sum F_x = 60\), \(\sum F_y = 30\):

$$F = \sqrt{(60)^2+(30)^2} = 67.1\ \text{lb}$$

questions.explanation: The ratio is y over x, and the sign of the result matters (the handbook arctan form does not itself resolve the quadrant).
questions.question: Forces on a particle sum to \(\sum F_x = 60\) lb and \(\sum F_y = 30\) lb. Using the handbook's arctan relation, what is the value of the resultant direction \(\theta\) with respect to the x-axis?
questions.solution:
Refer to Resultant (Two Dimensions) in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 95 (PDF page 101).

The handbook gives \(\theta = \arctan(\sum F_y/\sum F_x)\):

$$\begin{aligned}\theta &= \arctan\left(\frac{30}{60}\right) \\ &= 26.6^\circ\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The sign order matters: \(M_z = xF_y - yF_x\). Reversing it flips the sign.
questions.question: A force F = (4, -1, 2) lb acts at the point (x, y, z) = (2, 3, 1) ft. What is the z-component of the moment about the origin, \(M_z\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Moments (Couples) in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 95 (PDF page 101).

The handbook gives \(M_z = xF_y - yF_x\):

$$M_z = (2)(-1) - (3)(4) = -14\ \text{ft-lb}$$
questions.subtopic: Moment of a force about the origin

questions.explanation: The sign order matters: \(M_z = xF_y - yF_x\). Reversing it flips the sign.
questions.question: A force F = (2, 5, -1) lb acts at the point (x, y, z) = (1, -2, 3) ft. What is the z-component of the moment about the origin, \(M_z\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Moments (Couples) in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 95 (PDF page 101).

The handbook gives \(M_z = xF_y - yF_x\):

$$M_z = (1)(5) - (-2)(2) = 9\ \text{ft-lb}$$
questions.subtopic: Moment of a force about the origin

questions.explanation: The sign order matters: \(M_z = xF_y - yF_x\). Reversing it flips the sign.
questions.question: A force F = (-2, 4, 1) lb acts at the point (x, y, z) = (3, 1, 2) ft. What is the z-component of the moment about the origin, \(M_z\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Moments (Couples) in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 95 (PDF page 101).

The handbook gives \(M_z = xF_y - yF_x\):

$$M_z = (3)(4) - (1)(-2) = 14\ \text{ft-lb}$$
questions.subtopic: Moment of a force about the origin

choices: A single force acting at a distance
Two forces that meet at a point
Two forces equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and parallel to each other
Two forces equal in magnitude and collinear
questions.explanation: A collinear pair would produce no moment.
questions.question: Which description matches the handbook's definition of a couple?
questions.solution:
Refer to Moments (Couples) in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 95 (PDF page 101).

The handbook defines a couple as two forces equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and parallel.

questions.explanation: Tightening uses alpha + phi. The value with alpha - phi is the loosening moment; ignoring friction or the pitch angle gives other wrong values.
questions.question: A square-thread screw jack carries a load of 2000 lb. The mean thread radius is 0.5 in, the pitch angle is 6° and the coefficient of friction is 0.15. What moment tightens the screw (raises the load)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Screw Thread in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 98 (PDF page 104).

The handbook gives \(M = Pr\tan(\alpha \pm \phi)\), with + for tightening and \(\phi = \tan^{-1}\mu = 8.53^\circ\):

$$M = 2000(0.5)\tan(6+8.53) = 259\ \text{in-lb}$$

questions.explanation: The contact angle must be in radians. Dividing by the exponential gives the lower force, not the one needed to slip.
questions.question: A rope wraps 180° around a fixed drum with a coefficient of static friction of 0.3. The holding force on the slack side is 100 lb. What is the largest force on the tight side at impending slip?
questions.solution:
Refer to Belt Friction in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 98 (PDF page 104).

The handbook gives \(F_1 = F_2e^{\mu\theta}\) with \(\theta\) in radians (180° = 3.142 rad):

$$F_1 = 100e^{(0.3)(3.142)} = 257\ \text{lb}$$

choices: One in tension and one in compression
Both in tension with equal force
questions.explanation: Equilibrium of the joint in both directions forces both loads to zero.
questions.question: Two members meet at a truss joint and no external load or support reaction acts there. According to the handbook, what are the two members?
questions.solution:
Refer to Statically Determinate Truss in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 98 (PDF page 104).

The handbook states that if only two members form a joint and no external load or reaction acts on it, both are zero-force members.

choices: It carries the sum of the two collinear forces
It is redundant and must be removed
questions.explanation: The third member has no force component along the collinear line to balance.
questions.question: Three members meet at a truss joint with no external load or reaction. Two of them are collinear. What does the handbook say about the third member?
questions.solution:
Refer to Statically Determinate Truss in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 98 (PDF page 104).

The handbook states the third member is a zero-force member when two are collinear and there is no external load or reaction.

choices: Two (sum of horizontal forces and sum of vertical forces)
questions.explanation: A particle-type joint has no moment equation.
questions.question: How many independent equilibrium equations per joint does the handbook method of joints use for a plane truss?
questions.solution:
Refer to Plane Truss: Method of Joints in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 98 (PDF page 104).

The handbook states the method writes the two equilibrium equations \(\sum F_H = 0\) and \(\sum F_V = 0\) for each joint.

choices: By assuming all members are two-force members in tension only
By drawing a free body diagram of a portion of the truss so the force is an external force
By summing forces at a single joint
questions.explanation: The cut exposes the member force.
questions.question: In the handbook's method of sections for a plane truss, how is the unknown member force exposed?
questions.solution:
Refer to Plane Truss: Method of Sections in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 98 (PDF page 104).

The handbook states the method draws a free-body diagram of a portion of the truss so the member force appears as an external force.

choices: The two applied forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and collinear
The forces are parallel but offset
The forces are equal in magnitude and in the same direction
questions.explanation: Offset forces would create a moment.
questions.question: Which statement is the handbook's description of a two-force body in static equilibrium?
questions.solution:
Refer to Concurrent Forces in the Statics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 98 (PDF page 104).

The handbook states a two-force body has two equal, opposite, collinear forces.

questions.explanation: Static temperature rises across a shock, so the ratio exceeds 1.
questions.question: For a normal shock in air (k = 1.4) with upstream Mach number 1.5, what is the static temperature ratio T2/T1?
questions.solution:
Refer to Normal Shock Relationships in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 195 (PDF page 201).

The handbook gives \(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \left[2+(k-1)Ma_1^2\right]\dfrac{2kMa_1^2-(k-1)}{(k+1)^2Ma_1^2}\):

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{T_2}{T_1} &= [2+0.4(1.5)^2]\frac{2(1.4)(1.5)^2-0.4}{(2.4)^2(1.5)^2} \\ &= 1.320\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Temperature ratio across a normal shock

questions.explanation: Downstream flow is always subsonic.
questions.question: Air (k = 1.4) crosses a normal shock with \(Ma_1 = 1.5\). What is \(Ma_2\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Normal Shock Relationships in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 195 (PDF page 201).

The handbook gives \(Ma_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{(k-1)Ma_1^2+2}{2kMa_1^2-(k-1)}} = 0.701\), which is subsonic as the handbook states.
questions.subtopic: Downstream Mach number after a normal shock, check of subsonic result

questions.explanation: The head difference equals v²/2g.
questions.question: A pitot tube shows a velocity head v²/2g of 4.0 ft. What is the velocity? (g = 32.2 ft/s²)
questions.solution:
Refer to Pitot Tubes in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 200 (PDF page 206).

The handbook figure shows P0 raised above the static level by v²/2g, so \(v = \sqrt{2g(P_0-P_s)/\gamma}\) gives \(v = \sqrt{2(32.2)(4.0)} = 16.0\) ft/s.

choices: It depends on the fluid only
questions.explanation: Pumps lose energy to friction and leakage.
questions.question: Which handbook quantity is larger for a real pump: fluid power (\(\rho g H Q\)) or pump (brake) power \(\rho g H Q / \eta_{pump}\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Pump (brake) power in the Fluid Mechanics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 196 (PDF page 202).

Dividing by an efficiency below 1 makes brake power exceed fluid power.

questions.explanation: Angular acceleration is torque divided by inertia. Multiplying or inverting the ratio gives other quantities.
questions.question: A shaft with a mass moment of inertia of 8.0 kg·m² about its axis is acted on by a constant net torque of 120 N·m. What is its angular acceleration?
questions.solution:
Refer to Rigid Body Rotation About a Fixed Axis in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 110 (PDF page 116).

The handbook gives \(\sum T = I\alpha\) for rotation about the longitudinal axis of a shaft:

$$\begin{aligned}\alpha &= \frac{T}{I} \\ &= \frac{120}{8.0} \\ &= 15.00\ \text{rad/s}^2\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Angular velocity grows linearly with time under constant acceleration.
questions.question: The shaft has an angular acceleration of 15.00 rad/s² and starts at 2.0 rad/s. What is its angular velocity after 5 s?
questions.solution:
Refer to Rigid Body Rotation About a Fixed Axis (constant α) in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 110 (PDF page 116).

For constant angular acceleration the handbook gives \(\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t\):

$$\omega = 2.0 + (15.00)(5) = 77.0\ \text{rad/s}$$

questions.explanation: The one-half factor on the acceleration term is required. Using the final speed times time overstates the angle.
questions.question: A wheel starts at 2.0 rad/s with a constant angular acceleration of 15.00 rad/s². Through what angle does it turn in 5 s?
questions.solution:
Refer to Rigid Body Rotation About a Fixed Axis (constant α) in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 110 (PDF page 116).

The handbook gives \(\theta = \theta_0 + \omega_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2\):

$$\begin{aligned}\theta - \theta_0 &= 2.0(5) + \tfrac{1}{2}(15.00)(5)^2 \\ &= 197.5\ \text{rad}\end{aligned}$$
