questions.explanation: The relation uses squares of the speeds and a factor of 2 on the angle term.
questions.question: A flywheel speeds up from 10 rad/s to 30 rad/s while turning through 50 rad at constant angular acceleration. What is the angular acceleration?
questions.solution:
Refer to Rigid Body Rotation About a Fixed Axis (constant α) in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 110 (PDF page 116).

The handbook gives \(\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha(\theta-\theta_0)\):

$$\begin{aligned}\alpha &= \frac{30^2 - 10^2}{2(50)} \\ &= 8.00\ \text{rad/s}^2\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Angular acceleration from speeds and angle

questions.explanation: 12 counts each pair of links twice.
questions.question: A mechanism has 4 links, counting the ground. How many instantaneous centers does it have?
questions.solution:
Refer to Instantaneous Center of Rotation in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 111 (PDF page 117).

The handbook gives \(c = n(n-1)/2\):

$$c = \frac{4(4-1)}{2} = 6$$

choices: They all lie on the same straight line
They lie on a circle through the center of mass
questions.explanation: The collinearity is what lets the unknown center be found as the intersection of two lines.
questions.question: According to Kennedy's rule in the handbook, how are the three instantaneous centers of three bodies moving relative to one another arranged?
questions.solution:
Refer to Kennedy's Rule in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 111 (PDF page 117).

The handbook states: when three bodies move relative to one another they have three instantaneous centers, all of which lie on the same straight line.

questions.explanation: The distance is squared. The mass center value is the smallest inertia, so the offset axis must have a larger value.
questions.question: A body of mass 10 kg has a mass moment of inertia of 4.0 kg·m² about an axis through its mass center. What is its mass moment of inertia about a parallel axis 0.5 m from the mass center?
questions.solution:
Refer to Parallel-Axis Theorem in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 112 (PDF page 118).

The handbook gives \(I_{new} = I_c + md^2\):

$$I_{new} = 4.0 + (10)(0.5)^2 = 6.50\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$$
questions.subtopic: Mass moment of inertia, parallel axis

questions.explanation: The radius of gyration is the square root of the ratio, in meters.
questions.question: A body of mass 8 kg has a mass moment of inertia of 18.0 kg·m² about an axis. What is its radius of gyration about that axis?
questions.solution:
Refer to Mass Radius of Gyration in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 112 (PDF page 118).

The handbook gives \(r_m = \sqrt{I/m}\):

$$r_m = \sqrt{\frac{18.0}{8}} = 1.500\ \text{m}$$

questions.explanation: A rigid body in general plane motion carries both translational and rotational energy.
questions.question: A rolling body of mass 50 kg has a mass-center speed of 4.0 m/s, a centroidal mass moment of inertia of 2.5 kg·m² and an angular speed of 8.0 rad/s. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.solution:
Refer to Kinetic Energy in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 112 (PDF page 118).

The handbook gives \(T = mv^2/2 + I_c\omega^2/2\):

$$\begin{aligned}T &= \frac{50(4.0)^2}{2} + \frac{2.5(8.0)^2}{2} \\ &= 480.0\ \text{J}\end{aligned}$$
questions.subtopic: Kinetic energy of a rigid body

questions.explanation: The angular speed is squared and halved; it is not multiplied directly by the inertia.
questions.question: A body has a mass moment of inertia of 6.0 kg·m² about its instant center and an angular speed of 5.0 rad/s. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.solution:
Refer to Kinetic Energy in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 112 (PDF page 118).

For motion about an instant center the handbook gives \(T = I_{IC}\omega^2/2\):

$$T = \frac{6.0(5.0)^2}{2} = 75.0\ \text{J}$$
questions.subtopic: Kinetic energy about the instant center

questions.explanation: The speed must drop when the stationary rotor is added. The coupled system's inertia is the sum.
questions.question: A rotor with I = 10.0 kg·m² spins at 6.0 rad/s with no external torque. A second, initially stationary rotor on the same axis (I = 15.0 kg·m²) is coupled to it. What is the common angular speed?
questions.solution:
Refer to Conservation of Angular Momentum in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 112 (PDF page 118).

The handbook gives \(\sum(\text{syst. }H)_1 = \sum(\text{syst. }H)_2\) with \(H = I\omega\). Here the total inertia is \(I_1 + I_2\) after coupling:

$$\begin{aligned}I_1\omega_1 &= (I_1+I_2)\omega_2 \Rightarrow \omega_2 \\ &= \frac{10.0(6.0)}{10.0+15.0}\end{aligned}$$

$$\omega_2 = 2.40\ \text{rad/s}$$

questions.explanation: F = μk N applies once slip is already occurring.
questions.question: According to the handbook, which condition describes a body at the point of impending slip?
questions.solution:
Refer to Friction in the Dynamics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 110 (PDF page 116).

The handbook lists F < μs N for no slip, F = μs N at impending slip and F = μk N when slip is occurring.

questions.explanation: The sine of the angle opposite the unknown side goes in the numerator; swapping the sines gives the wrong side.
questions.question: In a triangle, side a = 12.0 ft is opposite angle A = 40°, and angle B = 65°. What is the length of side b opposite angle B?
questions.solution:
Refer to Law of Sines in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 39 (PDF page 45).

The handbook gives \(a/\sin A = b/\sin B\):

$$\begin{aligned}b &= a\frac{\sin B}{\sin A} \\ &= 12.0\frac{\sin 65^\circ}{\sin 40^\circ} \\ &= 16.92\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The minus sign belongs with the cosine term. The Pythagorean value applies only to a 90° angle.
questions.question: Two sides of a triangle are 9.0 m and 14.0 m with an included angle of 52.0°. What is the third side?
questions.solution:
Refer to Law of Cosines in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 39 (PDF page 45).

The handbook gives \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C\):

$$\begin{aligned}c^2 &= 9.0^2 + 14.0^2 \\ &\quad - 2(9.0)(14.0)\cos 52.0^\circ \\ &= 121.9 \\ c &= 11.04\ \text{m}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The angle belongs to the side that appears alone on the left of the law of cosines. Using the other sides' form gives a different angle.
questions.question: A triangle has sides a = 8.0, b = 10.0 and c = 13.0 (same units). What is angle A opposite side a?
questions.solution:
Refer to Law of Cosines in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 39 (PDF page 45).

Solve \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A\) for the angle:

$$\begin{aligned}\cos A &= \frac{10.0^2 + 13.0^2 - 8.0^2}{2(10.0)(13.0)} \\ &= 0.7885\ \Rightarrow\ A \\ &= 38.0^\circ\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: \(e^{j\pi/2}\) would be j; \(e^{j\pi}\) lies on the negative real axis.
questions.question: Using Euler's identity \(e^{j\theta} = \cos\theta + j\sin\theta\), what is \(e^{j\pi}\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Euler's Identity in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 39 (PDF page 45).

With \(\theta = \pi\): \(\cos\pi + j\sin\pi = -1 + j(0) = -1\).

questions.explanation: n = 1 gives 120° and n = 0 gives 0°.
questions.question: The handbook gives the k roots of \(r(\cos\theta + j\sin\theta)\) as \(w = \sqrt[k]{r}\,[\cos(\theta/k + n\,360°/k) + j\sin(\theta/k + n\,360°/k)]\). For the cube roots of 27 (r = 27, \(\theta\) = 0°), what is the angle of the root for n = 2?
questions.solution:
Refer to Roots in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 39 (PDF page 45).

Here k = 3, so the angle is \(0/3 + n(360°/3) = 120° n\). For n = 2 the angle is 240° (and \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\) is the magnitude).

questions.explanation: tan θ is y/x; cos θ is x/r.
questions.question: A point is at x = 12 and y = 5. What is sin θ for the angle θ from the x-axis to the line to the point?
questions.solution:
Refer to Trigonometry in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 39 (PDF page 45).

The handbook gives \(\sin\theta = y/r\) with \(r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} = 13\), so \(\sin\theta = 5/13\).
questions.subtopic: Trigonometric functions of a right triangle

questions.explanation: 0.28 is cos 2α, and 0.48 omits the factor of 2.
questions.question: If sin α = 0.6 and cos α = 0.8, what is sin 2α?
questions.solution:
Refer to Identities in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 40 (PDF page 46).

The handbook gives \(\sin 2\alpha = 2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha = 2(0.6)(0.8) = 0.96\).

questions.explanation: 0.91 forgets the factor of 2 and 0.18 is 2 sin²α.
questions.question: If sin α = 0.3, what is cos 2α?
questions.solution:
Refer to Identities in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 40 (PDF page 46).

The handbook gives \(\cos 2\alpha = 1 - 2\sin^2\alpha = 1 - 2(0.09) = 0.82\).

questions.explanation: The denominator carries the product term, with a minus sign for a sum.
questions.question: If tan α = 0.5 and tan β = 0.25, what is tan(α + β)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Identities in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 40 (PDF page 46).

The handbook gives \(\tan(\alpha+\beta) = (\tan\alpha+\tan\beta)/(1-\tan\alpha\tan\beta)\):

$$\frac{0.5+0.25}{1-(0.5)(0.25)} = 0.857$$

questions.explanation: 0.87 is cos(α/2) and 0.71 would result from dropping the 1/2 under the root incorrectly.
questions.question: If cos α = 0.5 and α is in the first quadrant, what is sin(α/2)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Identities in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 40 (PDF page 46).

The handbook gives \(\sin(\alpha/2) = \pm\sqrt{(1-\cos\alpha)/2} = \sqrt{(1-0.5)/2} = \sqrt{0.25} = 0.5\) (positive in the first quadrant). This is consistent with α = 60°, α/2 = 30°.

questions.explanation: cot² θ + 1 equals csc² θ, not sec² θ.
questions.question: Which expression equals sec² θ according to the handbook's identities?
questions.solution:
Refer to Identities in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 40 (PDF page 46).

The handbook lists \(\tan^2\theta + 1 = \sec^2\theta\). The companion identity \(\cot^2\theta + 1 = \csc^2\theta\) is for csc.

questions.explanation: The sum form uses a plus sign between the two sines for sin α cos β.
questions.question: Using sin α cos β = (1/2)[sin(α + β) + sin(α − β)], what is sin 75° cos 15°?
questions.solution:
Refer to Identities in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 40 (PDF page 46).

$$\begin{aligned}\sin 75^\circ\cos 15^\circ &= \tfrac{1}{2}[\sin 90^\circ + \sin 60^\circ] \\ &= \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + 0.866) \\ &= 0.933\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: bh/3 is the area of the other parabola figure, where the curve is tangent along an edge and the region is thinner.
questions.question: The handbook's first parabola figure (A = 2bh/3) has b = 6 ft and h = 4 ft. What is its area?
questions.solution:
Refer to Parabola in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 41 (PDF page 47).

The handbook gives \(A = 2bh/3 = 2(6)(4)/3 = 16.0\ \text{ft}^2\).

questions.explanation: 2bh/3 belongs to the first figure.
questions.question: The handbook's second parabola figure (A = bh/3) has b = 9 m and h = 5 m. What is its area?
questions.solution:
Refer to Parabola in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 41 (PDF page 47).

The handbook gives \(A = bh/3 = (9)(5)/3 = 15.0\ \text{m}^2\).

questions.explanation: The area uses the product of the semi-axes.
questions.question: An ellipse has semi-axes a = 5 in and b = 3 in. What is its area?
questions.solution:
Refer to Ellipse in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 41 (PDF page 47).

The handbook gives \(A = \pi ab = \pi(5)(3) = 47.1\ \text{in}^2\).

questions.explanation: The root contains the mean of the squared semi-axes, not their sum.
questions.question: Using the handbook's approximate ellipse perimeter, what is the perimeter of an ellipse with semi-axes a = 5 in and b = 3 in?
questions.solution:
Refer to Ellipse in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 41 (PDF page 47).

The handbook gives \(P_{approx} = 2\pi\sqrt{(a^2+b^2)/2}\):

$$P \approx 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{5^2+3^2}{2}} = 25.9\ \text{in}$$

questions.explanation: λ is 0 for a circle and approaches 1 as the ellipse flattens.
questions.question: In the handbook's series for the perimeter of an ellipse, λ = (a − b)/(a + b). What is λ for a = 5 and b = 3?
questions.solution:
Refer to Ellipse in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 41 (PDF page 47).

$$\begin{aligned}\lambda &= \frac{a-b}{a+b} \\ &= \frac{5-3}{5+3} \\ &= 0.25\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 60.00 ft² is the full sector. The segment is the sector minus the triangle, so the sine term subtracts.
questions.question: A circular segment of a circle with radius 10 ft subtends a central angle of 1.2 rad. What is the area of the segment (between the chord and the arc)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Circular Segment in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 42 (PDF page 48).

The handbook gives \(A = [r^2(\phi - \sin\phi)]/2\) with \(\phi\) in radians:

$$\begin{aligned}A &= \frac{10^2(1.2 - \sin 1.2)}{2} \\ &= \frac{100(1.2-0.9320)}{2} \\ &= 13.40\ \text{ft}^2\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The factor of 2 doubles the half-angle. Using arcsin instead of arccos gives the angle from the chord side.
questions.question: A circular segment in a circle of radius 10 m has a depth d = 2 m (from the chord to the arc). What is the central angle φ?
questions.solution:
Refer to Circular Segment in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 42 (PDF page 48).

The handbook gives \(\phi = 2\arccos[(r-d)/r]\):

$$\begin{aligned}\phi &= 2\arccos\left(\frac{10-2}{10}\right) \\ &= 2\arccos(0.8) \\ &= 1.287\ \text{rad}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Both s and r appear once. A full-circle area formula does not apply to a sector.
questions.question: A circular sector has radius 12 ft and arc length s = 15 ft. What is its area?
questions.solution:
Refer to Circular Sector in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 42 (PDF page 48).

The handbook gives \(A = sr/2\) (equivalently \(\phi r^2/2\) with \(\phi = s/r\)):

$$A = \frac{(15)(12)}{2} = 90.0\ \text{ft}^2$$
questions.subtopic: Circular sector area from arc length

questions.explanation: The angle must be in radians and the radius is squared. Without the 1/2 the area doubles.
questions.question: A circular sector has radius 8 m and a central angle of 1.5 rad. What is its area?
questions.solution:
Refer to Circular Sector in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 42 (PDF page 48).

The handbook gives \(A = \phi r^2/2\):

$$A = \frac{(1.5)(8)^2}{2} = 48.0\ \text{m}^2$$

questions.explanation: The diameter form has a 6 in the denominator. Using d where r belongs in 4πr³/3 overstates the volume eight times.
questions.question: What is the volume of a sphere with diameter 5 ft?
questions.solution:
Refer to Sphere in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 42 (PDF page 48).

The handbook gives \(V = 4\pi r^3/3 = \pi d^3/6\):

$$V = \frac{\pi(5)^3}{6} = 65.4\ \text{ft}^3$$

questions.explanation: 4πr³/3 is the volume, and πr² is a great-circle area.
questions.question: A spherical tank has a radius of 2.5 m. What is its surface area?
questions.solution:
Refer to Sphere in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 42 (PDF page 48).

The handbook gives \(A = 4\pi r^2 = 78.5\ \text{m}^2\).

questions.explanation: 11.36 ft is \(d_2\), which carries the plus sign.
questions.question: A parallelogram has sides a = 8 ft and b = 5 ft with an interior angle φ = 60° between them. What is the length of the diagonal \(d_1\) given by the handbook's formula \(d_1 = \sqrt{a^2+b^2-2ab\cos\phi}\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Parallelogram in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 43 (PDF page 49).

$$\begin{aligned}d_1 &= \sqrt{8^2 + 5^2 - 2(8)(5)\cos 60^\circ} \\ &= \sqrt{49} \\ &= 7.00\ \text{ft}\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The relation does not depend on the interior angle.
questions.question: The sides of a parallelogram are 8 and 5. The handbook states \(d_1^2 + d_2^2 = 2(a^2 + b^2)\). What is \(d_1^2 + d_2^2\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Parallelogram in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 43 (PDF page 49).

$$d_1^2+d_2^2 = 2(8^2+5^2) = 178$$

questions.explanation: The height is b sin φ, so the sine, not the cosine, applies.
questions.question: A parallelogram has sides 8 m and 5 m with an interior angle of 60° between them. What is its area?
questions.solution:
Refer to Parallelogram in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 43 (PDF page 49).

The handbook gives \(A = ab\sin\phi\):

$$A = (8)(5)\sin 60^\circ = 34.64\ \text{m}^2$$
questions.subtopic: Parallelogram area from sides and angle

questions.explanation: \(d_1 = d_2\) would make it a rectangle.
questions.question: According to the handbook, when is a parallelogram a rhombus?
questions.solution:
Refer to Parallelogram in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 43 (PDF page 49).

The handbook states: if a = b, the parallelogram is a rhombus.

questions.explanation: 45° is the central angle φ = 2π/n, not the interior angle.
questions.question: What is the interior angle θ of a regular polygon with 8 equal sides (a regular octagon)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Regular Polygon in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 43 (PDF page 49).

The handbook gives \(\theta = \pi(1 - 2/n)\):

$$\begin{aligned}\theta &= \pi\left(1-\frac{2}{8}\right) \\ &= 2.3562\ \text{rad} \\ &= 135^\circ\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 78.5 in² is the inscribed circle, smaller than the octagon.
questions.question: A regular octagon has a distance r = 5 in from its center to the middle of each side. What is its area using the handbook relations φ = 2π/n, s = 2r tan(φ/2) and A = nsr/2?
questions.solution:
Refer to Regular Polygon in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 43 (PDF page 49).

$$\begin{aligned}s &= 2(5)\tan(\pi/8) \\ &= 4.142\ \text{in},\qquad A \\ &= \frac{nsr}{2} \\ &= \frac{8(4.142)(5)}{2} \\ &= 82.8\ \text{in}^2\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: 168 ft³ is the average-end-area volume, which ignores the mid-section.
questions.question: A prismoid of height 12 ft has end areas 20 ft² and 8 ft² and a mid-height area of 13 ft². What is its volume using the handbook formula?
questions.solution:
Refer to Prismoid in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 43 (PDF page 49).

The handbook gives \(V = (h/6)(A_1 + A_2 + 4A)\):

$$V = \frac{12}{6}(20+8+4(13)) = 160\ \text{ft}^3$$

questions.explanation: A cone holds one third of the cylinder of the same base and height.
questions.question: What is the volume of a right circular cone with base radius 3 ft and height 8 ft?
questions.solution:
Refer to Right Circular Cone in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 44 (PDF page 50).

The handbook gives \(V = \pi r^2h/3 = \pi(3)^2(8)/3 = 75.4\ \text{ft}^3\).

questions.explanation: 80.5 m² is the side area only. The base adds 28.3 m².
questions.question: What is the total surface area (side plus base) of a right circular cone with r = 3 m and h = 8 m?
questions.solution:
Refer to Right Circular Cone in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 44 (PDF page 50).

The handbook gives \(A = \pi r(r + \sqrt{r^2+h^2})\):

$$A = \pi(3)(3+\sqrt{73}) = 108.8\ \text{m}^2$$
questions.subtopic: Right circular cone total surface area

questions.explanation: Areas scale with the square of the distance from the apex, not linearly.
questions.question: For a right circular cone of height 9 ft with a base area of 54 ft², what is the area of a cross-section parallel to the base at a distance x = 3 ft from the apex? (Use \(A_x : A_b = x^2 : h^2\).)
questions.solution:
Refer to Right Circular Cone in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 44 (PDF page 50).

$$\begin{aligned}A_x &= A_b\frac{x^2}{h^2} \\ &= 54\frac{3^2}{9^2} \\ &= 6.0\ \text{ft}^2\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Using d where r belongs overstates the volume by four.
questions.question: A cylindrical tank has a diameter of 4 ft and a height of 10 ft. What is its volume?
questions.solution:
Refer to Right Circular Cylinder in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 44 (PDF page 50).

The handbook gives \(V = \pi d^2h/4 = \pi(4)^2(10)/4 = 125.7\ \text{ft}^3\).
questions.subtopic: Right circular cylinder volume from diameter

questions.explanation: 125.7 m² is the side only, and 75.4 m² would be a cylinder with one end.
questions.question: A closed cylinder has radius 2 m and height 10 m. What is its total surface area (side plus both ends)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Right Circular Cylinder in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 44 (PDF page 50).

The handbook gives \(A = 2\pi r(h + r)\):

$$A = 2\pi(2)(10+2) = 150.8\ \text{m}^2$$

questions.explanation: A paraboloid holds half of the circumscribed cylinder, so the 1/4 cylinder factor becomes 1/8.
questions.question: A parabolic bowl (paraboloid of revolution) has a top diameter of 6 ft and a depth of 5 ft. What is its volume?
questions.solution:
Refer to Paraboloid of Revolution in the Mathematics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 44 (PDF page 50).

The handbook gives \(V = \pi d^2h/8\):

$$V = \frac{\pi(6)^2(5)}{8} = 70.7\ \text{ft}^3$$

questions.explanation: 0.7698 would be W(1.2), the area between -1.2 and 1.2, and 0.2302 is twice the tail.
questions.question: From a unit normal table, F(1.2) = 0.8849, where F(x) is the area under the curve from -∞ to x. Using the handbook's relation for negative arguments, what is F(-1.2)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Normal Distribution in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 68 (PDF page 74).

The handbook gives \(F(-x) = 1 - F(x)\):

$$F(-1.2) = 1 - 0.8849 = 0.1151$$

choices: At μ − σ and μ + σ
At μ − σ/2 and μ + σ/2
At μ and at μ + σ
questions.explanation: The curve changes from concave down to concave up one standard deviation from the mean.
questions.question: According to the handbook, where are the two points of inflection of a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ?
questions.solution:
Refer to Normal Distribution (Gaussian Distribution) in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 68 (PDF page 74).

The handbook states the mode is at x = μ and that the two points of inflection are each located a distance σ on either side of the mode.

questions.explanation: The denominator is the standard error s/√n, not s.
questions.question: A sample of n = 16 has a mean of 52 and a standard deviation of 6. What is the t statistic for testing μ = 50?
questions.solution:
Refer to t-Distribution in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 69 (PDF page 75).

The handbook gives \(t = \dfrac{\bar x - \mu}{s/\sqrt n}\):

$$t = \frac{52-50}{6/\sqrt{16}} = 1.333$$
questions.subtopic: t statistic for a sample mean

questions.explanation: The left-tail critical value has the same magnitude with a negative sign.
questions.question: A t table gives t(0.05, 10) = 1.812. Using the handbook's symmetry relation t(1−α, ν) = −t(α, ν), what is t(0.95, 10)?
questions.solution:
Refer to t-Distribution in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 69 (PDF page 75).

The handbook notes that, in view of the symmetry of the t-distribution, \(t_{1-\alpha,\nu} = -t_{\alpha,\nu}\). So \(t_{0.95,10} = -1.812\).

questions.explanation: One degree of freedom is used up by estimating the mean.
questions.question: A sample of 12 observations is used with the t-distribution. According to the handbook, how many degrees of freedom does it have?
questions.solution:
Refer to t-Distribution in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 69 (PDF page 75).

The handbook gives ν = n − 1 = 12 − 1 = 11.
questions.subtopic: Degrees of freedom for the t-distribution

questions.explanation: The degrees of freedom equal the number of squared normal variables in the sum.
questions.question: If Z1, Z2, ..., Z5 are independent unit normal random variables, how many degrees of freedom does χ² = Z1² + Z2² + ... + Z5² have?
questions.solution:
Refer to χ² - Distribution in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 69 (PDF page 75).

The handbook defines the sum of squares of n independent unit normal variables as chi-square with n degrees of freedom. Here n = 5.

questions.explanation: The total error is 0.25; the systematic part has to be taken out to leave the random part.
questions.question: A measurement x = 10.25 has reference value \(x_{ref} = 10.00\) and a systematic disturbance of 0.18. Using the handbook's model \(x = x_{ref} + d_{systematic} + d_{random}\), what is the random component?
questions.solution:
Refer to Measurement Error in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 69 (PDF page 75).

$$\begin{aligned}d_{random} &= x - x_{ref} - d_{systematic} \\ &= 10.25 - 10.00 - 0.18 \\ &= 0.07\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Each standard deviation is multiplied by the partial derivative, which for a product is the other variable.
questions.question: Two uncorrelated measurements are x1 = 10 with standard deviation 0.2 and x2 = 5 with standard deviation 0.1. Using the Kline-McClintock equation, what is the standard uncertainty of y = x1·x2?
questions.solution:
Refer to Measurement Uncertainty in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 70 (PDF page 76).

The handbook gives \(\sigma_y = \sqrt{(\partial f/\partial x_1)^2\sigma_1^2 + (\partial f/\partial x_2)^2\sigma_2^2}\). For y = x1x2, \(\partial y/\partial x_1 = x_2 = 5\) and \(\partial y/\partial x_2 = x_1 = 10\):

$$\begin{aligned}\sigma_y &= \sqrt{(5)^2(0.2)^2 + (10)^2(0.1)^2} \\ &= \sqrt{1 + 1} \\ &= 1.41\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: Uncorrelated standard deviations add in quadrature, not directly.
questions.question: Two uncorrelated measured lengths have standard deviations of 0.3 mm and 0.4 mm. What is the standard uncertainty of their sum, using the Kline-McClintock equation?
questions.solution:
Refer to Measurement Uncertainty in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 70 (PDF page 76).

For y = x1 + x2 both partial derivatives equal 1:

$$\sigma_y = \sqrt{0.3^2 + 0.4^2} = 0.5\ \text{mm}$$

questions.explanation: The derivative of x² is 2x, which doubles the relative effect of the side error.
questions.question: A side x = 3.0 m is measured with standard deviation 0.1 m. What is the standard uncertainty of the area y = x², using the Kline-McClintock equation?
questions.solution:
Refer to Measurement Uncertainty in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 70 (PDF page 76).

Here \(\partial y/\partial x = 2x = 6.0\), so \(\sigma_y = 6.0(0.1) = 0.6\ \text{m}^2\).

questions.explanation: k = 3 would give about 99.7%.
questions.question: A standard uncertainty is 0.5 units. At the handbook's coverage factor of k = 2, what expanded uncertainty is reported, and at about what confidence level?
questions.solution:
Refer to Measurement Uncertainty in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 70 (PDF page 76).

The handbook says expanded uncertainties are typically given at about 95% confidence with a coverage factor k = 2 (2 sigma): 2(0.5) = 1.0.

questions.explanation: The line passes through (mean x, mean y), so the intercept must be computed first.
questions.question: A regression has Sxy = 120, Sxx = 40, mean x = 5 and mean y = 30. What does the fitted line predict at x = 7?
questions.solution:
Refer to Least Squares in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 70 (PDF page 76).

The handbook gives \(\hat b = S_{xy}/S_{xx} = 120/40 = 3\) and \(\hat a = \bar y - \hat b\bar x = 30 - 3(5) = 15\):

$$\hat y = 15 + 3(7) = 36$$

questions.explanation: The slope uses sums of deviations about the means, not a ratio of totals.
questions.question: For the data (x, y) = (1, 2.1), (2, 3.9), (3, 6.2), (4, 7.8), (5, 10.1), what is the least-squares slope?
questions.solution:
Refer to Least Squares in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 70 (PDF page 76).

With mean x = 3 and mean y = 6.02: \(S_{xx} = \sum(x_i-\bar x)^2 = 10\) and \(S_{xy} = \sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y) = 19.90\).

$$\begin{aligned}\hat b &= \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} \\ &= \frac{19.90}{10} \\ &= 1.99\end{aligned}$$

questions.explanation: The divisor is n − 2 because two parameters were fitted.
questions.question: A regression with n = 5 has \(S_{xx} = 10\), \(S_{yy} = 40\) and \(S_{xy} = 19.9\). What is the standard error of estimate squared, \(S_e^2\) (the MSE)?
questions.solution:
Refer to Standard Error of Estimate in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 70 (PDF page 76).

The handbook gives \(S_e^2 = \dfrac{S_{xx}S_{yy} - S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}(n-2)}\):

$$S_e^2 = \frac{10(40) - (19.9)^2}{10(5-2)} = 0.133$$

questions.explanation: The residual is observed minus fitted.
questions.question: A fitted line is ŷ = 1.5 + 2.0x. At x = 3 the observed value is y = 8.0. What is the residual e?
questions.solution:
Refer to Residual in the Engineering Probability and Statistics section of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), printed page 70 (PDF page 76).

The handbook gives \(e_i = y_i - \hat y_i\). Here \(\hat y = 1.5 + 2.0(3) = 7.5\), so \(e = 8.0 - 7.5 = 0.5\).

questions.question: An activity has an early start (ES) of day 4 and a duration of 6 days. Its late finish (LF) is day 15. What is the activity's total float?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Total float is the slack between an activity's early and late schedule:

$$TF = LS - ES = LF - EF$$

$$\begin{aligned} ES &= 4 \\ \text{Duration} &= 6 \\ EF &= ES + \text{Dur} = 10 \\ LF &= 15 \end{aligned}$$

$$TF = LF - EF = 15 - 10 = 5\ \text{days}$$
questions.explanation: Total float = LF − EF. Using LF − ES (11) forgets the duration; 0 would only hold for a critical-path activity.

questions.question: Activity B has an early finish (EF) of day 12. Its only successor, activity C, has an early start (ES) of day 15. What is the free float of activity B?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Free float is the delay available before the earliest successor is affected:

$$FF = ES_{\text{successor}} - EF_{\text{activity}}$$

$$FF = 15 - 12 = 3\ \text{days}$$
questions.explanation: Free float uses the successor's early start minus this activity's early finish. It never exceeds total float.

questions.question: On a project, the planned value (PV) is $40,000, the earned value (EV) is $35,000, and the actual cost (AC) is $42,000. What is the cost variance (CV)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earned-Value Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Cost variance compares work performed against what it cost:

$$CV = EV - AC$$

$$CV = 35{,}000 - 42{,}000 = -\$7{,}000$$

A negative CV means the work is over budget.
questions.explanation: CV = EV − AC. −$5,000 is the schedule variance (EV − PV); a positive sign reverses the over-budget meaning.

questions.question: A project has an earned value (EV) of $35,000 and an actual cost (AC) of $42,000. What is the cost performance index (CPI)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earned-Value Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The cost performance index is earned value per dollar spent:

$$CPI = \frac{EV}{AC} = \frac{35{,}000}{42{,}000} = 0.83$$

CPI < 1 indicates a cost overrun.
questions.explanation: CPI = EV/AC = 0.83. 1.20 inverts the ratio; 0.88 would be the SPI if PV were $40,000.

questions.question: A project has a budget at completion (BAC) of $250,000. To date the earned value (EV) is $50,000 and the actual cost (AC) is $60,000. Assuming current cost performance continues, what is the estimate at completion (EAC)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earned-Value Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

With performance assumed to continue, EAC scales the budget by the cost performance index:

$$CPI = \frac{EV}{AC} = \frac{50{,}000}{60{,}000} = 0.8333$$

$$EAC = \frac{BAC}{CPI} = \frac{250{,}000}{0.8333} = \$300{,}000$$
questions.explanation: EAC = BAC/CPI. $260,000 wrongly adds the $10,000 overrun once; $208,333 multiplies by CPI instead of dividing.

questions.question: An activity has a normal duration of 10 days at a cost of $8,000, and can be crashed to 7 days at a cost of $12,500. What is the crash cost slope?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The cost slope is the added cost per day of time saved:

$$\text{Slope} = \frac{\text{Crash cost} - \text{Normal cost}}{\text{Normal time} - \text{Crash time}}$$

$$\text{Slope} = \frac{12{,}500 - 8{,}000}{10 - 7} = \frac{4{,}500}{3} = \$1{,}500/\text{day}$$
questions.explanation: Slope = Δcost / Δtime. $4,500 is the total added cost, not per day; $643 divides by 7 instead of 3.

questions.question: A contractor recorded 5 OSHA-recordable injuries over a period in which employees worked a total of 250,000 hours. What is the recordable incidence rate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Incidence Variable Values section in the Safety chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The OSHA incidence rate is normalized to 100 full-time workers (200,000 hours):

$$IR = \frac{(\text{cases})(200{,}000)}{\text{total hours worked}}$$

$$IR = \frac{(5)(200{,}000)}{250{,}000} = 4.0$$
questions.explanation: The 200,000-hour base represents 100 workers × 2,000 hr/yr. Using 100,000 gives 2.0; 500,000 gives 8.0.

questions.question: An excavator loads a haul truck in 5 minutes. Each truck's travel cycle (haul, dump, return, and spot) takes 20 minutes, excluding loading. How many trucks are needed to keep the excavator working continuously?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The number of trucks to balance the excavator is the full truck cycle divided by the loading time:

$$\text{Truck cycle} = \text{load} + \text{travel} = 5 + 20 = 25\ \text{min}$$

$$N = \frac{\text{truck cycle}}{\text{loading time}} = \frac{25}{5} = 5\ \text{trucks}$$
questions.explanation: Include the loading time in the cycle (25 min, not 20). Using 20/5 = 4 leaves the loader idle part of each cycle.

questions.question: A loader with a 3 LCY bucket has a cycle time of 30 seconds and operates at an efficiency of 50 working minutes per hour. What is its hourly production?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Production is bucket load times the number of cycles in the effective hour:

$$\text{Cycles/hr} = \frac{(50\ \text{min})(60\ \text{s/min})}{30\ \text{s}} = 100$$

$$\text{Production} = (100)(3) = 300\ \text{LCY/hr}$$
questions.explanation: Apply the 50-min efficiency hour. Using a full 60-min hour overstates output to 360 LCY/hr.

questions.question: Under OSHA 1926 (construction), at what height above a lower level is fall protection generally required at an unprotected edge?
questions.solution:
Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.501, fall protection is generally required in construction when a worker is exposed to a fall of 6 feet or more to a lower level.

The other heights are real OSHA triggers for different situations: 4 ft is the general-industry trigger (1910), 10 ft applies to scaffolds, and 15 ft is a steel-erection provision.
questions.explanation: The construction (1926) general trigger is 6 ft. 4 ft is general industry; 10 ft scaffolds; 15 ft steel erection.

questions.question: Per OSHA, a protective system (sloping, shoring, or shielding) is required for an excavation when it reaches what depth, unless it is made entirely in stable rock?
questions.solution:
Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.652, a protective system is required for excavations 5 feet or more in depth, unless the excavation is made entirely in stable rock.

Excavations deeper than 20 ft require a protective system designed by a registered professional engineer.
questions.explanation: The 5-ft threshold triggers a protective system; 20 ft is the depth that requires an engineered design.

questions.question: Under which project delivery method does the owner hold a single contract covering both the design and the construction of the project?
choices: Construction manager at risk (with separate designer)
questions.solution:
In design-build, the owner executes one contract with a single entity responsible for both design and construction, giving a single point of responsibility.

In design-bid-build the owner holds separate contracts with the designer and the contractor. CM-at-risk adds a construction manager but the designer is still under a separate owner contract. Multiple-prime splits construction into several owner-held contracts.
questions.explanation: Design-build = one contract for design + construction. Design-bid-build keeps them separate.

questions.question: For a project where the work items are known but the exact quantities are uncertain (e.g., earthwork), which contract type is most appropriate?
questions.solution:
A unit-price contract pays a fixed price per unit of each work item, so the final cost adjusts to the quantities actually measured in the field — ideal when item types are known but quantities are uncertain.

Lump-sum suits well-defined scope with firm quantities; cost-plus suits poorly defined scope; a GMP caps the owner's exposure under a cost-reimbursable arrangement.
questions.explanation: Unit-price fits known items with uncertain quantities. Lump-sum needs firm quantities to price accurately.

questions.question: A contractor completes $200,000 of work in the current pay period. The contract specifies 10% retainage. What is the current progress payment to the contractor?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Retainage is withheld from the amount earned:

$$\text{Payment} = \text{earned} \times (1 - \text{retainage})$$

$$\text{Payment} = 200{,}000 \times (1 - 0.10) = \$180{,}000$$

The withheld $20,000 is released later, typically at substantial completion.
questions.explanation: Withhold 10%: pay $180,000. $20,000 is the amount retained, not the payment.

questions.question: A continuous concrete footing is 60 ft long, 2 ft wide, and 1.5 ft deep. What is the concrete quantity in cubic yards?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Compute the volume and convert to cubic yards (27 ft³ per CY):

$$V = L \times W \times D = 60 \times 2 \times 1.5 = 180\ \text{ft}^3$$

$$V = \frac{180}{27} = 6.67\ \text{CY}$$
questions.explanation: Divide cubic feet by 27. 180 is the volume in ft³ (forgetting the conversion).

questions.question: A fill requires 10,000 CY of compacted soil. The borrow material has a shrinkage of 20%. How many bank cubic yards (BCY) must be excavated?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Shrinkage means compacted volume is less than bank volume:

$$CCY = BCY \times (1 - \text{shrinkage})$$

$$BCY = \frac{CCY}{1 - \text{shrinkage}} = \frac{10{,}000}{1 - 0.20} = 12{,}500\ \text{BCY}$$
questions.explanation: Divide by (1 − shrinkage). Multiplying by 0.80 gives 8,000, the wrong direction.

questions.question: On a site plan drawn at a scale of 1 in = 40 ft, a property line measures 3.5 in. What is its actual length?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Multiply the measured length by the scale factor:

$$L = 3.5\ \text{in} \times 40\ \text{ft/in} = 140\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: Multiply inches by ft-per-inch. Dividing (3.5/40) gives 11.4 ft.

questions.question: A roadway alignment runs from station 12+50 to station 27+00. What is the distance between these two stations?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

A station equals 100 ft, so convert each station and subtract:

$$12{+}50 = 1{,}250\ \text{ft}, \qquad 27{+}00 = 2{,}700\ \text{ft}$$

$$\Delta = 2{,}700 - 1{,}250 = 1{,}450\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: Each station is 100 ft; subtract the two. 1,500 ignores the +50 offset.

questions.question: A storm sewer invert drops from elevation 100.00 ft at station 0+00 to elevation 98.50 ft at station 3+00. What is the pipe slope?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Slope is the elevation change over the horizontal run (300 ft between the stations):

$$S = \frac{\Delta \text{elev}}{\Delta \text{distance}} = \frac{100.00 - 98.50}{300} = \frac{1.50}{300} = 0.005 = 0.50\%$$
questions.explanation: Divide the 1.50-ft drop by the 300-ft run. 1.50% forgets to divide by distance in hundreds of ft.

questions.question: A simply supported beam spans 8 m and carries a single 20 kN point load located 3 m from the left support. What is the maximum bending moment in the beam?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Beams section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Find the left reaction by moments about the right support, then the moment under the load:

$$R_A = \frac{P\,b}{L} = \frac{20(5)}{8} = 12.5\ \text{kN}$$

The maximum moment is under the load:

$$M_{max} = R_A \cdot a = 12.5 \times 3 = 37.5\ \text{kN·m}$$
questions.explanation: For a single point load the maximum moment is R_A·a. 60 would be PL/8×... using midspan PL/4; the load is not at midspan.

questions.question: At a truss joint, a horizontal member and a single diagonal member (inclined 30° above horizontal) meet, and a 10 kN load hangs vertically from the joint. What is the axial force in the diagonal member?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Plane Truss: Method of Joints section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Vertical equilibrium at the joint — only the diagonal has a vertical component to resist the 10 kN:

$$\sum F_y = 0: \quad F_d \sin 30^\circ = 10$$

$$F_d = \frac{10}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{10}{0.5} = 20\ \text{kN}$$
questions.explanation: Only the diagonal carries vertical load, so F_d = 10/sin30° = 20 kN. 17.3 kN uses cos30° (the horizontal component).

questions.question: A beam is supported at A (x = 0) and B (x = 6 m) with a 2 m overhang beyond B to a free end C (x = 8 m). A 10 kN point load acts at C. What is the magnitude of the vertical reaction at A?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Beams section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Sum moments about B to find R_A (the load at C is 2 m past B):

$$\sum M_B = 0: \quad R_A(6) + 10(2) = 0 \Rightarrow R_A = -3.33\ \text{kN}$$

The negative sign means R_A acts downward (uplift); its magnitude is 3.33 kN.
questions.explanation: The overhang load causes uplift at A: |R_A| = 10(2)/6 = 3.33 kN. 13.33 kN is the reaction at B.

questions.question: A cantilever beam 3 m long carries a 5 kN point load at its free tip. E = 200 GPa and I = 50×10⁶ mm⁴. What is the tip deflection?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Deflection of Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Tip deflection of a cantilever with an end point load:

$$\Delta = \frac{PL^3}{3EI}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P &= 5{,}000\ \text{N}, \quad L = 3\ \text{m} \\ EI &= (200\times10^9)(50\times10^{-6}) = 1.0\times10^7\ \text{N·m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\Delta = \frac{5{,}000(3)^3}{3(1.0\times10^7)} = 0.0045\ \text{m} = 4.5\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: Use PL³/3EI for a cantilever. 13.5 mm drops the factor of 3 (PL³/EI).

questions.subtopic: Simply supported central point load deflection
questions.question: A simply supported beam 6 m long carries a 30 kN point load at midspan. E = 200 GPa and I = 80×10⁶ mm⁴. What is the maximum deflection?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Deflection of Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Midspan deflection for a central point load on a simple span:

$$\Delta = \frac{PL^3}{48EI}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P &= 30{,}000\ \text{N}, \quad L = 6\ \text{m} \\ EI &= (200\times10^9)(80\times10^{-6}) = 1.6\times10^7\ \text{N·m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\Delta = \frac{30{,}000(6)^3}{48(1.6\times10^7)} = 0.00844\ \text{m} = 8.44\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: Central point load uses PL³/48EI. 33.75 mm uses /12EI (a cantilever-type factor).

questions.question: A pinned-pinned column is 5 m long with E = 200 GPa and I = 10×10⁶ mm⁴. What is the Euler critical buckling load?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Columns section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Euler buckling load with K = 1.0 (pinned-pinned):

$$P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{L^2}$$

$$\begin{aligned} EI &= (200\times10^9)(10\times10^{-6}) = 2.0\times10^6\ \text{N·m}^2 \\ P_{cr} &= \frac{\pi^2 (2.0\times10^6)}{(5)^2} = 790{,}000\ \text{N} = 790\ \text{kN} \end{aligned}$$
questions.explanation: K = 1 for pinned ends. 395 kN would use K = √2 effect wrongly; 1,579 kN doubles it.

questions.question: What is the theoretical effective length factor K for a column that is fixed at its base and free at the top (a flagpole-type column)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

For a column fixed at the base and free (and free to translate) at the top, the theoretical effective length factor is K = 2.0. The column buckles in a shape equivalent to half of a pinned-pinned column of twice the length.

The other values correspond to different boundary conditions: K = 0.5 (fixed-fixed, no sway), K = 0.7 (fixed-pinned), K = 1.0 (pinned-pinned).
questions.explanation: Fixed-free gives the theoretical K = 2.0. 0.5 is fixed-fixed; 0.7 is fixed-pinned; 1.0 is pinned-pinned.

questions.subtopic: Required moment of inertia for Euler load
questions.question: A pinned-pinned column 4 m long (E = 200 GPa) must carry an Euler critical load of 500 kN. What is the minimum required moment of inertia?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Columns section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Solve the Euler equation for I (K = 1.0):

$$P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{L^2} \Rightarrow I = \frac{P_{cr} L^2}{\pi^2 E}$$

$$I = \frac{(500{,}000)(4)^2}{\pi^2 (200\times10^9)} = 4.05\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}^4 = 4.05\times10^{6}\ \text{mm}^4$$
questions.explanation: Rearrange Euler for I. 2.03×10⁶ halves L² (uses L = 2 m); 8.11×10⁶ doubles it.

questions.question: A plane truss has 14 members, 3 reaction components, and 8 joints. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

For a plane truss, the degree of static indeterminacy is:

$$DSI = (m + r) - 2j$$

$$DSI = (14 + 3) - 2(8) = 17 - 16 = 1$$

Since DSI = 1 > 0, the truss is statically indeterminate to the first degree.
questions.explanation: Plane truss: DSI = m + r − 2j = 1. DSI = 0 would be statically determinate.

questions.subtopic: Plane frame indeterminacy with internal hinge
questions.question: A single-bay portal frame has both column bases fixed (6 reaction components total) and contains one internal hinge in the beam. The frame has no closed loops. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

With no closed loop, use external indeterminacy reduced by the released conditions:

$$DSI = r - 3 - c$$

where r = 6 reactions and c = 1 condition equation from the internal hinge:

$$DSI = 6 - 3 - 1 = 2$$
questions.explanation: Two fixed bases give 6 reactions (indeterminate to 3); the internal hinge releases one condition, so DSI = 2.

questions.question: A plane truss has 21 members, 3 reaction components, and 12 joints. Classify the truss.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Compare (m + r) with 2j:

$$m + r = 21 + 3 = 24, \qquad 2j = 2(12) = 24$$

Since (m + r) = 2j and the truss is properly arranged, it is statically determinate (DSI = 0).
questions.explanation: m + r = 2j gives DSI = 0, statically determinate. The count alone cannot prove stability, but with proper geometry it is determinate.

questions.question: A beam fixed at both ends spans 8 m and carries a uniformly distributed load of 15 kN/m. What is the magnitude of the bending moment at each support?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Beams section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

For a fixed-fixed beam under a full-span uniform load, the support (negative) moment is:

$$M = \frac{wL^2}{12} = \frac{15(8)^2}{12} = \frac{960}{12} = 80\ \text{kN·m}$$

The midspan moment for this case is wL²/24 = 40 kN·m.
questions.explanation: Support moment is wL²/12 = 80. 40 is the midspan moment (wL²/24); 120 is the simple-span wL²/8.

questions.question: An interior floor beam has a tributary width of 3 m. The floor dead load is 4.0 kPa and the live load is 5.0 kPa. What is the LRFD factored line load on the beam (use 1.2D + 1.6L)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Factor the area loads, then multiply by the tributary width:

$$w_u = (1.2D + 1.6L)\,(\text{trib width})$$

$$w_u = [1.2(4.0) + 1.6(5.0)](3) = (4.8 + 8.0)(3) = 12.8 \times 3 = 38.4\ \text{kN/m}$$
questions.explanation: Factor loads then apply trib width: (1.2×4 + 1.6×5)×3 = 38.4 kN/m. 27.0 uses unfactored (4+5)×3.

questions.question: A column carries a dead load of 20 kip and a live load of 15 kip (no other loads). Using LRFD, what is the controlling factored axial load?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Check the governing LRFD combinations:

$$1.4D = 1.4(20) = 28\ \text{kip}$$

$$1.2D + 1.6L = 1.2(20) + 1.6(15) = 24 + 24 = 48\ \text{kip}$$

The larger value controls: P_u = 48 kip.
questions.explanation: 1.2D + 1.6L = 48 governs over 1.4D = 28. 35 kip is the unfactored D + L.

questions.question: A steel tension member has a gross area A_g = 5.0 in² and F_y = 50 ksi. What is the LRFD design tensile strength for the yielding limit state?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Yielding on the gross section (φ = 0.90):

$$\phi_t P_n = \phi_t F_y A_g = 0.90(50)(5.0) = 225\ \text{kip}$$
questions.explanation: Yielding uses φ = 0.90 on F_y·A_g = 225 kip. 250 kip omits the φ factor.

questions.question: A compact, fully braced steel beam has a plastic section modulus Z_x = 60 in³ and F_y = 50 ksi. What is the LRFD design flexural strength?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Fully braced and compact, so the limit state is yielding (M_n = M_p), with φ_b = 0.90:

$$\phi_b M_n = \phi_b F_y Z_x = 0.90(50)(60) = 2{,}700\ \text{kip·in}$$

$$\phi_b M_n = 2{,}700 / 12 = 225\ \text{kip·ft}$$
questions.explanation: M_p = F_y Z_x, then φ = 0.90 and convert to kip·ft: 225. 250 omits φ; 203 uses S_x-type (0.9FyS).

questions.question: A steel column has KL/r = 150, A_g = 10.0 in², F_y = 50 ksi, and E = 29,000 ksi. What is the LRFD design compressive strength φ_c P_n?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Compare slenderness with the limit 4.71√(E/F_y) = 113.4. Since KL/r = 150 > 113.4, elastic buckling governs:

$$F_e = \frac{\pi^2 E}{(KL/r)^2} = \frac{\pi^2 (29{,}000)}{150^2} = 12.72\ \text{ksi}$$

$$F_{cr} = 0.877 F_e = 0.877(12.72) = 11.16\ \text{ksi}$$

$$\phi_c P_n = 0.90 F_{cr} A_g = 0.90(11.16)(10.0) = 100\ \text{kip}$$
questions.explanation: KL/r = 150 > 113.4, so F_cr = 0.877F_e (elastic). 114 kip skips the 0.877 factor; 82 kip mis-takes φ.

questions.question: A singly reinforced concrete beam has b = 12 in, d = 20 in, A_s = 3.0 in², f'_c = 4 ksi, and f_y = 60 ksi. Assuming it is tension-controlled, what is φM_n?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Depth of the equivalent stress block, then nominal moment with φ = 0.90:

$$a = \frac{A_s f_y}{0.85 f'_c b} = \frac{3.0(60)}{0.85(4)(12)} = 4.41\ \text{in}$$

$$M_n = A_s f_y\left(d - \tfrac{a}{2}\right) = 3.0(60)(20 - 2.21) = 3{,}203\ \text{kip·in}$$

$$\phi M_n = 0.90(3{,}203)/12 = 240\ \text{kip·ft}$$
questions.explanation: Find a, then φA_s f_y(d − a/2)/12 = 240. 270 omits φ; 300 ignores the a/2 lever-arm reduction.

questions.question: A reinforced concrete beam has b_w = 12 in, d = 20 in, and f'_c = 4,000 psi (normal-weight). Using V_c = 2λ√(f'_c) b_w d, what is the design shear strength φV_c?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Concrete shear with λ = 1.0, then φ = 0.75:

$$V_c = 2\lambda\sqrt{f'_c}\,b_w d = 2(1)\sqrt{4000}(12)(20) = 30{,}358\ \text{lb}$$

$$\phi V_c = 0.75(30{,}358) = 22{,}800\ \text{lb} = 22.8\ \text{kip}$$
questions.explanation: Apply φ = 0.75 to V_c. 30.4 kip is the unfactored V_c; 45.5 kip uses φ = 1.5 wrongly.

questions.question: An equal-tangent crest vertical curve 600 ft long joins a +4% grade to a −2% grade. The PVI is at station 30+00 at elevation 500.00 ft. What is the elevation of the PVC?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The PVC is half the curve length before the PVI, along the incoming grade:

$$\text{Elev}_{PVC} = \text{Elev}_{PVI} - g_1\left(\tfrac{L}{2}\right)$$

$$= 500.00 - 0.04(300) = 488.00\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: Back up L/2 = 300 ft along +4%: 500 − 12 = 488.00 ft. Adding instead gives 512.00 (that is toward the PVT direction).

questions.question: A crest vertical curve must provide a rate of vertical curvature K = 44 ft per percent. The grades are +3% and −3%. What is the minimum curve length?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Minimum length from the rate of vertical curvature and the total grade change A:

$$A = |g_1 - g_2| = |3 - (-3)| = 6\%$$

$$L = K A = 44 \times 6 = 264\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: L = K·A with A = 6%. Using A = 3% (one grade) gives 132 ft.

questions.question: An equal-tangent vertical curve 600 ft long joins a +4% grade to a −2% grade. What is the vertical offset between the tangent and the curve at the PVI?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The offset from the tangent to the curve at the PVI (the midpoint) is:

$$e = \frac{A L}{8}$$

with A as a decimal grade change, A = |0.04 − (−0.02)| = 0.06:

$$e = \frac{0.06(600)}{8} = 4.5\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: Mid-curve offset e = AL/8 = 4.5 ft. Using AL/4 doubles it to 9.0 ft.

questions.question: A horizontal circular curve has a radius of 500 ft and a deflection (central) angle of 30°. What is the length of the curve?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Arc length for a central angle Δ:

$$L = \frac{\pi R \Delta}{180} = \frac{\pi (500)(30)}{180} = 261.8\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: L = πRΔ/180 = 261.8 ft. 523.6 ft uses Δ = 60°; 150 ft drops the π (uses RΔ/100).

questions.question: A horizontal circular curve has a radius of 500 ft and a deflection angle of 30°. What is the tangent distance T (from PC or PT to the PI)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Tangent distance for a circular curve:

$$T = R\tan\!\left(\tfrac{\Delta}{2}\right) = 500\tan(15^\circ) = 500(0.2679) = 134.0\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: T = R·tan(Δ/2) = 134 ft. Using tan(Δ) = tan30° gives 289; halving gives 67.

questions.question: A horizontal circular curve has a radius of 500 ft and a deflection angle of 30°. What is the middle ordinate M?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Middle ordinate for a circular curve:

$$M = R\left[1 - \cos\!\left(\tfrac{\Delta}{2}\right)\right] = 500\,[1 - \cos 15^\circ] = 500(0.03407) = 17.0\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: M = R(1 − cos(Δ/2)) = 17.0 ft. Using cos(Δ) overstates it.

questions.question: Using the arc definition, what is the degree of curve for a horizontal curve with a radius of 500 ft?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Arc-definition degree of curve (100-ft arc):

$$D = \frac{5729.58}{R} = \frac{5729.58}{500} = 11.46^\circ$$
questions.explanation: D = 5729.58/R = 11.46°. 5.73° would use 2863; 22.9° halves the radius.

questions.question: A roadway has a design speed of 60 mph. Using a perception-reaction time of 2.5 s and a deceleration rate of 11.2 ft/s² on a level grade, what is the stopping sight distance?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stopping Sight Distance section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

SSD is the sum of the reaction distance and the braking distance:

$$SSD = 1.47 V t + \frac{1.075 V^2}{a}$$

$$= 1.47(60)(2.5) + \frac{1.075(60)^2}{11.2} = 220.5 + 345.5 = 566\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: Add reaction (220.5 ft) and braking (345.5 ft) = 566 ft. 345 ft omits the reaction distance.

questions.question: A horizontal curve is designed for 60 mph with a maximum superelevation e = 0.08 and a side-friction factor f = 0.12. What is the minimum radius?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Minimum radius from the point-mass curve equation:

$$R_{min} = \frac{V^2}{15(e + f)} = \frac{60^2}{15(0.08 + 0.12)} = \frac{3600}{3.0} = 1{,}200\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: R = V²/[15(e+f)] = 1,200 ft. Using only f or only e in the denominator changes the result.

questions.subtopic: Traffic density from flow and speed
questions.question: A freeway lane carries a flow rate of 1,800 veh/h at an average speed of 45 mph. What is the traffic density?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Flow Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The fundamental relationship q = k·u gives:

$$k = \frac{q}{u} = \frac{1800}{45} = 40\ \text{veh/mi}$$
questions.explanation: Density k = q/u = 40 veh/mi. Multiplying q·u instead gives 81,000.

questions.subtopic: Space mean speed from flow and density
questions.question: On a highway segment the flow is 1,500 veh/h and the density is 25 veh/mi. What is the space mean speed?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Flow Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

From q = k·u:

$$u = \frac{q}{k} = \frac{1500}{25} = 60\ \text{mph}$$
questions.explanation: u = q/k = 60 mph. Multiplying gives 37,500.

questions.question: An approach carries 2,000 vehicles in the peak hour, with 600 vehicles in the busiest 15-minute period. What is the peak hour factor (PHF)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Level of Service (LOS) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The peak hour factor relates hourly volume to the peak 15-minute rate:

$$PHF = \frac{V}{4 \times V_{15}} = \frac{2000}{4(600)} = \frac{2000}{2400} = 0.833$$
questions.explanation: PHF = V / (4·V15) = 0.833. A PHF of 1.0 would mean perfectly uniform flow.

questions.question: For an approach with a speed of 45 mph, a perception-reaction time of 1.0 s, and a deceleration of 10 ft/s² (level grade), what is the yellow change interval?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Signal Timing section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Yellow change interval (ITE), on a level grade:

$$y = t + \frac{1.47 V}{2a + 64.4 g} = 1.0 + \frac{1.47(45)}{2(10)} = 1.0 + 3.31 = 4.3\ \text{s}$$
questions.explanation: Reaction (1.0 s) plus motion time (3.31 s) = 4.3 s. 3.3 s omits the reaction time.

questions.question: An intersection is 60 ft wide and the design vehicle is 20 ft long. For an approach speed of 30 mph, what is the all-red clearance interval?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Signal Timing section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

All-red time clears the intersection plus the vehicle length:

$$r = \frac{W + L}{1.47 V} = \frac{60 + 20}{1.47(30)} = \frac{80}{44.1} = 1.8\ \text{s}$$
questions.explanation: Include the vehicle length: (W+L)/(1.47V) = 1.8 s. Using only W gives 1.36 s.

questions.question: A signalized movement has a saturation flow rate of 1,800 veh/h, an effective green of 30 s, and a cycle length of 90 s. What is the movement capacity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Level of Service (LOS) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Capacity is the saturation flow scaled by the green ratio:

$$c = s\left(\frac{g}{C}\right) = 1800\left(\frac{30}{90}\right) = 600\ \text{veh/h}$$
questions.explanation: c = s·(g/C) = 600 veh/h. Using the full saturation flow (1,800) ignores the green ratio.

questions.question: The current AADT on a roadway is 12,000 veh/day. Assuming 3% annual compound growth, what is the AADT 10 years from now?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Forecasting section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Compound annual growth:

$$AADT_n = AADT_0 (1 + r)^n = 12{,}000(1.03)^{10} = 12{,}000(1.344) = 16{,}100\ \text{veh/day}$$
questions.explanation: Compound: 12,000(1.03)^10 ≈ 16,100. Simple 3%/yr growth (1.30×) would give 15,600.

questions.question: A proposed development has 250 dwelling units. Using an average trip generation rate of 9.57 daily trips per unit, what is the estimated daily trip generation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Trip Generation section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Trips equal the number of units times the average rate:

$$T = (\text{units})(\text{rate}) = 250 \times 9.57 = 2{,}393\ \text{trips/day}$$
questions.explanation: 250 × 9.57 = 2,393 trips/day. 239 misplaces the decimal.

questions.question: A highway has an AADT of 20,000 veh/day. The K-factor is 0.10 and the directional distribution D is 0.60. What is the directional design hourly volume (DDHV)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Forecasting section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The DDHV applies the hour and direction factors to the AADT:

$$DDHV = AADT \times K \times D = 20{,}000(0.10)(0.60) = 1{,}200\ \text{veh/h}$$
questions.explanation: DDHV = AADT·K·D = 1,200 veh/h. Omitting D (0.60) gives 2,000 veh/h (both directions).

questions.question: A design lane carries 500 equivalent axles per day, each with a load equivalency factor of 2.3. What is the daily ESAL on the design lane?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Pavement Design section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

ESAL is the number of axles times the load equivalency factor:

$$ESAL = (\text{axles})(LEF) = 500 \times 2.3 = 1{,}150\ \text{ESAL/day}$$
questions.explanation: ESAL = axles × LEF = 1,150. Dividing by the LEF (217) inverts the relationship.

questions.question: Two concurrent forces act at a point: 300 N along the +x axis and 400 N along the +y axis. What is the magnitude of the resultant?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Resultant (Two Dimensions) section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The resultant magnitude of perpendicular components:

$$R = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2} = \sqrt{300^2 + 400^2} = \sqrt{250{,}000} = 500\ \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: Use the Pythagorean sum, not the algebraic sum. Adding 300 + 400 = 700 ignores the perpendicular directions.

questions.question: A coplanar force system has resultant components Rx = 6 kN and Ry = 8 kN. What is the direction of the resultant, measured counterclockwise from the +x axis?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Resultant (Two Dimensions) section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The direction is the arctangent of the component ratio:

$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{R_y}{R_x}\right) = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{8}{6}\right) = 53.1^\circ$$
questions.explanation: θ = tan⁻¹(Ry/Rx) = 53.1°. 36.9° inverts the ratio (tan⁻¹(6/8)).

questions.question: A simply supported beam spans 10 m, carries a uniform load of 4 kN/m over its full length, and a 20 kN point load 3 m from the left support A. What is the reaction at A?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Take moments about B. The UDL resultant is 40 kN at midspan (5 m from each support), and the 20 kN point load is 3 m from A, hence 7 m from B:

$$\sum M_B = 0:\ R_A(10) = 40(5) + 20(7) = 200 + 140 = 340$$

$$R_A = \frac{340}{10} = 34\ \text{kN}$$
questions.explanation: Sum the total load (60 kN) correctly by moments: R_A = 34 kN, R_B = 26 kN. Swapping them gives 26 kN.

questions.question: A beam has a pin at A (x = 0) and a roller at B (x = 4 m), with a 1 m overhang to a free end carrying a 12 kN point load at x = 5 m. What is the reaction at B?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Take moments about A (the load is 5 m from A):

$$\sum M_A = 0:\ R_B(4) = 12(5) = 60 \Rightarrow R_B = 15\ \text{kN}$$

Then R_A = 12 − 15 = −3 kN (downward).
questions.explanation: R_B = 12(5)/4 = 15 kN. The overhang makes R_A act downward (−3 kN).

questions.question: At a truss joint, a horizontal member and a diagonal member inclined 45° above horizontal meet, and a 10 kN load hangs vertically from the joint. What is the force in the diagonal member?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Plane Truss: Method of Joints section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Vertical equilibrium — only the diagonal resists the vertical load:

$$F_d \sin 45^\circ = 10 \Rightarrow F_d = \frac{10}{0.7071} = 14.14\ \text{kN}$$
questions.explanation: F_d = 10/sin45° = 14.14 kN. Using the horizontal component (cos45°) also gives 14.14; the vertical balance is what sets it.

questions.question: A 500 N block rests on a 25° incline with a static friction coefficient of 0.35. What force, applied parallel to the incline, is needed to keep the block from sliding down?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Friction section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The block tends to slide down (tan25° = 0.47 > μ = 0.35). Friction acts up the incline at its maximum; the applied force makes up the difference:

$$F = W(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta) = 500(\sin 25^\circ - 0.35\cos 25^\circ)$$

$$= 500(0.4226 - 0.3172) = 52.7\ \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: F = W(sinθ − μcosθ) = 52.7 N. Since tanθ > μ, the block is not self-retaining, so F ≠ 0.

questions.question: A block is on the verge of sliding when an incline is tilted to 30°. What is the coefficient of static friction?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Friction section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

At impending motion on an incline, the friction coefficient equals the tangent of the angle:

$$\mu_s = \tan\theta = \tan 30^\circ = 0.577$$
questions.explanation: μ = tanθ at the angle of repose. 0.500 and 0.866 are sin30° and cos30°.

questions.question: A T-section has a 120 mm × 20 mm flange on top of a 20 mm × 80 mm web (overall height 100 mm). How far is the centroid above the bottom of the web?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Centroids of Masses, Areas, Lengths, and Volumes section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Use the area-weighted average of the part centroids:

$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 120(20) = 2400\ \text{mm}^2,\ \bar{y}_1 = 90\ \text{mm} \\ A_2 &= 20(80) = 1600\ \text{mm}^2,\ \bar{y}_2 = 40\ \text{mm} \end{aligned}$$

$$\bar{y} = \frac{2400(90) + 1600(40)}{2400 + 1600} = \frac{280{,}000}{4000} = 70\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: Area-weighted: ȳ = 70 mm from the bottom. 50 mm would be the mid-height (ignoring the area weighting).

questions.question: What is the moment of inertia of a 100 mm wide by 200 mm deep rectangular section about its horizontal centroidal axis?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Moment of Inertia section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

For a rectangle about its centroidal axis:

$$I = \frac{b h^3}{12} = \frac{100(200)^3}{12} = \frac{8\times10^8}{12} = 6.67\times10^7\ \text{mm}^4$$
questions.explanation: I = bh³/12. Using bh³/6 doubles it; swapping b and h changes the result.

questions.question: A 50 mm × 100 mm rectangle (I about its own centroid = 4.17×10⁶ mm⁴) is located with its centroid 100 mm from a reference axis. What is its moment of inertia about that axis?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Moment of Inertia section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Parallel-axis theorem (A = 50×100 = 5000 mm²):

$$I = \bar{I} + A d^2 = 4.17\times10^6 + 5000(100)^2 = 4.17\times10^6 + 5.0\times10^7 = 5.42\times10^7\ \text{mm}^4$$
questions.explanation: Add A·d² to the centroidal I. Omitting the centroidal term gives 5.0×10⁷.

questions.question: A triangular distributed load varies linearly from 0 to 6 kN/m over a 4 m length. What is the magnitude of the equivalent resultant force?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Systems of Forces section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The resultant equals the area under the load diagram (a triangle):

$$R = \tfrac{1}{2}(w_{max})(L) = \tfrac{1}{2}(6)(4) = 12\ \text{kN}$$
questions.explanation: Triangular load resultant = ½·w·L = 12 kN. Using w·L (24 kN) treats it as uniform.

questions.subtopic: Moment of a force about a point
questions.question: A force F = (40, 30) N is applied at a point located at r = (2, 0) m from point O. What is the moment of the force about O?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Systems of Forces section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

In 2D the moment is the scalar cross product:

$$M_O = r_x F_y - r_y F_x = (2)(30) - (0)(40) = 60\ \text{N·m}\ (\text{CCW})$$
questions.explanation: M = r_x F_y − r_y F_x = 60 N·m. 80 N·m would use the wrong component (r_x·F_x).

questions.question: A 1000 N weight hangs from a point supported by two cables: one at 30° and one at 60° above the horizontal, on opposite sides. What is the tension in the 30° cable?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Resolve horizontally and vertically (T₁ at 30°, T₂ at 60°):

$$\sum F_x = 0:\ T_1\cos30^\circ = T_2\cos60^\circ \Rightarrow T_2 = 1.732\,T_1$$

$$\sum F_y = 0:\ T_1\sin30^\circ + T_2\sin60^\circ = 1000$$

$$0.5\,T_1 + 1.5\,T_1 = 1000 \Rightarrow T_1 = 500\ \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: Solving the two equilibrium equations gives T₁ = 500 N; the steeper 60° cable carries more (866 N).

questions.question: A round bar 25 mm in diameter carries an axial tensile load of 50 kN. What is the axial stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Stress is load over cross-sectional area:

$$A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4} = \frac{\pi(25)^2}{4} = 490.9\ \text{mm}^2$$

$$\sigma = \frac{P}{A} = \frac{50{,}000}{490.9} = 101.9\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: σ = P/A with A = πd²/4. Using πd²/2 would halve the stress.

questions.question: A 20 mm diameter bolt in double shear carries a load of 40 kN. What is the average shear stress in the bolt?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

In double shear the load is carried across two cross-sections:

$$A = 2\left(\frac{\pi d^2}{4}\right) = 2(314.2) = 628.3\ \text{mm}^2$$

$$\tau = \frac{P}{A} = \frac{40{,}000}{628.3} = 63.7\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: Double shear uses two areas. Single shear (one area) would give 127.3 MPa.

questions.question: A rectangular beam 100 mm wide by 200 mm deep carries a bending moment of 20 kN·m. What is the maximum bending stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stresses in Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Flexure formula with c = 100 mm and I = bh³/12 = 6.67×10⁷ mm⁴:

$$\sigma = \frac{M c}{I} = \frac{(20\times10^6)(100)}{6.67\times10^7} = 30\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: σ = Mc/I. Using the section modulus consistently gives 30 MPa; halving c (using 50 mm) gives 15 MPa.

questions.question: A solid circular shaft 50 mm in diameter transmits a torque of 2 kN·m. What is the maximum torsional shear stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Torsion section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

With c = 25 mm and J = πd⁴/32 = 6.14×10⁵ mm⁴:

$$\tau = \frac{T c}{J} = \frac{(2\times10^6)(25)}{6.14\times10^5} = 81.5\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: τ = Tc/J. Using the polar modulus for a hollow shaft or halving c changes the result.

questions.question: A steel bar is fully restrained between two rigid walls and heated 40°C. With E = 200 GPa and α = 12×10⁻⁶/°C, what is the thermal stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Thermal Deformations section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

A fully restrained bar develops a stress that would otherwise be free thermal strain:

$$\sigma = E\alpha\,\Delta T = (200\times10^3)(12\times10^{-6})(40) = 96\ \text{MPa (compressive)}$$
questions.explanation: σ = EαΔT for full restraint. The stress is independent of the bar length.

questions.question: A thin-walled cylindrical pressure vessel has an internal pressure of 2 MPa, an inner radius of 500 mm, and a wall thickness of 10 mm. What is the hoop (circumferential) stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Cylindrical Pressure Vessel section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Hoop stress in a thin-walled cylinder:

$$\sigma_h = \frac{p r}{t} = \frac{(2)(500)}{10} = 100\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: σ_hoop = pr/t = 100 MPa. The longitudinal stress pr/2t = 50 MPa is half as large.

questions.question: A steel rod (A = 600 mm², E = 200 GPa) is 2 m long and carries a 30 kN axial load. What is its elongation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Axial deformation:

$$\delta = \frac{P L}{A E} = \frac{(30{,}000)(2000)}{(600)(200\times10^3)} = 0.50\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: δ = PL/AE = 0.50 mm. Doubling comes from dropping a factor; be careful with unit consistency (N, mm, MPa).

questions.question: A solid shaft 40 mm in diameter and 1.2 m long transmits a torque of 1.5 kN·m. With G = 80 GPa, what is the angle of twist?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Torsion section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Angle of twist (J = πd⁴/32 = 2.51×10⁵ mm⁴):

$$\phi = \frac{T L}{J G} = \frac{(1.5\times10^6)(1200)}{(2.51\times10^5)(80\times10^3)} = 0.0895\ \text{rad}$$

$$\phi = 0.0895 \times \frac{180}{\pi} = 5.13^\circ$$
questions.explanation: Compute φ in radians then convert: 0.0895 rad = 5.13°. Reporting the radian value as degrees gives 0.0895°.

questions.question: At a point, the plane-stress state is σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa, and τxy = 30 MPa. What is the maximum principal stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Principal Stresses section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Principal stresses from the transformation equations:

$$\sigma_{1,2} = \frac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2 + \tau_{xy}^2}$$

$$= 50 \pm \sqrt{30^2 + 30^2} = 50 \pm 42.4$$

$$\sigma_1 = 92.4\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: σ₁ = 50 + 42.4 = 92.4 MPa. 50 MPa is the average (center of Mohr's circle); 42.4 MPa is the radius.

questions.question: At a point, σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa, and τxy = 30 MPa. What is the maximum in-plane shear stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Principal Stresses section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The maximum in-plane shear stress is the radius of Mohr's circle:

$$\tau_{max} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2 + \tau_{xy}^2} = \sqrt{30^2 + 30^2} = 42.4\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: τ_max is the Mohr's-circle radius = 42.4 MPa. It equals (σ₁ − σ₂)/2.

questions.question: A simply supported beam 8 m long carries a uniform load of 5 kN/m. What is the maximum bending moment?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

For a simply supported beam under a full-span uniform load:

$$M_{max} = \frac{w L^2}{8} = \frac{5(8)^2}{8} = 40\ \text{kN·m}$$
