questions.explanation: M_max = wL²/8 at midspan = 40 kN·m. wL²/16 (20) and wL²/4 (80) are wrong coefficients.

questions.question: A bar in uniaxial tension has an axial strain of 0.002. If Poisson's ratio is 0.30, what is the lateral (transverse) strain?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Lateral strain is opposite in sign to the axial strain:

$$\varepsilon_{lat} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{axial} = -(0.30)(0.002) = -0.0006$$
questions.explanation: ε_lat = −ν·ε_axial = −0.0006. The negative sign reflects contraction perpendicular to the load.

questions.question: A material has a modulus of elasticity E = 200 GPa and a Poisson's ratio of 0.25. What is its shear modulus G?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

For an isotropic material:

$$G = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)} = \frac{200}{2(1.25)} = 80\ \text{GPa}$$
questions.explanation: G = E/[2(1+ν)] = 80 GPa. Using ν = 0 gives 100 GPa.

questions.question: A 800 N weight hangs from a single movable (frictionless) pulley supported by two parallel rope segments. What is the tension in the rope?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Two rope segments share the load equally on a frictionless movable pulley:

$$2T = W \Rightarrow T = \frac{800}{2} = 400\ \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: Two supporting segments halve the load: T = W/2 = 400 N.

questions.question: A lever is pinned at a fulcrum. A 200 N load acts 0.5 m from the fulcrum on one side. What force applied 1.5 m from the fulcrum on the other side will balance it?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Moment balance about the fulcrum:

$$F(1.5) = 200(0.5) \Rightarrow F = \frac{100}{1.5} = 66.7\ \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: Balance moments: F = 200(0.5)/1.5 = 66.7 N.

questions.question: A cantilever 4 m long carries a triangular distributed load that is zero at the fixed end and increases to 9 kN/m at the free end. What is the reaction moment at the fixed support?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Resultant R = ½(9)(4) = 18 kN acts at 2/3 of the span from the zero (fixed) end, x = 2.667 m:

$$M = R \cdot x = 18(2.667) = 48\ \text{kN·m}$$
questions.explanation: Triangular resultant 18 kN acts at 2L/3 from the small end: M = 48 kN·m.

questions.question: At an unloaded truss joint, two collinear members and one non-collinear member meet, with no external load or support reaction applied. Which member carries zero force?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Plane Truss: Method of Joints section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

At a joint with two collinear members and one other, with no external load, equilibrium perpendicular to the collinear pair requires the non-collinear member to carry zero force; the two collinear members carry equal force.
questions.explanation: The lone non-collinear member is the zero-force member; the collinear pair transmits equal force.

questions.question: A rope is wrapped 180° (half a turn) around a fixed drum with a friction coefficient of 0.30. A 100 N tension is held on the slack side. What is the maximum tension on the tight side before slipping?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Friction section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Capstan (belt friction) equation with β = π radians:

$$T_2 = T_1 e^{\mu\beta} = 100\,e^{0.30\pi} = 100(2.566) = 257\ \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: T2 = T1·e^(μβ) = 257 N. Forgetting to apply e^(μβ) leaves 100 N.

questions.question: A 500 N block (base width 0.4 m, μ = 0.5) is pushed by a horizontal force applied at a height of 0.6 m. At what force, and in what mode, does motion begin?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Friction section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Slipping needs P = μW = 0.5(500) = 250 N. Tipping about the front edge needs:

$$P\,h = W\tfrac{b}{2} \Rightarrow P = \frac{500(0.2)}{0.6} = 167\ \text{N}$$

Since 167 N < 250 N, the block tips first.
questions.explanation: Tipping (167 N) occurs before slipping (250 N), so the block tips.

questions.question: Three equal 50 N forces act at a single point, directed at 0°, 120°, and 240°. What is the magnitude of the resultant?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Resultant (Two Dimensions) section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Three equal forces spaced 120° apart are symmetric; their vector sum cancels:

$$\sum F_x = 50(\cos0 + \cos120 + \cos240) = 0,\quad \sum F_y = 0$$

$$R = 0\ \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: Equal forces at 120° spacing sum to zero by symmetry.

questions.question: Two equal and opposite parallel forces of 100 N are separated by a perpendicular distance of 0.3 m. What is the moment of the couple?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Systems of Forces section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

A couple's moment is force times separation, independent of reference point:

$$M = F d = 100(0.3) = 30\ \text{N·m}$$
questions.explanation: Couple M = F·d = 30 N·m, the same about any point.

questions.question: A 200 N force acts at a point 0.5 m from point O. When this force is moved to act at O, what couple moment must be added to keep the system equivalent?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Systems of Forces section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Moving a force to a new point requires adding a couple equal to the moment of the original force about that point:

$$M = F d = 200(0.5) = 100\ \text{N·m}$$
questions.explanation: The added couple equals the force's moment about O: 100 N·m.

questions.question: A semicircular area has a radius of 60 mm. How far is its centroid from the flat (diameter) edge?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Centroids of Masses, Areas, Lengths, and Volumes section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Centroid of a semicircle from the flat edge:

$$\bar{y} = \frac{4R}{3\pi} = \frac{4(60)}{3\pi} = 25.5\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: ȳ = 4R/3π = 25.5 mm. 4R/3 (without π) gives 80 mm.

questions.question: A rectangular area is 60 mm wide and 120 mm deep. What is its radius of gyration about the horizontal centroidal axis?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Moment of Inertia section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Radius of gyration r = √(I/A), with I = bh³/12 and A = bh:

$$r = \sqrt{\frac{bh^3/12}{bh}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{12}} = \frac{120}{3.464} = 34.6\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: For a rectangle, r = h/√12 = 34.6 mm about the centroidal axis.

questions.question: What is the polar moment of inertia of a solid circular cross-section 40 mm in diameter?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Moment of Inertia section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Polar moment of inertia of a solid circle:

$$J = \frac{\pi d^4}{32} = \frac{\pi(40)^4}{32} = 2.51\times10^5\ \text{mm}^4$$
questions.explanation: J = πd⁴/32 = 2.51×10⁵ mm⁴. πd⁴/64 (1.26×10⁵) is the rectangular-axis I.

questions.subtopic: Bar supported by an inclined cable
questions.question: A horizontal bar is pinned to a wall at A and is 2 m long. A cable at the free end B runs up to the wall at 30° above horizontal, and a 400 N load hangs at B. What is the tension in the cable?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Take moments about the pin A (only the cable's vertical component and the load create moments):

$$\sum M_A = 0:\ (T\sin30^\circ)(2) = 400(2)$$

$$T\sin30^\circ = 400 \Rightarrow T = \frac{400}{0.5} = 800\ \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: Moment balance about A: T·sin30°·L = W·L, so T = 800 N.

questions.question: A 600 N crate rests on a level floor with a static friction coefficient of 0.40. What horizontal force is required to start it sliding?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Friction section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Maximum static friction on a level surface:

$$F = \mu_s N = \mu_s W = 0.40(600) = 240\ \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: F = μW = 240 N on a level surface (N = W).

questions.question: A simply supported beam 6 m long has a concentrated moment of 60 kN·m applied at midspan (no other loads). What is the magnitude of each support reaction?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

An applied moment is resisted by a reaction couple over the span:

$$R = \frac{M_0}{L} = \frac{60}{6} = 10\ \text{kN}$$

The reactions are equal and opposite (one up, one down).
questions.explanation: Reactions form a couple: R = M0/L = 10 kN, up at one support and down at the other.

questions.subtopic: Transverse shear stress in a beam
questions.question: A rectangular beam 100 mm wide by 200 mm deep carries a transverse shear force of 50 kN. What is the maximum transverse shear stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stresses in Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Maximum transverse shear stress in a rectangle is 1.5 times the average:

$$\tau_{max} = \frac{3V}{2A} = \frac{3(50{,}000)}{2(100\times200)} = 3.75\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: τ_max = 1.5·V/A for a rectangle = 3.75 MPa. The average V/A is 2.5 MPa.

questions.question: A 20 mm diameter bolt passes through a 10 mm thick plate and transmits 80 kN. What is the bearing stress between the bolt and the plate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Bearing stress uses the projected contact area (diameter × thickness):

$$\sigma_b = \frac{P}{d\,t} = \frac{80{,}000}{20(10)} = 400\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: Bearing uses projected area d·t = 200 mm²: σ = 400 MPa. Using πd²/4 (circular) gives 255 MPa.

questions.question: An unrestrained aluminum bar 3 m long is heated 50°C. With α = 23×10⁻⁶/°C, what is its elongation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Thermal Deformations section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Free thermal elongation:

$$\delta = \alpha\,\Delta T\,L = (23\times10^{-6})(50)(3000) = 3.45\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: δ = αΔT·L = 3.45 mm. No stress develops because the bar is unrestrained.

questions.question: A bar carries a constant 20 kN axial load through two 1 m segments in series: segment 1 has A = 400 mm² and segment 2 has A = 200 mm² (E = 200 GPa for both). What is the total elongation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Sum the elongation of each segment:

$$\delta = \frac{PL_1}{A_1E} + \frac{PL_2}{A_2E} = \frac{20{,}000(1000)}{400(200{,}000)} + \frac{20{,}000(1000)}{200(200{,}000)}$$

$$= 0.25 + 0.50 = 0.75\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: Add segment elongations (0.25 + 0.50): 0.75 mm. The thinner segment deforms more.

questions.question: A hollow shaft (outer diameter 60 mm, inner diameter 40 mm) transmits a torque of 3 kN·m. What is the maximum torsional shear stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Torsion section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

With J = π(d_o⁴ − d_i⁴)/32 = 1.02×10⁶ mm⁴ and c = 30 mm:

$$\tau = \frac{T c}{J} = \frac{(3\times10^6)(30)}{1.02\times10^6} = 88.1\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: Use the hollow J = π(d_o⁴−d_i⁴)/32. Treating it as solid understates the stress.

questions.subtopic: Normal stress on an inclined plane
questions.question: A bar is under uniaxial stress σx = 100 MPa (σy = 0, τxy = 0). What is the normal stress on a plane whose normal is oriented 30° from the x-axis?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Principal Stresses section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Transformation of a uniaxial stress onto an inclined plane:

$$\sigma_n = \sigma_x\cos^2\theta = 100\cos^2 30^\circ = 100(0.75) = 75\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: σ_n = σx·cos²θ = 75 MPa. Using sin²θ gives 25 MPa.

questions.question: A rectangular beam 100 mm wide by 200 mm deep carries a bending moment of 30 kN·m. Using the section modulus, what is the maximum bending stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stresses in Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Section modulus S = bh²/6 = 100(200)²/6 = 6.67×10⁵ mm³:

$$\sigma = \frac{M}{S} = \frac{30\times10^6}{6.67\times10^5} = 45\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: σ = M/S with S = bh²/6 = 45 MPa.

questions.question: A thin-walled cylindrical pressure vessel has an internal pressure of 4 MPa, an inner radius of 400 mm, and a wall thickness of 8 mm. What is the longitudinal (axial) stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Cylindrical Pressure Vessel section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Longitudinal stress is half the hoop stress:

$$\sigma_{long} = \frac{p r}{2t} = \frac{4(400)}{2(8)} = 100\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: σ_long = pr/2t = 100 MPa; the hoop stress pr/t = 200 MPa is twice as large.

questions.question: A thin-walled spherical pressure vessel has an internal pressure of 5 MPa, an inner radius of 300 mm, and a wall thickness of 6 mm. What is the wall stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Cylindrical Pressure Vessel section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Membrane stress in a thin-walled sphere (equal in all directions):

$$\sigma = \frac{p r}{2t} = \frac{5(300)}{2(6)} = 125\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: Sphere wall stress = pr/2t = 125 MPa, identical in every direction.

questions.question: A steel bar carries an axial stress of 150 MPa. With E = 200 GPa, what is the axial strain?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Hooke's law in one dimension:

$$\varepsilon = \frac{\sigma}{E} = \frac{150}{200{,}000} = 7.5\times10^{-4}$$
questions.explanation: ε = σ/E = 7.5×10⁻⁴ (stress and E in the same units, MPa).

questions.question: A simply supported beam carries a 40 kN point load at midspan. What is the maximum shear force in the beam?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

For a central point load, each reaction is P/2 and the shear is constant up to the load:

$$V_{max} = \frac{P}{2} = \frac{40}{2} = 20\ \text{kN}$$
questions.explanation: Each reaction (and the shear) is P/2 = 20 kN for a midspan load.

questions.question: At a point, the principal stresses are σ₁ = 100 MPa and σ₂ = 50 MPa (plane stress, σ₃ = 0). What is the von Mises effective stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Principal Stresses section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Von Mises stress for plane stress:

$$\sigma_v = \sqrt{\sigma_1^2 - \sigma_1\sigma_2 + \sigma_2^2} = \sqrt{100^2 - (100)(50) + 50^2} = \sqrt{7500} = 86.6\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: σ_v = √(σ₁² − σ₁σ₂ + σ₂²) = 86.6 MPa, not the simple sum or difference.

questions.question: An activity has an early start (ES) of day 4 and a duration of 6 days. What is its early finish (EF)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The early finish is the early start plus the duration:

$$EF = ES + \text{Duration} = 4 + 6 = 10$$
questions.explanation: EF = ES + duration = 10.

questions.question: An activity has a late finish (LF) of day 20 and a duration of 4 days. What is its late start (LS)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The late start is the late finish minus the duration:

$$LS = LF - \text{Duration} = 20 - 4 = 16$$
questions.explanation: LS = LF − duration = 16.

questions.question: An activity has ES = 5, duration = 3, and LF = 12. What is its total float?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Compute EF, then total float:

$$EF = 5 + 3 = 8,\quad TF = LF - EF = 12 - 8 = 4\ \text{days}$$
questions.explanation: TF = LF − EF = 4 days.

questions.question: An activity has an early finish of day 8. Its earliest successor has an early start of day 11. What is the free float?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Free float is the successor's early start minus this activity's early finish:

$$FF = ES_{succ} - EF = 11 - 8 = 3\ \text{days}$$
questions.explanation: FF = 11 − 8 = 3 days.

questions.question: In the network shown, activity A (3 days) precedes both B (5 days) and C (6 days), and both B and C precede D (4 days). What is the critical path duration?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Compare the two paths A-B-D and A-C-D:

$$A\text{-}B\text{-}D = 3+5+4 = 12,\quad A\text{-}C\text{-}D = 3+6+4 = 13$$

The critical path is the longest: 13 days.
questions.explanation: A-C-D (13 days) is the longest path, so it is critical.

questions.question: A project has PV = $50,000, EV = $45,000, and AC = $48,000. What is the schedule variance (SV)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earned-Value Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Schedule variance compares work performed with work planned:

$$SV = EV - PV = 45{,}000 - 50{,}000 = -\$5{,}000$$
questions.explanation: SV = EV − PV = −$5,000 (behind schedule).

questions.question: A project has EV = $45,000 and PV = $50,000. What is the schedule performance index (SPI)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earned-Value Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$SPI = \frac{EV}{PV} = \frac{45{,}000}{50{,}000} = 0.90$$

SPI < 1 indicates the project is behind schedule.
questions.explanation: SPI = EV/PV = 0.90.

questions.question: A project has a budget at completion (BAC) of $400,000 and an estimate at completion (EAC) of $450,000. What is the variance at completion (VAC)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earned-Value Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$VAC = BAC - EAC = 400{,}000 - 450{,}000 = -\$50{,}000$$

A negative VAC means a projected overrun.
questions.explanation: VAC = BAC − EAC = −$50,000.

questions.question: A project has an estimate at completion (EAC) of $450,000 and actual cost to date (AC) of $200,000. What is the estimate to complete (ETC)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earned-Value Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$ETC = EAC - AC = 450{,}000 - 200{,}000 = \$250{,}000$$
questions.explanation: ETC = EAC − AC = $250,000 (remaining cost).

questions.question: An activity can be shortened from a normal duration of 12 days ($20,000) to a crash duration of 8 days ($32,000). What is the crash cost slope?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$\text{Slope} = \frac{32{,}000 - 20{,}000}{12 - 8} = \frac{12{,}000}{4} = \$3{,}000/\text{day}$$
questions.explanation: Cost slope = Δcost/Δtime = $3,000/day.

questions.question: To shorten a project's duration at least additional cost, which activity should be crashed first?
choices: The activity with the longest duration
The critical-path activity with the lowest cost slope
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Crashing only helps if it shortens the critical path, and the cheapest time savings come from the critical activity with the smallest cost slope (lowest added cost per day saved).
questions.explanation: Crash the critical activity with the lowest cost slope first.

questions.question: A scraper hauls 20 LCY per cycle with a cycle time of 5 minutes, operating 50 minutes per hour. What is its hourly production?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Cycles per effective hour × load:

$$\text{Cycles/hr} = \frac{50}{5} = 10,\quad Q = 10(20) = 200\ \text{LCY/hr}$$
questions.explanation: Use the 50-min hour: 10 cycles × 20 LCY = 200 LCY/hr.

questions.question: An excavator has a 1.5 LCY bucket, a 20-second cycle time, and operates 50 minutes per hour. What is its hourly production?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$\text{Cycles/hr} = \frac{50(60)}{20} = 150,\quad Q = 150(1.5) = 225\ \text{LCY/hr}$$
questions.explanation: 150 cycles/hr × 1.5 LCY = 225 LCY/hr.

questions.question: A roller 2 m wide travels at 4 km/h, needs 4 passes, and works at 75% efficiency. What compacted area does it cover per hour?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$A = \frac{W \cdot S \cdot 1000 \cdot E}{\text{passes}} = \frac{2(4)(1000)(0.75)}{4} = 1{,}500\ \text{m}^2/\text{hr}$$
questions.explanation: Divide the swept area by the number of passes: 1,500 m²/hr.

questions.question: A crew places 2 CY of concrete every 10 minutes. What is the placement rate per hour?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$\text{Rate} = 2\ \text{CY} \times \frac{60}{10} = 12\ \text{CY/hr}$$
questions.explanation: 2 CY every 10 min = 12 CY/hr.

questions.question: A contractor had 3 OSHA-recordable injuries over 150,000 employee-hours. What is the recordable incidence rate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Incidence Variable Values section in the Safety chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$IR = \frac{(\text{cases})(200{,}000)}{\text{hours}} = \frac{3(200{,}000)}{150{,}000} = 4.0$$
questions.explanation: IR normalizes to 200,000 hours (100 workers): 4.0.

questions.question: Per OSHA, at what height above a lower level is fall protection required for workers on a scaffold?
questions.solution:
Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451, fall protection is required for workers on scaffolds more than 10 feet above a lower level.

Under OSHA 1926.451, scaffold fall protection is required above 10 ft (distinct from the 6-ft general construction trigger).
questions.explanation: Scaffolds: 10 ft (1926.451). General construction is 6 ft.

questions.question: An activity requires 0.5 worker-hours per unit for 200 units, at a labor rate of $40 per worker-hour. What is the labor cost?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$\text{Cost} = (0.5)(200)(40) = \$4{,}000$$

questions.question: A haul truck has a total cycle time of 30 minutes and is loaded in 6 minutes. How many trucks keep the loader working continuously?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$N = \frac{\text{cycle time}}{\text{load time}} = \frac{30}{6} = 5\ \text{trucks}$$
questions.explanation: N = cycle/load = 5 trucks.

questions.question: Under a CM-at-risk contract with a guaranteed maximum price (GMP), who absorbs costs that exceed the GMP?
questions.solution:
Under a construction-manager-at-risk arrangement, the CM commits to a guaranteed maximum price (GMP); costs above the GMP are the CM's responsibility, and savings below it are often shared with the owner.

The CM guarantees the maximum price, so overruns above the GMP are borne by the CM, not the owner.
questions.explanation: Costs above the GMP are the CM's risk.

questions.question: A lump-sum contract is most appropriate for which type of project?
choices: Work with a well-defined scope and firm quantities
questions.solution:
A lump-sum (stipulated-sum) contract is best suited to work with a well-defined scope and firm quantities, letting the contractor price the entire job for a single fixed amount.

Lump-sum pricing requires a well-defined scope so the contractor can price the whole job accurately.
questions.explanation: Lump-sum fits well-defined scope; uncertain scope suits unit-price or cost-plus.

questions.question: What does a performance bond primarily guarantee to the owner?
choices: Completion of the work per the contract
questions.solution:
A performance bond is a surety instrument that guarantees the contractor will complete the project in accordance with the contract terms; if the contractor defaults, the surety ensures completion.

A performance bond guarantees contract completion; a payment bond is what protects subcontractors and suppliers.
questions.explanation: Performance bond = completion guarantee; payment bond = payment to subs/suppliers.

questions.question: Detailed fabrication drawings a contractor submits for the engineer's review before fabrication are called:
questions.solution:
Shop drawings are contractor-prepared submittals (detailed fabrication/installation drawings) that the design professional reviews for conformance with the design intent before fabrication proceeds.

Shop drawings are reviewed before fabrication; as-builts/record drawings document final conditions.
questions.explanation: Shop drawings are submitted for review prior to fabrication.

questions.question: A footing requires 200 linear feet of reinforcing bar weighing 1.50 lb/ft. What is the total weight of steel?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$W = (\text{length})(\text{unit weight}) = 200(1.50) = 300\ \text{lb}$$

questions.question: A concrete wall is 20 ft long and 8 ft tall, formed on both faces. What is the formwork contact area?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$A = 2(\text{length})(\text{height}) = 2(20)(8) = 320\ \text{SF}$$
questions.explanation: Both faces: 2 × 20 × 8 = 320 SF.

questions.question: A soil has a swell of 25%. If 1,000 bank cubic yards (BCY) are excavated, how many loose cubic yards (LCY) result?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$LCY = BCY(1 + \text{swell}) = 1000(1.25) = 1{,}250\ \text{LCY}$$
questions.explanation: Swell increases volume: 1,000 × 1.25 = 1,250 LCY.

questions.question: A concrete item is 500 CY at a unit cost of $120/CY. With a 15% markup, what is the bid price for the item?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$\text{Direct} = 500(120) = \$60{,}000,\quad \text{Bid} = 60{,}000(1.15) = \$69{,}000$$
questions.explanation: Apply the 15% markup to the $60,000 direct cost: $69,000.

questions.question: On a plan at a scale of 1 in = 30 ft, a distance measures 4.5 in. What is the actual length?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$L = 4.5\ \text{in} \times 30\ \text{ft/in} = 135\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: Multiply by the scale factor: 135 ft.

questions.question: What is the distance between station 5+00 and station 18+50?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$\Delta = 1850 - 500 = 1{,}350\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: Each station = 100 ft; 1850 − 500 = 1,350 ft.

questions.question: At a station, the existing ground elevation is 102.5 ft and the proposed grade is 99.0 ft. What is the cut depth?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$\text{Cut} = \text{existing} - \text{proposed} = 102.5 - 99.0 = 3.5\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: Existing higher than proposed means 3.5 ft of cut.

questions.question: A pipe invert falls 2.0 ft over a horizontal run of 400 ft. What is the grade?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$S = \frac{\Delta \text{elev}}{\text{run}} = \frac{2.0}{400} = 0.005 = 0.50\%$$
questions.explanation: Grade = rise/run = 0.50%.

questions.question: A bolted lap splice uses three bolts in single shear. Each bolt has a nominal shear strength Fnv = 54 ksi and area Ab = 0.44 in². What is the LRFD design shear strength of the connection?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

LRFD bolt shear (φ = 0.75), three bolts in single shear:

$$\phi R_n = \phi F_{nv} A_b \times n = 0.75(54)(0.44)(3) = 53.5\ \text{kip}$$
questions.explanation: Single shear × 3 bolts = 53.5 kip. Double shear would double it to 107 kip.

questions.question: A square tied column is 16 in × 16 in (Ag = 256 in²) with four bars totaling Ast = 4.0 in², f'c = 4 ksi, and fy = 60 ksi. What is the LRFD design axial strength φPn?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components (ACI 318-14) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

For a tied column, φ = 0.65 and the 0.80 maximum-axial factor applies:

$$P_n = 0.85 f'_c (A_g - A_{st}) + f_y A_{st} = 0.85(4)(252) + 60(4) = 1096.8\ \text{kip}$$

$$\phi P_n = 0.65(0.80)(1096.8) = 570\ \text{kip}$$
questions.explanation: Apply both 0.80 and φ = 0.65 to the nominal squash load. Omitting them overstates capacity.

questions.question: A simply supported beam spans 10 m and carries a 20 kN load 3 m from A and a 30 kN load 7 m from A. What is the reaction at A?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Sum moments about B:

$$R_A(10) = 20(7) + 30(3) = 140 + 90 = 230 \Rightarrow R_A = 23\ \text{kN}$$
questions.explanation: R_A = 23 kN, R_B = 27 kN (the heavier load is nearer B).

questions.question: A 3/4 in bolt bears on a 1/2 in thick plate with Fu = 58 ksi (deformation a consideration, factor 2.4). What is the LRFD design bearing strength at the bolt hole?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

LRFD bearing (φ = 0.75):

$$\phi R_n = 0.75(2.4\, d\, t\, F_u) = 0.75(2.4)(0.75)(0.5)(58) = 39.2\ \text{kip}$$
questions.explanation: φ·2.4·d·t·Fu = 39.2 kip. 52.2 kip omits φ.

questions.question: A steel tension member has an effective net area Ae = 4.0 in² and Fu = 65 ksi. What is the LRFD design strength for the rupture limit state?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Rupture uses φ = 0.75 on the effective net area:

$$\phi P_n = 0.75 F_u A_e = 0.75(65)(4.0) = 195\ \text{kip}$$
questions.explanation: φ = 0.75 for rupture: 195 kip. 260 kip drops φ.

questions.question: A 1/4 in fillet weld, 10 in long, uses E70 electrodes (FEXX = 70 ksi). What is the LRFD design strength of the weld?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Weld strength on the effective throat (0.707w), φ = 0.75:

$$\phi R_n = 0.75(0.6 F_{EXX})(0.707 w)(L) = 0.75(42)(0.1768)(10) = 55.7\ \text{kip}$$
questions.explanation: Use the 0.707w throat and φ = 0.75: 55.7 kip. 74.2 kip omits φ.

questions.question: A compact, fully braced steel beam has Zx = 54 in³ and Fy = 50 ksi. Using ASD (Ω = 1.67), what is the allowable flexural strength?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

ASD allowable moment:

$$M_n = F_y Z_x = 50(54) = 2700\ \text{kip·in};\quad \frac{M_n}{\Omega} = \frac{2700}{1.67} = 1617\ \text{kip·in} = 135\ \text{kip·ft}$$
questions.explanation: Divide Mp by Ω = 1.67, then convert: 135 kip·ft. 225 kip·ft is the nominal Mp.

questions.question: For a steel column with Fy = 36 ksi and E = 29,000 ksi, what is the slenderness limit 4.71√(E/Fy) that separates inelastic from elastic buckling?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$4.71\sqrt{\frac{E}{F_y}} = 4.71\sqrt{\frac{29{,}000}{36}} = 4.71(28.38) = 133.7$$
questions.explanation: For Fy = 36 ksi the limit is 133.7 (it is 113.4 for Fy = 50 ksi).

questions.question: What is the shape factor (ratio of plastic to elastic section modulus, Z/S) for a solid rectangular cross-section?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

For a rectangle, Z = bh²/4 and S = bh²/6:

$$\text{shape factor} = \frac{Z}{S} = \frac{bh^2/4}{bh^2/6} = 1.5$$
questions.explanation: Rectangle shape factor = 1.5; a typical wide-flange is about 1.1–1.12.

questions.question: A reinforced-concrete beam has As = 2.0 in², fy = 60 ksi, f'c = 4 ksi, and b = 10 in. What is the depth of the equivalent (Whitney) stress block, a?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components (ACI 318-14) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$a = \frac{A_s f_y}{0.85 f'_c b} = \frac{2.0(60)}{0.85(4)(10)} = \frac{120}{34} = 3.53\ \text{in}$$

questions.question: A beam has b = 12 in, d = 20 in, f'c = 4,000 psi, and fy = 60,000 psi. What is the minimum flexural reinforcement As,min?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components (ACI 318-14) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

As,min is the larger of 3√(f'c)/fy and 200/fy, times b·d:

$$\frac{200}{f_y} = \frac{200}{60{,}000} = 0.00333\ \text{(governs)};\quad A_{s,min} = 0.00333(12)(20) = 0.80\ \text{in}^2$$
questions.explanation: 200/fy governs here: As,min = 0.80 in².

questions.question: Per ACI 318, what is the strength reduction factor φ for a tension-controlled flexural member?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components (ACI 318-14) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

For a tension-controlled section (net tensile strain ≥ 0.005), ACI 318 uses φ = 0.90. Compression-controlled tied members use 0.65, and shear/torsion use 0.75.
questions.explanation: Tension-controlled φ = 0.90; tied compression members 0.65; shear 0.75.

questions.question: Per ACI minimum-thickness tables, a simply supported one-way slab spanning 12 ft (normal-weight concrete, Grade 60) needs a minimum thickness of L/20. What is the minimum thickness?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components (ACI 318-14) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$h_{min} = \frac{L}{20} = \frac{12(12)}{20} = \frac{144}{20} = 7.2\ \text{in}$$
questions.explanation: L/20 with L in inches: 144/20 = 7.2 in.

questions.question: For normal-weight concrete with f'c = 4,000 psi, what is the modulus of elasticity using Ec = 57,000√(f'c)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components (ACI 318-14) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$E_c = 57{,}000\sqrt{f'_c} = 57{,}000\sqrt{4000} = 3{,}605{,}000\ \text{psi} \approx 3{,}600\ \text{ksi}$$
questions.explanation: Ec = 57,000√f'c ≈ 3,600 ksi (f'c in psi).

questions.question: A cantilever beam 10 ft long carries a uniform load of 3 kip/ft over its full length. What is the maximum bending moment?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Beams section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$M_{max} = \frac{w L^2}{2} = \frac{3(10)^2}{2} = 150\ \text{kip·ft}$$
questions.explanation: Cantilever UDL: M = wL²/2 at the fixed end = 150 kip·ft.

questions.question: A simply supported beam 10 m long carries a single 40 kN point load 4 m from the left support. What is the maximum bending moment?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$R_A = \frac{P b}{L} = \frac{40(6)}{10} = 24\ \text{kN};\quad M_{max} = R_A a = 24(4) = 96\ \text{kN·m}$$
questions.explanation: Max moment under the load = R_A·a = 96 kN·m.

questions.question: A continuous beam rests on four supports (one pin and three rollers) with no internal hinges. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Reactions r = 2 (pin) + 3(1) (rollers) = 5; equations = 3:

$$DSI = r - 3 = 5 - 3 = 2$$
questions.explanation: Five reactions minus three equations = 2nd-degree indeterminate.

questions.question: A single-bay, single-story rigid frame has two fixed column bases and rigid beam-column joints (no internal hinges). What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Two fixed bases give r = 6 reaction components; with three equilibrium equations:

$$DSI = r - 3 = 6 - 3 = 3$$
questions.explanation: Six reactions minus three equations = 3rd-degree indeterminate.

questions.question: A flat roof has a ground snow load pg = 40 psf, with Ce = 1.0, Ct = 1.0, and Is = 1.0. What is the flat-roof snow load pf = 0.7·Ce·Ct·Is·pg?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design Loads section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$p_f = 0.7 C_e C_t I_s p_g = 0.7(1.0)(1.0)(1.0)(40) = 28\ \text{psf}$$
questions.explanation: pf = 0.7·pg = 28 psf with all factors 1.0.

questions.question: Compute the velocity pressure qz = 0.00256·Kz·Kzt·Kd·V² for V = 115 mph, Kz = 0.85, Kzt = 1.0, and Kd = 0.85.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design Loads section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$q_z = 0.00256(0.85)(1.0)(0.85)(115)^2 = 0.00256(0.7225)(13{,}225) = 24.5\ \text{psf}$$
questions.explanation: Apply all factors to 0.00256V²: 24.5 psf.

questions.question: A member has an unreduced live load L0 = 50 psf, KLL = 4, and a tributary area AT = 400 ft². Using L = L0(0.25 + 15/√(KLL·AT)), what is the reduced live load?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design Loads section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$L = 50\left(0.25 + \frac{15}{\sqrt{4(400)}}\right) = 50\left(0.25 + \frac{15}{40}\right) = 50(0.625) = 31.3\ \text{psf}$$
questions.explanation: Reduced to 31.3 psf; reduction cannot go below 0.5·L0 for this case.

questions.question: A member carries a dead load of 20 kip and a live load of 30 kip (no other loads). Using ASD, what is the controlling required strength?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design Loads section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The governing ASD gravity combination is D + L:

$$D + L = 20 + 30 = 50\ \text{kip}$$

(LRFD's 1.2D + 1.6L = 72 kip is a factored value, not ASD.)
questions.explanation: ASD uses unfactored D + L = 50 kip.

questions.question: A cantilever 3 m long carries a uniform load of 5 kN/m. With E = 200 GPa and I = 50×10⁶ mm⁴, what is the tip deflection?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Deflection of Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$\delta = \frac{w L^4}{8 E I};\ EI = (200\times10^9)(50\times10^{-6}) = 1.0\times10^7\ \text{N·m}^2$$

$$\delta = \frac{5000(3)^4}{8(1.0\times10^7)} = 0.00506\ \text{m} = 5.06\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: Cantilever UDL: δ = wL⁴/8EI = 5.06 mm.

questions.question: A simply supported beam 6 m long carries a uniform load of 8 kN/m. With E = 200 GPa and I = 80×10⁶ mm⁴, what is the maximum deflection?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Deflection of Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$\delta = \frac{5 w L^4}{384 E I};\ EI = 1.6\times10^7\ \text{N·m}^2$$

$$\delta = \frac{5(8000)(6)^4}{384(1.6\times10^7)} = 0.00844\ \text{m} = 8.44\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: Simple span UDL: δ = 5wL⁴/384EI = 8.44 mm.

questions.question: A fixed-fixed column (K = 0.5) is 5 m long with E = 200 GPa and I = 5×10⁶ mm⁴. What is the Euler critical load?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Columns section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{(KL)^2};\ KL = 0.5(5) = 2.5\ \text{m},\ EI = 1.0\times10^6\ \text{N·m}^2$$

$$P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 (1.0\times10^6)}{(2.5)^2} = 1{,}579\ \text{kN}$$
questions.explanation: Fixed-fixed K = 0.5 gives 4× the pinned load (395 kN).

questions.question: A fixed-fixed beam 10 m long carries a 30 kN point load 4 m from end A (6 m from end B). What is the fixed-end moment at A?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$M_{AB} = \frac{P a b^2}{L^2} = \frac{30(4)(6)^2}{10^2} = \frac{30(4)(36)}{100} = 43.2\ \text{kN·m}$$
questions.explanation: FEM at A = Pab²/L² = 43.2 kN·m; at B it is Pa²b/L² = 28.8 kN·m.

questions.question: A steel section has a plastic section modulus Z = 60 in³ and Fy = 50 ksi. What is the plastic moment Mp?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$M_p = F_y Z = 50(60) = 3000\ \text{kip·in} = 250\ \text{kip·ft}$$
questions.explanation: Mp = Fy·Z = 3000 kip·in = 250 kip·ft.

questions.question: A column base plate 12 in × 12 in bears on concrete with f'c = 4 ksi (A1 = A2). Using φPp = φ(0.85 f'c A1) with φ = 0.65, what is the design bearing strength?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components (ACI 318-14) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$\phi P_p = 0.65(0.85 f'_c A_1) = 0.65(0.85)(4)(144) = 318\ \text{kip}$$
questions.explanation: φ(0.85 f'c A1) = 318 kip; 490 kip omits φ.

questions.question: A steel I-beam web has an area Aw = 5.0 in² and Fy = 50 ksi (web shear coefficient Cv = 1.0). Using LRFD (φv = 0.90), what is the design shear strength?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Steel Components section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$\phi_v V_n = \phi_v (0.6 F_y A_w C_v) = 0.90(0.6)(50)(5.0)(1.0) = 135\ \text{kip}$$
questions.explanation: φ·0.6·Fy·Aw = 135 kip. 150 kip omits φ.

questions.question: A closed four-sided traverse has corners A(0, 0), B(300, 0), C(350, 200), and D(50, 250), with coordinates in feet. What is the enclosed area in acres?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Area by Coordinates section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Apply the coordinate (shoelace) rule, then convert (43,560 ft²/acre):

$$2A = \left|\sum (x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i)\right| = |60{,}000 + 77{,}500| = 137{,}500$$

$$A = 68{,}750\ \text{ft}^2 = \frac{68{,}750}{43{,}560} = 1.58\ \text{acres}$$
questions.explanation: Shoelace gives 68,750 ft²; divide by 43,560 for acres = 1.58.

questions.question: A closed traverse of total length 1,200 ft has a latitude misclosure of +0.12 ft and a departure misclosure of −0.16 ft. Expressed as 1:X, what is the precision (X, rounded)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Latitudes and Departures section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Linear misclosure, then precision:

$$e = \sqrt{0.12^2 + 0.16^2} = \sqrt{0.04} = 0.20\ \text{ft}$$

$$\text{Precision} = \frac{1200}{0.20} = 6000 \Rightarrow 1{:}6000$$
questions.explanation: Misclosure 0.20 ft over 1,200 ft gives 1:6000.

questions.question: Differential leveling starts at BM elevation 100.00 ft. Readings (ft): BS 4.20 at BM; FS 6.50 to TP1; BS 5.10 at TP1; FS 3.40 to point P. What is the elevation of P?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Leveling section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Height of instrument then turning points:

$$HI_1 = 100.00 + 4.20 = 104.20;\ TP1 = 104.20 - 6.50 = 97.70$$

$$HI_2 = 97.70 + 5.10 = 102.80;\ P = 102.80 - 3.40 = 99.40\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: Add backsights to get HI, subtract foresights: P = 99.40 ft.

questions.question: In a closed traverse (perimeter 1,200 ft) with a departure misclosure of +0.16 ft, what is the compass-rule correction to the departure of a 300 ft course?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Latitudes and Departures section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The compass (Bowditch) rule distributes the misclosure in proportion to course length:

$$C = -(\text{dep misclosure})\frac{\text{course}}{\text{perimeter}} = -(0.16)\frac{300}{1200} = -0.04\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: Correction is opposite the misclosure, scaled by length: −0.04 ft.

questions.question: A project has BAC = $500,000 and is 40% complete. PV to date is $220,000 and AC is $190,000. Assuming current cost performance continues, what is the estimate at completion (EAC)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earned-Value Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Earned value first, then CPI, then EAC:

$$EV = 0.40(500{,}000) = 200{,}000;\quad CPI = \frac{EV}{AC} = \frac{200{,}000}{190{,}000} = 1.053$$

$$EAC = \frac{BAC}{CPI} = \frac{500{,}000}{1.053} = \$475{,}000$$
questions.explanation: EV = %complete×BAC = 200k; EAC = BAC/CPI = $475k (ahead on cost, so below budget).

questions.question: In the network shown, A (4 d) precedes B (6 d), C (8 d), and D (3 d); all of B, C, D precede E (5 d). What is the total float of activity B?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

The critical path runs through the longest parallel branch (C):

$$\text{Critical: } A\text{-}C\text{-}E = 4+8+5 = 17\ \text{d}$$

$$\text{Path through B: } A\text{-}B\text{-}E = 4+6+5 = 15\ \text{d};\quad TF_B = 17 - 15 = 2\ \text{d}$$
questions.explanation: B's branch is 2 days shorter than the critical C branch, so its total float is 2 days.

questions.question: A dozer produces 300 LCY per hour and its combined owning-and-operating cost is $180 per hour. What is the unit cost of production?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Unit cost is hourly cost divided by hourly production:

$$\text{Unit cost} = \frac{\$180/\text{hr}}{300\ \text{LCY/hr}} = \$0.60/\text{LCY}$$
questions.explanation: $180/hr ÷ 300 LCY/hr = $0.60/LCY. Inverting gives 1.67 (LCY per dollar).

questions.question: A steel bar (E = 29,000 ksi, yield 60 ksi) 10 in long carries a stress of 50 ksi. What is its elongation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Below yield, use Hooke's law for strain then elongation:

$$\varepsilon = \frac{\sigma}{E} = \frac{50}{29{,}000} = 0.001724;\quad \delta = \varepsilon L = 0.001724(10) = 0.0172\ \text{in}$$
questions.explanation: ε = σ/E = 0.001724, then δ = εL = 0.0172 in (elastic since 50 < 60 ksi).

questions.question: A steel rod (E = 200 GPa, α = 12×10⁻⁶/°C) sits between rigid walls with a 0.5 mm gap over its 1,000 mm length. After the gap closes, the rod is heated an additional 20°C. What stress develops?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Thermal Deformations section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Only the heating beyond gap closure produces stress (the gap-closing expansion is free):

$$\sigma = E\alpha\,\Delta T_{extra} = (200\times10^3)(12\times10^{-6})(20) = 48\ \text{MPa (compressive)}$$
questions.explanation: The 0.5 mm free expansion closes the gap; only the extra 20°C is restrained: 48 MPa.

questions.question: What is the larger eigenvalue of the matrix [[4, 1], [2, 3]]?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Solve det(A − λI) = 0:

$$\lambda^2 - (\text{tr})\lambda + \det = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 5,\ 2$$
questions.explanation: Trace 7, determinant 10 give λ = 5 and 2; the larger is 5.

questions.question: Using Newton-Raphson to solve x² − 10 = 0 starting from x₀ = 3, what is the first iterate x₁?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Numerical Methods section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$x_1 = x_0 - \frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)} = 3 - \frac{3^2 - 10}{2(3)} = 3 - \frac{-1}{6} = 3.167$$
questions.explanation: x₁ = 3 − (−1/6) = 3.167, converging toward √10 ≈ 3.162.

questions.question: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test is 95% sensitive and 90% specific. If a person tests positive, what is the probability they actually have the disease?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Bayes' Theorem section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Bayes' theorem with false positives from the 99% healthy:

$$P(D|+) = \frac{(0.95)(0.01)}{(0.95)(0.01) + (0.10)(0.99)} = \frac{0.0095}{0.1085} = 0.088 = 8.8\%$$
questions.explanation: Despite a positive result, the low prevalence makes P(disease) only 8.8%.

questions.question: A sample of n = 16 has a known population standard deviation σ = 8. For a 95% confidence interval on the mean (z = 1.96), what is the margin of error?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Confidence Intervals section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$E = z\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = 1.96\frac{8}{\sqrt{16}} = 1.96(2) = 3.92$$

questions.question: A rectangular channel 3 m wide flows 1.5 m deep with Manning n = 0.013 on a slope of 0.001. What is the discharge (SI, use Q = (1/n)AR^(2/3)S^(1/2))?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Open-Channel Flow section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Geometry, then Manning:

$$A = 3(1.5) = 4.5\ \text{m}^2;\ P = 3 + 2(1.5) = 6\ \text{m};\ R = 0.75\ \text{m}$$

$$V = \tfrac{1}{0.013}(0.75)^{2/3}(0.001)^{1/2} = 2.01\ \text{m/s};\ Q = VA = 9.0\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}$$

questions.question: Water discharges through a sharp-edged orifice of area 0.05 m² under a head of 3 m, with a discharge coefficient Cd = 0.60. What is the flow rate (Q = Cd·A·√(2gh))?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Orifices section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$Q = C_d A\sqrt{2gh} = 0.60(0.05)\sqrt{2(9.81)(3)} = 0.03(7.67) = 0.23\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}$$

questions.question: A normally consolidated clay layer 3 m thick has Cc = 0.30 and e₀ = 0.80. The effective stress increases from 100 kPa to 200 kPa. What is the primary consolidation settlement?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Consolidation Settlement section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

$$S_c = \frac{C_c}{1+e_0}\,H\,\log\frac{\sigma_0'+\Delta\sigma}{\sigma_0'} = \frac{0.30}{1.80}(3000)\log\frac{200}{100}$$

$$= 0.1667(3000)(0.301) = 150\ \text{mm}$$

questions.question: A crest vertical curve joins a +3% grade to a −2% grade and must provide a stopping sight distance of 600 ft. Assuming S < L (use L = A·S²/2158), what is the required curve length?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Grade change A = |3 − (−2)| = 5. Assume S < L:

$$L = \frac{A S^2}{2158} = \frac{5(600)^2}{2158} = \frac{1{,}800{,}000}{2158} = 834\ \text{ft}$$

Since 834 ft > 600 ft, the S < L assumption is valid.
questions.explanation: L = AS²/2158 = 834 ft; verify S < L (834 > 600), so the assumption holds.

questions.question: Water flows at 0.02 m³/s through a 100 mm diameter pipe. What is the velocity head (V²/2g)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Continuity Equation section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Velocity from continuity, then velocity head:

$$V = \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{0.02}{\pi(0.05)^2} = 2.55\ \text{m/s};\quad \frac{V^2}{2g} = \frac{2.55^2}{2(9.81)} = 0.33\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: A = 7.85×10⁻³ m², V = 2.55 m/s, velocity head = 0.33 m.
